en: *The Scripture on the Original Vows of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva*, Fascicle One, with Annotations.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Qinglian of Kuāngān in Yán, whose secular surname was Língchéng.
Having already explained the title of the scripture above, △ next, the Translator.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan during the Tang Dynasty.
"Tang" was the name of that era. The Li clan possessed the mandate over all under heaven;

because they first established their legacy at Pinyang, the ancient capital of the lineage of Tàodáng, the state was named Tang (the Li clan’s ancestor, Lǐ Hǔ, assisted the Western Wei and Emperor Mǐn of the Zhou; having received the abdication from the Western Wei, he was posthumously enfeoffed as the Duke of the State of Tang. Hǔ begot...).
Bing. Bing’s son was Yuan; both inherited the title of Duke of Tang and thereby established their state). Yutian—properly called *Gostana*, which in the language of Tang means "earth-milk."
Because the king had no heir, he prayed before an image of Vaiśravaṇa. A baby boy emerged, split open from the forehead of the statue; he did not drink human milk.
The ground before the deity suddenly rose up in the shape of a breast, and the divine child suckled from it (the character *cǔ* is pronounced *zǐ yú*, with the first tone).
He eventually grew to maturity, and thus the country was named after this event. It is also said that [the name] is *Huàn nà ān dùn huò qiě* (the character *qiě* is pronounced *zǐ yú*).

Ju and Qu-dan are all alternative names for this country. According to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-candragarbha-sūtra*, the World-Honored One entrusted the thousand-member retinue of the Devaputra Duryodhana, as well as the Great Yakṣa Saṃjñeya and Vaiśravaṇa, to jointly protect the territory of Khotan.
Consequently, many sages and worthies have followed in succession; it is, therefore, the native land of the translators. (3)

"Treasury" (藏, *piṭaka*). In Sanskrit it is called *kośa*, which here is translated as "treasury. Just as a worldly treasury accumulates wealth and property, the Three Treasuries of the Dharma accumulate both text and meaning.
Because each of the three names contains all principles and expressions, they are called "treasuries. *Āgama* is the Treasury of Concentration (*samādhi-piṭaka*);
*Vinaya* is the Treasury of Precepts (*śīla-piṭaka*); and *Abhidharma* is the Treasury of Wisdom (*prajñā-piṭaka*). "Śramaṇa," in its correct pronunciation, is...
*Śramaṇa*. This means "merit" (*guānláo*). It refers to one who has merit from cultivating the path yet undergoes much toil.

It is also called "one who quiets the mind. The *Ruìyìng* (Sutra of Auspicious Responses) states: "One who quiets the mind reaches the fundamental source; therefore, he is titled a śramaṇa. This is correct.
However, translators of various sutras all referred to him as a "Dharma Master" (*fǎshī*). The current title of "śramaṇa" is an expression of the translator's humble virtue. Realakṣa...

Nanda (translated into Chinese as Xuexi, "Delighting in Learning"). At that time, Empress Wu, who illuminated the sun of the Buddha’s teachings and held the Mahāyāna in high esteem, learned from afar that the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* existed in Khotan.
Because the existing Chinese translations were incomplete in their assemblies and chapters, she dispatched envoys to invite Śikṣānanda.
Accompanying the scripture, he arrived in Luoyang to produce a new translation.

△ Third, the exegesis following the text is divided into three sections: the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Propagation. 1. The first chapter, the Introduction, concludes with the Assembly of the Emanated Bodies. 2. The Main Body consists of nine chapters;
the section on the comparison of giving concludes with the "Earth Deity Protecting the Dharma" chapter. 3. The Propagation section consists of three chapters. Question:
The smiling face and the emission of light may be termed the "Initiation"; the questions and answers concerning the stage of the causal ground [are found in] the "Elder" chapter.

The chapter on "The Noble Woman Who Arouses the Mind Rescuing Her Mother" logically belongs to the "Correct Text," while the chapter on "Earth Deities Protecting the Dharma" and its benefits for those who see and hear it should properly belong to the "Main Body.

Only the "Entrusting" chapter can be called the "Circulation. Why is it that none of these are currently so designated? Answer: Our ancestor, the Great Master Zhiyi, said: "When dividing the text, it is based on human sentiment; human sentiment universally regards the Preface as such. Thus, the classification follows the conventional understanding of the people. It is not that the principles are incorrect, but rather that the categorization is made according to the common perception of the time. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the "Entrusting" chapter is placed at the end because it serves as the conclusion for the entire work, ensuring that the teachings remain intact and are transmitted to future generations. This is why it is specifically termed "Circulation. As for the other chapters, their placement is determined by the flow of the narrative and the thematic structure of the text, which is why they do not conform to the aforementioned expectations. This is the underlying meaning.

Before the Dharma has been fully elucidated and its circulation has ceased, one must not yet discuss the finality of cause and effect. As for the three sections, they cannot be arbitrarily severed or isolated;
the introduction serves as the introduction to the main body, the main body serves as the main body to the introduction, and the circulation serves as the circulation to the main body.
Each section possesses the three meanings of being "good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end. If these were to be abruptly severed, how could they be called "good"?

How could it be appropriate for the introduction to lack flavor and cause the circulation [of the teaching] to decline at the end? Now, because the assembly has gathered in great numbers, Mañjuśrī asks about past vows and practices;
the World-Honored One’s response recounts former events. This is precisely the prologue to the gathering of the emanated bodies. Why then do you say this is not the introduction?
As for the earth goddess Dharmapālā, her witnessing and hearing of the benefits constitute the essential matter of the main circulation. What is there to object to?

As for the statement that it still belongs to the main body of the orthodox teaching (*zhengzong*), why not examine the words of the Great Master himself? He states: "Sentient beings who attain the Way have indeterminate capacities;

there is no harm in explaining the orthodox within the preface. Furthermore, the presence of the orthodox serves as an even greater incentive for diligent practice, which does not contradict the intent of the sutra.
Now, following the patriarchal injunctions rather than mere human sentiment, I shall explain the preface in two parts: first, the title of the initial chapter.
Chapter One: The Supernatural Powers in the Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
Chapter Two: The Explanation. [The subsequent chapters] follow this pattern. △ Regarding the sequence of divisions, there are two parts. First, the General Preface (Sūtra-Preface).

Since all sūtras possess this, it is also called the "Preface of Certification and Faith" (*saddharma-śraddhā-prativedha-nidāna*); for when these five matters are present, people will believe. It is also called the "Sūtra-Preface."

The preceding section is called the "Preface" (or *nidāna*) because it marks the beginning of all sūtras; it is also called the "Sūtra Preface. The subsequent section is called the "Colophon" (or *parinidāna*) because it was established by the compilers; it is also called the "Introductory Section" (*upodghāta*) because it specifically introduces this particular sūtra and initiates the formal exposition. Regarding the "Certification of Faith" (*śraddhā-pratyaya*), there are two parts: first, citing five matters to certify faith; second, identifying the purpose for which the three months were spent. The first of the four intermediate sections concerns the essence of the Dharma as it was heard. Thus,
the Great Master, having deeply awakened to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, elucidated its wondrous purport by explaining the initial title through five layers and four [sections].
To explain and clarify the textual passages: since this sutra is identical to the *amṛta* (the finest essence), how could its commentary be of inferior flavor?

Moreover, as it is the opening proclamation of all sutras and the ultimate discourse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, Nanyue performed three recitations of the text, and Tiantai realized that a single thought-moment contains [all meanings].
Since the principle is of one body, the text must accord with the fourfold progression; yet later generations, following their own inclinations, have sought brevity.
Those of dull faculties in the final age may find the details cumbersome; therefore, I shall now provide a moderate account—perhaps three, two, or one [section].

The priority lies in grasping the essential meaning, so as not to weary you with excessive writing. For one who acts thus, faith is perfected. The great ocean of the Buddha’s Dharma is entered through faith;
when the mind possesses pure faith, one can enter the sea of the Dharma. Thus, those who lack faith say that this matter is not so, like an ox.
If leather is not yet supple, it cannot be bent or folded. "Faith" means that one says, "This matter is thus.

Just as when cowhide has become supple, it can be fashioned according to its use, so too when faith exists, the principle of what is spoken becomes compliant; when there is compliance, the way of teacher and disciple is perfected.
Therefore, this is placed at the beginning. Furthermore, when names do not differ, this is called being without error. Ānanda transmitted the perfect teachings spoken by the Buddha.
The Sūtra is like pouring water from one vessel into another; there is no difference. When the words accord with the underlying principle, they are entirely appropriate and without error.

Thus, the words are as they are and the principle is as it is; therefore, it is said, "Thus" (*evam*). This very "thus" is not without universal sameness, for the inconceivable nature-consciousness is the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Its essence is free from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), and its characteristics transcend the hundred negations. [This applies to] mind, Buddha, and the multitude...
They arise; there is no difference among the three. Furthermore, how could it be that this is only so at the beginning of the sutras within my Buddha’s legacy?

Even at the very beginning of this very sutra, it is likewise so. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The suchness (*tathatā*) of past phenomena is precisely the suchness of future and present phenomena."
The suchness of present phenomena is the very same as the suchness of past and future phenomena.
The suchness of future phenomena is the very same as the suchness of past and present phenomena. Why is this? Because suchness is one and without differentiation.

Thus, from the time Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva first resolved his mind toward enlightenment until the present day when he received his mandate in the celestial palace, he has always acted through this perfect suchness.
Cultivating oneself, one likewise benefits others through this very perfection. Regarding the three stages of planting, ripening, and liberation, these are never abandoned from time to time;
that which accords with and is identical to the matters of our Buddha’s original and manifested traces is precisely what is called the "Thusness" revealed in this present sutra.
When a practitioner can, by means of this perfect, eternal, and correct truth, contemplate the mind that possesses all within a single thought-moment, this is it.
The cultivation of evil arising from the mind is precisely inherent evil; it is called the "evil dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*). There is no phenomenon that it does not encompass.

Its essence is the three virtues (*triguṇa*), and it is also termed the "three truths" (*tisraḥ satyaḥ*). When one contemplates in accordance with these truths, the illumination of the object is non-different [from the subject]; this is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*).

When both object and contemplation are simultaneously extinguished, and faults and transgressions are forever severed, this is called "Is-ness" (*asti*). To believe in this manner is for faith to be perfected. △ Second, the Capable [Subject].
"I have heard from people.
"I have heard" means that one's hearing is perfected. This, Ānanda, personally testifies that there was direct transmission; it is forever distinct [from hearsay].
"Outsider! To take 'mastery' as its meaning is the foremost of the sixteen views and the root of the five sharp outflows.

Therefore, ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle cling to a self within persons and phenomena. Yet Ānanda is a Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma, one among those for whom the *Lotus Sūtra* granted a prediction;
he transmits this Perfect Sūtra, which must accord with the two kinds of emptiness. Why, then, do you speak of a 'self'?"
One must know that ordinary persons possess three kinds of "self": [the self of] views, pride, and conventional names. Ānanda has already been free from views and pride;
he follows only conventional names. Since he lacks a [substantial] self and lacks [the need for] hearing [the Dharma], his transformative teaching would cease.

Therefore, although he knows there is no self, for the sake of transmitting the transformative teaching, he employs provisional designations according to worldly convention—just as when one exchanges gold coins for copper, the method of buying and selling remains, yet people do not [regard the copper as the original value].
As for the one who laughs and the one who hears: the faculty of hearing is unimpaired, the sound is within the range of audibility, and the mind is applied to listen attentively.
Through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, hearing occurs; thus, it should be said that "the ear hears.

However, because I am the master of hearing and hearing is my function—the master being a conventional person and the function being a real dharma—if the meaning of "master" is understood, the meaning of "hearing" becomes self-evident. Yet, the master is merely a composite whole.

Discussing the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination) of "having heard" (*śruta*), this differs slightly from the separate explanation given there for the sake of listening. This is Ānanda directly manifesting the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
it is the true self’s hearing with the mind, intended to cause people to awaken and enter [the truth] directly.

Yet, the true self is neither self nor non-self; the hearing with the mind is neither hearing nor non-hearing. For the sake of ensuring the transmission and transformation of the Dharma remains uninterrupted, it is said: "I have heard. Thus, "hearing."
Thus, the accomplishment was achieved. △ Third, the time of hearing and upholding.
Regarding "at one time":
this should record the specific year and month. That it is now stated as "at one time" is likely because the calendars of the two lands differ; when the sutra was preached...
There are differences between the preceding and the following; therefore, they are collectively subsumed under "one" for the time being. However, "one" is the unification of the Way (*Dao*).

It embodies the purity of celestial virtue, the source of form and breath, the beginning of numbers, and the *qi* (the odd line) of the *Yi*. It gives birth to heaven and earth, and all things arise from it. There is nothing that does not begin with "one.
Thus, the hexagrams and lines of Fuxi, as well as the characters of Cangjie, all [originate from it].
It arises from the One. The One is the great mother of all characters. Above, it has the form of a celestial canopy; below, it has the form of the earth’s foundation;

in the middle, it has the form of a person bearing a burden. "Shi" (時) means change and transformation. As the processes of creation and transformation shift subtly, who among humanity perceives them?
Nothing is more visible than the sun; therefore, we take the path of the sun as our standard, for this is the convergence.
[The Master] said: "Because the substance of the heavens is most vast, the subtlety of its operation resides in the sun. In the Buddha’s world, there are two ways of discussing time:

first, *kāla*, which refers to short duration and actual time; this is taught so that internal disciples may eat according to the proper time and observe the signs of the light of wisdom (*prabhāsa*).

Second, *samaya*, which refers to long duration and conventional time; this is because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to time as being substantial, and thus [the Buddha] revealed [this distinction]."
"Time is provisional. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "Since the various sutras are numerous, the term 'at one time' is used as a general expression;

this encompasses both long and short durations and includes both the refined and the coarse. Now, it is said that the Dharma-activity of the Buddha, the King of Awakening, is nearing its end, at a time of a sublime assembly in the celestial palace.
The listeners were moved to request the teaching, and the speaker expounded in response to their capacity. When the matters of speaking and listening were concluded, [the assembly] collectively..."
This is called "simultaneity. The essential point is to bring the faculties to maturity so that the six realms of existence return to the one mind. The Great Master said:
"If prior thought and subsequent awakening are distinct, these two are not one. When delusive thought and awakening are severed and one attains sudden enlightenment, it is just like this now.
△ Fourth, the Buddhas and their abodes.
The Buddha was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Tiantai clarifies the six levels of Buddhahood (*liuji*). Here, we focus on the level of ultimate Buddhahood (*jiongjiu ji*), which has three aspects: based on the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), there is the Buddha of sixteen feet;
based on the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), there is the Honored One of Special Distinction (*viśeṣa*) of sixteen feet; and based on the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is...
Regarding the Dharma-body Buddha, these three Buddhas are neither identical nor different; they are neither identical nor different, yet they are both identical and different.

Now that the secret treasury has been revealed in its entirety, they are one and the same Perfect Buddha. Both identity and difference are forgotten. To say they "are" for a moment is a temporary expression;

to say they "abide" over a long duration is a designation of persistence. This is merely a conventional way of speaking. Now, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "abiding" (*sthiti*) is used to explain "being present" (*vartate*). As for "abiding," it is one of the four modes of deportment.
The Buddha is the dweller; the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is the place of dwelling. There are two types of dwelling places:

first, the place of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-sthāna*), which is the realm of travel for the purpose of transforming those who remain in the secular world; second, the place of reliance (*niśraya-sthāna*), which is for the governance of the community of renunciants.

Here, it refers to the place of the objective sphere. Furthermore, there are four types of dwellers: namely, devas, Brahmās, noble ones (*ārya*), and Buddhas. This refers to the "deva-dwelling" (*deva-vihāra*).

The so-called "six desires" have as their cause the virtues of generosity, ethical discipline, and a wholesome mind. The "Brahma-abodes" range from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
their cause is the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). The "Noble abodes" belong to those of the three vehicles; their cause is the three samādhis.

The "Buddha-abode" consists of the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, the hundred and eight samādhis, and so forth. However, one must necessarily abide by means of the Truths (*satya*); therefore, the six-foot Buddha abides in the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is consistent.
The Body-Buddha abides in the midst of reality; the Dharma-body Buddha abides in the Middle Way.

This means that we, within a single mind, perfectly cultivate the three contemplations without ceasing from moment to moment, constantly dwelling in the three truths. This is precisely the abiding of contemplative practice.

Therefore, know that one who can understand the spiritual capacity and the nature of the mind will, in every thought-moment, perfect the fruit of Bodhi; even the slightest arising of intention constitutes a great function.
Manifest before one’s eyes; without attainment and without reliance, neither grasping nor rejecting. Arising from the Truth to manifest practice, essence and function mutually encompass one another.

Through practice, one accords with the Truth; in its unfolding and rolling up, they share a single boundary. Spontaneously, mind after mind merges with the Way, and thought after thought darkly accords with the Truth.

This concludes the "Chapter on the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Seeing the Title. II. Regarding the purpose for which this section was established over the course of three months: Why was this division established?

The Mother’s recitation of these Dharma verses belongs to the *śraddhā-prasāda* (faith and confidence) section; however, because their underlying intent contains the *nidāna* (introductory narrative), they cannot be subsumed under the general category, nor can they be included elsewhere.

Therefore, they are established separately. Furthermore, these verses constitute the primary source for the Tathāgata’s ascent to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for the three-month summer retreat, serving as the foundational basis for Kṣitigarbha’s making of vows on behalf of his mother. This was done, first, to refute the non-Buddhist heretics.

The doubts and slanders of the six heretical teachers arose next, followed by the filial reflections of the fourfold assembly of later generations; though the words briefly touch upon these matters, their meaning truly encompasses them all.
Thus, he preached the Dharma for his mother.
According to the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisāgara-sūtra*, the father-king addressed the Buddha, saying that he should go to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother.
The Buddha said, "You should proceed like a Wheel-Turning King, inquiring after the welfare of your donors.
According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, however, it was Śakra who invited him; it is said that all Buddhas ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for their mothers. As [stated]...

The Tathāgata should also come to preach the Dharma for his Holy Mother. Thereupon, the Tathāgata, together with a thousand bhikṣus, ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven at the city of Kuśinagara in the kingdom of Andhra to preach the Dharma for his mother, thereby repaying the kindness of her giving birth to his physical body.
In Sanskrit she is called Mahāmāyā; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "Great Artifice" or "Great Illusion. In the *Dīrgha Āgama*, she is named...

Regarding the Great Transformation (*Daihō*), the *Myōgen* states: "Māyā is the mother of the thousand Buddhas; she is a great provisional embodiment of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) who has attained the stages (*bhūmi*).
How could an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) be capable of conceiving the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa? Therefore, in the Jin translation of the *Avataṃsaka*, Lady Māyā replies to Sudhana:
'I have already accomplished the dharma-gate of the illusion of the wisdom of great vows. Having attained this dharma...'"

Therefore, she is the mother of Vairocana Tathāgata. In the city of Kapilavastu in Jambudvīpa, within the palace of King Śuddhodana, she gave birth to Prince Siddhārtha from her right side, manifesting inconceivable and sovereign supernatural powers.
This explanation regarding the parents and others is according to the Hīnayāna; if according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), they are all like illusory manifestations, just as with the Buddha.
He addressed the Devaputra of the Moon Dynasty, saying: "As for that bodhisattva, they do not dwell upon birth, nor is there any arising;
yet, by virtue of their original vow, they manifest as being born. The deva asked: "If the bodhisattva does not dwell upon what is born, nor undergo birth, [how is this so?]"
"How is it that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for his biological kin, ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for three months at once?
Was the Tathāgata not born from Queen Māyā? The Buddha told the devaputra:
"The Bodhisattva was not born from Queen Māyā; he was born from the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā). Why is this so? Because..."

The thirty-two marks of a great man, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, and even the Buddha-eye as vast as space, as well as the supernormal powers and skillful means—all these merits did not arise from Queen Māyā;
rather, they arose from the Perfection of Wisdom. This is why the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for the sake of the Holy Queen.
The Dharma that was preached consists of three fascicles, all of which are titled as "Discourses on the Origin" (Ben-zhi Tan). II.

The Specific Introduction (*Prastāvanā*) Since this text does not relate to other sutras, it is called a "Specific Text. It is divided into three sections: 1. The Introductory Section Praising the Assemblage of Fruits and Causes;
2. From "At that time, the Tathāgata... onwards, the Section Manifesting Signs and Gathering the Assembly; 3. From "At that time, Śākyamuni... onwards, the Section of Questions and Answers.

Preface to the Dispelling of Doubts: If one summarizes the sequence of their mutual arising, it is because the praise of the cause and the accumulation of the fruit led the World-Honored One to emit light, whereby devas, nāgas, and others assembled.
Because the assembly was so vast, the Buddha questioned Mañjuśrī regarding the number of those present.
Mañjuśrī, harboring doubts, posed questions, and the Tathāgata responded by recounting past events. Thus, the questions and answers dispel doubts through manifestation.
The assembly gathers through signs; the gathering of the assembly arises from the convergence of cause and fruit. Praising the sequential and inverse arising, they are linked like a chain of hooks.
If it were merely this, the *pratītyasamutpāda* would be exactly the same as the single interpretation of causal conditions by Guangzhai, which is incomplete.

Yet, regarding the teachings of the provisional and the real, the fundamental and the trace, and the contemplation of the mind, there is no further direction [to be found]. One must know that the three prefaces serve to introduce the central teaching.

This is the explanation of the causal conditions (*nidāna*). If categorized according to the teachings, this introduction (*nidāna*) introduces the main body; it does not belong to the *Tripitaka*, the *Shared*, or the *Distinct* [teachings], but rather introduces the *Perfect* [Teaching]. 1. The mutual praise between the fruit and the cause, and the description of the assembly gathered there. 2. The manifestation of auspicious omens, describing the principle. 3. The mutual praise between the fruit and the cause, describing the person. 4. Mañjuśrī’s inquiry and reflection, describing practice. 5. The exchange of questions and answers, describing the teaching. This is the explanation of the causal conditions.
If one examines the teachings, this introduction serves as the preface to the main text; it is not of the Tripitaka, Shared, or Distinct vehicles, but is the introduction to the Perfect Teaching.

To speak precisely, if we consider the matter from the perspective of the fundamental and the provisional (honji-suijaku), from the incalculable eons prior to the original beginning of Kṣitigarbha down to the present day, one may understand that each of the fourfold aspects of the One Vehicle (*ichi-ichi*) was spontaneously realized through the contemplation of the mind (*kanjin*) while receiving the entrustment in the celestial palace.

Furthermore, since the *Lotus Sūtra*, the King of Sutras, has already established these fourfold aspects of the One Vehicle, how could the present sutra be compared to it? [This is] the answer given by the golden mouth of the Tathāgata.
The *Profound Praise* states that the wisdom, supernatural powers, and so forth of Kṣitigarbha are all inconceivable. The Great Master [Zhiyi] says that the "wondrous names" are inconceivable;

why then does he not allow for a fourfold or singlefold introduction? If one follows the *Myōgen* (the *Fahua xuanyi*), where each of the ten wonders is discussed in terms of both the original and the manifested aspects (*honjaku*), one should indeed clarify the ten inconceivabilities according to the original and the manifested aspects respectively. However, those in the final age delight in brevity.

Therefore, one should preserve this and refrain from further discussion; it must be understood that the *Perfect Sūtra* (Vajraśekhara) is not to be interpreted otherwise. Now, for the first part, there are two sections.
First, the simultaneous gathering:
At that time, from the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, all the unspeakably unspeakable Buddhas and great [bodhisattvas]...
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas all gathered together.
"At that time" refers precisely to when the Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma for the Noble Mother. Since the Buddhas are so numerous, it is difficult to distinguish their individual lands;
therefore, they are collectively referred to as the "innumerable worlds of the ten directions. "Innumerable" means that their measure cannot be grasped. There are...
What are these? "Worlds" (*loka*) refer to temporal flux; "realms" (*dhātu*) refer to spatial directions. East, west, south, north, above, and below constitute the realms;
the past, future, and present constitute the worlds. There are two types: first, the world of sentient beings, which is the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
2. The Receptacle World (*bhājanaloka*). This is the environment-retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*). The number of these environments and their inhabitants is so vast that it cannot be described.

This is one among the two hundred and twenty-five numbers in the *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* chapter of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. "Universal" (*pǔjí*) is called "one" (*yī*); "exhausting the limit" (*jìnjì*) is called "all" (*qiè*).
Not being merely one is called "various" (*zhū*). Being supreme and honored is called "Buddha" (*fó*). Each is attended by a single Great Bodhisattva as a retainer.

Therefore, it is said "and. "Bodhi" means the Way; "Sattva" means the mind. One who personally practices this Way and is further able to transform others, establishing supreme practice based on a supreme state, is a Great Being of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Thus, one speaks of a "Mahāsattva Mahāsattva," wherein the principal and the attendants are together, the cause follows the fruit, and the principal does not differ from the attendants, nor do the attendants differ from the principal; they are both principal and attendants, yet are not [separate].
They are different yet not distinct. When they come, they come together; when they gather, they gather as one. Thus it is said that "all have come to assemble.
At this moment, like the radiance of pearls in Indra’s net, layer upon layer, inexhaustible, the practitioner’s single thought darkly accords with its midst.
Then, the wisdom of initial awakening and the wisdom of original awakening merge into a single boundary, and the mind of ignorance and the mind of bodhi interpenetrate.
The two streams flow together; thus, the boundless ocean of lands is not separated from the tip of a single hair. Ten ages of past and present do not depart from the present moment of thought.
The mind is the master of total retention (dhāraṇī); one must never for a moment cease this perfect contemplation.
Please each reflect upon this. II. Jointly Expressing Praise, Part One: Together Praising the Difficult Deeds of Śākyamuni.

I praise Śākyamuni Buddha, who, within this world of five turbidities and evil, manifests the power of inconceivable great wisdom and supernormal penetrations to subdue beings of stubborn and unruly nature, and who understands the dharmas of suffering and pleasure.
Śākya is his clan name; in the *Benqijing* (Sūtra on the Original Arising), it is translated as "Capable Benevolence" (*Néngrén*).

According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, in the past, King Ikṣvāku (of the sugarcane clan) listened to the praises of his secondary consort and banished his four crown princes to the north of the Snow Mountains. There they established cities and settled, attracting people through their virtue.
Within a few years, they had become a powerful nation. Their father, the king, dispatched an envoy to summon them, but the four sons declined the invitation, citing their transgressions.
He did not return. His father, the King, sighed three times, saying, "My son is a Śākya. Because of this, he was named after his clan. "Muni" is his personal name;

in the *Benxing jing* (Sūtra of Past Deeds), it is translated as "Silent One" (*jìmò*). Because the members of the Śākya clan were arrogant and talkative, when they saw the Prince, they all became silent.
The King said, "It is fitting that his name be Muni. As for his surname, derived from compassion and benefiting sentient beings, he therefore does not abide in nirvana.

The characters [of the name] capture the wisdom that accords with the profound principle; thus, one does not abide in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). This is precisely the meaning of praising the ability to "name" [the Buddha].

In the world of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), it is like clear water into which dust and soil are thrown; its appearance becomes turbid, and this is what is called "turbidity. There are five aspects of turbidity:

namely, the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*)—which has no separate essence and is designated by way of the other four turbidities—the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*)—which has the five deluded afflictions (*kleśa*) as its essence—and so forth.

The turbidity of afflictions (having the five dull fetters as its essence), the turbidity of sentient beings (a designation established based on the retribution of views and pride), and the turbidity of lifespan (having the continuity of matter and mind as its essence).
Of these five turbidities, afflictions and views are the root. From these two turbidities, the turbidity of sentient beings arises; from sentient beings, there is the continuity of lifespan.
The duration of these four is called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). During the period of disorder in the turbidity of the eon, sentient beings...
Because defilements are heavy, and because stinginess, greed, and envy have brought about the various unwholesome roots, it is called an "evil world.

In the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Śāntamati asks: "For what cause and by what condition does our present World-Honored One abide within this impure evil world of the five turbidities, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and preach the Dharma of the three vehicles? For what reason does he not take up a pure [land]?"
The world is far removed from the five turbidities of the evil age. The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:
"By virtue of my original vow, I have taken up a pure and wondrous land; yet by virtue of my original vow, I have also taken up an impure land.
Because the Bodhisattva has perfected great compassion, he takes up this defiled, evil, and impure land. Therefore, by means of my original vow, I dwell in this impure, foul, and evil world."
[The Buddha] attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (and so forth). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The great compassion of all Buddhas penetrates to the very marrow of their bones;
regardless of whether the world is favorable or unfavorable, they teach and transform those to be saved according to what is appropriate for them, just as a compassionate mother loves her child."
Although you were submerged in a latrine, you diligently sought deliverance without regarding it as foul;

therefore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas praise those who are able to subdue stubborn and unruly sentient beings within this evil world of the five turbidities. This refers to the manifest [Buddhas] in terms of their transformative methods.
Originally he was the Elder Śreṣṭhin Muktaka, yet he manifested as one with a base and defiled body; this is to conceal the great and manifest the small.

According to the Buddha’s intention, he was originally a Perfect Buddha (paripūrṇa-buddha), yet he descended to manifest the appearance of one newly attaining the Three Piṭakas; this is to conceal the reality and manifest the provisional.
Regarding his great wisdom and supernormal powers, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is said that he is able to subdue the great treatises of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Because he deliberates with the masters of the assembly as well as Śakra and Brahmā, he is named "Great Wisdom.

According to the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, after the six heretical teachers had been defeated, King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying: "The six teachers are deluded and lack self-awareness;

they have come to the World-Honored One seeking to compete in displays of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). The Buddha has manifested miraculous transformations that are wondrous and inconceivable; the six teachers are now cowed and shrunken, possessing not a single skill."
He threw himself into the water and died; his followers were dispersed and scattered. Thus he was named "One of Great Supernatural Power.
The power of the Buddha’s physical merit surpasses that of a hundred thousand precious white sandalwood elephants; this is the power of the physical strength inherited from his parents.
As for the power of his supernatural merits, it is immeasurable and limitless. Such great wisdom and supernormal powers are unknown to those of the Three Vehicles, nor to humans or devas.
It is unfathomable; thus it is called "inconceivable. By the power of this wisdom-penetration, he tames sentient beings who are stubborn and fierce.
The Layman Vimalakīrti said: "The sentient beings of this land are stubborn and difficult to transform;
therefore, the Buddha speaks words of severity to tame them, saying: 'This is hell,' 'this is the animal realm,' 'this is the realm of hungry ghosts,' and so forth, even unto..."

Ignorance. Such is the retribution of ignorance and so forth. Because those who are difficult to transform have minds like monkeys, or like elephants and horses—*luoli* (the first character pronounced *lóng*, the second *lì*;
*luoli* means extremely stubborn and wicked)—they are unruly, such that even the most piercing of punishments, reaching to the very bone, cannot subdue them.
Thereafter, they are subdued. Because such beings are stubborn and difficult to transform, it is only through words that are entirely harsh and urgent that they can be brought into the discipline.
Therefore, our Buddha is titled the "Tamer and Teacher of Gods and Humans. Suffering and pleasure refer to the three baskets (*piṭaka*), arising and ceasing, and the four noble truths.

Because their delusion regarding reality is profound, they are designated according to their engagement with phenomena. Furthermore, suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*) are one and the same dharma.
By dividing cause and effect, two [pairs] are established; the same applies to the Path (mārga) and Cessation (nirodha).

Because these two are the causes and effects of worldly suffering, while the other two are the causes and effects of supramundane happiness, they are simply referred to as the "dharmas of suffering and happiness. Their meaning is defined by "guiding" (naya) and "sustaining" (dhāraṇa).
These dharmas of the Four Truths were not created by Buddhas, devas, humans, śramaṇas, or brahmins; they exist solely due to the past perversion of ignorance.
It is the natural law that the performance of various formations (*saṃskāra*) within an inverted mind can produce the bitter fruits of the six realms in this present life;
naturally, good and evil differ. For one who knows this, when the Wheel of Dharma was turned three times at the Deer Park, its characteristics were shown, saying:
"This is suffering; you should know it," and so forth. This was the initial accomplishment of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), wherein expedient means were first employed to subdue [beings].
Regarding the capacities of the three vehicles: Śrāvakas are tamed by means of the Four Noble Truths;

Pratyekabuddhas are tamed by means of Dependent Origination; and Bodhisattvas are tamed by means of the Six Perfections. Whether it be the Truths, Dependent Origination, or the Great Vows, all rely upon the Four Noble Truths;

therefore, they are collectively described as "knowing the dharmas of suffering and joy. This is the specific capacity of Śākyamuni; thus, cause and fruit mutually praise and together extol one another. △ Second.
Each dispatched an attendant to inquire after [the Buddha’s] welfare.
Each dispatched an attendant to inquire after the World-Honored One’s welfare.

An "attendant" (*upasthāyaka*) is one who stays close by, follows instructions, and serves; in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, they are called "administrators" (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*). This refers to those such as [Pūrṇa] in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

"And as for the various servants. The commentary states: "Servants" refers to attendants and messengers. This is a metaphor for expedient means (*upāya*) and knowledge-and-vision (*jñāna-darśana*), which are all fully perfected.
Blending their light within the six realms of existence, they comply with the myriad capacities of beings;

these are the servants of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). Because true wisdom presides internally, it is that which sends forth; because provisional wisdom (*prajñā*) operates externally, it is that which is sent forth. As for "inquiry": [text continues].
To inquire after one's health is to ask about their affairs. It is as if the various emanations of the Buddhas each dispatched their attendants to inquire, saying:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your strength and well-being secure? This extends to the assemblies of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, all of whom are equally at peace.

Because he must respond to the five turbidities of this evil age, he asks about the strength of his illness as a means of instruction; this is because the Buddha manifests himself in accordance with the human condition.

△ Second, manifesting signs to assemble the multitude, which has two parts: first, manifesting auspicious omens. These "omens" (ruì) are simply secret intimations, while the "signs" (xiàng) are extraordinary wonders.
What do these signs represent? They represent the profundity of the wondrous principle, which is most difficult to explain and beyond the reach of ordinary human sentiment.

Since those who are distant and unable to show respect must rely on supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to manifest auspicious signs (*praṇidhāna-lakṣaṇa*) as a subtle expression of the underlying principle:

just as the world regards a spider’s web as a sign that joyful news is approaching, or the cawing of a magpie as a sign that a traveler is arriving—where even small things portend the great—so too should the manifestation of omens from the near to indicate the distant be understood in this way. This manifestation of omens is divided into two parts.

First, the emission of clouds of light; second, the production of subtle and wondrous sounds. These indicate that our Buddha manifests his body and preaches the Dharma as the prototype for the form and voice of Kṣitigarbha.

First, he awakens them through supernatural powers; subsequently, he proclaims the teaching through wisdom and eloquence. Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, a general demonstration.
At that time, the Tathāgata smiled and emitted hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great clouds of radiance.
"At that time" means when the path of response and stimulus intersected, and his original station was revealed as he manifested his fundamental nature.

It was the moment when the Tathāgata attained the capacity for entrustment and the Great Being received the command to deliver and save. Now is precisely this time; it is like the *udumbara* flower, which appears only at such a time. Now...
Having attained [this state] at that time, he therefore smiles and emits light. "Encompassing" (*han*) means "closing. It refers to closing the mouth and remaining still.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, a smile issues from the mouth and all the pores open; thus it is called a "smile. Because one laughs with the mouth out of joy, it is so named.
All the pores of his body open. Now, among Buddhas, there are two distinctions regarding radiance: the constant light (*nityaprabhā*) and the emitted light (*visṛtaprabhā*).

As for the constant light, it is a radiance extending one *zhang* on each of the four sides of the Buddha’s body; it is present from birth and is one of the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*).

This is called the "one-zhang radiance mark. In other realms, the constant light is immeasurable; however, because sentient beings have meager merit, they cannot endure such brilliance, and thus Śākyamuni Buddha accepted a limit of one zhang.

This present emission of light signifies that he establishes teachings according to the capacities of beings to shatter delusions, eliminate doubts, and manifest function from the essential body (*tattva*).
Yet, while in various sutras the light is invariably withdrawn after being emitted, it is not seen to be withdrawn here.
Regarding these passages on "light" (*ābhāsa*): they employ the emission of light to illuminate present events and the gathering of light to encompass future events.
Since the current section clarifies the manifest events of Kṣitigarbha, it briefly omits the passages concerning the gathering of light. The *Guangming xuán* (Profound Meaning of Light) states:

*Pobopo* is translated as "light" (*ābhāsa*); *Yùduōmó* is translated as "illumination" (*prakāśa*). As for "clouds," they are the vapors of mountains and rivers; they are the patterns of Heaven. When Yin and Yang gather together, they form [clouds].
Clouds drift and spread upward, naturally forming patterns. The *Nèijīng* (Inner Classic) states: "The vapors of the earth rise to become clouds; the breath of heaven descends to become rain.

Thus, the character for "cloud" (*yún*) is composed of "rain" (*yù*). It represents the shifting and transforming forms of swirling shapes, signifying that the Tathāgata manifests his body like a cloud and preaches the Dharma like rain.
Just as clouds emerge from mountain clefts without intention and disperse into the void leaving no trace, they gather in dense, vast masses.
The spreading of sweet rain falls in torrents, clearly manifesting the Tathāgata’s non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). When conditions are met, he manifests his body;

when the capacity [of beings] invokes him, he preaches the Dharma, causing the sprouts of *bodhi* to grow spontaneously within sentient beings. "Hundreds of thousands of myriads of millions" refers to the great number of clouds of light.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Body-light is the root of all lights; from this root, branches and streams flow forth in immeasurable numbers."
Innumerable. For example, it is like the *kālakūṭa* insect: its body is minute, yet upon encountering the wind, it grows vast; the radiance of the Tathāgata is likewise.
Upon encountering sentient beings who can be saved, it increases boundlessly; thus there are hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis.
One must know that the light of the Tathāgata originally flows forth from the mind of wisdom; thus, within a single thought-moment of ours, the three [bodies] are inherently complete.

The thousand natures and characteristics, the hundred realms and the thousand suchnesses—thus, the hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of mental radiances are mutually complete.
They are non-dual and indistinguishable from the wisdom-radiance of the Tathāgata. Therefore, the three vehicles all converge and the six paths are simultaneously opened;
they share this one radiance, which is inconceivable. △ Second, the specific explanation.
That is to say: the great perfection cloud of light; the great compassion cloud of light;
the great wisdom cloud of light; the great prajñā cloud of light; the great samādhi cloud of light; the great auspiciousness cloud of light;
the great merit cloud of light; the great virtue cloud of light; the great refuge cloud of light; the great praise cloud of light.
"Clear Clouds.

As for the term "so-called," it is a word used for indication. In terms of the literal text, it refers to ten kinds of light-clouds; in terms of its underlying meaning, it refers to the inherent virtues of the nature of sentient beings.

This is intended to allow one to know the meaning by beholding the form, so that the Way may be perceived through direct observation, and cultivation may arise entirely from the nature, whereby the cause is perfected.
As a result, one then perceives that Vairocana pervades all places, and that there is no difference between the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.

Therefore, according to the ten-fold contemplative method (*daśa-yāna-dhyāna*) of our school, we correlate and explain the ten kinds of light-clouds, enabling practitioners to attain the gateway through cultivation.

One sees that [this teaching] is not in vain. Therefore, Siming said: "Although these ten dharmas were proclaimed by the Great Sage (Zhizhe) during the Semblance Age, if one departs from these ten, there is no other method for cultivation.
Now, following his intent, I shall explain this text so that these ten dharmas may become a vehicle (*yāna*) to transport one back to the precious abode.
*The Great Perfection Cloud of Radiant Light* serves as the ten lights.

First: It radiates nine rays of light. It directly confronts the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*), standing at the beginning of the ten vehicles and serving as the foundation for the nine vehicles.

Great Perfection (*mahāparipūri*) refers to the three bodies (*trikāya*) of the Tathāgata’s fruition-merit and the one thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) of sentient beings’ three thousand realms (*trisahasra*).
These are fully present without deficiency; this very realm lacks no dharma whatsoever, and is therefore called "perfect. It is the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
"Is it not found herein? Thus he answered. ○ Regarding the "Cloud of Great Compassion and Radiant Light," this corresponds to the second [category]:
those who have truly resolved their minds toward Bodhi. Since they have already contemplated the wondrous realm, what further need is there to resolve the mind?

It is because, although these ten dharmas are all perfect and eternal, there are three grades of capacity among those of perfect realization that are not equal: those of superior capacity require only one dharma; those of middling capacity require two.
Alternatively, there are seven; those of inferior capacity must possess all ten. Now, those of middling and inferior capacities do not attain awakening by contemplating the object alone;

they must further cultivate the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Thus, relying on the wondrous object, they give rise to the four great vows of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Compassionating themselves and feeling pity for others, they seek the highest [enlightenment] above and transform beings below.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s compassion that extracts suffering and bestows happiness—it is the very bodhicitta generated by us.
This does not accord with the text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Fearing it would be too cumbersome, the following sections are all abbreviated.

○ Regarding "The Great Cloud of Wisdom-Light" in contrast to the third [section], "Skillful Settling of Mind through Calm Abiding and Insight": the cause is named "calm abiding and insight," while the fruit is named "concentration and wisdom.
The wisdom that arises from concentration is called "great wisdom. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Wisdom universally knows; there is no dharma that it does not [know]."
Exhausted. When wisdom is great, the light is great; it is like a large casket having a large lid. Thus one knows that the Buddha-wisdom on the level of fruition is immeasurable.

Because the causal mind skillfully establishes *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, cause and fruit manifest each other, and cultivation and realization mutually support one another; therefore, they are set in opposition.
The "Great Prajñāpāramitā Cloud of Radiance" corresponds to the fourth [section], "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas," which refers to the three contemplations as one.
The mind: there is no delusion that it cannot shatter. This is precisely the cultivation of Prajñā. For indeed, among all the various gateways of the teachings, non-arising (*anutpāda*) is foremost;

it universally shatters all delusions, and by means of non-arising, one enters into all gateways. Thus, both vertically and horizontally, everything is shattered, causing the essence of consciousness to become pervasive.

This pervasiveness of the essence of consciousness is the *dharmatā-prajñā* (the Prajñā of the true mark); entering the various gateways is the *pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā* (the Prajñā of contemplative observation).
Prajñā. This is contrasted with the "transverse and longitudinal shattering" of this *prajñā* of words.
○ Regarding the "Great Samādhi Cloud of Radiance," it corresponds to the fifth consciousness’s "penetration and obstruction.

This precisely uses the sovereign samādhi to illuminate the obstructions of the Four Truths (suffering and accumulation), the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the six hindrances, the dust-like [afflictions], and ignorance; there is nothing that does not become the Way.

Extinction. The wisdom of the causes and conditions of extinction, the six perfections, and the penetration of the three contemplations within one mind: that which is open is protected; that which is blocked is broken through.
Where there is no blockage, there is no lack of penetration; this is called the Great Samādhi.

When samādhi and wisdom are in profound accord, what blockage would not be penetrated? Therefore, these are set in opposition [to the sixth path]. ○ The Cloud of Great Auspicious Radiance corresponds to the sixth path-factor, *samprajanya* (clear comprehension).

Regarding "the appropriate": the Great Master said that "auspiciousness" (*śrī*) is a term for benefit and profit. Present benefit is called "meaning" (*artha*), while future benefit is called "profit" (*lābha*).
The *Mahākaruṇā-śūnyatā-jñāna-sūtra* states: "Auspiciousness refers to non-dual wisdom.

Now, in these chapters on the path of non-action, each is harmonized and entered according to what is suitable. This employs untainted *prajñā* to guide the truths, the conditions, and the perfections.
All myriad practices reach *sarvajñā* (omniscience). Prajñā guides these practices; this non-dual wisdom reaches *sarvajñā* and attains meaningful benefit.
Therefore, it is set in opposition [to the preceding]. The "Great Cloud of Merit and Radiance" corresponds to the seventh category, the "Aids to Counteraction and Opening.
Here, merit refers to giving (*dāna*) and so forth, which are the aids to the path; untainted (*anāsrava*) prajñā is...
The Right Path. The Right Path has many obstacles; the Perfect Principle remains unopened. One must cultivate the merit of phenomenal practice to assist in its opening.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The afflictions of sentient beings are not of a single kind; the Buddha has taught immeasurable gates of counteractive treatment (*pratipakṣa*).

One who does not believe in the existence of such counteractive treatments should be known as a person who has not yet understood right practice; therefore, these are provided as a remedy for them. [This constitutes] Great Merit.
The Cloud of Radiance. Regarding those who know their own stage and position as the eighth: this refers to practitioners who avoid the arrogance of overestimation (*adhimāna*).
For when beholding this cloud of light, all gain the merit of extinguishing evil and the virtue of generating goodness;

yet there are inevitably differences in the depth and clarity of their contemplative wisdom. Nevertheless, those who harbor arrogance claim they are equal to the Buddha, though in reality they have not yet attained realization.
To claim for oneself that one has attained realization is not merely to lose one's station; one will instead fall back into the *niraya* hells.

If one knows that the essence of sentient beings and Buddhas is identical and true, and that the causal and resultant aspects of the semblance [of reality] do not overlap in terms of sequence, then one should diligently apply the three contemplations internally and perform the five repentances externally.

Thus, one avoids the arrogance of overestimation (*adhimāna*) and accomplishes great merit. Therefore, this is set forth as a remedy. The Great Refuge: Clouds of Radiance. This corresponds to the second [section].

Ninth is the patience of being able to remain tranquil: this refers to remaining serene and unmoved amidst both adverse and favorable conditions, thereby exerting oneself to advance through the five stages and enter the six faculties.

For the practitioner of the perfect contemplation who has first entered the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), external fame and profit are summoned, while internal latent obstructions are stirred.

Because of this, one is ruined and shattered; how could one possibly advance on the Path? Now, seeing the clouds of light manifesting the image of taking refuge, one immediately returns to one's own nature.
Relying upon the Triple Gem, whose essence is radiantly adorned, one dwells in the unborn and advances spontaneously.
Thus, it is used to respond [to this]. ○ The "Great Praise of the Clouds of Radiance" responds to the tenth stage, the "Detachment from the Love for Dharmas that Accord with the Path.
This means one must not cling to the provisional path of the Ten Faiths; rather, one must enter the true principle of the First Abode (*prathama-vihāra*).

Since one has already practiced detachment from craving, one enters the Bronze Wheel (*tāmra-cakra*) of the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), where the hundred realms manifest as emanations, and the one and the many are mutually identical, occurring spontaneously.
Flowing spontaneously into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-encompassing wisdom), one is praised and comforted by all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time;

therefore, this is presented as a response. Question: Regarding the ten kinds of clouds of light, which are the functions of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the fruition-awakening, and the ten vehicles of contemplative methods (*dhyāna-dharma*).
This concludes the section on the initial gateway of cultivation and progress. [Objection: To equate the fruit with the cause results in a discrepancy between cultivation and realization. [Response:
Now, in discussing the method of contemplation (*guanfa*), if one does not take the awakening of the fruit as its essence, it is not the practice of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanxing*).

If one does not take the nature of immediate awakening as the object of illumination, it is not the wondrous object (*miaojing*), nor is it the ultimate principle. Herein, we do not permit the beginner and...
If the fruition and enlightenment are of the same substance, then how could the Tathāgata’s clouds of light have any connection with sentient beings?

And why would devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits gather everywhere by riding upon that light? Only when one knows that the beginning and the end are non-dual does it manifest that cause and effect share the same path.
This is what is called the Buddha of the inherent virtue of sentient beings: neither self nor other, neither cause nor effect; this is precisely the Great Perfect Eternity.

This is the essence of awakening. Therefore, one should know that the perfectly luminous essence of the Buddha of fruition is the inherent nature and virtue (xingde) originally possessed by us ordinary beings.

How can it be said that the cloud of light of the Buddha of fruition is not the wondrous function of the initial mind of the Perfect Teaching? △ Second, the manifestation of subtle and wonderful sounds.
Part One: Concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent.
Having emitted such unspeakable clouds of light as these, there further issued forth various subtle and wondrous sounds.
"Emitting" (fang) connects equally with what precedes; "again" (you) introduces equally what follows. *Vaja-ni-sa-pa* forest—this is translated as "Sound.

According to the *Māra-rakṣa-luàn-jīng* (Sūtra on Māra’s Disturbance), the Sanskrit name is *Vilū*, which is translated as "Sound"; later translations rendered it as "Resounding Sound" (*Hóngyīn*). [This refers to] Kulu Qin, a disciple of the Buddha.
[This is the definition of their names]. The *Baihutong* says: "Sheng" (sound) means "to cry out"; "yin" (tone) means "to drink.
When hardness and softness, clarity and turbidity harmonize, they "drink" one another. The *Jingyun* says: "Yin" is when sound forms a pattern;
that which is dispersed and spread is "sheng. Without this [pattern], it cannot cause vibration. That which contains and stores more than is fully revealed is "yin. Without this... [text ends]
This, however, cannot achieve a complete integration. By uttering two characters, the processes of opening and closing, as well as development and withdrawal, are fully provided for.

Now, the sound that expresses principle is called "sound" (*yin*). The sounds uttered by the Buddha are refined and elegant in their diction; those who hear them never grow weary, and those who listen never find it sufficient.
As for being able to act as the cause and condition for bestowing joy upon all and uprooting suffering, nothing compares to hearing this sound.
Furthermore, it is by cultivating speech with loving-kindness that one possesses the eight qualities of voice: first, an exceedingly beautiful voice; second, a soft and gentle voice;

third, a harmonious and pleasing voice; fourth, a voice of noble wisdom; fifth, a voice free from feminine timbre; sixth, a voice free from error; seventh, a deep and far-reaching voice; eighth, an inexhaustible voice.
These various subtle and wondrous qualities arise from the causes and conditions of the Buddha’s cultivation of virtuous vocal qualities in previous lives.

Therefore, within the throat one obtains the subtle and wondrous four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which are able to produce various kinds of exquisite sounds that reach both far and near, pervading the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions. Now, the clouds of light emit sound; it flows forth according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

It severs the emotional views of the conceptualizing mind and manifests the penetration of non-discriminative wisdom. When these sounds resonate with one another, they are called "subtle" (*miao*); that—
This lack of confusion is called "wondrous. This indicates that Kṣitigarbha manifests bodies according to the various species and preaches the Dharma in response to their capacities.
Since the objects [of his teaching] are not uniform, his voices are likewise manifold. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"From within all the radiances emerge wondrous sounds, which pervade all lands throughout the ten directions, proclaiming the various merits of the Buddha-sons and enabling them to enter the sublime path to Bodhi. Indeed.
This is what is meant by that. △ Second, the actual explanation of the various sounds:
namely, the sound of the dāna-pāramitā; the sound of the śīla-pāramitā; the sound of the kṣānti-pāramitā;
the sound of the vīrya-pāramitā; the sound of the dhyāna-pāramitā; the sound of the prajñā-pāramitā; the sound of compassion (maitrī); and the sound of sympathetic joy (muditā).
The sound of relinquishment; the sound of liberation; the sound of the untainted; the sound of wisdom; the sound of great wisdom; the sound of the lion’s roar; the sound of the great lion’s roar;
the sound of clouds and thunder; the sound of the great clouds and thunder.
The teaching of the six perfections and so forth has two intended meanings. First, it represents the body of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas, which is the Dharmakāya;

it arises from the merits of all dharma-gates. Second, it represents the preaching of the Dharma by the Buddha and Bodhisattvas, which does not transcend the dharma-gates of the six perfections and so forth.
With great wisdom, they let out the lion’s roar, moistening all things and solemnizing the assembly like the thundering clouds. (From the *Fan*)
"Dāna" means "generosity" (bōshī) in the language of Qin. Dāna is a precious treasury; it is a field of merit for wealth, nobility, peace, and security.
Dāna can destroy suffering and serves as a raft for attaining the Way and Nirvana. Because its benefits are so manifold, Guangyunshou praised it.
Śīla is translated as "intrinsic goodness" (xing shan). It is also translated as "stopping and attaining" (zhì dé), meaning to cease evil and attain goodness.
If a person seeks great and wholesome benefits, they should firmly uphold the precepts as if cherishing precious treasures or protecting their own life. It is, for example, like the great earth.
It is that upon which all things depend and abide. Precepts are the dwelling place for all wholesome dharmas; therefore, clouds of light flow forth. ○ *Kṣānti* means patience.

There are patience toward sentient beings (*sattvakṣānti*) and patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*). When a bodhisattva practices patience toward sentient beings, they obtain immeasurable merit.
When they practice patience toward phenomena, they obtain immeasurable wisdom. Thus, they become fully endowed with both merit and wisdom. Regarding this matter:
Matters were accomplished according to his wishes; for this reason, he proclaimed the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) with radiant speech.

*Vīrya* means diligence (*vīrya*). There is bodily diligence, which is the diligent cultivation of wholesome dharmas; and there is mental diligence, which is the diligent practice of the path of goodness.

This is because one desires to attain the Buddha-way. Generally, there are two gates: first, merit (*puṇya*), namely generosity, ethical discipline, and patience; second, wisdom (*prajñā*), namely reality...
The Prajñā of Characteristics: entering the gate of merit brings about the elimination of all transgressions and the fulfillment of all aspirations;
entering the gate of wisdom entails neither aversion toward saṃsāra nor attachment to nirvāṇa. Those who wish to enter Prajñā must rely upon dhyāna-concentration;

those who wish to cultivate dhyāna-concentration must necessarily practice diligence (*vīrya*). Therefore, Guangyun extensively proclaimed this to inspire others to enter the gate of the perfection of diligence. ○ Dhyāna.
That is called "cultivation through reflection. When a bodhisattva practices dhyāna, the five pāramitās harmoniously assist and perfect it.
Within each state of dhyāna, they practice great loving-kindness and compassion, uprooting the offenses of immeasurable kalpas and attaining the wisdom of the true mark of all dharmas.

Therefore, they are remembered by the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas. For this reason, they proclaim and expound the Light-Sound (Prabhāsvareśvara), giving rise to the gateway of human meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). *Prajñā* is translated as "wisdom" (*hui-zhi*).

It illuminates all phenomena (*dharmas*) such that none are found to be obtainable, yet it is able to penetrate all things without obstruction; this is called wisdom. From their initial aspiration, the Bodhisattvas...
Mind. One who seeks all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) should study all dharmas to attain all wisdom. This is why the Light-Sound (*Prabhāsvara*) proclaims this:

to give rise to the roots of wisdom in sentient beings. Although the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are common to the four teachings, here they are presented by opening up the preceding matters and principles to form a complete and perfect whole;
this refers to the principle of the six perfections. ○ The Sound of Compassion, the Sound of Joy and Equanimity. This...

He proclaims the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*). These four teachings are cultivated by both [types of] bodhisattvas. To be able to bestow happiness upon others is called the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*).

To be able to extract suffering from others is called the mind of compassion (*karuṇā-citta*). To rejoice in others' attainment of happiness is called the mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā-citta*). To be without hatred and without attachment is called the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*).
There are three types of loving-kindness: first, that which takes sentient beings as its object; it contemplates all sentient beings with the thought that they are like one's parents or kin.

Second, the conditioned object (*sālambana*): seeing that all phenomena arise from conditions. Third, the unconditioned (*anālambana*): not dwelling upon the marks of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) or the marks of sentient beings (*sattvalakṣaṇa*).

Compassion (*karuṇā*) likewise has three types, with names identical to those of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Because these are now the Tathāgata’s four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇacitta*), each is called "great.
In reality, they are able to bestow happiness and extract suffering for others; they are not merely conceptual constructs.

The reason for listing these two sounds here is that compassion (*karuṇā*) and pity (*anukampā*) are the root of the Buddha-way. Joy (*muditā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) arise from compassion and pity;

therefore, they are listed separately to demonstrate that compassion is the essential core. Now, as the Light-Sound [Bodhisattva] proclaims, he correctly opens up the four provisional and limited minds of the previous stage, so that they all become the Tathāgata’s four true and great immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*) that are free from conditions (*nirālamba*). Liberation (*vimukti*).
*Śabda*. The Sanskrit name is *mukti*, which here means "liberation" (*vimokṣa*). The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "First, true nature; second, real wisdom;
third, skillful means. The Sūtra says: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess a liberation called 'inconceivable.
If a Bodhisattva dwells in this liberation, he can place the height and breadth of Mount Sumeru inside a mustard seed, and so forth. This is it.
The inconceivable meaning of the three kinds of liberation. What are they? The liberation of the Bodhisattva is itself true nature (*dharmatā*).
The Bodhisattva’s abiding therein is itself true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*). A mustard seed within Mount Sumeru is itself skillful means (*upāya*).

Now, the flowing light and sublime sound precisely represent the inconceivable skillful means, supernatural powers, and wondrous functions of Kṣitigarbha. ○ This is the untainted sound (*anāsrava-śabda*). This...

Within this context, one should explain the causal conditions, the Four Noble Truths, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Here, however, these are subsumed under the term *anāsrava* (outflow-free).

In the Sanskrit language, it is *upasaṃ* or *satya*; here it is translated as "existence" (*yu*). What is the meaning of "existence"? It refers to all phenomena characterized by outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*).

This does not rely on the Small Vehicle’s perspective of the four truths involving arising and ceasing, wherein suffering and its origin are taken as the causes and effects of outflows, while the path...

Cessation (*nirodha*) constitutes the cause and fruit of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Now, as this refers to the perfect outflow-free state, the seven stages of expedient means (*upāya*) are all termed "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*).

This is because the six classes of ordinary beings (*ṣaḍ-gati*) fall into the extreme of existence, while those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) of the two teachings fall into the extreme of emptiness; as for the bodhisattvas of the three teachings...
[Those who] fall into the two extremes are now [reached by] the light-clouds proclaiming the truly non-outflowing (anāsrava) sound.

This assembles those of the seven stages of expedient means (upāya), causing them all to abide in the Middle Way, never again falling into the two extremes. Regarding the "Sound of Wisdom" and the "Sound of Great Wisdom":

"Wisdom" (jñāna) is designated by its ability to exhaustively penetrate the subtle; "Insight" (prajñā) is named for its power of discernment and decision. These two sounds are listed because the "Sound of Wisdom" extends throughout the seven [stages].
Expedient means (*upāya*). These are the twenty kinds of wisdom listed in the "Excellence of Wisdom" section of the *Myōzen* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra).

The "Sound of Great Wisdom" refers to the Tathāgata’s two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate truth; it is as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profound and immeasurable," and so forth. Question:
Previously it was stated that the Sanskrit term *prajñā* translates into Chinese as "wisdom. Why is it listed again here? Is it not a redundancy?

"Is it not [the case that] they are not valued? Answer: Since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, "If one wishes to attain the wisdom of the path (*mārga-jñatā*), the wisdom of the aspects of the path (*mārgākāra-jñatā*), all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*," it follows that *prajñā* can give rise to these various wisdoms;

therefore, this [term] is used as a translation for them. This is like naming a mother after her child, in the sense that the mother is able to produce the child. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) says: "The 'aspects' (*ākāra*)..."
Regarding "Wisdom-Prajñā": it inherently possesses all dharmas and is able to possess all marks; thus, Prajñā inherently possesses the three names: reality (śūnyatā), equality (samatā), and so forth.
Furthermore, because wisdom is not without causes at its time, there are the two meanings of provisional and real. Therefore, these are not considered redundant. Now, Guangyin proclaims this:
it correctly opens up the provisional, the small, and partial wisdom, such that there is nothing that is not the Middle Way, the true and wondrous wisdom. Great!
The Treatise states: "The Buddhas of the three periods and the ten directions emit great radiance from their bodies, which shines universally throughout the ten directions and destroys all darkness.
From their minds they produce the radiance of wisdom, which destroys the dark gloom of ignorance in sentient beings. This is precisely the meaning intended here.
The Lion’s Roar Sound; the Great Lion’s Roar Sound. In the Sanskrit language, *saṃgha* is translated as "little lion.
The Sanskrit name *saṃghapati* is translated as "lion"; he is a great lion. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Like a lion king, born from a pure lineage, dwelling in deep mountains and vast valleys... (and so forth). "Roaring" (*hu*) means stretching and yawning; by means of the mouth...

He strikes the ground, manifesting great majestic power to represent the strength of the lion king. Here, "lion's sound" refers to the teaching of provisional and lesser methods for the sake of the three vehicles;
"great lion's roar" refers to the teaching of the Mahayana for the sake of the Separate and Perfect [teachings]. Together, these represent fearlessness.

The New Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "For example, when a great lion roars, the young lions who hear it all become courageous and vigorous, while all other birds and beasts flee far away and hide in crouch.
When the Buddha-lion roars, if the bodhisattvas hear it, they praise the sound of the bodhicitta, which nourishes their dharma-bodies;
those sentient beings with false views feel ashamed, submit, and disperse. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra says:

It is like a lion, which can cause the herds of beasts to be cowed and subdued; this is it. That the light now flows and spreads means that he intends to proclaim the Dharma of the Six Perfections and so forth.
To do so, one must necessarily possess great wisdom. Once wisdom is sufficient, one utters the lion’s roar, and sentient beings receive its nourishment;
therefore, the passage concludes with "clouds and thunder. [The names] Cloud-Thunder Sound and Great Cloud-Thunder Sound refer to the Dharma.
Huā said: "It is like a great cloud that covers everything. The cloud of wisdom contains moisture; lightning flashes brilliantly;

thunder resounds afar, bringing joy to all beings. Its rain falls equally, saturating the entire land. The cloud is a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) preaching the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
hence it is called the 'cloud of wisdom. The body emits great radiance, and the mouth thunders with the four types of eloquence, just like the flashing of lightning."
The sound of thunder proclaims and pours down the rain of the Dharma; all receive its benefit and profit, yet the benefits received differ.

Thus, while the clouds and thunder are distinct, they are both produced from the same ground and moistened by the same rain. Differentiation is itself non-differentiation. The manifestation of signs is concluded.
△ Second, the gathering of the assembly. First, concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent:

Having uttered such unspeakably unspeakable sounds, immeasurable billions of devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits from the Sahā world and other lands also gathered at the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The *Xiyu ji* states that the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system of the Sahā universe is the domain transformed and sustained by a single Buddha.
Formerly it was called "Saha. The *Beihua jing* asks: "Why is it named Saha? It is because the sentient beings therein endure the three poisons and all afflictions;
