Thus, regarding the matters of Kṣitigarbha’s salvation of sentient beings as taught by the Buddha, how could he fail to believe and accept them with reverence? He naturally penetrates and understands them without obstruction.
It is obstructed. △ Second, the raising of doubts and slanders by the assembly:

Although the śrāvakas of the small fruits, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, and all sentient beings of future ages hear the Tathāgata’s words of truth, they will inevitably harbor doubts and suspicions; even if they receive them upon their heads, they cannot avoid giving rise to slander.

First, the occasion for doubt and slander is raised; next, the intent behind the rise of such slander is revealed. This is truly because those of the Lesser Vehicle hear only of the Truths and Conditions;
their wisdom is as shallow as water in a cow’s footprint, and their faculties are so narrow that they fail to recognize the vast ocean.

The Eight Classes of Devas and Dragons, being of mixed species and inferior capacity, lack the concurrent cultivation of the Vehicle and the Precepts. How could they hope to deeply understand the Great Way? As for the sentient beings of the future, their resolve...
Their natures are not firm; they are entangled by karmic obstacles and difficult to liberate. How could their majestic spiritual power be fathomed?

Thus one knows that these three types of people, though they hear the Tathāgata’s words of sincerity and truth, will inevitably harbor fox-like doubts and confusion. They speak against the Way, saying, "Though the words are thus, how could the facts truly be so?
Though their outward demeanor seems to involve receiving and practicing [the teachings], within their hearts they must perversely give rise to [doubt].

To slander [the teaching] through doubt is a grave transgression that will inevitably lead to rebirth in the Avīci Hell; therefore, it is necessary to inquire clearly into the origins of the causal ground and elucidate the matters of practice and vows.

Only then can those of the three types of capacity receive [the teaching] with a single mind, so that they do not fall into the state of icchantika and may forever ascend the path to Buddhahood. 2. Vowing to Expound the Practice and Vows.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively explain what practices the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha performed and what vows he established during his stage as a causal bodhisattva,
whereby he was able to accomplish such inconceivable deeds.

Based on this meaning of "seed" (*bīja*), the term "ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to one's own mind. Because it inherently possesses the three causes—the seed of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*)—and because the discerning cause (*vibhāva-hetu*) has not yet given rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), while the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) has not yet engaged in preparatory practice (*prayoga*), the nature-cause (*svabhāva-hetu*), the contributing cause, and the discerning cause are all designated by the same name: the primary cause (*mūla-hetu*).

This refers to the three causes of the principle-nature (*li-xing*). Now I ask: when this Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha first initiated his resolve in the stage of the causal ground (*yin-di*), what gate of practice did he perform and what vows and aspirations did he establish, such that he was able to accomplish these inconceivable deeds?
The two characters "er" (二) are words of inquiry. This is because among the bodhisattvas of the four teachings, there are none who do not cultivate practice and make vows.

If the three preceding teachings involve expedient practices and vows that all belong to the realm of birth-and-death causes and conditions, then how can one who takes a mind of birth-and-death as the fundamental cause for cultivation achieve the non-arising, non-ceasing nature of the ground of fruition?

Therefore, I pray that you will explain its causes extensively, so that those of lesser capacities may believe and accept them without giving rise to doubt or slander. As for practice and vows, they must both be asked about as before.
As for this, aspiration is that which leads, while practice is that which initiates action. If there is aspiration but no practice, the aspiration is empty;
if there is practice but no aspiration, the practice is isolated. Because aspiration exists, practice is not isolated; because practice exists, aspiration is not empty.
As aspiration and practice support one another, the realization of the fruit is all the more swift. This is why they are asked together. △ Second, the World-Honored One.

Citing the cause to answer the question regarding the salvation of others; Part Two: First, a brief praise of the merit; Second, an extensive explanation of the practices and vows. Within the first [section], there are again two parts:
First, clarifying the merits of the stages of fruition in both the Great and Small Vehicles; Third, citing a metaphor.

The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "Suppose, for example, that all the grasses, trees, forests, rice, hemp, bamboo, reeds, mountains, rocks, and motes of dust within a trichiliocosm were each counted as a single Ganges River, and the sands of each such Ganges River were likewise counted."

One grain of sand constitutes one world-system. Within one world-system, each particle of dust represents one kalpa. Within one kalpa, the total number of accumulated particles of dust fills the entirety of that kalpa.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "What is a trichiliocosm? It answers:

"As explained in detail in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, one thousand suns, one thousand moons, one thousand Jambudvīpas, and so on up to one thousand Mahābrahmās—this is called a 'small chiliocosm' (the term *cūlika* [small] is the Sanskrit name).
Taking one thousand such small chiliocosms as a single unit, and counting in this manner until..."

A thousand [small worlds] is called a "two-thousandfold intermediate world system. Taking one such two-thousandfold intermediate world system as a single unit, when that count reaches one thousand, it is called a "trichiliocosm" (three-thousandfold great world system).
The first thousand are small; the second thousand are intermediate; the third is called the "great" (mahāsāhasra). Because it is a thousandfold multiplication of thousands, it is named "great.
Because it exceeds a thousand by another factor of a thousand, it is called "three-thousand. Taken together, this is termed a hundred.
From one hundred million suns and moons up to one hundred billion Great Brahmā Heavens, this is called a trichiliocosm (the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world).
This great trichiliocosm rests in the void; upon the wind is water, upon the water is earth, and upon the earth are humans.

The grasses and trees and so forth are situated upon the earth. "Cong" means a cluster or gathering. A cluster of trees is called a forest. Rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds serve as metaphors for existence.
There are two kinds: first, that which uses a metaphorical illustration; second, that which uses a literal illustration. Here, it is a metaphorical illustration.
Because these four things grow in clusters, are densely interwoven, and are numerous in their varieties, and because people commonly see them, they are easily believed.

The same applies to the minute particles of mountain rock. Now, from among such a multitude of things, if one were to take a single count from each object and make it a Ganges River, since the objects are infinite, how could the rivers ever be exhausted? This is reckoning the number of rivers based on the objects;
thus, the rivers cannot be ended. Furthermore, from within the sands of a single Ganges River (some versions say "a single Ganges filled with sand"), if one takes a single [particle]...
Each grain of sand constitutes a world-system. Since the sands are difficult to exhaust, how could the world-systems ever be exhausted?

This calculation of world-systems based on the sands of a single river shows that the world-systems are inexhaustible. Furthermore, within each of these world-systems, there is even a single mote of dust.

This is what is called one *kalpa*. Since the atoms (*paramāṇu*) are difficult to know, how could the *kalpas* be measured? This is based on calculating *kalpas* according to the number of atoms in a world-system;

thus, the *kalpas* cannot be exhausted. Now, if one were to take the number of atoms accumulated within a single *kalpa* and use every one of those atoms to constitute a *kalpa*, the duration of time would be so long that the accumulated atoms would naturally be vast. Based on such a multitude of *kalpa*-atoms—
"Numerous kalpas. How could kalpas be numbered? Kalpas are inconceivable.

Thus, through these successive metaphors, it is revealed that even if a master mathematician and his disciples were to employ their spiritual minds and skillful hands to attempt to calculate the number of kalpas since the Great Being Kṣitigarbha first resolved upon the *saṃnāha* (armor of resolve), the total would still be as in the aforementioned metaphor; in the end, they would be unable to reach it.
No one is able to know [the number of its sands]. It is necessarily the Ganges that is cited because its sands are so numerous.
Furthermore, it is because the Buddha was born there and wandered there, and his disciples have seen it with their own eyes. Moreover, among the four rivers, the Ganges is the greatest;

all people regard it as a river of merit and auspiciousness, and those who enter it to wash have all their defilements and impurities removed. Because people revere and serve this river, [it is used as an example].
This is known through collective consensus. Furthermore, the names of various rivers change from age to age, whereas the Ganges remains constant;
therefore, the Ganges is used as a metaphor. Question: How many grains of sand are there in the Ganges? Answer: This cannot be known by any form of calculation;
only a Buddha or a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body can know it. The Sanskrit term *kalpa* corresponds to the Qin (Chinese) term for "division" (*fen*).
There are different time periods: small kalpas (*antarakalpa*), intermediate kalpas (*madhyakalpa*), and great kalpas (*mahākalpa*). Here, we shall speak in terms of the great kalpa.
II. The Main Explanation.

Since the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha attained the fruit of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), he has been [in this state] a thousand times more than the aforementioned metaphor; how much more so for the earth itself?
The Bodhisattvas are concealed within the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This passage first correctly uses the Mahāyāna as a primary metaphor, and secondly, it contrasts it with the minor fruits [of the Hinayana].

As for the mention of only the ten *bhūmis*, this is an abbreviation of the virtuous stages of *vihāra*, *caryā*, and *mukha*; it compares them solely in terms of the realization of the sages (*ārya*). This is according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*). If...
According to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), from the first stage (*zhù*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*děngjué*), there are forty-one stages in total, all of which are positions of true causes.

For now, we shall follow the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*). First: the Stage of Joy (*huānxīdì*). From this point on, one employs the Middle Way contemplation (*zhōngdào guān*) to shatter a portion of ignorance (*wúmíng*).
This reveals one aspect of the three virtues; this is the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), as well as the stage of effortlessness (*anābhoga*).

Here, the hundred realms manifest Buddhahood, achieving the eightfold signs of enlightenment to benefit sentient beings. Having traveled five hundred *yojanas*, one first enters the unobstructed realm of true reality (*tathatā*) and first reaches the precious destination;
therefore, it is named "Joy" (*pramuditā*). Second is "Freedom from Defilement" (*vimalā*); third is "Radiance" (*prabhākari*); fourth is "Blazing Wisdom" (*arciṣmatī*).
5. Difficult to Conquer (Durjayā); 6. Manifest (Abhimukhī); 7. Far-Reaching (Dūraṅgamā); 8. Immovable (Acalā); 9. Excellent Wisdom (Sādhumatī); 10. Dharma-Cloud (Dharmameghā).
In each of these stages, one abandons one grade of ignorance and realizes a portion of the Middle Way (and so forth).
Yet, from the time Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva entered such fruitive stages—whether distinct or perfect—until this very day, the number of kalpas has been vast and long.
Compared to the number of kalpas accumulated over the kalpas of the upper realms, this exceeds it by more than a thousandfold.

How much more so for those who traverse the Great Vehicle of the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications; and how much more so for those in the lesser fruits of the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
Those who realize the fruit upon hearing the sounds of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—are called "those who hear" (śrāvaka).
I have heard that there are both provisional and ultimate [teachings]. As for the ultimate, it is as previously explained.

As for the provisional, according to the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, together with eighty hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of Bodhisattvas, manifested in the form of Śrāvakas through their supernormal powers and came from the south to pay homage to the Buddha and offer praise. Judging the present by the past, how could this not be so? (From the *Fan*)

Regarding *pratyekabuddha*, this is translated as "Pratyekajñāna" (Solitary Realizer). Because they awaken to the Way by contemplating conditions, it is also translated as "Solitary Buddha" (*dokaku*).

Because they appear in worlds where no Buddha exists, one should also discuss their provisional and ultimate aspects (and so forth). Herein, there is no comparison made between the Great and Small Vehicles.
This merely reveals that the passage of time is vast and remote. Regarding such a stage of practice, who could fathom its duration?
△ Third, the conclusion and manifestation:
"Mañjuśrī, the majestic power and vows of this Bodhisattva are inconceivable."

This mastery of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) for subduing Māra and restraining outsiders, as well as the vow-mind and great vows for the universal salvation of all classes of beings, are none of them measurable by the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Since those on lower stages are unable to speak of them, the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* records the Buddha saying to the Bodhisattva Subhāṣtaparipṛcchaka:
"The merit and roots of goodness of such a Mahāsattva are such that all the devas and humans in every world..."

The assembly was unable to fathom the depth or shallowness of his measure. If the Tathāgata were to explain at length such meritorious roots and virtues of this Great Being, all the multitudes of gods and humans in the world would become bewildered and distressed, or perhaps fail to believe and accept them.
Thus, this Great Being has accomplished immeasurable and inconceivable, supreme merits.
He is well able to awaken to and enter the realm of the Tathāgata; he has already attained mastery over all Buddha-dharmas.
Desiring to bring all sentient beings to maturity, he dwells in every Buddha-land where he may be (and so forth). Inconceivable. [This is from] the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Name: [Title].
It is not determinable; because its transformative activities cannot be definitively determined, it is called "inconceivable.
△ Second, showing the merit of hearing, praising, and making offerings to the image.
If, in future ages, there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who hear the name of this bodhisattva,
or praise it, or gaze upon and pay homage to it, or recite its name, or make offerings to it— even by painting, carving, sculpting, or lacquering its image—
such persons shall be reborn thirty-three times in the Heaven of the Thirty-three and shall never again fall into the evil realms.
The word "if" (*ja*) is an indefinite term. It is likely because those who practice evil are many, while those who practice good are few;
it is also a phrase used to express hope, meaning: "Should there be any sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing the name of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, cultivate reverence for him."
One shall certainly and eternally attain the Hall of Blessings. This does not restrict [the practice] to the two groups of the laity alone;
as the *Daśacakra* Sūtra refers to Kṣitigarbha as "good son," it follows that all seven assemblies and the three vehicles may likewise be so addressed. For [as it is said]: "Commit no evil."
"Practice all that is good. Within the Buddha-dharma, who would not comply with and practice this? Hearing the names of Bodhisattvas and so forth constitutes planting the seeds;

when there is a resonance, there is a response. This is like a great bell hanging on its frame: it rings whenever it is struck. To explain the name: it is like threads being strung together. "Zi" (字) means "to nourish and transform.
Only after a man has a wife and a woman has a home can they give birth and raise children. It is written with the radical *mián* (pronounced mián, resembling a house).

This arises from the transformations of the mind and possesses no reality. As the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says: "The sinner before King Yama is not..."
These beings—when the sinners see them, they perceive these beings as holding flaming iron tongs in their hands.
When that hell-being’s evil karma is exhausted, he no longer sees the jailers of Yama;
just as there is no lamp when the oil and the wick are spent, so it is when karma is exhausted: one no longer sees the jailers of Yama. Now, these beings...

As long as the evil karma one has produced has not yet been exhausted, one will naturally experience false visions in the intermediate state. △ Second, being fearless through the power of mindfulness of the Buddha:
At that time, because of the power of mindfulness of the Buddha, the Brahmin woman was naturally free from fear.
This is because of the causal power of mindfulness of the Buddha. Although one may encounter various forms, there will naturally be no fear.

This is because one knows that all objects arise from the mind, and the mind manifests through objects. Since the mind is fundamentally empty, how could objects exist? When both mind and objects have vanished, [fear ceases].
From what does fear arise? In the *Cittabhūmi-parivarta* of the *Buddhānusmṛti-sūtra*, the Buddha tells Mañjuśrī:

"Suppose there is a dense and lush forest where lions, white elephants, tigers, wolves, and other predatory beasts dwell in hiding. When their venom is unleashed, they harm people, and all traces of human passage are utterly severed.
At that time, a wise person sets fire to the forest, so that none of these great and evil beasts remain. [The mind is like this forest.]
The same applies to the cessation of the view of emptiness. Furthermore, the Mahāyāna Ratnavyūha Sūtra says:
"For example, it is like a painter who creates an image of a ghost and is immediately struck with fear.

In this same way, Kāśyapa, all foolish commoners create for themselves the phenomena of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, and thus they revolve in birth and death, not knowing that these phenomena are likewise [illusory]."
Now the Holy Woman understands that all dharmas arise in form from the mind and manifest as appearances due to the heart-mind.

She knows that the mind is like an illusion, possessing no fixed pattern; what is perceived varies and arises or perishes according to the mind. Since she knows it is like an illusion, why should she feel fear or dread?
△ Second, the Demon King Welcomes and Praises Her.
There was a king of ghosts named Wudú (Non-Venomous) who bowed his head in greeting and came forward to welcome her. He addressed the Holy Woman, saying, "Excellent, O Bodhisattva!
For what reason have you come here?"

"Poison" (dú) means harm. In the world, there are plants that harm people, such as those called *chúmǎng* (a class including *yégé*). In the Dharma, that which harms people is called the "three poisons. This ghost harbors a compassionate heart toward all beings;
he manifests in the form of a ghost as a skillful means, yet his mind is devoid of poisonous harm, thus manifesting this auspicious name.

However, there is the "Poison-Subduing" (Shèdú) mentioned previously and the "Evil Poison" (Èdú) mentioned later; although the names for poison are the same, their underlying intentions differ. To investigate the origin...
Their benefit to others is no different [from that of the heavens]. The *Book of Rites* says: "To nourish and foster them is how spring and summer cause growth;
to frost and snow them is how autumn and winter bring maturity. Is this not all the teaching of Heaven?
To bow the head until it touches the ground, lingering for a short while—when the King of Ghosts bows to welcome him, one observes that his physical appearance is not [that of a ghost].
In general, his majestic demeanor is extraordinary; truly, he has not come here as one burdened by transgressions, but must have arrived by means of supernatural powers.
Therefore, it is said: "Excellent! O Bodhisattva, for what reason have you come here? *Brahma* is named *Sādhu*, which translates here as "Excellent.
This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva King of Joy. If a practitioner recites this a thousand times before the Buddha every day, they will attain the mind...
Pure. One receives the praise of all Tathāgatas, and all dharmas are fully accomplished.

This is detailed in the *Xiangruji* (Record of Incense and Milk) concerning the sequence of offering food. △ Third, the question-and-answer regarding the hells, in two parts: first, a general inquiry as to whether hells exist;
second, the specific inquiry as to where my mother was reborn. Within this, there are two sections: first, a brief question and answer.
At that time, the Brahmin woman asked the King of Ghosts, "What place is this?
Wudu replied, "This is the first layer of the ocean on the western side of the Great Iron Ring Mountains."
First, when the Holy Woman asks, "What place is this? it is a word of startled doubt, arising because it differs from what she has seen at other times.

Second, the King of Ghosts replies: in Sanskrit, *Cakravāḍa*; translated as "Wheel Mountain. The old translation was "Iron Encircling Mountains" (*Tiewei Shan*); here, "encircling" (*wei*) carries the same meaning as "wheel" (*lun*).
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Qishi Jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World), and other texts, this is the center of the four continents and is Mount Sumeru.
Mountains. Outside these mountains, there are eight other mountains, continuing until the salt ocean beyond them, which is of infinite breadth.
Beyond the ocean is a mountain, which is the Great Iron Encircling Mountain (*Mahā-cakravāḍa*). According to the *Lishi apitan lun* (Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra), it says:

"Beyond the great salt ocean, there is a mountain named Iron Encircling (*Cakravāḍa*), which enters the water for three hundred and twelve *yojanas*, and likewise emerges above the water for the same distance."
The breadth is likewise. From the southern limit of Jambudvīpa to the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) is three hundred and sixty million, six thousand, six hundred, and sixty-three yojanas.

From the water’s edge of the Iron Ring Mountains to the extreme western water’s edge of the Iron Ring Mountains, the distance across is twelve billion, two hundred and eighty-two million, five hundred yojanas. [This is] from the water’s edge of the Iron Ring Mountains...
Its circumference is thirty-six billion, eight hundred and forty-seven million five hundred thousand yojanas. The first layer of the ocean is situated therein.
Some say there are separately three layers of the karma-ocean; I have not yet examined this in detail and await further investigation.

△ Second, the extensive question-and-answer session, which has two parts: first, the question-and-answer regarding the existence or non-existence of hells; second, the question-and-answer regarding where the hells are located.
The first [section] further has three parts: first, the question-and-answer as to whether the reality of the hells exists or not.
The noble lady asked: "I have heard that within Mount Cakravāḍa there are hells in its center; is this true?
Wudou replied: "There truly are hells."
First, the Holy Woman asked: "I have heard it said in the sutras that there are hells within Mount Cakravāḍa.
Is this true, or not? Next, the King of Ghosts replied: "This is real and not false. It is simply because hell is fundamentally empty, yet people themselves make it real.
As stated in the *Ayaḥpuraniraya-sūtra*, the Buddha admonished the śramaṇas, saying: 'I behold with my divine eye...'"

Regarding all people in the world—whether in life or death, whether good or ugly, those who attain the good path and those who attain the evil path—it is so that among people in this world, those who commit evil with their bodies, speak evil with their mouths, and harbor evil thoughts in their minds, who constantly delight in cooking and killing to sacrifice to ghosts and spirits, shall upon the death of their bodies enter the *niraya* (hell).
Is this not, in truth, entering hell by one's own hand? △ Second: Question and Answer on "What Am I?"
Upon arriving at the prison, the Holy Woman asked, "How have I now reached this place of imprisonment? Wudu replied, "It must be either through spiritual power or the force of karma;
without these two things, one could never arrive here."
First, the holy woman was struck with alarm and doubt, thinking to herself: "The hells are the prisons where the guilty are confined.
Reflecting upon my own heart, I have reverently placed my faith in the Triple Gem; my person is without fault. By what cause have I now arrived at this place of hell?
Second, the King of Ghosts replied: "Those who arrive here are of two kinds: first, spirits of majestic power."

Regarding those who pass through: some do so for the sake of rescuing and delivering others, while others do so for the sake of sightseeing. Alternatively, there may be those whose evil karma has matured such that they ought to undergo retribution in hell;
it is for this reason that they arrive here. Apart from these two cases, there is ultimately no one else capable of reaching this place.
III. Question and Answer on the Suffering Realms of the Ocean of Hells. Part One: Inquiry Based on the Realm.
The noble lady asked again: "For what reason does this water surge and boil? Why are there so many sinful beings and evil beasts?
This describes the scene she beheld upon first arriving at the seashore. "Sea water" is the general question; "for what reason" is the term of inquiry.
First, she wonders for what reason this water surges and boils. Second, she wonders for what reason there are so many sinful beings within the water.

3. Regarding the doubt as to why there are so many malevolent beasts within the waters by the seashore: according to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, these are all produced by the karmic retribution of those sentient beings themselves.
Having created the ten causes of habitual practice, they undergo the sixfold intersecting retributions; thus the waters surge and boil.
Due to the habituation of pride (*māna*), they give rise to mutual reliance; flowing without ceasing, there is thus surging and rushing. The accumulation of these waves forms water.
Furthermore, due to the habituation of deception (*māyā*), mutual cheating leads to the existence of drowning, leaping, flying, falling, drifting, and sinking.

Regarding various evil beasts: because contact with them brings about the retribution that draws forth evil fruits, the conscious spirit consequently perceives a great iron city, fire-snakes, fire-dogs, tigers, wolves, lions, and so forth. △ Second, the direct answer based on facts, in three parts:
first, the formal answer.
Wu Du replied, "These are newly deceased sentient beings from Jambudvīpa who committed evil deeds.
After forty-nine days have passed, they have had no one to succeed them in performing meritorious acts to rescue them from their suffering and hardship.
Furthermore, having no roots of goodness from their past lives, they must now proceed naturally across this sea toward the hells, as determined by the retribution of their original karma."
Regarding Jambudvīpa, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: To the south of Mount Sumeru, there is a continent named Jambudvīpa.
Its land is narrow in the south and broad in the north, measuring seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth. There is a great king of trees named Jambu;
it is seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height, with its branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all directions. Thus it begins.
The world-sūtra differs slightly [from this]. A sentient being who commits evil refers to one who fully commits the ten non-virtuous actions.
In the Sanskrit language, *kumāra* means "evil person" (*pāpaka*) or "unwholesome person. That which can extinguish the sense faculties is called "death. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Death is the relinquishing of the body one has received. There are two kinds: first, death through the exhaustion of the life-span, which is of three types. First, [death] through the exhaustion of the life-span... [and so forth].
1. This is the exhaustion of merit. 2. This is the exhaustion of merit, but not the exhaustion of life. 3. This is the exhaustion of both merit and life.

Regarding the second [type], there are three ways of dying due to external conditions: 1. Death through self-inflicted harm beyond one's proper measure; 2. Death through being unjustly killed by another;

3. Death through both [causes]. Furthermore, there are three kinds of death: 1. Death through negligence; 2. Death through breaking the precepts; 3. Death through the destruction of the life-faculty. 40.

Regarding the nine days and so forth: according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, when a person dies, they possess an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*; that is, the *antarābhava* body). If one is extremely virtuous, one is reborn in a pure land or the heavens;

if extremely evil, one enters hell—neither of which involves passing through the intermediate state. If virtue and evil are not fixed, one undergoes the intermediate state and passes before the authorities of the underworld. If the conditions for rebirth have not yet been met...
It remains for a maximum of seven days. After dying, it is born again; thus it cycles through birth and death until the seventh week, at which point it definitely attains rebirth.

However, if there are conditions for rebirth, this is not fixed. The *Shishi Yaolan* states: "Nowadays, when someone dies, one must invariably prepare a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*) every seven days to cultivate merit for them;
this is called 'the seven-day feast' (*zhāi qī*). It is intended to prevent the seeds of existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) from undergoing further rebirth."

This refers to the evil realms. Now that the seven-times-seven days have passed, and since no one has continued the lineage to perform meritorious deeds for them to extinguish evil and give rise to good, who will rescue them from their suffering?

This first statement means that if no one performs funeral rites for the deceased to secure merit for the afterlife, they will inevitably fall into suffering. The subsequent statement means that the deceased did not cultivate virtue themselves while alive.
Even the slightest good will inevitably lead to falling into suffering, as the King of the Netherworld (Yama) examines and adjudicates good and evil.
Based on the karma one has committed during their lifetime, those who ought to fall into hell will certainly go to hell. As stated in the *Nāgasena Bhikṣu Paripṛcchā Sūtra*:
"The good and evil that a person performs follow that person, just as a shadow follows a form. When a person dies, it is only their [physical] body that perishes."
The body does not lose its actions. It is like writing at night by the light of a fire: when the fire is extinguished, the characters remain; when the fire returns, they are once more visible.
Thus it is that what one performs in this life is realized in a future life. This is the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*): it is brief and free from any sense of artificiality or forced effort.
King Yama says to the transgressors: "Your sins arose from yourself; you must now undergo their consequences. (From the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*)
He said: "You are of wrong views and deluded; you are a person bound by the snares of ignorance who has now fallen into this hell within the great ocean of suffering.
Therefore it is said: 'One naturally crosses this sea first. △ Second, pointing out the category.
Ten thousand yojanas to the east of the sea, there is another sea; its suffering is twice that of the former.
To the east of that sea, there is yet another sea; its suffering is again doubled.
Preface: The first layer of the ocean on the western side of the Cakravāḍa mountains already encompasses these two layers.
Regarding the fact that their sufferings increase twofold at each stage, the *Niraya Sūtra* states: "The Salt Water Niraya is several thousand li in length and breadth.
The water is salty like salt and boils with surging waves. Within the water there are birds with beaks made of iron; they peck at human flesh and gnaw at people."
The bones [exposed]. The person could not endure this pain and tried to cross the water to leave. The *niraya* (hell) guardian spirit said, "You wicked dead man!
What do you seek? The person replied, "I suffer from hunger and thirst.

The spirit then used a hook to pull apart his upper and lower gums (the flesh at the roots of the teeth), causing his mouth to gape wide open. He then poured molten copper into his mouth, filling his lips, tongue, and throat.
Their bellies are completely scorched; the copper then sinks downward. The person can no longer endure it and returns to the boiling brine.
Because the person committed such extreme evil during their lifetime in the world, they seek release but cannot find it.
They rise and fall with the waves, swirling and sinking, their suffering redoubled—how could it be described in words? △ Third, the conclusion of the name.
It is summoned and manifested by the evil causes of the three karmas; this is the place commonly known as the Ocean of Karma (*karma-sāgara*).
The evil causes of the three karmas refer to the ten non-virtuous actions of body, speech, and mind. Due to these causes, one summons the retribution of the ocean of hells.

However, that which is summoned is summoned by oneself, and that which is manifested is manifested by oneself. As the *Xingqi xing jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of Practice) states: "In previous lives..."
One has created these conditions oneself and must inevitably experience them; there is no place from which to escape.
These consequences were not made by one's father, nor by one's mother, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor were they created by śramaṇas or brahmins. They were originally created by oneself.
Now, one receives [the consequences] oneself. Therefore, the Buddha taught that there are two essential principles for sentient beings: first, by doing this, one obtains this;
second, by not doing this, one does not obtain this. Within the three realms and five destinies, the defilements of sin and the suffering of affliction do not exist apart from action.
There is no misfortune for anyone. The sins and merits one has committed follow like a shadow follows a form or an echo responds to a sound;
not even as much as a hair’s breadth shall be lost. Therefore, these three places are all called "Oceans of Karma. What the Noble Lady had previously heard with her ears, she now reaches in person.
2. Question and Answer: Where are the hells located?
The Holy Woman again asked the King of Ghosts, Wudu, "Where is hell located? Wudu replied, "Within the Three Seas lie the great hells;
they number in the hundreds and thousands, each distinct from the others. Among them, the largest consists of eighteen;
next there are five hundred, where the bitter poisons are immeasurable; and next there are a thousand, which likewise involve immeasurable suffering."
First, the Holy Woman asked: "If it is said that there are indeed hells within the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), why do we now see only this Sea of Karma?
I do not understand where these hells actually reside. Second, the King of Ghosts replied: "Within the three seas lies the Great Hell;
how could there be one apart from this? It is because sentient beings emerge from the Drum of the Treasury Sea [that they perceive it]."
Wind gives rise to the waves of the three poisons; therefore, one is reborn in hell, which lies within the three seas.
However, upon examining various sūtras and śāstras, hells are fully subsumed under three categories: first, the hot; second, the cold; and third, the peripheral.
The eight hot hells are situated beneath Jambudvīpa, stacked one upon another, where beings undergo the torments of heat. The eight cold hells are located beyond the Cakravāḍa Mountains.
[The hells] face upward and dwell there, suffering the pains of cold and freezing. There are three peripheral hells: among the mountains, among the waters, and in the wilderness;
there one undergoes the retribution for specific karmic actions. These [peripheral hells] should be understood as receiving a mixture of cold and heat.

Now, since it has already been stated that there are eighteen great hells, yet it is also said there are five hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand, why is this? It is because these are fixed locations, as clarified above; whereas the others are unfixed locations.
It is not improper that the peripheral and the central [realms] are raised together. [If you argue that] cold and heat are experienced in a mixed manner, this is not so;

for how could the central and the peripheral hells be distinguished? The "three seas" and so forth are general designations. Each of the eight cold and eight hot hells has sixteen *utsada* (subsidiary) realms.

Briefly stated, there are one hundred and thirty-six in each; extensively stated, the number reaches hundreds of thousands. As for their individual distinctions, they arise from the various karmas performed.
There are degrees of severity: the heavy [karma] involves traversing all [hells], the middling does not traverse them all, and the inferior is further reduced.

This is because the kalpas [spent there] also vary in length. Regarding what is called "inferior," it is explained specifically as follows: the "great" consists of eighteen [hells]. There are two interpretations.
First, according to the *Diyu jing* (Sūtra on the Hell Realms), the "eighteen kings" refers to those who preside over the eighteen hells; this is one interpretation by Kātyāyana.

The *Dian nili* (Director of Niraya) and so forth, up to the *Guan shen dian yang tong* (Observing the Body in Boiling Copper), refer to the names of the hells and their presiding directors who are restricted to eighteen specific locations.
As the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra* states: "In the Avīci Hell, there are eighteen minor hells;
within each of these minor hells, there are eighteen cold ice hells, as well as the Dark, the Minor Heat, and so on."
Up to and including the Hell of Drinking Copper, there are eighteen [hells] for each. Thus, within the Great Avīci Hell, there are these eighteen hells.
Within each individual hell, there are separately eighteen compartments (the term *gé* is pronounced *tǒng jì*; it is a type of cauldron).
Beginning from the Cold Ice Hell up to the Hell of Drinking Copper, there are a total of one hundred and forty-two compartmentalized hells. This is what that sūtra refers to.

Because the Avīci hell is considered the greatest, those [other hells] that each possess eighteen [subsidiary hells] are regarded as small. Now, it is said that the "great" ones fully possess eighteen;
alternatively, because they do not correspond to the Avīci hell, each is called "great. This is, for example, like the kings of the world:
when not compared to the Son of Heaven (devaputra), each is titled a "Great King," but when compared to the Supreme Sovereign, they are called "Small Kings. This is what the sutra states.
The same applies here; there is no need for forced interpretation. Next, there are five hundred [hells], which is likewise a fixed number. However, the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states:
"There are five hundred billion Sword-forest hells, Thorn-forest hells, Copper-pillar hells, Iron-mechanism hells, and Iron-net hells—each numbering five hundred billion.
Thus, the numbers in the two sutras differ significantly; there is also no need to forcibly reconcile them. The bitter poisons are immeasurable.
According to the *Niraya Sūtra*, the Buddha said: "If you wish to know that which is most unbearable in its diligent suffering, it is found only in *niraya*.
As for *niraya*, its extreme suffering cannot be fully described; it is like a worldly rebel who has been captured by high officials."
When he was about to be brought before the King, he was pierced by three hundred spears. "Was it not agonizingly painful?
The bhikṣu replied, "If a person were struck by a single wound, their entire body would ache; how much more so when pierced by three hundred wounds?

The Buddha said, "The pain in the niraya hells is hundreds of thousands of millions of times greater than the pain of a spear wound; even that does not compare to the pain of the niraya. Within the hells, the hell-guardians further..."
Pain and poison reach everywhere. Although the suffering in the hundreds and thousands of hells is immeasurable, when compared to the five hundred hells, its pain is slightly less;
yet compared to the sufferings of the world, it does not equal even a ten-thousandth part. Suffering is indeed immeasurable. Thus concludes the general inquiry as to whether the hells exist or not.
II. The Proper Inquiry into the Realm Where My Mother Was Reborn. A. The Holy Woman’s Question Regarding Her Mother’s Birth.
The noble woman again asked the Great King of Ghosts: "My mother has been dead for not long; I do not know to which realm her soul and spirit have gone."
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "In all worlds, there are none who do not age and die. It is the constant law of sentient beings that as they are born again and again, they all return to death.
Although my mother has been dead for but a short time, I know not at all to which realm her soul and spirit have now gone.
The *Jiyi* says: "Qi is the manifestation of the spirit; the hun is the manifestation of the ghost. The Daoist scriptures say:
The *hun* is the spirit of the vital breath (*qi*); the *po* is the spirit of the essence (*jing*). The yang-spirit is the solar *hun*; the yin-spirit is the lunar *po*.
My teaching points to the eighth consciousness. As the *Dharmapada Sūtra* says: "This body is a dead thing; the spirit is a formless dharma."
One creates for oneself suffering and pleasure; when the body dies, the spirit does not perish. The conscious spirit constructs the three realms—good, evil, and the three intermediate states.
Moving in concealment and arriving silently, its destination is like an echo responding to a sound. Thus, one knows that it must inevitably proceed according to karma.
△ Second, the King of Ghosts inquires into her origins. Part two: First, the inquiry and response regarding her past conduct;

second, the initial inquiry and the response. The King of Ghosts asked the Holy Lady: "As the mother of a Bodhisattva, what kind of practices did you cultivate during your lifetime? The Holy Lady replied:

"My mother held wrong views and reviled the Triple Gem; even if she occasionally believed for a moment, she soon again failed to show respect. Although her death was but recent, we do not yet know the place of her rebirth."
"Conduct" (*caryā*) means advancing toward; "karma" (*karman*) refers to the act of performing. This refers to the construction of good and evil deeds through the three types of karma.
As the *Dharmapada* says: "According to the karma one performs, there is the retribution of sin or merit. Evil karma leads to falling into hell; good karma leads to birth in the heavens.
Noble conduct leads to birth in the good realms, and one attains untainted *nirvāṇa*. [The text] does not clarify the mother of the Bodhisattva regarding...
"What kind of karma do these three types of action produce? The Noble Lady replied: "My mother was attached to false views and reviled the Triple Gem.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: 'It is better to refrain from acting than to follow a wrong path; when the body perishes and life ends, one falls into the evil realms.
Furthermore, she was inconsistent in her intentions and unstable in her character; she would occasionally listen to advice and believe it for a short time."
Suddenly, following a deviant path, he reviled and slandered [the Buddha]. Although his death has been but a few days, it is certain that he will fall into suffering according to his karma.
Therefore, I am urgently desirous of knowing where he has been reborn, yet I have not yet succeeded. △ Second, the question and answer regarding his surname and clan; first, the question.
Wu-du asked: "What are the clan and family name of the Bodhisattva’s mother?
A 'clan' (xing) is that which binds together a lineage for a hundred generations so that it is not divided;
a 'family name' (shi) is that which distinguishes the descendants according to their origin. In the land of India, there are four classes of clans: first, the Kṣatriya, the royal caste."
The Brāhmaṇas are those of pure conduct. The Vaiśyas (formerly called Piśas) are merchants. The Śūdras (formerly called Shuduos) are the common people.
Of these, the first two are noble, while the latter two are lowly. Now, I do not yet know what the clan and family name of the Bodhisattva’s mother are, nor whether she is of low or noble birth.
Since one’s clan and family name are clear and easy to verify, it is necessary to inquire about them.
This refers to her clan name. △ Second, the response in two parts: First, the noble maiden directly answers regarding her clan name.
The noble maiden replied: "Both my father and my mother are of the Brahmin caste. My father’s name is Śīlasudarśana; my mother’s name is Mṛgajā."
"Father" (*pitṛ*) means "to begin"; it refers to the one who first gives birth to oneself. "Mother" (*mātṛ*) means "to cover"; it refers to the one who contains and gives birth to oneself.

Since both belong to the Brahmin caste, they naturally cling to heterodoxy and slander the orthodox. The non-Buddhist practitioners of the Western Heaven exclusively maintain that the Brahmin caste is the foremost and most honored.
As stated in the *Brahmacārya-Āpastamba-prcchā-jāti-viśeṣa-sūtra*: "Originally, at the beginning, [he] arose upon the earth..."
"In former times, we were all of the Brahmin caste. Our lineage is the most honored;
we first emerged from the mouth, while the people of the world emerged from below. We are the descendants of the seventh son of Brahmā.
Yet the Buddha, on the contrary, speaks of only one kind in the world, placing our caste on equal footing with the Kṣatriyas, the Vaiśyas, and the Śūdras. We shall die [in this state]."
All were reborn in the Brahma Heaven. The Buddha, on the contrary, treats us as equal to ordinary people. The Buddha said: "In my sutras, the practice of giving (*dāna*) is the foundation.
Those who practice the goodness of giving are the most eminent among the great classes. Those who are most honored and noble in the world all obtain this by practicing the goodness of giving;
it is not obtained by birth. *Śīla* is a Sanskrit word; it translates as 'inherently good. One who delights in practicing..."
"Good path. Because one does not indulge in self-indulgence. "Śubhānita" is the Chinese term; its Sanskrit name is Subhūti.

"Yuetdili" (悅帝利) is not yet fully understood. Their names and titles are equally auspicious, yet their mental orientations are each perverse. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The sin of wrong views is heavy."
Therefore, even if one maintains the precepts and the actions of body and speech are virtuous, if they all follow wrong views, the evil mind acts like a seed;

Thereafter, he preached the Four Noble Truths for him, and those who heard it simultaneously attained the Way. At that time, in the Pārileyyaka Garden, this was the first assembly where the Dharma was preached; nine [thousand]...
One billion six hundred million people attained arhatship. At the second assembly for preaching the Dharma, one billion four hundred million people attained arhatship.
At the third assembly for preaching the Dharma, one billion two hundred million people attained arhatship.
Thus, in the *Womb Sutra* (*Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*), the Buddha told Maitreya: "The people of your three assemblies were those whom I previously transformed; they number nine hundred million."

Six hundred million people who received my five precepts, followed by those who took the three refuges—nine billion two hundred million of whom merely uttered "Namo Buddha"—all attained the Way of the Buddha;
this is what is meant. In the Sanskrit language, it is *vyākaraṇa*; here it is translated as "prediction" (*jùjì*). The holy words that bestow [the name] are called "bestowing" (*shòu*);

when the fruit is granted in accordance with the mind’s aspiration, it is called a "prediction" (*jì*). This refers precisely to the prediction corresponding to the first stage of abiding (*prathamā-bhūmi*).
This is all because our Buddha entrusted [the teaching] to Kṣitigarbha in the celestial palace, so that he might await those who would appear in the world during the time of Maitreya.
II. Kṣitigarbha’s Embodiment Accepts the Teaching. A. Kṣitigarbha Properly Accepts the Teaching.
B. The Tathāgata’s Praise and Joy. 1. First, an account of the fundamental basis of the unified body.
At that time, the various manifestations of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva from all worlds merged back into a single form.
Shedding tears of sorrowful longing, he was as described in the *Daśacakra Sūtra*: "He is steadfast and immovable, like the great earth.

Now, this Great Being Kṣitigarbha made his vow before kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and received his entrustment after the path of Maitreya; he endures this turbid impurity to transform and deliver those mired in suffering.
The plow is like the earth. That which unites divided bodies into a single form takes one as the root of all bodies; thus, the branches are united to honor the root.
This arises from when the Earth Store Bodhisattva practiced the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) while cultivating the perfection of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāramitā*).
They experience various kinds of miraculous powers: transforming a single body into countless bodies, and returning those countless bodies to a single body;
they exercise mastery over appearing and disappearing. Yet, they do not become attached to these miraculous powers, because their intrinsic nature is empty.
Because it is detached; because it is unarisen; and because it has no abiding place, whether internal or external, large or small.

By the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*), it swiftly pervades all bodies and returns with equal speed. In the twelfth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, Śāriputra says: "As for the realization of the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vidhi*):"
Following the mind of samādhi, one manifests countless supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*): transforming a single body into countless bodies, and merging countless bodies back into a single body.
To boast of such supernatural powers is the conduct of base and inferior ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*);
it is not that which is practiced by the noble ones (*ārya*). Regarding all things in the world, whether they be pleasant forms or unpleasant forms, one abandons both.
Having thus cultivated impartial protection and maintained focused mindfulness without forgetfulness, this is what is called the "spiritual power (ṛddhipāda) of the noble ones.

If even those of the Hīnayāna are like this, how much more so the Great Bodhisattvas! Just as the reflection of a single moon appears in all waters, yet the moons in all waters are subsumed within that single moon—this is the principle of the identity of the principal body and its emanations. There are four meanings for his weeping and sorrowful longing: first, compassion...
First, the karma created by beings in the six realms has not been rectified; second, sentient beings are stubborn and difficult to transform; third, the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is about to set;
and fourth, the task of entrusting the celestial palaces is of great importance. Thus, one knows that his weeping and sorrowful attachment truly stem from a sense of necessity.
△ Second, the application of transformative activities and the reception of the mandate, in two parts: first, the Buddha leads the messenger to attain supernormal wisdom.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since the distant kalpas of the past, I have been guided by the Buddha, enabling me to attain inconceivable spiritual powers and to be endowed with great wisdom."
In this passage, Kṣitigarbha personally declares the supernormal wisdom (*abhijñā*) he has attained, comparing it to the supernormal wisdom of the Buddha. He says:
"As for my supernormal wisdom, it is that which I have obtained through the Buddha’s rescue and guidance over the course of kalpas long ago; it is indeed the supernormal wisdom of the Buddha himself.
Now, as the Buddha entrusts sentient beings of the final age to me, I should naturally guide them just as the Buddha guided me."
To receive and guide them, causing them likewise to attain this penetrating wisdom, is precisely my own duty;

it is only right that I should reach upward to grasp the profound root and look downward to uplift those who have lost their way. △ Second, manifesting transformation bodies throughout the sands of worlds to benefit sentient beings, part one:
dividing the body to save people.
My manifested bodies fill hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. In each world, I manifest hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodies;

with each body, I deliver hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of people, causing them to take refuge in and revere the Triple Gem, forever leaving birth and death behind to attain the bliss of nirvana.
The text herein contains two meanings. Manifesting bodies throughout as many lands as there are grains of sand clarifies inconceivable spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*).

Delivering beings so they may realize the fruits of enlightenment clarifies inconceivable wisdom (*prajñā*). Spiritual power and wisdom are the very foundation for manifesting bodies to deliver sentient beings.
The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* states in brief: "This son of good family has accomplished inconceivable dharmas of merit, possesses firm vows, and is courageous and diligent.

For the sake of bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he may at times manifest as the body of Mahābrahmā, or even manifest as a jailer of the hells. All such [beings]...
The *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) manifests in these and other such infinite and innumerable bodies of diverse types to teach the Dharma to all sentient beings as is appropriate for them.
According to their needs, it establishes them in the stage of non-retrogression within the three vehicles (*yāna*). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"One who is fully endowed with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) can, at one and the same time, manifest transformations throughout worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
They manifest immeasurable bodies to make offerings to all Buddhas, listen to the Dharma, preach the Dharma, and deliver sentient beings;
none except a Buddha can equal them. These are the Bodhisattvas in their final body, and thus they are able to extensively deliver many people.
"Taking refuge" (歸) has the meaning of returning; it causes them to turn away from the heterodox and return to the orthodox. "Venerating" (敬) means single-minded sincerity.
The meaning is this: it causes one to abandon delusion and return to the truth. The Three Jewels are the vanguard against evil and the first chapter for entering the Path;
they are the vessel for crossing the sea of suffering and the essential way to reach Nirvana. Therefore, one must take refuge.

Through the phrase "forever departing from [suffering]" and so forth, both types of birth-and-death are severed, the afflictions of the five stages are utterly extinguished, and the secret treasury of the three virtues is realized as one.
It is perfectly realized. The *Five Mothers and Sons Sūtra* says: "If one uproots the very source, one can attain liberation. It is like a person who does not sow seeds;
they shall simply enter *nirvāṇa*. This *nirvāṇa* is bliss. △ Second, obtaining benefit through minor good deeds.
Whatever wholesome deeds are performed within the Buddha-dharma— be they as small as a single hair, a single drop, a single grain of sand, a single speck of dust, or even a mere hair’s breadth—
I shall gradually deliver those beings and cause them to attain great benefit.
Within the Buddha-dharma, there are degrees of goodness, ranging from superior to inferior.

That which is performed now is the inferior kind of goodness—lighter than a single hair, smaller than a single drop, more minute than a single grain of sand, and even finer than a single speck of dust;
yet it is still lighter than the goodness of a mere hair’s breadth. Nevertheless, I shall cause you to escape birth and death and attain great benefit. (From the *Xianyu jing*, by the Buddha.)
He addressed Ānanda: "If there are sentient beings who plant even a small amount of goodness within the field of merit of the Triple Gem, they shall obtain the fruit of the infinite.

This is precisely when the minor virtues of humans and devas in this assembly return to the vastness of the One Vehicle. It is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which universally opens the way for the six realms of existence;
even those who merely bow their heads, raise their hands, snap their fingers, or scatter flowers are originally [beings of] the human and celestial realms."
"Virtue! To open it now is precisely to provide the causal condition for the Buddha-seed, enabling one to obtain great benefit. Why, then, should there be any doubt?
△ Third, comforting the World-Honored One not to worry:
'I only pray that the World-Honored One will not harbor concerns regarding sentient beings who commit evil deeds in future lives. Thus he addressed the Buddha three times."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will not harbor concerns regarding sentient beings who commit evil deeds in future lives.
To comfort those who need no such concern is to demonstrate one’s own capacity to undertake the task.
This is because all afflictions, the sixty-two views, and so forth, are all seeds of the Tathāgata; even those of icchantika nature do not sever their inherent goodness. Should...
Encountering the conditions for the Dharma, their roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) are awakened once more. When even a single root of goodness arises, ten thousand evils are entirely eliminated.
This is like a spark of fire consuming ten thousand acres of fuel, or the seven poisons claiming the lives of many people. As the *Daśacakra-sūtra* states:
"In whatever place sentient beings dwell, because their greed, hatred, and delusion are all so fierce and sharp, they commit the ten paths of unwholesome action (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*)."

If there are those who, with a sincere mind, invoke the name, recite the mantra, take refuge, pay homage, and make offerings to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, all their afflictions will be completely extinguished;
they will distance themselves from the ten non-virtuous actions and accomplish the ten virtuous actions;
they will give rise to a heart of compassion and a heart of benefit toward all sentient beings. This son of good family accomplishes such meritorious virtues and wondrous samādhi.
By the power of his majestic spiritual authority and through courageous diligence, within the duration of a single meal, he is able to traverse immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields.
In each of these fields, during that same interval of a single meal, he is able to liberate immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings—
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— who are to be converted, causing them to leave behind all suffering and attain peace and happiness, establishing them according to their respective needs.
Setting aside the paths to rebirth in heaven and nirvana, he no longer has cause for concern regarding sentient beings who commit evil deeds in future lives.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s praise and joy.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent! Excellent! I rejoice with you.
You have been able to fulfill the great vows you made throughout kalpas long ago; as your extensive work of saving beings is nearing completion, you shall immediately realize Bodhi."
Having received the entrustment and comforted the Buddha, Kṣitigarbha was praised by the Tathāgata with words of approval and joy. The double exclamation of "Excellent! (Sādhu) was for two reasons:

first, because he was able to embody the Buddha’s mind and reverently accept the solemn command; second, because he would manifest emanations to benefit sentient beings without omitting even a hair’s breadth of merit.
The reason for this joy was that it fulfilled my own heart and completed your vow. As for the two words "Extensively Deliver," they refer to me—
Even if the Buddha were to grant his request, Kṣitigarbha would surely know the proper time himself.

If, as the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance) states, "He does not dwell in saṃsāra, nor does he abide in nirvāṇa," and thus received the prediction of bodhi, then Kṣitigarbha must have long ago realized great bodhi;
why then wait until the completion of his vast work of universal salvation?
