The first section is divided into three parts: first, describing the name of the Buddha and the kalpa of the king.
In the distant past, immeasurable, incalculable, nayuta, and unspeakable kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha named Sarvajñatā-saṃpanna Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi,
Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. The lifespan of that Buddha was sixty thousand [kalpas].

*Kalpa*. First, the duration of the *kalpa* is described. From the words "At that time" (*er shi*) onwards, the name of the Buddha is presented. The character for "Ancient" (*gu*) is composed of "mouth" (*kǒu*) and "gāo" (phonetic *kǎo*).
If the radical "tiger" (*hǔ*) is added, it is pronounced *háo*; it refers to the roar of an angry tiger or a loud cry. *Hào* means to wail or lament. Thus, ancient and modern [traditions] accumulate.

This is an error that is very difficult to correct. The Sanskrit name is *sarvajñatā*; *pratyutpanna* is translated as *sayun* in Qin (Chinese), meaning "the aspect of all-knowledge" (*sarvajña-lakṣaṇa*).
Because one attains the three knowledges within a single mind, once such true wisdom (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) is attained, it is fully accomplished.
Thus, by riding upon this, one attains perfect enlightenment; therefore, he is named the Tathāgata Accomplished in All-Knowledge (*Sarvajñatā-siddha*).

He is worthy of receiving the supreme offerings of all devas and humans, and is thus named Arhat (*Worthy of Offerings*). He is "Right" (*Samyak*) because he is immovable and indestructible regarding all phenomena. He is "Universal" (*Vibhu*).
It is not called [the knowledge] of one dharma or two dharmas; because it fully knows all dharmas without remainder or exhaustion, it is called "Perfectly Complete Knowledge" (samyak-saṃbuddha).
"Clarity" (vidyā) refers to the three types of clarity, as explained later. "One whose practice is perfected" (vidyā-caraṇa-sampanna):

To the place where he has gone, the Buddha likewise goes; ascending to the supreme state, never to return again, he is called the Sugata (Well-Gone).
"Understanding" (*vid*) means knowing. Knowing all aspects of the afflictions and purifications within the world and the realm of sentient beings, he is called the Lokavid (Knower of the World).
Among all phenomena, Nirvana is supreme; among all sentient beings, the Buddha is supreme. Because of this...
One who has severed [all afflictions] is called the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara*). The Buddha is able to subdue sentient beings and skillfully guards the gates of the sense faculties.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "He skillfully governs the six contacts, guarding and subduing them just as one levels the ground for a chariot drawn by four horses;
a skilled driver holds the whip and reins, ensuring the vehicle does not stray from its path. If one were to say he "subdues women," it would be disrespectful.

Therefore, he is called the "Tamer of Men" (*Puruṣadamyasārathi*). Because the Buddha delivers fewer sentient beings from the other realms and delivers more sentient beings among gods and humans, he is called the "Teacher of Gods and Humans" (*Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*).
Because he has accomplished all wisdom and knows the dharmas of sentient beings and non-sentient beings, as well as the categories of the conditioned and the unconditioned, he is called the "Buddha.
Possessing these ten titles, he is universally honored by the world; therefore, he is called the "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*).
The lifespan is sixty thousand kalpas. Is this the lifespan of a Buddha of Supreme Response in a pure land? However, regarding the enumeration of time, there are four types of kalpas:

first, the intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*); second, the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*); third, the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*); and fourth, the great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). If these are further expanded, there are six distinct kalpas:
first, the intermediate; second, formation; third, abiding (*sthāyikalpa*); fourth, destruction; fifth, emptiness (*śūnyakalpa*); and sixth, the great. If [these are] further...

When these are grouped together, there are three types of kalpas: first, the small; second, the medium; and third, the great. From a human lifespan of ten years, it gradually increases to eighty thousand years, passing through a vast period of time;

then, from eighty thousand years, it gradually decreases back to ten years—this constitutes one *antarakalpa* (a "separate" kalpa, so called in contrast to the "total" kalpa, specifically referring to the kalpa of increase and decrease).

The small kalpa is thus the *antarakalpa*. The medium kalpa consists of either the period of formation (*vivartakalpa*) or the period of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*). The great kalpa is the total cycle of formation and [destruction].
Eighty *kalpas* of destruction combined constitute one great *kalpa*. The present mention of sixty thousand *kalpas* should be understood as analogous to the long lifespan of the Buddha of Sukhāvatī;
it ought not to be definitively determined according to the three types of *kalpas* specific to this land.

"Again" (yòu) signifies the convergence of aspirations. When aspirations converge, they assist and benefit one another; therefore, the superior and inferior are taken together.

Secondly, by observing their intent to cooperate, the two lines regarding "practicing together" correctly explain the meaning of "furthermore. This means they share the same resolve and the same path.

The ten wholesome deeds (*daśa-kuśala*) are the opposite of the ten unwholesome deeds (*daśā-akuśala*). Generally, all four types of Wheel-Turning Kings (*cakravartin*) transform the people and establish customs through the ten wholesome deeds;
for the ten wholesome deeds are the very foundation for rebirth in the heavens. Now, these minor kings likewise practice the ten wholesome deeds, and thus they are equally universal.
This is the heart of compassion. Regarding the fortunes and misfortunes of serving the Buddha, the sutras state: "The ten unwholesome acts are like enemies; the ten wholesome acts are like close kin.
To settle the spirit and attain the Way, all arises from goodness. Those who can maintain their faith will naturally receive blessings and rewards; proceeding from good to even greater good."
It is not bestowed by a deity; therefore, he proclaims the Dharma teachings and manifests them to the people to serve as a field of merit.

Those who have faith may plant seeds therein, so that they shall have no sorrow in future lives. In this way, he benefits the common people and does not fail in the transformation of a benevolent king.
△ Second, the narration of the vows made by the two kings, in two parts: first, the origin of their vows.
The people within the neighboring kingdom committed many evils; the two kings deliberated and devised extensive skillful means.

The people are the foundation of the state. "People" refers to sentient beings. At the beginning when Heaven and Earth gave birth to humanity, they were outwardly simple and rustic, and inwardly true and pure.
Each person was fully endowed with a primordial unity (*hun-tun*). Those who opened the Way of Heaven are called the "people of Heaven."

Those who open themselves to others are merely common people; hence they are called "the people. When there is much evil, they fully commit the ten unwholesome karmas, which are the direct opposites of the ten wholesome virtues.
The *Sūtra on the Auspicious and Inauspicious Signs of Serving the Buddha* states:

"If one neither burns incense, lights lamps, nor performs prostrations, but constantly harbors doubt, anger, verbal abuse, harsh speech, and envy toward the worthy; furthermore, if one does not observe the six fast days and kills..."
They follow the ways of the living and do not revere the Buddhist scriptures. When afflicted by illness, they summon shamans to perform divinations and offerings to heterodox deities.

These people have come from evil paths due to their past actions; as sinners in the present life, they will enter the hells after death, where they shall be subjected to tortures and punishments beyond description. All this arises from the accumulation of evil, for their conduct has been unwholesome. (2)

The King deliberated and calculated: "Ultimately, how may I extensively establish skillful and expedient methods to rescue these people of manifold evils, so as not to lose the transformative influence of a sovereign-teacher? II. The Actual Formulation of the Vow A.
First, the King himself first attains Buddhahood 1. The King first delivers sentient beings (Note: Originally divided into two sections, they are now merged.)
The commentator adopts this phrasing for the sake of literary convenience.
One king made a vow: "May I quickly attain the Buddha-way and deliver these multitudes, leaving none remaining. Another king made a vow: [the same].
"If I do not first deliver them from the suffering of sin and affliction, bringing them to peace and happiness so that they may reach Bodhi, I shall never vow to become a Buddha.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are two ways of maturing sentient beings: there are those who first perfect their own merits and virtues and then deliver sentient beings, and there are those who first mature sentient beings and afterwards perfect their own merits and virtues. This refers to the two kings, Mahāsammata and Māndhātṛ.

The intent of this vow is that the attainment of Buddhahood is the very foundation for delivering sentient beings and enabling the widespread propagation of the Way; therefore, one vows to attain Buddhahood.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "When one person appears in the world, many people receive blessings and joy, and are enriched with benefit—this refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
Therefore, one must first achieve self-perfection before being able to deliver these wicked multitudes, leading them all into *nirvāṇa* without exception.

This is precisely what is meant by attaining perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta. When a king thinks, "Before I have attained deliverance myself, I shall first deliver sentient beings"—this alone is the generation of the mind of a Bodhisattva.
How could it be appropriate to act for oneself first? As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The Buddha..."
"I declare that with my purified divine eye, I see all sentient beings dying here and being born there, receiving various retributions according to their good and evil karma.
I should now first deliver those who are sinful, enabling them to attain the bliss of unsurpassed nirvana.
Rather than allowing them to remain long in birth and death, I vow never to wish for my own attainment of Buddhahood until this is done. This is the true arousal of the *saṃnāha* (armor).

Regarding their initial resolve, they ultimately concluded with great compassion in responding to the crisis; thus, while the vows of the two kings appear to differ slightly, [they are essentially the same].
△ Third, concluding the comparison of the two kings across past and present.
The Buddha told King Sovereign of Samādhi: "The king who made the vow to attain Buddhahood early is none other than the Tathāgata Sarvajñatā-saṃpādaka.
The king who made the vow to eternally deliver sentient beings from the suffering of sin, without wishing for his own attainment of Buddhahood, is none other than the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha."
When a king of men makes the vow to attain the Way, it is like taking possession of goods by holding a promissory note. Thus it is said: "The nature of phenomena is like a great ocean;
it does not speak of right or wrong. Whether ordinary person or sage, all are equal without high or low. It depends solely upon the extinction of mental defilements."
To attain realization is as easy as turning over one’s palm. Examining this king, it is indeed so.
Yet, that events from kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges appear as vividly as today is because the Buddha-eye knows no dharma unknown and sees no event unseen.
△ Second, the vows made by the girl Prabhāvatī. Part One: Describing the names of the Buddhas and the duration of their kalpas and lifespans.
Furthermore, in the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Pure Lotus-Eye Tathāgata.
That Buddha’s lifespan was forty kalpas.
Regarding the appearance of a Buddha in the world: taking the present Śākyamuni as an example, he is identical to the Buddhas of antiquity. As the *Caixin jing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) states:

"When the Bodhisattva’s meritorious practices are fulfilled and his rank has reached the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), he occupies the position of the 'One Life Remaining' (*ekajātipratibaddha*) and is born in the Tuṣita Heaven.

When the appointed time approaches and he is about to descend to become a Buddha, he immediately contemplates five matters: first, he contemplates those who are mature, those who are immature, and those who are not yet mature; second, he contemplates..."
1. Contemplating whether the time has arrived or not; 2. Contemplating which country is central; 3. Contemplating which clan is noble and flourishing; 4.

Contemplating past causes and conditions—identifying who served as his parents. Having completed these contemplations, he descends to be born. Judging the present by the ancient, it is exactly like this.
The "Pure Lotus Eye" is one of the thirty-two marks [of a Great Man]. As the Jewel Woman asked the Buddha, so did the Tathāgata...
There are thirty-two marks of a Great Man. What meritorious deeds did he perform in his past lives to bring about these marks that are spread across his entire body?
The Buddha said: "The mark of a Great Man wherein the Tathāgata’s pupils are deep blue like sapphire—"
In ages long past, because he constantly observed all people with eyes of loving-kindness, the Tathāgata’s eye possesses the mark of a great man like the newly risen moon.

Furthermore, in ages long past, because his will was free from coarseness and violence and his nature was harmonious and gentle, that Buddha established his name based on the marks he had attained, namely: "The face is like the pure, full moon; the eyes..."
If it is a blue lotus, it signifies that he has repaid his debt to the Buddhas and is called "Pure and Perfect.

Because all evils have been utterly exhausted and all virtues are fully perfected, he has attained a naturally wondrous eye like a pure lotus flower. △ Second, the manifestation of Arhats saving sentient beings.
Part one: Narrating past vows and deeds. Part two: Concluding by correlating the ancient and the present. Within the narrative of the first part, sub-part one: The sinful mother falls.
Part Two: The Vows of the Two Filial Daughters. Section One: First, the presentation of the Arhat capable of delivering others.
During the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was an Arhat who, through his merit, delivered sentient beings.
The Semblance Dharma (Saddharma-pratirūpaka) lies between the end of the True Dharma and the period of the Final Dharma; it is the time when stūpas and monasteries are firmly established.
Because one practices only conditioned meritorious deeds, this is the underlying intent for the subsequent passages concerning the molding of clay and painting of images. Regarding the Arhat:

by name they are called "mendicants" (bhikṣu), and as a fruition they become "worthy of offerings" (arhat). The *Sarvadharmaguṇavyūharāja Sūtra* states: "Four practices and four attainments; eight riches..."
Kāla, you should receive the offerings of the world’s devas and humans; you are worthy of reverent homage with palms joined, for you are the unsurpassed field of merit.
Thus, in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, King Dṛḍhadhyāna, the Wheel-turning Monarch, said to his crown prince:

"Regarding all the śramaṇas within your realm who practice with purity and integrity, who are fully endowed with merit, who have alone attained nirvāṇa, and who are tireless in their benevolence regarding food, clothing, and—"
Contented, he carried his alms bowl and went begging for food for the sake of blessing sentient beings; thus it is said that he "blessed and delivered sentient beings.
△ Second, an account of the filial daughter he encountered, in three parts: first, stating her name.
Following this, he proceeded with his teaching and encountered a woman named Guangmu (Light-Goal). She prepared food as an offering.
Since the Tathāgata had already entered parinirvāṇa, the Arhats successively taught people to transform evil into good and to change from the mundane state into the state of sainthood.
Regarding the name Guangmu, according to the *Lingshu Jing* (The Pivot of the Spirit), the essential qi of the five viscera and six bowels all ascends...

The essence is concentrated in the eyes, forming the pupils (the character *jing* being interchangeable with *qing*). The nest of this essence is the eye; the essence of the bone is the pupil (*tongzi*);

the essence of the sinews is the black sclera. Generally, the shape of the eye resembles a sphere, with the pupil situated in its center and facing forward, like the sun and moon shining brilliantly in the southeast while fading in the northwest. Yet, the eye is able to emit light because of the internal organs (*zangfu*).
The essences of these [organs] all receive their sustenance from the spleen-earth. The spleen is the head of all the yin organs, and the eyes are the sovereign of blood and qi.
Therefore, when the spleen is depleted, the essential qi of the five viscera all lose their respective functions and cannot return to the clarity of the eyes.
Now that this Holy Woman is able to be filial and obedient toward her two parents and reverent toward the Triple Gem, she naturally possesses divine unguents, divine waters, and divine radiance;
as well as true qi, true blood, true essence, and the moisture that nourishes the eyes. Her brilliance manifests in an extraordinary manner.

If we discuss this according to the Dharma, the eyes manifest concentration (*samādhi*), and the light manifests wisdom (*prajñā*). Because concentration gives rise to wisdom, and the light of wisdom is focused upon the eyes, this auspicious sign is established.
This is what is meant by "providing. One should prepare food as an offering. Food is the external life-force of sentient beings;

when a person holds food and gives it to others, there are five merits that enable them to attain the Way: first, the gift of life; second, the gift of physical form; third, the gift of strength; fourth, the gift of peace; [and fifth, the gift of wisdom].
5. The eloquence of giving. These constitute the five blessings. If one gives to an Arhat, the merit is a hundredfold.
For example, in the past, Nārada offered a single meal to a Pratyekabuddha; he subsequently received the retribution of never being poor for ninety-one kalpas and attained the fruit of the Way.
Therefore, one must make offerings. △ Second, the inquiry regarding vows.
The Arhat questioned him: "What do you wish for?
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones and Worthy Recipients, that after a meal they invariably ask what one's aspiration is, as when Kāśyapa questioned the poor mother.

"Mother, what is the wish in your heart now? Whether it be the wealth and nobility of the world, the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*), the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, or Brahmā among the various devas;
or if you desire to attain the fruit of a Stream-Enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to that of a Buddha—whatever fruit you seek, that is the fulfillment of your vow.
△ Third, the announcement of the matter, in two parts: first, the filial daughter relates her situation.
Guangmu replied, "On the day my mother passed away, I performed meritorious acts to rescue and deliver her. However, I do not yet know in which realm or destiny she has been reborn.
'Wang' (亡) means to depart; it means no longer remaining. It is composed of the radical 'to enter' (from) and the phonetic 'yin' (乚). This signifies entering into a hidden place. Thus it is said.
To provide for the merit of one’s deceased mother is the proper duty of a filial son. My parents gave birth to my body; relying upon their nursing, I grew to adulthood.
This kindness and this virtue are difficult to repay throughout kalpas. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "One who recognizes kindness is the foundation of great compassion;
one who does not recognize kindness is worse than a beast. Now, the girl Guangmu wishes to know where her mother has been reborn.

Regarding his place of birth, it may be said that he recognized his debt of gratitude and recovered his origin, thereby transcending ordinary sentiments. △ Second, the Arhat enters meditative concentration.
Part one: Describing what he saw of his mother while in concentration.

The Arhat took pity on her and entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to observe. He saw that the mother of the girl Guangmu had fallen into the evil realms (*apāya*), undergoing extreme suffering.
Out of compassion for her exceptional filial piety, he entered concentration to observe her mother. [The character "字" (zi) belongs to the end of the preceding phrase. This clarifies [the context].

The eye of wisdom that is able to observe is the subject, while the female mother is the object of observation—the realm of suffering. This is based on the Great Master’s commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding the verse:
"With my Buddha-eye, I behold the sentient beings of the six realms. He analyzes the character "behold" (*jian*) and assigns it to the preceding category.
The Buddha possesses the eye that is able to see; the sentient beings of the six realms possess the five turbidities that are seen.

In that sutra, even for a five-character gāthā, one still analyzes the character "下" (xià) and attaches it to the preceding line; how much more so for this continuous passage—how could one not read it in this way?
Otherwise, if one takes the two characters "觀見" (guānjiàn) as the beginning of the following sentence, it is even more consistent with the union of wisdom and its object.
This is clear. "The ultimate great suffering" refers to the Avīci Great Hell. Question:

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) does not perceive sentient beings as being either entirely extinguished or characterized by identity and difference; it does not apprehend any phenomena.

Because the wisdom-eye cannot deliver sentient beings and is devoid of conceptual discrimination, the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) arises. Now, the wisdom-eye of an Arhat clearly realizes emptiness and quiescence, just as...
"How can one see one's mother suffering? He replied: "The wisdom-eye knows emptiness, meaning it does not cling to objects;
how could it be like one born blind, who sees nothing at all? Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

'The Bodhisattva with the wisdom-eye sees no dharma that is not seen, knows no dharma that is not known, and recognizes no dharma that is not recognized. This is the purity of the wisdom-eye. This clear text serves as authoritative evidence."
How much more so when, through sequential teaching and transformation, there already exists the intention for Bodhisattvas to emerge from their provisional state.

For since Arhats have already eliminated the four abodes (*catur-vāsa*)—the same as those eliminated during the ten practices (*daśa-pratipatti*) of the Separate Teaching—they are naturally able to further sever the "dust and sand" (*reṇu-sikata*) afflictions within the realms.

Thus, Siming stated: "There is also compassion based on the Dharma (*dharmālambana-karuṇā*), which benefits sentient beings in accordance with the world. △ Second, the description of emerging from meditative absorption and posing questions.

Answer: Regarding the first of the two questions on karmic actions, the Arhat asked Guangmu: "What kind of karmic actions did your mother perform while she was alive, that she now dwells in the evil realms and undergoes such extreme suffering?"
The agent and the act of creating: as the Buddha has taught, the defilements of sin and the suffering of the three realms and five destinies do not exist apart from action.
Nothing occurs by chance, nor is it bestowed by a celestial deity; rather, one creates for oneself and reaps the results for oneself. "Formation" (saṃskāra) takes the meaning of flux and transition.
Among the five aggregates, it refers to mental factors that arise due to the delusion of past ignorance. It initiates the three...

Karma: The performance and creation of various phenomena is called "karmic activity. Because karma brings about the manifestation of retribution, one falls into the evil realms and undergoes extreme suffering.
△ Second, the answer concerning what has been practiced, in two parts: first, describing the situation and seeking rescue.
Guangmu replied, "The habits of my mother were such that she took pleasure only in eating the flesh of fish and turtles. Of the fish and turtles she ate, she mostly consumed their offspring;
whether by frying or boiling, she ate them to her heart's content. Calculating the number of those lives, it amounts to ten million and more."
Venerable One, have compassion. How may you pity and rescue me? As for "what is practiced":

it refers to the nature of practice, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and the seeds of evil habits that internally permeate and manifest as active states (*samudācāra*), thereby transforming one's practice into evil.
The following clarifies the performance of karma. The term "only" (*wei*) means "solitary. "Loving" (*hao*) means to cherish and not let go. "Woman" (*nü*).

Your nature is gentle yet stagnant. When you have something you like, you cherish it and cannot let go. Now, the mother of Guangmu alone has a fondness for eating the young of fish and turtles, and her feelings cannot be released from this.
The *Biya* states: "The turtle hears with its eyes; it has a high-backed shell connected to its ribs and belongs to the class of armored insects.
It is also called Shen-shou (Guardian of the Spirit). [When turtles reach three hundred and sixty in number], the dragon leads them in flight."

It emerged from the water (the turtle within did not leave). The *Gujin zhu* names it the "Attendant of the River Lord" (*Hébó cóngshì*). [In] the *Fàngshēng shī* (Poem on Releasing Living Beings) by Táo Xiè'ān of Kuàijī, there is the line: "The Attendant grieves at being confined."
The lines from the *Bōchén* [poem] state, "Suffering from being tossed about. The poem says, "Boiled soft-shelled turtles and fresh fish," referring to minced raw fish (*huài*) among the fresh fish.
"Boiled soft-shelled turtles and minced carp" means that when cooked, there are boiled soft-shelled turtles, and when raw, there is minced carp. Did the mother of Guangmu habitually enjoy these?
This clarifies the taking of life; what follows clarifies the rules for eating. It is simply a fondness for the offspring of fish and turtles, fried...
If one cooks them for food at will, it causes both mother and offspring to perish. Yet while the mother’s life is but one, the lives of her offspring are beyond counting.
From the time they have a home until their death, they take this as a constant practice; such is the number of lives of mothers and children that are thereby killed.
It cannot be calculated; hence it is said to be "ten million times more. This involves seeking out many lives to provide for a single meal.
It is not only a matter of a cruel heart, but also a loss of merit. Su Dongpo said: "With knives [the character is pronounced 'wan,' meaning to carve], one prepares fish and turtles as fine dishes.
Those who eat find them very delicious, while those who die suffer greatly. Zhou Yong said: "Life and death are of such gravity to those beings..."
This is most urgent. That the flavors of the world may be indulged in can wait; these words are all from the pained compassion of benevolent men.
As for "feeling" (*qíng*), it is the spontaneous resonance with external objects that stirs the desires of one's nature. One cannot call human desire "feeling.

When the physical constitution (*qìzhì*) moves recklessly, one flees from Heaven and doubles over one's true feelings. People are constantly constrained and restrained out of fear that they might run wild; were they ever to let themselves loose even once...
It runs wild; it cannot be suppressed or cut off. Thus, Master Fu Daoshi said: "Solitary emotion—its reality transcends names and sounds.
When one investigates the four phases [of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing], they are all non-arising. Where could the thorny thickets grow?
This may be called skillfully curbing deluded emotions while following the true nature. Below this, the Venerable One seeks compassionate rescue, saying: "Since my mother’s karma is profound..."
The offenses are grave; one undergoes such great suffering. I now earnestly entreat the Venerable One’s compassion and pity.
Ultimately, how may you show mercy and deliver us? △ Second, Deliverance through Expedient Means, Part Three: First, Contemplating the Buddha and His Image.

The Arhat took pity on her and devised a skillful means, exhorting Guangmu, saying: "You should recite the name of the Tathāgata Pure Lotus Eye with sincere devotion and also fashion images of him through sculpture or painting;
then both the living and the deceased shall receive their retribution."

To practice the visualization of the Buddha’s image is the method for compassionate salvation. That which the mind maintains is called *zhi* (will/volition); it is composed of the radical for "mind" (*xin*) and the radical for "stopping" (*zhi*).
The image embodies a sense of profound depth and firm determination. True virtue is called *cheng* (sincerity); it is the root of one's nature and life.
Heaven attains it and becomes heaven; Earth attains it and becomes earth; humans attain it and achieve self-perfection. To lack sincerity is to fail oneself.

It destroys and shatters the very root of life, causing the heavens and earth of our being to collapse. From "accomplishing" (*cheng*), one establishes the intent to point directly to the true mind of man.
Yet, when following through with words, they disperse my sincerity; nothing leaks the primordial source (*tianyuan*) more than speech.

To cultivate one's expression and establish sincerity, there must be no lack of reality. That which issues forth in speech and action is all the operation of my sincerity. To bring this to fulfillment—

This is the first merit. To recollect the Tathāgata Pure Lotus Eyes is precisely the means to expel the roots of perverse delusion, uproot the foundation of greed and hatred, cultivate the cause of Buddha-recollection, and realize the fruit of seeing the Buddha.
Therefore, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "After my parinirvāṇa, if one invokes my name, the merit obtained shall be immeasurable and boundless."
Therefore, the instruction is to invoke the name of the Buddha, the Original Teacher. Regarding the creation of images:
molding clay to represent an object is called *sù* (modeling), while applying five colors with a brush is called *huà* (painting). For instance, King Udayana asked the Buddha:
"If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there are sentient beings who create images of the Buddha, what merit shall they obtain? The Buddha told the king: "If there should be someone who..."
The merit of a Buddha image is immeasurable and beyond calculation. In every lifetime one is born into, one shall not fall into the evil realms;
among gods and humans, one will receive blessings and happiness, even attaining the rank of Great Brahmā King with incomparable physical beauty.
Ultimately, all shall be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Life, becoming great Bodhisattvas, most honored and foremost, and shall surely attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha has entered the path of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, I now urge you to practice two matters so that both the living and the deceased may obtain their retribution.

Second, regarding the painting of images and making offerings and prostrations: having heard this, Guangmu immediately relinquished what she loved and promptly painted an image of the Buddha to make offerings to it, further doing so with a heart of reverence.
Weeping with grief, he gazed upon and paid homage to the painted image, making offerings to it—acts easily performed by others. Yet, to renounce what one loves is difficult for anyone to do;

now, having renounced his own affection to pay respectful homage and weep before the image, he relies on the Buddha to save his mother and repays his kin through the Way. Such is the heart of pure filial piety.
It has shone brilliantly through the ages. △ Third, the dream of seeing the Buddha at night, in two parts: first, the filial daughter sees the Buddha and receives his words;
second, the sinful mother is entrusted to be reborn in the house of a maidservant. The first part further has two sections: first, the daughter beholds the sublime marks.
Suddenly, after the night had passed, she saw the Buddha’s body in a dream; it was golden and radiant, like Mount Sumeru, emitting a great light.
Regarding the dream of the Buddha’s body at night, the *Sūtra of the Storehouse of Various Jewels* states: "The Buddha-dharma is vast and wide, its salvation boundless.
If one seeks the Way with a sincere heart, there is no fruit that cannot be obtained; even [the merit of] playful laughter does not go to waste. Therefore, the Filial Daughter abandoned...
He loved the painted image and gazed upon it with tears of sorrowful devotion. The Buddha immediately manifested his body and again emitted radiance.

The person of supreme attainment responds to spiritual resonance and compassionately accords with the capacities of sentient beings; thus, through his physical form and light, he consoled him in his dreams and grief. According to the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, there are four kinds of dreams:

first, dreams resulting from the disharmony of the four great elements (such as seeing mountains collapsing, flying through the air, or being pursued by tigers, wolves, and bandits); second, dreams of prior perception (seeing black or white men and women during the day).

3. Dreams of Celestial Beings (celestial beings manifest auspicious or inauspicious dreams, causing people to encounter good or evil matters). 4. Dreams of Conception (due to the presence of merit, transgressions, or obstacles from previous lives, auspicious or inauspicious dreams appear in the present).
Of these, the first two are unreal, while the latter two are real. The present case refers to the latter two types of dreams. The *Sūtra on the Birth of the Bodhicitta* states:
"If one sees in a dream the form of the Buddha, his body fully adorned with all the marks..."
Those who have given rise to [right] views should rejoice, mindful that he will surely become a Teacher who Tames [beings].
Is it not the case that what Guangmu dreamed of today was a response to such auspicious signs, brought about solely by her supramundane great filial piety moving the Heaven of Ultimate Truth?
As for the golden [mountains] and so forth: the eastern side of Great Sumeru, as well as the seven mountains of the Lesser Sumerus, are composed entirely of pure gold. The Buddha...
Her body shone brilliantly, just like that mountain, emitting even greater radiance; her physical features were increasingly wondrous.
△ Second, the Buddha tells her place of birth.
He said to Guangmu: "Your mother shall soon be born into your family. As soon as she perceives hunger or cold, she will immediately speak."
The Buddha’s body emitted light in a dream to inform his mother of the place of his birth; this was an extraordinary event.
To comfort her regarding the place of his birth, he spoke immediately, secretly indicating his need for rescue. II. The Mother of Sin Entrusts Her Birth to a Maid’s House.
A. Birth and Subsequent Seeking of Rescue.
Subsequently, a maidservant in the household gave birth to a son. Before three days had passed, he spoke; bowing his head and weeping piteously, he addressed Guangmu, saying:
"The karmic conditions of birth and death result in retribution that one must experience for oneself. I am your mother; I have long dwelt in the darkness."
"Since I parted from you, I have repeatedly fallen into the great hells. Only by virtue of your meritorious power have I now attained rebirth as a person of low station;
moreover, my life is short, lasting but thirteen years, after which I shall fall again into the evil realms. What plan do you have to enable me to escape this?"
The text is divided into three sections. The first describes the circumstances of his birth. From "Life and death... onwards, it describes the realm of suffering. From "Having received your...
onwards, it describes the expression of gratitude and the plea for rescue. As for the term "slave-child" (*bīji*), it refers to a son born of a female slave; its Sanskrit name is *Dāsaka*.
This is translated as "slave" (nú). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "When a male enters into sin, he is called a slave; when a female enters into sin, she is called a maidservant.
A maidservant is one of the lowest among women. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "If a child is born who can speak upon hitting the ground, he is therefore named 'King of Sound' (*Śabdavādin*).
Just as people today are terrified if a newborn is able to speak, such a child is called 'Terrifying. Now, when a small child is three days old..."

He immediately prostrated himself and wept as he spoke, for this was yet another manifestation of the extraordinary nature of his circumstances. It was the power of the Buddha that enabled him not to forget his past karmic conditions.
These two lines concerning birth and death are steeped in profound pathos. As the sages of old said: "Birth and death are truly momentous; how could they not be painful?
The causes are the ten non-virtuous actions of karmic conditioning, and the retribution is the abode of the three miserable realms. As the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
The three fruits [of killing] are: first, the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), which refers to the three evil realms;
second, the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*), which refers to being born among humans with much illness and a short lifespan;

and third, the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*), which refers to external objects all having little luster because they do not endure for long. The *Jyotiṣka-sūtra* says: "What is most defiled? Birth and death are most defiled. What falls...
As for the hells: the ten evil deeds lead one to fall into hell; one receives the retribution for what one has done oneself, and there is no one who can receive it on one's behalf.

As the sutra says: "By doing this, one obtains that; all is brought about by one's own actions. There is no one who bestows these things arbitrarily. Since the matter is thus clear, he expresses his general lamentation over it.
Regarding "those who have long dwelt in darkness and obscurity," the *Wǔkǔ zhāngjù jīng* (Sūtra on the Five Chapters of Suffering) says:

"Merely sitting and eating out of stinginess and greed, one falls into the Black Rope City, between the two mountains of Cakravāḍa. Deep and how utterly dark it is! Therein the consciousness falls, seeing not the essence of the sun or moon;
turning and rolling about, they do not see one another, but hear only the sounds of wailing. This is what is meant. As for "separated from others" and so forth:
Furthermore, the Verse on Impermanence says: "Relatives and acquaintances all abandon him; he is led away by the ropes of Yama, King of Death.
According to his karma he receives retribution: through evil karma he falls into hell (niraya), where the suffering of his own actions cuts into his very flesh.
Thus he goes from one great hell to another. From the phrase "Having received your [protection]" onwards, it first describes how he was liberated through the power of merit.

Regarding past offenses, one subsequently seeks rescue and liberation from future suffering through the power of merit. By invoking the name and fashioning an image [of the Buddha], one is released from hell and receives rebirth.

Although heavy karma may result in a light retribution—such as being born into a lowly station with a short life—the remaining karmic residue is not yet exhausted, and one may still fall back into the evil realms.
His Sanskrit name is *Sakula*, which translates here as "Seller by Family"; he was a person of low status. Thus, four such individuals appear.
The Sūtra says: "There may be those born into lowly families or other impoverished and base families who lack food and drink;
even if they obtain food, it is foul and disgusting, difficult to taste. Being born into such families is due to the evil conduct of their body, speech, and mind."
Regarding short-lived beings: the lifespan in the world consists of three grades. In the lower realm it is sixty years; in the middle realm, eighty years;
and in the upper realm, one hundred and twenty years. Now, even the lower lifespan is further diminished; how could this not be considered a short life? As for "life" (*jīvitendriya*):

according to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, at the stage of the *kalala*, there are already three things: first, life; second, warmth; and third, consciousness. The inhalation and exhalation of breath is what is termed [the faculty of life].

Life-force: the seeds of this consciousness are themselves the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). It is provisionally established based upon the mind; life-force is the dependent, and the mind is the basis.
Now, having been born into a lowly station, moreover being short-lived, and further falling into the evil realms—these three fruits are fully assembled.

"How bitter this is! Therefore, one immediately seeks a means to escape it. △ Second, the detailed inquiry into karmic conduct, which has two parts: first, the direct questioning regarding the original offense;
second, the further investigation into the retribution of the hells. The first part has two sub-sections: first, the inquiry as to what kind of karma was committed.
Having heard this teaching, Guangmu knew her mother’s situation beyond doubt; she choked with sobs and wept bitterly, saying to the maidservant’s son:
"Since she was my mother, you ought to know her original transgressions. What karma did she perform that caused her to fall into the evil realms?"
First, regarding the narrative: having heard the aforementioned account, the facts were so true that he knew with certainty this was his mother;
there was no need for further doubt, and thus his voice was choked with sobs as he wailed and wept in grief. Regarding the phrase "since it is already... and below:

once the textual definitions have been explained, since she is indeed my mother, one ought to know the original transgressions she committed. The reason for the repeated interrogation is that [the author] fears...
This is merely an error. △ Second, the answer regarding retribution for killing and reviling:
The servant replied, "I am receiving retribution for the two karmas of killing and reviling.
Had it not been for your grace in rescuing me from this calamity, due to these karmic deeds, I would not yet have attained liberation."

First, I shall directly answer regarding the retribution for one's fundamental karma. It is solely through the two karmas of body and speech—namely, killing and reviling—that such retribution in hell is incurred.
Thus, in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, the daughter Sumanā told her sons: "As for the sin of killing..."

When one enters hell, one undergoes various sufferings and afflictions for many tens of millions of years, constantly being hunted and shot by the *ābāng* hell-wardens who have the heads of deer, rabbits, and various other birds and beasts.
For incalculable ages, though one longs for liberation, [one remains there].
What is the reason for this? Xunzi said: "Kind words spoken to others are warmer than cloth and silk; harmful words spoken to others are deeper [in their injury] than spears and halberds.

How much more so, then, is the case of slander and abuse! Therefore, the *Cheng lun* states: "If a person speaks with evil words and utters various kinds of insults, they will receive retribution corresponding to those words.
Thus, both of these karmic actions result in rebirth in hell. If it were not for the lower realms, conversely, this would clearly manifest as blessings.
To save and liberate: taking life stands at the head of all transgressions, and slander and abuse precede the myriad evils.

Had it not been for my daughter receiving the instructions of an Arhat, invoking his name, fashioning his image, and seeking merit to rescue me from this calamity, what hope would there have been for liberation from the retribution for my two karmas of killing and abuse? △ Second, turning to interrogate the retribution of hell.
Guangmu asked, "What are the circumstances of the retributive punishments in the hells? The servant’s son replied, "The matters of such sinful suffering are unbearable to recount;
even in a hundred thousand years, one could never finish describing them."
First, Guangmu questions; next, the maidservant’s son answers. "Unable to bear" means that the words cannot be uttered from the mouth.
Even if one wished to speak of them, they could not be fully described even in part. "Zu" (卒) means to exhaust; "jing" (竟) means to conclude.

Even if one were to spend hundreds or thousands of years describing the matters of white-robed [monks] committing sins and suffering pain, it would likely be difficult to reach the end. △ Second, the Filial Daughter.

The first part, "Making Vows," has two sections. The first section, "Guangmu hears of her suffering and makes vows for her mother," has two parts. The first part, "Weeping toward the void to recount her mother’s karmic retribution," further has two sub-sections.
The first is the vow to liberate [her mother] from the retribution of the present life.
Having heard this, Guangmu wept and wailed with tears streaming down her face, addressing the empty realm: "May my mother be forever liberated from hell;
until the end of these thirteen years, may she never again commit grave offenses nor pass through the evil realms."

"Shào" (Hào) means to wail loudly. The inner heart is rent with pain, while the exterior is filled with loud lamentation. When one weeps for a long time until the voice is choked, it is called "qì" (nī).
Holding this grief, she addressed the empty realm, saying: "May my deceased mother be forever liberated from hell.
May she exhaust the brevity of these thirteen years of life and dissolve the length of her suffering in the eighteen hells. May she never again traverse the evil paths to receive [retribution]."
The suffering is immeasurable. △ Second, the vow to be liberated from retribution in future births:
"May all Buddhas of the ten directions, out of compassion and pity for me, grant that I may fulfill this vast vow made on behalf of my mother.
If it be granted that my mother shall forever leave the three miserable realms and this lowly station, and never again receive a female body for even an eon."

Regarding the seeking of all Buddhas currently living and residing in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions: first, it reveals the vastness of the aspirational mind;
second, it earnestly manifests the Buddhas’ compassion for those in the three miserable realms and the lowly. As the *Cittabhūmi-parivarta* states:
"There are some who, out of greed for great wealth, regard their own treasures with fear; they constantly seek to accumulate them and never enjoy them."

How much more so for one who is able to give to impoverished sentient beings, yet develops deep attachment to their own wealth and treasures, and desires to diminish the wealth and treasures of others?
By reason of these causes and conditions, after the end of life, they fall into the great hells and undergo immeasurable suffering.
Such a retribution of suffering is called the primary fruit of direct karmic result. Emerging from hell, they receive...
In the bodies of animals, they are constantly subjected to toil and suffering; water and fodder are insufficient.

Having spent a long period of time repaying and exhausting the wealth of others, such sentient beings are called those who experience the second direct retributive fruit. After undergoing these punishments, they are born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Due to the suffering of hunger and thirst, for immeasurable thousands of *kalpas* they do not even hear the names of beverages, water, food, or drink. Their throats...
Like a needle, its belly is as vast as a mountain; even if it obtains food and drink, these immediately transform into fire.
Such a body of suffering is called the third fruit of direct retribution. Once this retribution is exhausted, one will be reborn among humans, poor and lowly.
Being driven by others, one finds it difficult to obtain the wealth and treasures one seeks; at all times, one lacks autonomy.
Such other names as these correspond exactly to the "resemblance fruits" (*nāmānurūpa-phala*). The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers back to the aforementioned matters.
That is to say, once I have attained liberation from the retribution of my mother’s present life and future births, I shall immediately make a vast vow before the Buddha to deliver all living beings.
△ Second, the vow to make my solemn resolve before the Original Buddha.
I vow that from this day forward, before the image of the Tathāgata Viśuddhapadmākṣa, throughout the course of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas hereafter,
for whatever worlds there may be, I shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings suffering from the karmic retribution of sins in the hells and the three evil realms,
causing them to leave behind the hells, the miserable destinies, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and such like retributions for their offenses.
"Once all beings have attained Buddhahood, only then shall I achieve perfect enlightenment.
From this day forward, he marked the beginning of his resolve; for indeed, one cannot reach the destination ten thousand *li* away without first taking the initial step.

The merit of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* cannot be accomplished without the initial resolve. Thus, the old *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If one departs from the initial resolve, then the unsurpassed path will not be achieved;
all merits reside within the initial resolve. Therefore, we know that this sutra clarifies Kṣitigarbha’s generation of the resolve through four successive stages.
Each subsequent stage is the fulfillment of the preceding one, and the present moment is the very beginning; hence it is said: "From..."
Now, before the Buddha image, he is the Lord upon whom all rely. Through hundreds of thousands of millions of *kalpas*, he has traversed every period of time.
There must be worlds that encompass all lands where beings dwell. As for "the hells and so forth," it means that all those in the realms of suffering are delivered.

From the words "In this way" below, it clearly reveals that after delivering all sentient beings without exception, he then attains perfect enlightenment for himself. He repeatedly makes vows, saying: "May [it not be otherwise]..."
It is not always so. Therefore, one knows that the merit of the initial arousal of the bodhicitta cannot be fully extolled even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
△ Second, the Buddha, moved by filial piety, praises the vow and announces his birth. Part One: Validating the Previous Vow.
Having made this vow, she heard the Tathāgata Pure Lotus Eye say to her: "Guangmu, you possess great compassion;
it is well that you have been able to make such a great vow for the sake of your mother."
"Equipped" means complete, sufficient, and fully endowed with having heard his words. "Greatly compassionate and merciful" means universally taking the entire dharma-realm as an object of focus.
"Well able to act as a mother and make vows" praises the wisdom of her resolve; for if she had merely resolved to be a mother, what goodness or capability would there be?
Rather, it is by means of a mind of vast salvation that she seeks to exhaust the karmic offenses of her mother, just as a great flood extinguishes [fire].

A small fire—how could it fail to be extinguished? Therefore, he praises him for being both virtuous and capable. △ Second, the announcement regarding the transformation of future retribution, in two parts:
first, the transformation into a Brahmin in the present; second, the transformation into the fruit of Buddhahood in the future.
These two sections are explained together because the text is divided while the meaning remains continuous.
I observe that when your mother’s thirteenth year has ended and she has cast off this retribution, she will be born as a brahmin with a lifespan of one hundred years.
After this retribution is exhausted, she shall be born in the land of No-Sorrow, where her lifespan will be incalculable kalpas. Thereafter, she will attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
They extensively deliver humans and devas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
They cause them to leave behind low-born families and be born into pure lineages; they transform those of short lifespans into long-lived immortals (*ṛṣi*).

This is the power of this filial daughter’s resolve to sculpt an image of the Buddha while recollecting him. *Brahmin* (*brāhmaṇa*) translates literally as "pure lineage"; it refers to the pure scion of Brahmā.
The descendants inherited and practiced the Dharma of the Brahmā Heaven. Because they claimed to have been born from the mouth of Brahmā, they alone adopted the name "Brahman.
This exists only in the five regions of India and not in other countries; in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, they are called *brāhmaṇas*.

One son sought the Buddha and resolved his mind [on enlightenment], while his mother’s three karmic retributions were all transformed. Initially born into a lowly station, she was transformed from her previous retribution; subsequently, she was born...
O Brahmin, by transforming his present retribution, he will later attain the fruit of Buddhahood;

by transforming his future retribution, he will reach the land of No-Grief—which is precisely the Land of Ultimate Bliss—thus transforming sorrow into joy. Indeed, when he was first born in hell, he took being burned and boiled as his sorrow;

next, when born into a maidservant’s household, he took his lowly status as his sorrow; and upon reaching the age of thirteen, he took the prospect of falling again into the evil realms as his sorrow.
Those born later as brahmins were filled with anxiety due to their pride in their own heterodox practices; now, all such anxieties have ceased, and thus they are born in the Land of No-Anxiety.
The lifespan of the people under that Buddha is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), which is why it is said that their lives span uncountable kalpas.
As for "extensively delivering humans and devas": in the past, she was a sinful mother who was delivered by means of the hells.
This prisoner was to become a Tathāgata—the Great Awakened One capable of transforming gods and humans.
He resolved to fashion an image, a merit beyond compare. Thus, in the *Sarvadharma-uttara-rāja-sūtra*, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"From the very day a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first resolves upon Bodhicitta, they have already surpassed all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
The Bodhisattva is the field of merit for all sentient beings. All sentient beings are born from within the Bodhisattva and are those transformed by the Bodhisattva;
therefore, the multitude of those transformed by him is as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. △ Second, the conclusion correlating the ancient and the present.
The Buddha told King Sovereign of Samādhi: "At that time, the Arhat named Puḍuo Guangmu was none other than the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati.
The mother of Guangmu was none other than the Bodhisattva Vimukti. The daughter Guangmu was none other than the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha."

In the past they achieved the minor fruits; now they become great beings. This is the turning from the small toward the great. As for "Inexhaustible Intent," it is explained in detail in the *Separate Commentary* (*Biexingshu*).
Now, according to the *Record* (*Ji*), they receive the name "inexhaustible" because both their vows and practices are inexhaustible, and because they are all non-active (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
They are all the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), for they contain all Buddha-dharmas. Regarding the "liberated Bodhisattvas": in the past...
She fell into an iron city and underwent every kind of hardship. Next, she was born into the household of a maidservant and again met with a short life.
Later, she became a Brahmin, but ultimately fell into heterodox currents. Now, through successive stages, she has become a practitioner of inconceivable great liberation;

the fruit of Buddhahood may be expected for her. Thus, Guangmu attained the state of an Arhat through the instruction of another, while the mother of the girl ascended to a higher realm because of Guangmu.
Now, as my Buddha’s transformative influence nears its end and he is about to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, both the subject and the object have reached their completion;

mother and child have come together. Though separated by sands of kalpas, they remain present in this single assembly. "Beating the drum and playing the lute, we return once more as one family"—is this not what that means?
Part Two: Showing the Benefits of the Present. Section One: Concluding the Reference to the Great Vow.
This section appears to conclude the preceding passage; however, its placement as the opening of the subsequent section serves to summarize his great vow and point it out directly.
This is precisely the foundation for future sentient beings who have committed evil to take refuge, make offerings, and be liberated from suffering.
The subtlety of this structural arrangement—acting as the "needle and thread" of the composition—is something later scholars must not fail to recognize.
In the distant past, across kalpas as long ago as the sands of the Ganges, he thus cultivated compassion and made vows as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to extensively deliver sentient beings.
From the initial arousal of the mind until the final entrustment, the number of kalpas is so vast and remote that it is beyond calculation.

These phrases on "compassion" briefly summarize the four preceding sections and broadly point to his vows throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. (The *Miaoxuan* quotes the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.)
It is said: If someone asks, "What is the root of all virtues? one should reply, "It is loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

If this loving-kindness is not endowed with the Buddha’s ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), it is the loving-kindness of the *śrāvakas*.
If it is fully endowed with these, it is the loving-kindness of the Tathāgata; it is the great mass of Dharma, it is Great Nirvāṇa. The power of loving-kindness is vast and profound.
He is fully endowed with the adornments of all merit and virtue. Now, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, with a mind of Great Nirvāṇa, cultivates the noble practices and attains the stage of fearlessness.
He possesses the twenty-five royal samādhis and manifests great, unimpeded functions; this is true brahma-conduct.
Thus, the moment he speaks of compassion, his merits and virtues are complete. △ Second, the praise and exhortation to take refuge and pay homage (in two parts).

Regarding those who initially commit evil but turn to take refuge and pay homage to escape their retribution: in future ages, if there are men or women who do not practice goodness but instead commit evil—
even those who do not believe in cause and effect, who engage in sexual misconduct or false speech, who use double-tongued or harsh words, or who slander the Mahāyāna— just as...

These sentient beings with such karma will inevitably fall into the evil realms. However, if they encounter a virtuous friend who exhorts them to take refuge in the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha for even the duration of a finger-snap, these sentient beings will immediately attain liberation from the retribution of the three evil paths.

The first section of the text enumerates the assembly of the wicked. If one encounters the lower [states], taking refuge transforms the retribution. The two dharmas of good and evil are generated within the mind;
they are compared to water and fire, which follow different paths in their manifestation. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One should cultivate wholesome karma and abandon unwholesome conduct.
Wholesome merit pursues a person like a shadow follows a form; it cannot be separated from them. Such is the nature of transgression and merit."
It is all like this. Do not harbor doubts, lest you fall into the evil realms yourself. Virtue and transgression are distinct;
believe them with clarity and do not be deluded. Wherever one may be, the Buddha’s words are most sincere; they never deceive people.
Those who do not believe in cause and effect are icchantikas, such as the brahmin Pāyāsi, who constantly harbored heterodox views, claiming that there is no other world and no further rebirth.
He claimed that there is no retribution for good or evil deeds. He constantly told people: "The śramaṇas hold divergent views.
They say that those who commit killing up to holding wrong views will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, all enter hell;

whereas those who refrain from killing up to refraining from wrong views will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, all be reborn in the heavens. I have never yet seen anyone who has died return to speak of what they experienced."
Because one falls into such states, I do not believe in future lives or the retribution for good and evil deeds.

This is likely because they fail to understand the distinctions within karmic retribution, and thus they propagate talk that denies cause and effect. As for the phrase "and so forth," evil matters are manifold and cannot be summarized by merely one or two;
however, because the gravity of their offenses is not widely recognized, these are specifically singled out. "Sexual misconduct" refers to the third of the three physical unwholesome paths of action.
It is not that violating external forms is considered "deviant"; rather, it is simply that the moment a thought arises, one becomes licentious and loses rectitude.
This is truly because worldly people do not realize that their entire bodies are impure, yet they falsely cling to the seductive and beautiful.

Thus, they deviate from the Way of Brahma, obstruct the karma for Bodhi, and become causes for the four modes of birth, resulting in the fruits of the three miserable realms. Because the moisture of such karma is particularly heavy, the Sage established this precept at the very beginning.
Lying (*mṛṣāvāda*) means that which is false and unreal. According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, lying distresses others and causes one to lose the merit of truth;
it is always like darkness, and though one has life, it is as if dead. The sword of speech cuts one's own tongue, being more terrible than blazing fire or venomous snakes.
At the end of life, one falls into hell, with pus and blood issuing from the mouth. Slander (*paiśunya*) means speaking two different things from a single mouth.
Speech. It seems as though one possesses two tongues. A sutra says: "Excessive delight in much talk increases greed and causes others to fear;

verbal transgressions include self-aggrandizement and boastfulness, with double-tongued speech being the foremost. As for harsh speech (*pāruṣya*): it refers to using coarse and evil words to revile others and so forth.

The *Dharmapada* says: "Though one may be a śramaṇa, if one does not restrain body and speech, using coarse words and evil speech to cause much injury and harm, one will not be loved by the multitude nor cherished by the wise.
When the body dies and the spirit departs, one revolves through the three miserable realms;
dying and being born again, one undergoes immeasurable suffering and affliction, which neither the Buddhas nor the noble sages cherish. Even if one’s body [is otherwise]..."
[Answer: It is so. By failing to guard one’s verbal karma, one likewise falls into the evil realms. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: There was once a ghost whose head resembled that of a pig;
foul-smelling insects issued from its mouth, yet its body possessed a golden radiance. This ghost had been a bhikṣu in a previous life.
Because he maintained pure precepts in his physical conduct, he possessed this radiance; however, because his mouth uttered evil words, foul odors emerged.

Worms emerge from the mouth. Thus, the *Ekottarika-āgama* says: "It would be better to cut one's own tongue with a sharp sword than to utter evil words or coarse speech that causes one to fall into the three evil realms.
To slander the Mahāyāna—whether in the past or the future—such karmic actions of sentient beings are, in summary, the failure to practice virtue and so forth;
they will inevitably lead to rebirth in the evil destinies. This concludes the section on the locus of sin. If one encounters..."
"Good spiritual friend. "Departing for clear liberation. The word "if" (*ruò*) is an indefinite term;
it means that if there is even a hair’s breadth of goodness within evil, one might perhaps encounter such a person, but otherwise they are difficult to meet. The *Wénjù* states:

"Some say that 'knowing' is merely consciousness (*shí*), while others say that hearing the name is 'knowing' and seeing the form is 'consciousness'. Now, this teaching [instructs us] to take refuge in Kṣitigarbha in the mere blink of an eye.
The Bodhisattva is a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), for by him one immediately attains liberation from the retributions of the three evil realms.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, twenty moments (*tatkṣaṇa*) constitute one instant (*nimeṣa*); twenty instants are called one finger-snap (*acchaṭā*).

According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, in the time it takes a strong man to snap his fingers, sixty-four *kṣaṇas* elapse. Yet, by merely taking refuge [in the Bodhisattva] for the duration of a single finger-snap, one’s evil...
The liberation attained through a thousand lifetimes of practice on the Path is due to the power of taking refuge, which is beyond measure; therefore, I exhort you to do so.
△ Second, receiving blessings by serving with a sincere mind.
If one can reverently take refuge with a sincere heart, gaze upon [the image], pay homage, and offer praise;

or if one serves by offering incense, flowers, robes, various precious jewels, or even food and drink—such a person shall, throughout future hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, constantly dwell among the devas and enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss.
When their celestial merit is exhausted and they descend to be born in the human realm, they shall still serve as emperors for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
One is able to recollect the origins and details of past lives and their causes and conditions.

First, the offering is clarified; the initial phrase provides a general indication of the "resolute mind" and so forth, as in the text. Regarding incense and flowers, they are explained according to the teachings of the Secret Division (Guhyatantra).
Incense is the Samādhi of Delighting and Gladdening; by making offerings with this, one immediately attains the unimpeded wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Flowers are the Samādhi of Jewel Adornment; by making offerings with these, one swiftly attains the forty-eight wondrous marks of the Tathāgata.

In the Sanskrit language, *vastra* means "clothing. Here it is translated as "clothes" (*yi*). "Clothing" (*yi*) implies that which one relies upon; its purpose is to provide shelter from cold and heat and to conceal what is unseemly.
Because there are various kinds of precious jewels, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of "immeasurable seven-jeweled [robes]. Regarding food and drink:
*bhojana-pāna*—in the language of Tang, this means "the five types of solid food," namely rice, cakes, parched grain flour, and so forth. These are called "proper meals" (*bhojana*). From here...
From the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m. until the hour of the Horse (11 a.m.–noon), one may eat as one pleases; after midday, one must not eat.

"Half" refers to *khādaniya*, which here means the five types of chewed food—namely, roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits. These are called improper foods (*asama-bhojana*). This means that after the fast has been observed, one does not eat fruits or vegetables.
Such is the phrase for "rendering service," which concludes the preceding discussion on offerings and establishes them definitively. Not yet... [text ends].
They descend to manifest their karmic rewards (*puṇyavipāka*). This specifically clarifies being born in the heavens to receive blessings.

If they descend from heaven, it reveals that there remains further merit, as in the *Śatapañcāśatkathā* (The Sūtra of One Hundred Causes), regarding the causal conditions for the Chinese man who offered flowers to the Buddha: at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Furthermore, when the bhikṣu Candanagandha was born, sandalwood fragrance issued from all the pores of his body, and the scent of an utpala lotus issued from his mouth.
This was because he had made offerings of sandalwood incense to the stūpa of Vipaśyin Buddha. One whose virtue matches that of heaven and earth is called an Emperor (Di);
one born of benevolence and righteousness is called a King (Wang). This is like the Five Emperors and Three Kings of this land. He also recalled his past lives and so forth.
One attains the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*). As stated in the *Āmaṇḍa Sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"With a mind that is concentrated, pure and stainless, supple and disciplined, one is able to recollect and recognize numerous and manifold matters of past lives.

One can remember from a single life up to countless lives—the cycles of kalpas of formation and destruction, dying here and being born there, as well as names, surnames, lineages, and the food and drink [of those lives]."
He clearly remembers and recognizes all things—his likes and dislikes, the length of his lifespans, the suffering and joy he has experienced, and his physical forms and appearances.
Thus, although he descended from the heavens to become an emperor, he clearly recalls events from hundreds of thousands of kalpas past.
He understands that his initial cause for being born in the heavens was his reverent worship of Kṣitigarbha, and this constitutes the very root of his original birth in the celestial realm.
Even up to the present time, as the final period of your reign, there is nothing that I do not recall or understand with complete clarity.
It is like a person who travels from their own village to another kingdom or town, where they walk, stay, speak, or remain silent;

Regarding all the lands where consciousness travels—from here to there, and from there to here—whether walking, staying, speaking, or remaining silent, one remembers them all.
Is this not the inconceivable power of Kṣitigarbha’s majestic spiritual authority? The explanation of the benefits is concluded.

Such are the phrases that bind and enable one to cross over. There are also phrases that manifest what is applied.

We, the many hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, shall certainly, by relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, extensively expound this sutra throughout Jambudvīpa to benefit sentient beings."

However, because the people of the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa) are of unsettled disposition and character, and their evil karma is particularly prevalent, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others must focus their efforts specifically upon Jambudvīpa.
