Therefore, the Heavenly King of the North, who governs the three directions, rose from his seat, reverently received the essential teachings of the Dharma, and with a heart filled with yearning and admiration, joined his palms in respectful salutation. △ Second, the Heavenly Kings recount their doubts.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, since the distant kalpas of the past, the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha has made such great vows;
why is it that even until now his deliverance of beings continues without ceasing? He has further made this vast and great vow.”
Having heard these four rounds of great vows, he stepped upon his previous doubts and questioned [the Buddha], essentially saying:

"Since the Great Being has, throughout kalpas as long ago as that, made such great vows, he ought naturally to have completed the deliverance of all sentient beings by now; yet, they are not yet exhausted."
As for the reason for raising this question again: is it because the power of his vows has not yet reached its full extent? Or is it because sentient beings are so difficult to save?
Thus he asks, "How is this? △ Third, he requests the Buddha to explain.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will speak for us;
for when he speaks for us, there is a relevant matter. While we are currently protecting the four directions, Jambudvīpa is particularly replete with evil karma.
Although those [beings] harbor the intention to rescue them as Great Beings, we likewise embrace the duty of protection and maintenance.
This is a loss for the world; therefore, we pray that you will explain it, so as to deliver us from this city of doubt and to comfort sentient beings regarding the future.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s subsequent answer and explanation, in three parts: first, praise and permission.

The Buddha addressed the Four Heavenly Kings: "Excellent, excellent! For the sake of bringing extensive benefit to you and the multitudes of devas and humans of the future and present, I shall now speak of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha within Jambudvīpa in the Sahā world."
Within the path of birth and death, there are skillful means for compassionately rescuing and delivering all sentient beings who suffer from transgressions.
The double praise of the Heavenly Kings consists of one who skillfully poses questions and one who skillfully protects the world.
To speak of "Sahā" includes the great trichiliocosm; to mention "Jambudvīpa" specifically refers to the southern continent. Within this path of birth and death...
This is because all six realms of existence possess birth, old age, sickness, and death. Now, "birth" encompasses "old age," and "death" includes "sickness";

thus, by mentioning the beginning and the end, the middle stages are abbreviated. Rising and sinking alternate, suffering and joy intersect, and the cycle of birth and death revolves without ever ceasing.
Therefore, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, through his unconditional great compassion, provides rescue and deliverance.
Regarding "sentient beings suffering from the retribution of their sins," the Buddha said:
"All sentient beings are constantly within a long prison, surrounded by twelve concentric walls and enclosed by three layers of thorny hedges. Six bandits with drawn swords lie in wait there.

To be able to escape from within it is most difficult, most difficult. The "long prison" refers to the triple world (*triloka*). The "twelve concentric walls" refers to the twelve [links of dependent origination].

As for the causal conditions: the threefold thorny fence refers to the three poisons. Now, Kṣitigarbha, through these sentient beings, employs skillful means to deliver them, causing them to realize the emptiness of the triple world and refrain from practicing within the three realms of existence; thus they are delivered from the triple world.

By knowing the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination, one can transcend the root of ignorance and emerge from the city of twelve layers. [One must likewise] know lust, anger, and delusion.
When the three impurities are no longer entangling and the mind no longer clings, one has uprooted the triple thorny fence.

When one clearly understands that the six sense-faculties have neither beginning nor end, one leaves behind the six sword-wielding thieves. These are all the matters of the Great Being’s skillful means, his work of delivering and liberating beings.
△ Second, the aspiration to hear.
The Four Heavenly Kings said, “Indeed, World-Honored One, we wish and delight to hear it.
Bodhisattva Vimukticandra of the *Avataṃsaka* said: “They gaze at one another with mutual reverence; with single-minded devotion, they all look up toward him.
Like bees longing for fine honey, or like those parched with thirst yearning for nectar, so it is now. Therefore, they say, ‘We wish and delight to hear it.’”
△ III. The Formal Announcement, Part Two: First, a brief indication of the resolve to fulfill the vow once more.

The Buddha addressed the Four Heavenly Kings: "Since the distant kalpas of the past until the present day, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva has been delivering sentient beings, yet his vow remains unfulfilled.
Out of compassion for the suffering beings of sin in this world, he further contemplates the immeasurable kalpas of the future."
In the midst [of this], because the continuity of the vines was not severed, for this reason, he again made a solemn vow.
First, he recounted his previous compassionate vows; next, he demonstrated his renewed intention, beginning with "Out of compassion for this world... and so forth. The *Ānanda-vibhaṅga-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha’s grace is not small, yet sin arises from sentient beings. Because the world is turbid and full of evil people, it returns upon itself..."
Falling into perversion, one creates the root of manifold transgressions; when life ends, one goes to the Avīci Hell.

There, swords and blades dismember the body, molten copper is poured into the mouth, and one encounters myriad calamities and hardships with agonizing pain beyond description. If one is reborn as a human again...

Because they are among those who are lowly, base, and impoverished, the Great Being compassionately delivers and liberates them. Furthermore, he contemplates the future and so forth, as the Sūtra says:
"To harm life and truncate a living being's existence—no sin is greater than this. Hostilities will be requited one against another without end."
In this present life there is no peace; one frequently encounters calamities and misfortunes. Upon death, one enters hell.

Escaping from that human form, one shall fall among the animals, where one is slaughtered and disemboweled by humans for their meat, with no end in sight. Life after life, they become enemies, repaying one another for past deeds.

Though their spirits are the same, their forms differ; such is the depth of their transgression. Since these matters arise from karmic conditions and evolve through mutual causation, it is like [the following analogy]: [The text continues with a detailed analogy comparing the cycle of rebirth to a series of causes and effects.]
It is like the *gelei* (pronounced lěi) vine clinging to the *jiǎo* (pronounced jiū) tree; it winds and entangles without ceasing. "Màn" refers to the genus of the *ge* vine.
Just as the *ge* vine spreads and extends, the *Zuǒzhuan* says: "Do not allow it to grow into a thicket; once it has become a thicket, it is difficult to manage.
Now, the accumulation of karma binds the body, just like the *ge* vine spreading through the valley; one sees only its leaves flourishing lushly—how could there be any severing?
This is because afflictions nourish karma; karma moistens birth; birth again creates karma; and karma leads once more to suffering.
For this reason, the Great Being Kṣitigarbha again exerts himself and makes an exceedingly profound vow, just as the poem says:
"The *gé* (knotweed) spreads across the valley and grows luxuriantly. II. Extensively explaining the preaching of the Dharma according to individual capacities. 2.
First, the explanation of the Great Being’s deliverance and the exhortation for the Heavenly Kings to provide protection; this section has two parts, the first of which further has two sub-sections.
First, a general demonstration of skillful means: Thus, within the Sahā world, in Jambudvīpa, the Bodhisattva employs hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of skillful means.

For the sake of teaching and transforming others, the light of transformation should have pervaded the entire Sahā world; yet, though his compassionate vows were proclaimed far and wide, they instead flowed only toward Jambudvīpa.
As the *Miaoxuan* says: "The three karmas of a Bodhisattva are nothing other than benefiting sentient beings; yet here it speaks only of manifesting the body and preaching the Dharma."

It is not called "intention" (*manas*) because it employs those two types of karma without erring regarding the capacities of sentient beings; this is precisely the skillful means (*upāya*) of intention.

Now, by means of skillful means, both the wheels of body and intention are encompassed, manifesting supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to observe their capacities. The following phrase refers specifically to the wheel of speech (*vāk-cakra*) preaching the Dharma.

"Hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis" indicates that the mental aspirations and karmic functions differ, and thus the skillful means employed for transformation are each distinct. As it is said:

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 17, states: "Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas manifest immeasurable transformation bodies to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, yet the mind of the Bodhisattva remains free from discrimination.
It is like the lute of the asuras, which constantly produces sound that accords with one's wishes;
there is no one who tires of it. There is neither a distracted mind nor a concentrated mind, for it is born of the retribution of merit; thus, it follows the person."
Sound issues forth from the mind. It is the same for the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas: they have no conceptual discrimination, no distracted mind, and no marks of preaching the Dharma.
Because of their immeasurable merit, meditative concentration, and wisdom, various sounds of the Dharma issue forth according to their will.
Thus, the *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra-stotra* says: "They manifest various bodies and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. They are fully endowed [with these qualities].
This refers to one who possesses the merit of giving and has compassion for all sentient beings. △ Second, the specific explanation of preaching the Dharma, in two parts:
first, the actual explanation of teaching and transforming according to capacities; second, the summary showing the distinctions in karmic retribution.

This is because those who can preach the Dharma differ in their use of gentle or harsh speech, while those who receive the instruction differ in their realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) or the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). By reason of this...
Question: Since these karmic retributions of suffering are not virtuous matters, why not simply speak of the wholesome and cause [beings] to practice it?
Why is it necessary to describe them according to their nature as "suffering" and "karma"? Answer: The laws of cause and effect regarding good and evil must be presented in contrast to one another.
If one does not explain that greed and so forth are faults, by what means could generosity be revealed?
If these virtues were not proclaimed, the suffering of the three miserable realms could not be revealed, nor could the happiness of humans and devas be made known;
therefore, it is necessary to teach the transgressions of ordinary beings so that they may recognize them, cultivate weary detachment, and return to the wholesome.

When those of dull faculties hear of these karmic sufferings and develop weary detachment, they immediately seek worldly happiness; consequently, their minds are transformed as they cultivate various meritorious deeds.
If those of sharp faculties, upon hearing of this suffering and karma, give rise to revulsion and detachment, they immediately seek liberation;

because they can thereby transform their minds and cultivate the contemplation of the path, they are able to give rise to the cause for emergence from within the afflictions. Therefore, the Sūtra says that all afflictions are the seeds of the Buddha.
Thus, one knows that suffering and karma are the basis for revulsion and detachment, and the conditions for giving rise to the wholesome.
Therefore, it must be explained; for if this were not explained, sentient beings would fail to recognize these evil karmas as transgressions and would continue to practice them without interruption.

Although one may describe their various faults and evils according to the facts, from the perspective that there is no separate karma or suffering external to the mind, the ignorant do not yet understand this.

Thus, it is necessary to definitively declare their offenses. Consequently, relying on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one teaches them with words of harsh reprimand. This is the first [section].
The Four Heavenly Kings: If Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva encounters one who has committed killing, he explains the retribution of past calamities and a short life span.

If he encounters one who has committed theft, he explains the retribution of poverty and bitter suffering. If he encounters one who has committed sexual misconduct, he explains the retribution of being reborn as a sparrow, a pigeon, or a mandarin duck.

First, the retributions for the ten non-virtuous actions are set forth. Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are the three physical evils. Because the transgression of killing is most grave, it is mentioned first.
For every person cherishes their own life, and every creature craves its own existence; all sentient beings, down to the smallest insect, possess Buddha-nature.
To kill and eat them is to kill all Buddhas, and one will constantly remain in the three miserable realms, undergoing immeasurable suffering. Even if one should later obtain a human birth...
Their faculties are incomplete and their lifespans are diminished. As in the *Ghosts’ Questions to Maudgalyāyana*:
"I have given birth to sons and daughters, yet they all die young. Thinking of them brings me to a breaking point; by what sin has this been caused? He replied:

"When you were a human being, you saw children killing living beings, and you assisted them with joy, eating the flesh together. Because of the killing, your life was short; because of the joy, you suffer such bitter agony. [The text ends with] "stealthily."

Regarding "thieves," Xunzi says: "To steal goods is called being a thief. Wealth, money, jade, and silk are what one relies upon externally; banners, flowers, and the property of the Sangha are internal offerings.

Stealing from the external can be expiated through repentance, but stealing from the internal is difficult to save. One will constantly dwell in the three miserable realms, undergoing immeasurable suffering.
Even if one should obtain human form, one will be poor, destitute, and afflicted; the devas will abandon them, leaving them with no external support.
O Protector. Because one lacks internal merit and virtue, one encounters poverty and suffering. The *Dīpaṅkara-sūtra* states: "One should know that poverty is comparable to hell;
to live in poverty is no different from death. Its bitter afflictions and hardships have no peer in this world.
The sūtra contains several thousand words extensively lamenting the sufferings of poverty. ○ Regarding sexual misconduct, as before, the Sanskrit name is...
*Mayūra*. This is translated here as "peacock. By nature it is jealous and envious, and it prizes its own tail feathers.

It does not necessarily require a mate, yet it also mates with snakes; it is among the most lustful of creatures. Its Sanskrit name is *kapota*, which in the language of Tang means "pigeon. Pigeons take the greatest pleasure in mating.
While all other birds have the male mount the female, this bird has the female mount the male; therefore, the peacock has offspring throughout the four seasons, whereas the pigeon... [follows].
The moon has a son named *Cakravāka* in Sanskrit, which in this language is translated as "mandarin duck.
They are a pair of birds that remain coupled when at rest and fly together as a duo; male and female never part from one another. If a person captures one, the other dies of longing for it.

Therefore it is said: "The magpie loves the external; the mandarin duck loves internal reflection. According to popular tradition, the male is called the *yuān* (mandarin duck) and the female is called the *yāng*.
If born among humans, one receives two kinds of retribution: engaging in litigation with close relatives and being subjected to royal law.

If one encounters those who speak with harsh words, one should explain the retribution of strife among one's kinsmen. If one encounters those who slander, one should explain the retribution of a tongueless mouth and sores.

This demonstrates the four types of retribution for the mouth: harsh speech constitutes one, while slander subsumes the other three, because at the time of slandering, one possesses [the other three].

Regarding the phrase "and so forth": when one is subsequently reborn among humans, there are two remaining retributions; namely, constantly hearing evil sounds and perpetually being involved in disputes.
Thus, the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "When a person is born into this world, calamity issues from the mouth.
One should guard the mouth more carefully than a fierce fire. While a fierce fire blazes, it burns only worldly wealth; yet the blazing of evil speech [burns much more]."
It burns away the seven noble riches. For all sentient beings, calamity issues from the mouth; this refers precisely to the axe that destroys the body and the disaster that extinguishes one’s life.
Regarding "slander": it means to insult and defame. The *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states:
"Those who slander the Dharma commit an extremely grave offense; they fall into the three evil realms, from which it is difficult to escape."
Because of slandering others, one will undergo great suffering and affliction for seventy kalpas;
how much more so for that foolish person who, possessing no true knowledge at all, is conceited and even slanders a single four-line verse?
Such a person is certain to fall into hell and never again see a Buddha, receiving the retribution of being blind and tongueless. Therefore, one must not fail to be cautious.

If one encounters those who are prone to anger, one speaks of the retribution of ugliness and physical deformity; if one encounters those who are stingy, one speaks of the retribution of having one's requests thwarted and wishes unfulfilled;
if one encounters those who lack moderation in food and drink, one speaks of the retribution of hunger, thirst, and throat ailments.
This indicates the distinction between the three types of retribution for the intention. Regarding the arising of good and evil, a sutra states:

"If a person in this world constantly delights in anger and fails to distinguish between good and evil, upon death they will enter Mount Tai (the Hell of Great Mountains) for many tens of millions of years.
When reborn as a human, their countenance will always be hideous. Those we see today with an ugly appearance all owe this to the anger of their past lives. Regarding the stingy and miserly:
The preceding sutra says: When a person acquires property and wealth, they are stingy and greedy, refusing to practice giving. They do not look upon their households with affection;
they do not provide for the poor, nor do they serve śramaṇas or practitioners of the Way.
They give nothing to beggars or the sick. They dare not eat to their fill, nor dare they wear complete clothing. People call such a person a "slave who guards wealth," and they constantly bear shame.
Shame! Upon death, one falls among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). Seeing water and running toward it to drink, it instantly transforms into molten copper, pus, and blood.

Even when reborn as a human, one is poor and famished, unable to satisfy one's hunger. Those who are currently poor beggars are all the result of the seeds of stinginess, greed, and delusion from past lives.
Food and drink are indeed indispensable to human life; however, there must always be moderation in their consumption.
The *Sūtra on the Nine Untimely Deaths* states that failing to measure one's food leads to such a death; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* likewise maintains that eating in excess results in untimely death.

Therefore, one must exercise moderation (lack of restraint is delusion). Xunzi says: "Those who are indolent and avoid labor, lacking integrity and shame while being addicted to food and drink, may be called wicked youths.
The *Wǔkǔ zhāngjù* states: "To eat without moderation and to crave the taste of wine [are faults]."

This is your heavy burden. Those who do not cast off this burden will later enter hell. Based on this, it follows that hunger, thirst, and throat ailments are merely the "flower-retribution" (the preliminary manifestation).
Regarding the character for "throat" (*yānhòu*): the character *yān* (咽) is pronounced with the *yin* (因) and *jiān* (堅) initials.

The two apertures of the throat and the esophagus emerge from the same tube (the stomach organ), yet they function differently. The throat is positioned in front and governs exhalation; it serves as the essential passage for the inhalation and exhalation of breath.

The throat (*yan*) is located behind; it is the gateway for the transport of food and drink. The "throat" in the term for "throat disease" (*yanbing*) is pronounced with the *qie* of *xie* (meaning "to block").

It refers to the disease of *ei-ge* (dysphagia). This is because the transformation of the *qi* in the three *jiao* (triple burner) does not proceed, causing the *qi* to become obstructed and flow upward within the chest and diaphragm, making it difficult for food and drink to enter the throat.
The *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "Just as in the case of the disease of a blocked throat, one is immediately able to..."
Taking life is truly a precursor to becoming a hungry ghost (*preta*).

If one encounters those who indulge in hunting for their own pleasure, they will receive the retribution of being terrified, driven mad, and losing their lives. If one encounters those who are rebellious and unfilial toward their parents, [they will likewise suffer such consequences].
He speaks of the retribution of calamity and slaughter from Heaven and Earth; if one encounters those who burn mountain forests and trees, he speaks of the retribution of madness and seeking death.
If one encounters parents who are malicious and poisonous before or after birth, he speaks of the retribution of being whipped and beaten in return while manifest in this life.
If one encounters those who net and capture fledglings, he speaks of the retribution of having one's own flesh and bones torn apart.
Next, the retribution for miscellaneous karmas is explained. Hunting began with the Lord Fuxi;

because there were many beasts in the world, he taught the people to hunt, driving out birds and animals to clear the fields of harm. Thus, the spring *sou*, summer *miao*, autumn *xian*, and winter *shou* were all termed hunting.
Today, however, it is practiced solely for profit and the gratification of the senses and body, killing and harming at will; therefore, one falls into the three [evil realms].

[The karmic retribution for] smearing [poison] is to be born among humans and suffer the fate of madness and loss of life, such as falling into a river, tumbling into a ditch, being trampled by horses, or injured by carts.

(Formerly, there was a wealthy elder who had an only son. Seven days after his marriage, while gathering flowers with his wife, he fell from a tree and died. His mother was Lady Pei; she gave birth to Junping in her youth and thereafter conceived no more. Her parents loved him as their own eyes. When he reached the age of twenty, they would not allow him to live elsewhere.

Consequently, his father sent him out of the house, but his mother took pity on him and had a secret affair with him. Later, when the father returned home, he and his mother killed him and buried his corpse in the rear garden. Heaven sent down a thunderbolt, which struck the father’s corpse and caused it to emerge.

Subsequently, the thunderbolt struck Junping’s own body, manifesting the full details of the causal connection. Neighbors reported this to the authorities, and the matter reached the imperial ear. An edict was issued to execute Lady Pei, and she was not permitted to be buried. This was because she had committed incest with her son, murdered her husband, and thus acted against principle and violated human ethics—a pig or dog among men who had offended the sovereign. Therefore...
To manifest this outwardly). ○ To burn mountain forests and trees causes great injury to living beings. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states:
"If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, sets fire to mountain forests or vast wildernesses, they must not intentionally burn any living creatures."

However, all worldly people harbor cruel and poisonous intentions in their hearts; they burn mountains and wilds, or perhaps release fires driven by the wind, thereby harming and distressing all beings.
For this reason, they receive the retribution of becoming deranged and dying in madness. (Formerly, Du Sima of Quzhou was initially a magistrate of Luoyang.

At Wuchao Bridge south of the city, there was a civilian house that had been burned down, killing several people. Suddenly, a man arrived at the county gate staggering; he ran out and then back in again. Du seized him and questioned him. He confessed, saying: "I am the one who killed the residents of Wuchao Bridge. Five of us formed a band to commit robbery... )

He possessed several hundred thousand pieces of wealth, which he set on fire and burned. At that time, wishing to escape, his feet could not move forward. He went out in the morning and traveled south, but a fire blocked his way; consequently, he fled north, yet another fire scorched his heart and drove him toward the county gate.

Knowing he could not escape, Du arrested all the members of the bandit gang and sent them to the prefecture to be executed). According to the *Sanfadu lun* (Treatise on the Three Dharma-measures), the "Crying Hell" (*Rudana-naraka*) is the place of retribution for those who burn vast wildernesses or smoke-out creatures living in burrows. ○ "Previous and subsequent parents" refers to a stepfather.
Mothers, because their children are not born of them, may treat them with malice and poison, as was the case with the stepmothers of Great Shun and Min Dun.

Some even go so far as to inflict flogging and beatings, suffering the consequences in this very life. Do not say that the workings of destiny are indifferent or that the cycle of rebirth turns like a wheel, such that retribution will only be meted out in a future existence.
Even within this present life, one may lose control and cause death, thereby incurring public punishment for the sin committed.

In court, some parents, driven by extreme emotion, instead resort to whipping and beating [their children]. How can such matters be settled? People today do not understand this principle and indulge their passions in flogging and beating;
I fear that the retribution in this present life will not fail to arrive. ○ Regarding "netting and capturing fledglings": a fledgling (*chú*) is the offspring of a bird.
A bird that is newly born and capable of pecking for itself is called a fledgling. Whether caught in a net or seized by hand, all such acts invite calamity.

This is the retribution for separating flesh from its source. Although the bodies of humans and birds differ, the affection between mother and child is the same. (In Xin Gan there was a man named Yang who made his living by trapping birds with nets.

One day, a small sparrow perched upon a tree; Yang set up a sticky pole and climbed onto a branch. The branch snapped and he fell, his head impaled on the pole, piercing his brain so that blood flowed profusely until he died).
Therefore, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna equally prohibit such acts.

If one encounters those who slander the Triple Gem, it is said that they will receive the retribution of being blind, deaf, and mute. If one encounters those who treat the Dharma lightly and are arrogant toward the teachings, it is said that they will receive the retribution of dwelling forever in the evil realms.
If one encounters those who misappropriate or waste the property of the Sangha, it is said that they will receive the retribution of wandering in hell for billions of kalpas.
If one encounters those who defile the pure life or falsely accuse the monks, it is said that they will receive the retribution of remaining forever among the animals.
This clarifies the retribution within the Three Jewels: the Buddha is like a king of physicians, the Dharma is like excellent medicine, and the Sangha is like a nurse attending to the patient.
Those who now slander them lack faith. The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* states:
"If there are Kṣatriyas who are outcasts (caṇḍāla) and give rise to evil thoughts toward the Three Jewels, no Buddhas can save them; they will constantly fall into the hells."
They fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Even if they obtain human birth, they will be blind, deaf, mute, or speech-impaired.
Alas! Being blind, they shall never behold the marks of the Triple Gem. Being deaf, they shall never hear the names of the Triple Gem.

Being mute and speech-impaired, they shall never be able to praise the virtues of the Triple Gem. Though they live, they are as if dead; they are as obscured as the long night. Therefore, a sutra says: "It would be better to swallow..."
Yet, one must not slander the Triple Gem. Regarding those who treat the Dharma lightly and are arrogant toward the teachings, the *Dṛḍhamati-sūtra* records that the Buddha told Ānanda:

"I am now in meditative concentration. I feel compassion for the people of the world who do not understand that the Buddha-way is truly profound and vast, yet who, with shallow, false, and frivolous words, wish to speak out of a jealous heart, slandering the roots of the Way or destroying the Dharma."
Those who disparage śramaṇas and upāsakas, and who speak with harsh words and falsehoods, should be understood as being dragged away by their own transgressions.
Thus, the *Sūtra of the Superior Son of Heaven* states: "If there is a Dharma master who circulates this sūtra, this very place is where the Tathāgata walks.
Toward that Dharma master, one should give rise to the thought of him as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and a heart of reverence. As it says:

With a mind like that of the Buddha, even if I were to remain in the world for an eon, or slightly less than an eon, I could not exhaustively describe the merits of a Dharma teacher who propagates this sutra.
Now that people thus slight the Dharma and treat the teachings with contempt, who will provide protection?

They shall dwell forever within the three evil realms, undergoing thousands of millions of billions of sufferings and afflictions. To obtain a human body again would be like a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log.
[Regarding] the embezzlement and misuse of permanent property, as before. [Regarding] defiling the *brahmacarya*, as before. [Regarding] slandering the Sangha.

If one slanders another bhikṣu with a groundless charge of a pārājika offense—just as Kokālika slandered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana—one will consequently develop malignant sores on the body and fall into the Great Lotus Hell.
There, one’s great tongue will be driven with five hundred nails and plowed by five hundred plows; thus one shall remain forever among the animals, no different from being in hell.
This is the residual retribution of a ghost.
If one encounters those who inflict harm upon living beings through boiling water, fire, or execution by sword, one explains the retribution of successive repayments within the cycle of saṃsāra.

If one encounters those who violate the precepts or break the fast, one explains the retribution of being reborn as a hungry bird or beast. If one encounters those who use things unrighteously or wastefully, one explains the retribution of having all one's requests frustrated and cut off.
As for the retribution: if one encounters those who are conceited and arrogant, they shall receive the retribution of being born lowly and base;

if one encounters those who are double-tongued and divisive, they shall receive the retribution of being tongueless or having a hundred tongues; if one encounters those with wrong views, they shall receive the retribution of taking birth in a borderland.
This clarifies the retribution for mixed karma. Being boiled in cauldrons, burned in fire, and subjected to hacking and chopping are the methods of killing.

They are scalded with boiling water to remove their fur, their bodies are roasted with fire, or their heads are severed, or their feet are hacked off. As the Sūtra says: "Because humans eat sheep, when the sheep dies it becomes a human;
thus they devour one another in a cycle that has no end. Therefore, it is said that they revolve through saṃsāra, repaying each other in turn. ○ Regarding those who break the precepts:
If one breaks the disciplinary code (*vinaya*), gross offenses are easy to perceive, whereas subtle evils resemble the marks of one who maintains the precepts and are difficult to know.
In the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*, the Buddha told Kāśyapa: "There are four kinds of bhikṣus who break the precepts yet appear as if they maintain them.

First, there is a bhikṣu who is able to practice all the rules within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* in their entirety, yet he asserts the existence of a self (*ātman*). Second, there is one who recites and upholds the sūtras..."
1. Regarding the Vinaya: though they guard their conduct of the precepts, they do not move away from nor abandon the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi).
2. There are those who practice the twelve dhūta ascetic virtues, yet they perceive all phenomena as truly existent. 3. There are those who direct a mind of loving-kindness toward sentient beings;

upon hearing that all conditioned formations are characterized by non-arising, their minds become terrified. This is called breaking the precepts while appearing to uphold them, and violating the fasts, just as [described] by the Buddha.
I replied to Śāriputra: "One who eats at an improper time is a person who has broken the precepts; they are a person who commits theft.
The same applies to the one who gives it. Such a person is not my disciple; they are called a person who steals food through unrighteousness.

Both the thief who gives and the thief who receives—even for a fragment of salt or a drop of vinegar—shall die and fall into the Hell of the Scorched Entrails. There, they shall swallow glowing iron balls. Upon emerging from that hell, they shall be reborn as pigs."
Among dogs, they eat various impurities; furthermore, they are born as evil birds whose cries people find strange. Even among hungry ghosts, they eat excrement; among humans, they are poor and lowly.
According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, they receive the body of a *caṭaka* bird (likely the Sanskrit term for a turtledove;
await further investigation). They drink only the rain from heaven, receiving it by tilting their mouths upward, and may not drink any other water; therefore, they are constantly distressed.
This refers to hunger and thirst. ○ To destroy or misuse [an object] contrary to reason: "use" here refers to utensils and implements.

These may be destroyed by one's own temperament, or damaged toward others through an evil mind. This is because such utensils are essential to human life: farmers have plows and hoes; craftsmen have axes and chisels.

In the home there are utensils for daily use; on the road there are umbrellas and travel gear; in boats and carriages there are oars, paddles, yokes, and axles (the upper character *e* refers to the shaft;

the lower character *yue* refers to the curved wood at the front of the carriage that holds the crossbar). Now, suddenly and without cause, you destroy these; you will naturally experience the retribution of having your needs and requirements cut off.

(Formerly, there was a man surnamed Shen at the head of the Great Granary Sands. Whenever a neighbor had fishing nets, traps, carts, or plows, he would inevitably borrow them and secretly damage them. One day, his son’s wife returned to her parents’ home for a visit...)

Before they had traveled one *li*, a sudden and violent thunderstorm broke out. A dragon entered their home, sweeping everything away with a great upheaval until nothing remained; the entire family, both old and young, perished. Regarding the term "wú-wǒ gònggāo" (self-conceit): "Wú" refers to one's own person.

"Gòng" (pronounced with the departing tone) means to offer up. To present goods from a subordinate to a superior is called an "offering" (*gòng*). In this context, it refers to the act of offering oneself up as a tribute.
One must certainly hold it aloft and offer it. Now, those who grasp at themselves as great elevate themselves and disparage others, just like the manner of offering an object;
this is the very root of birth and death. Thus, the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"Among all views, only the view of self can immediately sever the life-force of wisdom. The *Wǔkǔ zhāngjù* says: "Prideful regarding one's own lineage, arrogance..."
To be haughty and arrogant, to rely on one’s own wisdom to despise the foolish, and to treat others with contempt—these are your heavy burdens.

One who does not cast off these burdens will later enter hell. Therefore, when emerging from hell, if one should happen to become a human being, one will certainly be born into a lowly household of servants or the base.
As Xun Qing said: "Arrogance and insolence are the calamities of man. This is proven by this very case.
...so it is. As for those who engage in double-tongued speech and incite strife: they take the crooked to be straight and the straight to be crooked;

they report what was said to this person to that person, and what was said to that person to this person. They instigate disputes over right and wrong and destroy the fundamental social order. The *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra* states: "There are immeasurable kinds of litigation, conflict, and contention;
they deceive and insult one another, using coarse and malicious words to cause estrangement, practicing slander, treachery, and deceitful confusion. While alive..."
Through divisive speech that incites strife, one will in future lives personally experience the retribution of being tongueless or having a hundred tongues.
Regarding wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): everything that arises in contradiction to reason is a wrong view. To specify them individually now is because this view is the most evil.

Because they are able to sever the roots of goodness, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* clarifies two types [of wrong views]: first, destroying worldly happiness by asserting that there is no merit or demerit, nor sages or worthies;
second, destroying the path to nirvāṇa by being greedily attached to a self and discriminating between existence and non-existence.

Both are termed "wrong views" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and thus result in further retribution, causing one to be born in a frontier region. As the *Wǔkǔ zhāngjù* states: "In borderlands, there is no righteous principle."

Father and son bite one another (the character *xiè* here means laughter; it also has the pronunciation *dié*, meaning to gnaw). Within your households, you sell one another to others to become slaves, constantly subjected to being driven and commanded.
Whether moving or at rest, you are met with the infliction of canes and whips. Though you possess human form, you share the same companions as beasts.
Therefore, practitioners of the Mahāyāna still fear taking birth in the borderlands. Yet, [the text] first raises the matter of killing.
This is because it is the root of all evils, the ultimate culmination of false views, and a vast abyss for the flowing stream of karma. II.
Concluding Summary on the Differentiations of Karmic Retribution:
Such sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, through the fruits of their habitual evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, undergo hundreds of thousands of retributions.

Now, this has been explained in brief. In such ways, according to the differences in the karmic retributions of sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva employs hundreds of thousands of skillful means to transform and teach them.

The first phrase generally indicates those who commit evil through the actions of body, speech, and mind; this clarifies the cause of karma. The phrase regarding "evil habits" clarifies the fruit of habituation.

The phrase regarding "hundreds of thousands of retributions" clarifies the fruit of maturation. As for "body, speech, and so forth," when ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) create karma, there are many varieties:
some cases where the mind accords with body and speech, and some cases where body and speech contradict the mind. In all movements...
Body and speech are both driven by the mind; therefore, the three karmas all have the mind as their root.
Regarding the fruition of evil habits, according to the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, there are three types: first, the fruit of retribution, such as being born in the hells and other realms;
second, the fruit of habitual tendencies, such as being born among humans where, based on killing, there is the fruit of short life, and so on, up to [the fruits] based on wrong views.

Therefore, when delusion increases (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The monk Gomukha came from among oxen; he looked at himself in a mirror. The courtesan came from among women; Maudgalyāyana leaped about in sport. [The monkey] came from among monkeys," and so forth).

3. The Dominant Fruit (*adhipati-phala*). Based on those ten types of unwholesome paths of action, all external objects lack power and majesty, resulting in hundreds of thousands of such retributions.
According to the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, when sentient beings create karma, there are...

There are four kinds of retribution: first, retribution in the present life (karma performed in this life is experienced immediately in this life); second, retribution in the next life (karma created in this life is experienced in the body immediately following);

third, retribution in subsequent lives (karma created in this life is experienced only after two or three lifetimes or more); fourth, non-retribution (such as neutral karma). There are further four types of non-retribution.

1. Determination of time, but indeterminacy of retribution (*kāla-niyata-vipāka-aniyata*). This is determined and unalterable across three periods [of existence], yet because karma can be transformed, the retribution is indeterminate. 2. Determination of retribution, but indeterminacy of time (*vipāka-niyata-kāla-aniyata*).

Because the power of karma is fixed, the retribution cannot be altered; however, because the timing can be shifted, it is indeterminate as to when it occurs. 3. Determination of both time and retribution (*ubhaya-niyata*). Because the karma is fixed, the timing is likewise fixed.

4. Neither Time nor Retribution is Fixed (because the karma is not determined, both time and retribution are not fixed). Furthermore, regarding nirvāṇa, it clarifies the remaining retributions of afflictions and so forth;
such hundreds of thousands of retributive responses are here described only in brief. Thus, below, the distinctions are formally concluded.

Depending on the karma performed by sentient beings, there are cases where [the conditions] are complete or incomplete. If one first forms the intention and subsequently performs the act, it is called "karma as performance" (*kṛta-karman*).
It is complete. If one acts directly without prior intention, it is called incomplete action.
Furthermore, there is that which is incomplete action, meaning that after the deed has been performed, the retribution is not certain. There is also that which is both completed and complete.
The time and the circumstances are both fixed. Since the karmic retributions of sentient beings differ, the Bodhisattva’s edification likewise employs hundreds of thousands of skillful means.
As stated in the *Daśacakra-sūtra*, the Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhaśuddhāśaya: "O son of good family..."
Since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed; long ago he was already able to cross the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

Yet, by virtue of his original vows, he manifests transformations throughout the ten directions, and his transformative benefits are particularly abundant in this world of five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
This is due to the conditioning of the power of his original vows, as well as the karma of sentient beings who are ready to receive his transformation. Thus, from the tenth...
For one kalpa, he has adorned this world and brought sentient beings to maturity;
therefore, within this assembly, his physical form is dignified and majestic, and his spiritual power is preeminent—none can surpass him except for the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, regarding the emanated activities he performs, none can equal them except for the great bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra and Avalokiteśvara. For this reason, [he is] a bodhisattva...
By the power of his original vows, he swiftly fulfills all the requests of sentient beings,
can extinguish all their grave transgressions, and removes all obstacles so that they obtain peace and security in the present life.

He is also called the "Skillful Comforter," for he is adept at expounding the profound Dharma and is able to skillfully guide beginners who have resolved to seek the Mahāyāna, ensuring they do not become timid or weak.
By means of such causes and conditions, sentient beings receive transformation and attain deliverance; the teaching through hundreds of thousands of skillful means is just like this.
△ Second, exhorting the Heavenly Kings to provide protection.
These sentient beings will first undergo such retributions as these, and subsequently fall into the hells, where they will remain for kalpas without any prospect of release.
Therefore, you who protect people and protect the nation must not allow these various karmic actions to delude sentient beings.
First, the intention of what is to be protected is shown. Why is it urged that the Heavenly Kings provide protection?
It is because sentient beings first receive the aforementioned flowers of retribution (*puṣpa-vipāka*), and subsequently fall into hell due to receiving the fruits of retribution (*phala-vipāka*).
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "There are those who do not understand such karmic conditions; throughout immeasurable lifetimes, they wander through birth and death. Although...
They are born in the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception with a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas; yet when their merit is exhausted, they fall back into the three evil realms.
Thus, they may remain there for as long as a thousand kalpas without any prospect of escape, as recorded in the *Jiuzapiyu jing* (Sutra of Old Miscellaneous Parables).
Formerly, there were six men who traveled together and committed crimes; they all fell into hell. When the Buddha saw them, he smiled. Maudgalyāyana asked why he was smiling, and the Buddha said:

Six people fell into hell and were together in a single cauldron. Each wished to recount their original transgressions, but as the boiling hot water surged and bubbled, they were each pushed downward after uttering but a single word.
The first said, "Sha" (Sā). "In the world, sixty billion years constitute but a single day in Niraya;
when will it ever end? The second said, "Na" (Nā). "There is no time for escape; one knows not when it shall be attained."

"Tuō" (脫). The third word: "Tè" (特). It means: "Alas! Alas! I intended to manage my livelihood, yet I could not restrain myself; my mind was stolen away by the five families, and I failed to provide for the Three Honored Ones.
Now that I am foolishly poor and lack everything, what benefit is there in regret? The fourth word: "Shè" (涉). It means: "I managed my livelihood, yet I did not practice with sincerity;
my property belongs to others, and because of this, I have come to suffer. The fifth word: "Gū" (姑). It means: [The text here appears to be fragmentary or incomplete].
"Who will guarantee that I shall emerge from hell, so that I may no longer violate the prohibitions of the Way and attain the bliss of rebirth in heaven? Thus it was said.
As for "Dhara," this matter was originally not considered by the mind. It is like a charioteer who loses the road;
the axle breaks and the chariot is destroyed, yet regret comes too late (text). Therefore, one wanders through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, with no time of emergence from hell.

Therefore, below, the two characters "zhèngquàn" (正勸, *zhèngquàn*) serve as a transition to formally exhort [the practitioner], demonstrating the intent of the exhortation to protect. Regarding the phrase "protecting persons and so forth," according to the *Guānmíng shū* (Commentary on the *Guānmíng jīng*), this is explained through the contemplation of the mind (*guānxīn*).

Concerning the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings (*lokapāla-deva-rāja*), it is said: the East is Accumulation (*jì*), the South is Suffering (*kǔ*), the West is the Path (*dào*), and the North is Cessation (*miè*).
These are the four truths (*catvāri satyāni*). The wisdom that contemplates these four truths constitutes the Four Kings; protecting the realm of the four truths is what is termed [their function].

To protect the kingdom is to protect the mental factors (*caitta*), which is to protect sentient beings. "The world" refers to others. To explain the mental factors for the sake of others is called protecting others.

If sentient beings do not illuminate the principle of the Four Noble Truths, the two delusions of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi- and kleśa-saṃyojana*) will assail the mind-king (*cittarāja*), destroying its realm.
When the mind-king perishes, the kingdom of the realm collapses, and the subjects—the mental factors—scatter in all directions; thus, both the realm and the wisdom are ruined.

When one is afflicted by ghosts and spirits, one can contemplate suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*). By restraining views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the state becomes peaceful and the people tranquil.
Being able to explain the Four Truths (*catur-āryasatya*) to others is to protect other lands; it obstructs their views and afflictions, causing them to dwell in peace and happiness.

This is what is meant by the Four Heavenly Kings (*catur-mahārāja*) protecting the world through the contemplation of the mind. If one does not act in this way, how could one cause sentient beings to [attain] this?
"Is karma not delusive? Aṅgulimāla replied, "To protect the true Dharma is what is meant by 'protecting the world.
△ Upon hearing this, the three heavenly kings withdrew in sorrow.
Having heard this, the Four Heavenly Kings wept and lamented with grief; they joined their palms and withdrew.

This was because, upon hearing the signs of the distinctions in the retribution of superior karma, it resonated deeply within their hearts, whereby they realized that the fundamental nature is empty and quiescent.
Hearing is itself non-hearing; this is called "hearing with the mind. Thus it is said, "having heard. Alas, sentient beings fail to understand this and falsely engage in conceptualization.
Because of deluded attachment, there are tears and weeping. There is no time across the three periods; there is no realm within the ten directions.
The six realms remain unknowing, and every movement spans kalpas. Thus, one sighs in sorrow. Thereupon, the self-mind unifies with the One, ceasing all deluded fluctuations.

Retreating into the secret treasury, one waits in stillness for the Dharma-sound. Therefore, one joins the palms and withdraws. Thus, one knows that by means of power and the Dharma, one may [attain] oneself...
The Protectors of Beings. These are known as the Four Heavenly Kings who Guard the World (*Lokapāla*).

Part Three: Showing the Differences in Karmic Retribution. First, the Title of the Chapter:
Chapter Five, The Names of the Hells.
△ Section Two: The Text of the Two Chapters. Part One: Samantabhadra’s Request for the Teaching.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, saying:
"O Benevolent One, for the sake of the fourfold assembly of devas and nāgas, as well as all sentient beings of the future and present, please explain [the nature of] the Sahā world and Jambudvīpa."

To cause sentient beings of the future age during the final dharma to know these retributions— the places where those who commit offenses and suffer the pains receive their retribution, the names of the hells, and matters such as the evil karmic results.
Next, following the discussion on the conditions of karma and the retribution of karma, he asks about the specific characteristics of the karmic retributions of the hells;
therefore, it says, "At that time. His Sanskrit name is *Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa*, or *Samantabhadra*, which is translated here as "Puxian" (Universal Worthy).
According to the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Beihua jing), he was the fifth prince of King Araṇemin in a past age, named [Avalokiteśvara].
He is fearless because his practice surpasses that of all other bodhisattvas; therefore, the Buddha Ratnagarbha changed his name to Samantabhadra. The text states:
"At the summit of the path of subduing, its cause is all-pervasive, hence it is called 'Universal' (Samanta). Following the path of severance, he is adjacent to the ultimate sage."
It is said: "The Worthy" (*xian*). Guang’s *Shu* states: "The stages of the True and the Semblance follow one another stage by stage; there is no stage where they are not present.

For example, when Samantabhadra has perfected the practices of Samantabhadra, his rank is adjacent to the ultimate supremacy. This 'semblance' is thus high. The *Ji* states: "That which has been realized is called 'True';

that which has not yet been realized is called 'Semblance. Since Samantabhadra at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is viewed in relation to the ultimate [Buddhahood], he is termed 'semblance,' and thus the name 'Worthy' is established for this chapter."

Regarding the arousal [of the bodhicitta]: it is by means of Samantabhadra that one’s practice pervades the entire Dharma-realm, thereby enabling compassionate vows to be universally and extensively propagated.
This is because Samantabhadra represents the Tathāgatagarbha which is the object of faith, and further symbolizes the Dharmakāya manifested as free from entanglements.

It is precisely to cause all sentient beings to realize that the environment and inhabitants of the Avīci hell are entirely situated within the most supreme state—the Vairocana body and land of one’s own mind—without ever transcending it.
Even a single thought of an ordinary person can realize the original source and perfect supreme wisdom. When supreme wisdom reflects back upon itself, it is no different from the initial resolve.
Now, the virtues and ranks of these two Great Beings are nearly equal, and their wisdom and conduct are likewise matched. How could they not know the name and the reality of hell?
It is simply because Kṣitigarbha has manifested emanations within the netherworld to teach and transform those in the hells, making his vow before the assembly.

How could anyone not believe and accept this? Therefore, I have specifically raised this question. "Benevolent One" (*ren*) is a title of supreme honor. Benevolence is the comprehensive embodiment of the virtues of the heart.

Since the great virtue of Heaven and Earth is said to be "generation," human beings, containing this principle of generation within them, naturally possess a feeling of compassion and loving-kindness, sharing the springtime with all things.
Thus, the meaning of the character is derived from "human" (*ren*) and "two" (*er*). The "two" represents the heavens above.
In the lower realms, if a person can overcome their own self, they will become one with Heaven and Earth in a state of total integration, vast and open like the Great Duke.
With the Buddhas manifesting in heaven and sentient beings manifesting on earth, the human mind mediates between them; it directly causes the living and the Buddha to be of one essence.
Therefore, it is said that those who possess benevolence aspire to become devas, nāgas, and so forth;
yet because they hear [the Dharma] without distinction between male and female, they all equally undergo the retribution for their sinful karma, and thus it is called "Avīci" (the Uninterrupted).

Furthermore, having heard that all sentient beings have not yet attained liberation, he prayed and entreated Kṣitigarbha to preach for their sake. These sentient beings suffering from the retribution of their sins are indeed able to receive [his teachings].
Regarding the places where retribution is received: generally, these refer to the six realms; specifically, they pertain only to the hells.

There are briefly nine types of environments experienced at the time of receiving such retributions for evil deeds and the like. For instance, if one hears the Dharma and uses double-tongued speech to sow discord among others...
Those who fall into the state of a dog with drooping ears will not find pleasure in hearing the Dharma; they fall among long-eared donkeys and eat alone out of stinginess and greed;
they fall among hungry ghosts and, when born as humans, are poor and famished, providing foul food for others; they fall among pigs, swine, and dung beetles for plundering the property of others;
they fall among sheep, where humans flay their skin and eat their flesh; and those who delight in stealing the property of others [fall likewise].
They fall among oxen and horses; when born as humans, they become lowly servants.

They delight in speaking falsehoods and spreading evil of others, thereby falling into hell, where molten copper is poured into their mouths and their tongues are pulled out and plowed with an ox-yoke. Delighting in drinking wine until intoxicated, they fall into the Niraya of Boiling Excrement;
upon emerging, they become orangutans, or if born as humans, they are stubborn and foolish, subjected to lashes from above with no one to whom they can appeal. Thus they fall into hell.
To explain in detail those who emerge as water buffaloes, with their noses pierced and burdened by heavy loads to repay their karmic retribution, there are indeed immeasurable instances.
This is intended for future generations to clarify the true meaning of hell: that sentient beings undergo suffering solely because they do not understand the law of karmic retribution.
Now, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), non-existence, signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) constitute the essential wisdom of the Path; these cannot be [fully grasped] through mere effort.

Newly initiated practitioners say that upon hearing that nothing exists, they become despondent in mind and no longer cultivate the precepts, claiming that since all things are empty, what is there to be done?

Now, when a spiritual friend wishes to instruct a new practitioner, they speak gradually of the works of Māra, causing them to guard against the causes and conditions for Māra, and making the sufferings of birth and death and the distinctions of the five realms of existence clear. They cause them to believe in sin and merit, so that every matter is understood with clarity.
Only then can one speak of the Way; thus, it is intended merely to let future sentient beings know of karmic retribution. △ Second, Kṣitigarbha’s Response, in three parts:
First, humbly accepting the request to speak.
Kṣitigarbha replied: "O Benevolent One, I now rely upon the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and the strength of this Great Being to briefly explain the earth..."
Regarding the names of the hells and the matters of karmic retribution and evil consequences:

it is certainly appropriate to say that one relies upon the supreme Sage, the Teacher, by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*). But as for what is meant by "the power of the Great Being" (*mahāsattva*):
Samantabhadra is the legitimate son of the Buddha, his honor being peerless. Because the power of his conduct and vows is profound, he [is able to]—by means of the Great...
The term "Shi" (士) is a respectful designation. The *Zhuangzi* says: "One who comprehends antiquity and the present, and can discern right from wrong, is called a Shi.
"Shi" means "action" (事). It is composed of "ten" (十), symbolizing the multiplicity of affairs; everything within the universe is a matter that falls within one's own vocational duty.

It is composed of "one" (一), signifying that all is unified by this One. Thus Confucius said: "To extend the One and harmonize it with the Ten is to be a Shi. The myriad practices of Samantabhadra are likewise so.

From one to ten, and so on up to from a thousand to ten thousand; by comprehending the single nature of these myriad practices, one delivers sentient beings within a single mind and is able to establish matters of the utmost magnitude;
therefore, they are called "Great Beings" (*mahāsattva*). The term "briefly explained" is a word of humility.
△ Second, the response explaining the retribution of the hells has two parts: first, answering regarding the names of the hells; second, answering regarding the offenses.
The first part of the report on evil deeds is divided into two sections. First, a general indication of the location of the hells:
"O virtuous one, to the east of Jambudvīpa there is a mountain called Cakravāḍa. That mountain is dark and profound, where the light of the sun and moon does not reach."
The *Dīrgha Āgama*, Sūtra 19, the *Lokadhātu-vibhaṅga-sūtra*, Chapter on the Hells. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"These four continents are surrounded on their exterior by eight thousand continents. Furthermore, a great ocean of water completely encircles these eight thousand continents.
Beyond the great ocean of water, there is a Great Diamond Mountain (*vajra-parvata*) which encircles it. Outside of this Diamond Mountain, there is furthermore..."
The second is the Great Vajra Mountain. Between these two mountains, it is profound and pitch-black;
even the sun, moon, and divine deities of great power cannot illuminate those eight great hells with their light. Therefore, they are called "dark and deep."
"Profound" (*sui*) means deep and remote. "Black and profound" refers to the ultimate limit of darkness. Thus, the *Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra* states:
"The World-Honored One has spoken of a great hell named 'Darkness' (*andhakāra*). It exists at the outer edge of each respective world-system; it is entirely without covering.
Within this place, sentient beings cannot see even their own raised hands or eyes. Although... [the text continues].
The light of the sun, the moon, and all those possessing great majestic power does not illuminate that city.
Only when Buddhas appear in the world does a great radiance shine everywhere; by means of this light, they are able to see one another.

They dwell in the worlds between two mountains, on the outer edge of the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), which is called "Outside the Realm" (Wén). Because it lies to the east of Jambudvīpa, it is said that there is a mountain in the eastern direction.
...and so forth. △ Second, the specific enumeration of the names of the hells, in two parts: First, the primary principal hells.
There is a great hell named Ultimate Uninterrupted (Ānantarya). Furthermore, there is a hell named Great Avīci.
Regarding the two great hells of Avīci and Anantarya: whether they are combined or separate has been difficult to determine since antiquity.
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama* and the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi Sūtra*, they are combined into a single hell. That sūtra itself asks and answers: "What is named the Avīci Hell?
This is translated here as the "Hell of No Interval" (Anantarya). In this sūtra and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, they are treated as two distinct hells. The sūtra says: "Nine..."
With one thought-moment of emotion, they descend into the wheel of fire; their bodies enter the wind-fire, passing through the ground where the two intersect.

Those with slight emotion are born in the *Avīci* (Abyan) hell, while those with heavy emotion are born in the *Avīci* (Wujian) hell. When emotion is pure, they sink directly into the *Avīci* (Abi) hell.

This scripture exists in different translations by various masters, which causes the separation or merging of these two hells to differ. I privately say it is like, for example, two surnames living together in one [house].
The two hells share one gate for entry and exit, each having its own retinue. To an outsider observing them, there is no lack of both similarity and difference.
Since they emerge from the same gate, what prevents us from saying they are "one"? Since they belong to two different clans, what prevents us from saying they are "two"?

Because the two hells are situated in the same location and the punishments endured therein are roughly the same, the designations "one" or "two" are not fixed. *A* means "non-existent," and *ni* means "obstructing. Or...
Regarding the terms "rescue" (*jù*) and "no-rescue" (*wújiù*), they are combined to form the name "Unobstructed" (*wúzhē*).

According to the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, it is taught that the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) are the most extreme evils. Furthermore, there are four kinds of great sins equal to these four heinous crimes;
those who commit such fundamental offenses (and so forth) will, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, all fall into the Avīci Hell. Thus the Buddha told Saṃgharakṣita:
There are nine kinds of persons who dwell perpetually within the Great Avīci Hell: first, those who consume the property of the Sangha;

second, those who consume the property of the Buddha; third, those who kill their father; fourth, those who kill their mother; fifth, those who kill an Arhat; sixth, those who cause a schism in the harmonious Sangha;

seventh, those who violate the pure precepts of a bhikṣu; eighth, those who violate a bhikṣuṇī of pure conduct; ninth, those who become icchantikas. These nine kinds of persons remain forever therein.
Regarding the hells, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that the suffering of the Avīci Hell exceeds that of the ten great hells by a thousandfold, and its lifespan lasts for one kalpa.
Furthermore, the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra* says: "The Avīci Hell is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
it has seven layers of iron walls and seven tiers of iron nets, with forests of knives and forests of swords, each [situated] separately."
There are seven layers, each containing eighteen hells such as the Cold Ice Hell. These—the Flying Blades and so forth at the four corners below—are all retinues of the Avīci Hell.
Thus, after the *Lokasthāna-abhidharma* has finished explaining the eight further hells, it proceeds to explain the ninth section:
the "Chapter on the Outer Encircling Hells. The Hot Ashes, Excrement, and Filth hells are all situated therein.
In the middle [section], the subsequent text establishes the headings based on the retinues; this is a definitive conclusion established for all time, which later scholars must know.

The repetition of the phrase "there is furthermore" indicates that these are all subsidiary hells of the Great Avīci Hell. Their varieties are extremely numerous;

therefore, they are indicated by two characters [to represent the category]. Regarding the four corners, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "There are those who, though not actually śramaṇas..."
Gate. One who calls himself a śramaṇa, upon hearing the sounds of women singing, dancing, laughing, playing, or the tinkling of their ornaments, fails to examine them wisely;

his mind becomes stained with lust, he emits impurity, and at the dissolution of the body after death, he falls into the Saṃghāta Great Hell, specifically the Iron Dust Fire location (the sixteenth location of the Saṃghāta Hell), namely the Hot Iron Quadrangular Hell, which surrounds...
An iron wall five hundred *yojanas* high rains fire and iron from above, causing all parts of the body to be scattered into powder;
they are constantly boiled and constantly burned. According to the *Lokasthāna-abhidharma*, the Black Rope (*Kālasūtra*) Hell is entirely made of iron and burns day and night.
Within it, the sinners are seized by the hell-wardens, who throw them down to lie upon the ground, following the black [ropes].
Bound by ropes, they are hacked with broad axes (the character *fēi* [pronounced *fān*] refers to a wide-bladed axe). Their bodies may be made into eight-sided, six-sided, or four-edged shapes.
Furthermore, from the neck down to the feet, they are severed into fine pieces like the joints of sugarcane.

This is because in their previous lives among humans, they committed acts of killing others, severing and hacking off hands, feet, noses, and ears, or cutting the flesh from their backs and so forth; it is for these reasons that they undergo rebirth therein. ○ Flying.
"Knife" refers to the Knife-Wheel (Kṣuramārga) Hell. The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisāgara-sūtra*, fascicle five, states:
"As for the Knife-Wheel Hell, there are mountains of knives on all four sides; among these mountains, knives are piled up like bricks.

In the void above, there are eight hundred trillion extremely large knife-wheels that descend in succession like falling raindrops. This is what is referred to as the "Sword" (Khaḍga) in the *Lokasthāna-śāstra*.
Rains of axes and other weapons fall; wherever they strike, their bodies are severed and their heads separated, scattered in disarray like wood chips being split.

Having previously lived among humans, they engaged in warfare, provided others with swords and staves to incite combat, gathered large crowds, and slaughtered at will. Due to these roots of karma, they are born there.

○ Regarding the "Rocket Hell" (*huo-jian*): According to the *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha*, this corresponds to the Iron-Mechanism Hell (*tie-ji di-yu*) of five hundred billion realms.

Therein is an iron bed, four hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth, exactly equal in all dimensions. Upon it are placed various rows of needles (*ji*), and between each needle there are ten billion iron crossbows.
The tips of these iron crossbows are whirled, possessing ten billion sharp blades. When a sinner enters this iron mechanism, [the crossbows strike him].
Above, ten trillion iron shackles are suspended from below; as they move, the iron shackles rise and fall.
Simultaneously, immeasurable iron crossbows are drawn, and each one shoots an iron arrow into the heart of the sinner. In a single day and night, they undergo six hundred billion births and deaths.

The *Lishi* (Establishment of the World) states: "Sentient beings in this world who are deluded, out of greed and desire, fail to be filial toward their parents, fail to respect their teachers and elders, do not follow wholesome teachings, kill sentient beings, and feed various wicked people; for these reasons, they undergo this retribution.
Regarding the *Jiashan* (Mount Jiashan), the *Sanfadu* (Threefold Dharma Measure) states: "As for the Saṃghāta Hell, it is where sentient beings with transgressions [suffer]."
Terrified by the hell-wardens, who number in the hundreds of thousands, they flee into the mountains. Once inside, fires spontaneously arise before and behind them, blocking their path.
Two mountains close together like a grinding mill; blood flows like a river, and their flesh and bones are completely consumed.
Among these beings, those who take pleasure in grinding others are foremost. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "The two mountains are solid whips, with iron flames and fire."

However, the two sides assume their positions and come together simultaneously, crushing the denizens of hell. Having crushed them, they grind them until their bodies are completely dispersed and nothing remains to be seen.
After being thus ground, they are reborn once more; then the two mountains crush and grind them again as before.
In this manner, they are repeatedly crushed and ground for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years. This is due to their manifold karmas.

[This is] caused by [karmic conditions]. ○ Regarding *tōshō* (通槍): *Shō* (槍) means a spear (*śakti*). Furthermore, piercing wood to injure a thief is called *shō*. The *Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra* states:

"When a sinner has passed through the *Gūthamṛttika* (Feces and Filth) Hell and sees the *Asipattravana* (Sword-Leaf) Hell, a mind of attachment arises toward it as if it were a grove of mango trees (*āmra-vana*).
This is the path of the Sword-Forest, where various sharp spikes, seven-edged razors, and the blades of knives and swords are spread everywhere."
As for that ground: when sinners travel along the paths of this forest, they undergo various sufferings such as being pierced and impaled.

These are experienced as the predominant karmic retribution for killing, primarily induced by acts such as waging war. ○ Regarding the Iron Chariot, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The bonds of retribution for thoughts cause the breath to cease."
This constitutes the "Fire Chariot" hell. According to the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, it was precisely in this hell that Śākyamuni first gave rise to a mind of compassion.
Regarding the "Iron Bed": according to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the habit of sexual misconduct results in an iron bed and a copper pillar. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
"If one commits lewd acts in this life, upon death one enters hell and is laid upon an iron bed, or forced to embrace a copper pillar; the hell-demons then kindle fires [to heat them]."
It burns their bodies. Thus, the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisūtra* states: "When a sinner’s life ends, they sit upon an iron bed;
like a king of geese soaring through the air, they fall into a place of pitch darkness. Iron wheels, moving up and down, hack and mince their bodies. [Regarding] the iron ox, see the details below.
[Regarding] the iron garments, the *Lokasthānābhidharma* states: "At times, the hell-wardens revile and terrify those undergoing punishment."
The wicked beings arise; having arisen, they do not move. At that time, immeasurable sinners stand in great terror and agitation, like a forest of banners.
Then, countless tens of millions of red iron *kāṣāyas* and red iron garments descend from the sky.
The sinners cry out, "The garments! The garments! Once these garments have arrived, each one wraps and envelops their skin, flesh, tendons, and bones.

Once they have all been scorched and withered, their iron garments fall away of their own accord. This is because in their past human lives, they whipped and beat sentient beings who were still alive;
furthermore, as renunciants who had broken their precepts, they made use of the lands, clothing, and waist-bands belonging to others.
Due to the retribution of these karmic deeds, they are reborn therein. An ancient master said: "We see now that the *kāṣāya* leaves the body, and in the future, iron will strip it away."
"Enveloping the body. This refers precisely to this. Regarding "a thousand blades," according to the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*:

"There are sentient beings who do not follow their teacher’s instructions, giving rise to evil and rebellious intentions; they fail to recognize the kindness of their upbringing, stealing from their teacher or harming them, defiling the teacher’s pure food, sitting upon the teacher’s seat, seizing the teacher’s alms bowl, reviling and slandering the teacher, beating the teacher, or even killing the teacher. By means of... [text continues]
Various poisons were taken and given to their teachers—whether śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas—who committed various unrighteous acts without shame or remorse;
they stripped images and destroyed stūpas, plundered the property of the Dharma-treasure, and killed their uncles, paternal aunts, parents, brothers, and sisters.
Such a sinner, at the end of life, sits upon a great bed of swords. Ten billion sword-blades, each emitting fire, burn and pierce his body.
Fire-wheels from the sky descend from above, cleaving straight through the crown of his head;
his body shatters into thousands of pieces. [The following sections describe: ○ An iron donkey as below; ○ Boiling copper as above; ○ Embracing a pillar.

The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* (or *Buddha-dhyāna-samādhi-sūtra*) states: "Ignorant sentient beings of the world, defiled by lustful attachment to illicit sexual conduct, at the end of their lives are born atop copper pillars where fierce flames blaze and incinerate their bodies.
In their terror, they look down and see a beautiful woman upon an iron bed; if they are women, they see a handsome man. A mind of passionate attachment arises, and from the copper..."
Upon a pillar, they wish to throw themselves to the ground; yet copper pillars pierce their bodies and iron nets ensnare their necks. Iron-beaked insects swarm and devour their limbs.
They fall upon iron beds, where male and female simultaneously experience flames erupting from their six sense organs.
There are iron-beaked insects that enter through the eyes and emerge from the male organ. If one has defiled the precepts, there are additionally ten billion other minute insects.
They are like the *śvitra* (a type of leprosy) worm; this worm has twelve beaks, and from the tips of these beaks, fire issues forth as it gnaws and devours its own body.
This is the retribution for sexual misconduct. In a single day and night, one undergoes nine hundred billion births and deaths. [This is] the "Flowing Fire" hell.

The *Tridharmaka-śāstra* names this the Great Wailing Hell (*Mahā-rāva-naraka*). It is said that there are great iron mountains entirely ablaze with fire, where the four quarters are utterly devoid of any place to go.
The malevolent hell-wardens are devoid of compassion; they shout in rage, "Where do you wish to flee?

Without cause or reason, they take iron pestles and incinerate them with fire, then strike and shatter the heads [of the denizens]. Because those beings caused suffering to the myriad people in this world, they are born there.
