Among these, according to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, regarding the two characteristics of retribution for taste, the second is that one’s exhaled breath flies up as a fierce fire, which sears and rots the marrow and bones;
this is it. ○ Regarding the plowing of the tongue, see below. ○ Regarding the decapitation:
the *Tri-dharmaka-vinaya-śāstra* states that in the Reviving Hell (*sañjīva*), the hell-wardens use sharp knives and axes to flay, hack, and mince the sinful beings, just as one would mince [meat].

The sheep-head [hell]: the skin and flesh fall apart. The *Lishi apidamo lun* (Abhidharmakośa-śāstra) states: "In former lives among humans, there were sentient beings who struck and smashed the heads of living creatures—such as fish, snakes, centipedes, and various other species.
Due to such diverse karmic actions, one receives the retribution of having one's head crushed. ○ The Burning Feet [hell].
In the *Lishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of the World), it is called "Hot Ashes. When a sinner emerges from the Great Hell, he sees hot ashes outside that appear like a level, empty plain.
Seeing this sign, a thought arises in his mind: "I should go there. Thereupon, the sinner goes into its midst.
When his feet tread upon hot ashes, his skin and flesh immediately rot away, like a lump of wax cast into a fierce fire.
As soon as he lifts his foot, his skin and flesh are restored; this occurs whether the heat reaches his knees, his navel, or his neck, or until he is submerged and no longer visible.
In former lives among humans, he took living beings and placed them in fire, in hot ashes, or in hot sand, or committed sexual misconduct with others.
Wife. Transgressing the laws of the world, or leaving the household life and breaking the precepts, one dwells within a *saṃghārāma* while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
or one treads upon the grounds of the four *caityas*, as well as stepping on the shadows of a *caitya*. By the retribution of this karma, one takes birth therein.
○ Regarding "eating eyes": The *Utpatti-sūtra* (Qishi jing) states that in the minor hell of the Forest of Sword-leaves (*Asipatravana*), by means of immeasurable...
As a retribution for unwholesome karma, iron-beaked crows suddenly appear. They fly toward the two temples of the hell beings;
having settled their feet upon them, they immediately peck out the eyes of those sinners with iron beaks and depart.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "When sinners enter the Great Sword-Tree Forest and the Iron Grove, there are iron vultures."
Birds peck out their eyes and drink their marrow; this is the retribution for the evil karma of providing alcohol in the past.
○ Iron balls are as described before. ○ Regarding the iron hatchets: the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that those who emerge from the Iron Ball Hell flee in terror and panic.
Seeking self-preservation, they are dragged by the force of their past karma and suddenly find themselves in the *Kiṇākhya* (Adze and Axe) Hell, which is five hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth.
The hell-wardens angrily seize the offenders and throw them onto glowing red-hot iron.
With heated iron adzes and axes, they hack at their hands, feet, ears, noses, and bodies. In bitter agony and distress, they wail and shriek. As the verse says: "O man..."

The axe is within one’s own mouth; it is that which cuts one’s body because of evil speech. To praise those who deserve condemnation and to condemn those who deserve praise—this is an evil karma committed by the mouth, for which the body receives the retribution.
Contentious debate and excessive anger, though categorized as two distinct hells, share a single cause.
Contentious debate arises from greed and envy; because of greed and envy, one consequently gives rise to much hatred.
Because they experience results corresponding to their causes, they are born therein. The *Tridharmaka-śāstra* states:
"Furthermore, due to evil transgressions, iron claws naturally grow from their hands; they are as sharp as blades and shaped like half-moons.
Each harbors a mind of resentment, thinking, 'He once oppressed me, and now I shall oppress him in return. From this arises anger, and they further tear and claw one another."
It is like cutting bamboo or reeds; because one dies there with a heart bound by resentment, one is born in that place.
One must know that all phenomena are entirely false and deceptive; yet sentient beings, out of ignorance, respond to anger and abuse with further harm, even unto the taking of life.

The five aggregates are all empty; there is no self and no person. Yet, by grasping at signs and engaging in strife, they recklessly inflict poison and harm, giving rise to these grave offenses and thus falling into the three miserable realms to undergo immeasurable suffering. For this reason, the Bodhisattva says to sentient beings:
"Do not engage in strife within the fundamental emptiness. Even a human body is difficult to obtain, let alone encountering a Buddha. Now..."
"Once you have fallen into hell, it will be too late for regret. △ Second, pointing out the extent:
Kṣitigarbha said, "O Benevolent One, within the Iron Ring Mountains, there are such hells as these, their number being infinite."

The phrase "such as these" refers to the various hells within Mount Cakravāḍa mentioned above. Regarding the phrase "infinite in number," it means that within each individual hell there are further minor hells, which cannot be fully described.
As for the statement that they "exist," it is because ordinary beings falsely give rise to craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*), taking conditioned existence (*bhava*) as their object;
thus, there is cause and effect, and there is suffering and pleasure. Therefore, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only): [text continues].
It is said: All things are like the hells; that all alike see hell-wardens and the like who can inflict torment is entirely the manifestation of the sinful karma of the offenders' own minds.
There are no actual copper dogs, iron snakes, or other such things existing externally to the mind.
All phenomena and events in the world are likewise so. △ Second, the different names of the hells, part one: listing the names.
Furthermore, there are the Screaming Hell, the Tongue-Extraction Hell, the Excrement and Urine Hell, the Copper Chain Hell,
the Fire Elephant Hell, the Fire Dog Hell, the Fire Horse Hell, the Fire Ox Hell, the Fire Mountain Hell, the Fire Stone Hell,
the Fire Bed Hell, the Fire Beam Hell, the Fire Hawk Hell, the Saw-Toothed Hell, and the Flaying Hell.
The hells: the Blood-Drinking Hell, the Hand-Burning Hell, the Foot-Burning Hell, the Downward-Thorned Hell, the Fire-House Hell, the Iron-House Hell, and the Fire-Wolf Hell.
Raurava (The Screaming Hell). According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, eight great hot hells are enumerated. The fourth is Raurava and the fifth is Mahāraurava;

each has sixteen auxiliary hells (*utsada*). Because the hell-wardens seize the offenders and hurl them into large cauldrons where boiling hot water surges and seethes, and again onto large griddles where they are repeatedly scorched and broiled, they wail and scream; thus it is called Raurava. Furthermore...
It is a place of great wailing and screaming. However, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states:
"In the Black Rope Hell, there is a location called Equal Screaming. There, one is horribly burned and undergoes uninterrupted suffering.

Being lifted onto a precipitous cliff many yojanas high, and having been bound and fettered with glowing black ropes, one is subsequently pushed down onto a ground of hot iron blades, where iron dogs devour one."

All parts of the body are torn apart limb by limb; one utters cries and roars. Based on this, the two hells of Raurava (Crying) and Mahāraurava (Great Crying) are situated within the second hell, Kālasūtra (Black String).
Since all eight hells are generally interconnected, they are described collectively. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"Because of harboring poison through anger and hatred, one commits various evil deeds and thus falls into the Raurava Hell. This is due to habitual practice...
Driven by various wrong views and pulled by the net of craving, they commit strange and loathsome deeds and fall into the Great Howling Hell.

[The punishments of] having the tongue pulled out and being defiled by excrement and urine are as described below. Regarding the Copper Shackles: the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states that those in the Black Rope Hell...
There are eight hundred iron chains and eight hundred iron mountains. A great iron banner is erected, with its two ends bound to their necks.
The rakshasa jailers drive the sinners, forcing them to carry the iron mountains and run upon iron ropes. Unable to bear the weight, they fall to the ground and drop into cauldrons of boiling liquid.
The rakshasas drive them back up; in desperate thirst, they drink iron and swallow stones. They undergo this for one day and one night.

They have undergone suffering ninety thousand times over. This is caused by ignorant sentient beings, the seven classes of disciples, and the ninety-six kinds of brahmins, who proclaim what is not the Dharma as the Dharma and what is the Dharma as not the Dharma, or who violate minor precepts and fail to repent for a long time.
○ As Saṃgharakṣita proceeded forward, he saw a white elephant whose body was being consumed by blazing fire.
The Buddha said, "Those whom you see as elephants are people from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were renunciants who served as kitchen attendants for the Sangha.
When various donors brought offerings to the monastery to give to the monks, these men would sometimes arrive after the meal had already been consumed."
The donor said, "Venerable Sir, it is still not yet time; please strike the *ghanṭā* to assemble the Saṃgha for the offering of food.
The bhikṣu replied to the layperson with harsh words: "These bhikṣus are like white elephants; they can never be satiated by food."
Having finished eating, he remained there for another day. Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and received the body of a white elephant;
he suffers from being burned by fire, and this has continued without end until now. Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"If a person harbors such a thought as, 'When an elephant is intoxicated, it can kill many people; thus I shall gain the victory,' and provides alcohol to cause the elephants to fight."
They are made to drink [molten metal] and fall into the Raurava Hell. There, great elephants are born whose bodies are entirely ablaze; every part of their bodies is capable of striking and touching.
Having seized those persons, they touch and break their limbs until they are shattered and fall down. Because they cry out with a loud wail, these fire-elephants are born.
Regarding the Fire Dogs, the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states: "On both banks of the river of boiling hot ashes..."
All the dogs there have bodies that are blackish-purple, filthy and greasy, and terrifying;

they devour the flesh of the sentient beings in that hell, biting and eating it piece by piece. The *Tridharmaka-śāstra* states: "The ground is ablaze with fire and iron, driving the sinful beings to roast them until they are cooked.
Once they are cooked, they are driven out again to be eaten by evil dogs. When their flesh is completely consumed, the wind blows and causes it to grow back."
They return to their former state. Because they raised silkworms and boiled or roasted them in this world, they are born there.

Regarding the "Fire Horses" and "Fire Oxen," according to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, if someone sees a female ox or a stallion and sexual desire arises in their mind, they will be reborn as such.
This is no different from [intercourse with] a woman. He engages in sexual desire and, because of this, falls into the Saṃghāta Great Hell, being born in the Piṇḍa (Mass) region.
Seeing those oxen and horses, he recalls them as human women as before; his lustful mind becomes intensely blazing, and he runs toward the oxen and horses.
Once that person has approached the private parts of the oxen and horses, due to the cause of his evil karma, he enters their private parts.
He immediately enters its belly, which is filled with hot fire, and there he suffers. Regarding the "Volcanic Mountain" and the "Flaming Rock":
according to the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra*, this is the hell named Saṃghāta (Crushing). Beings are born between two mountains called "White Sheep";
they eat blazing, most fierce flames with their mouths. When they enter within those mountains, the two mountains grind, strike, and rub against one another.
Having thus completed the joining, rubbing, striking, and wiping, they return to their original abodes.
It is like the *vikaṭa* and *rāvikaṭa* (these two are names for lightning) which, after joining, rubbing, wiping, and striking one another, each returns to its original place.
Furthermore, the jailers take large iron stones, blazing with fierce flames, and strike the sentient beings in that hell, forcing them to lie supine upon the hot iron stones;
they then take other stones and cover them over, just like a worldly millstone.
Having been ground, they are ground again; the great millstones reduce them to powder, which is then ground even finer until they are pulverized into dust.
One sees only pus and blood flowing out, while nothing remains but the empty marrow, bones, dust, and powder. ○ The Fire Bed is the same as the previous Iron Bed.
○ Within the Hell of the Fiery Beam, the iron beams and iron pillars are entirely composed of fire; alternatively, the offenders are taken and suspended from the beams.
They are burned; or they are burned while their bodies are pressed down by iron beams. ○ Regarding the Fire Hawk: it is the same as the aforementioned Iron Hawk.
In the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, it is called Mount Kukūla. That mountain is ablaze, with flames reaching five thousand yojanas in height.

There are iron trees upon it, and on these trees are iron crows. The bodies of the crows are ablaze, filling the tops of those trees. When the offenders reach that place, the flaming crows [attack them].

As for "breaking their heads": they take the brains; they take the eyes; they take the noses; they take the cheeks; they take the hearts; they take the lungs; they take the small and large intestines.
These various crows devour the hell-beings, eating them piece by piece. Due to the power of their karmic offenses, once they have been eaten, they are reborn.
The case of the hawks and crows is the same. Regarding "saw-teeth": the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states that the hell-wardens seize those beings...
Born there, they are cast upon the ground of glowing-hot iron. With black iron cords, their bodies are measured out; then, with iron saws, their bodies are sawn asunder.
Having been split once, they are split again, until they are utterly shattered. Since they have had their bodies sawn, why should their tusks not also be sawn?
This is brought about by the four evil karmas of the mouth. ○ Flaying the Skin: The *Lishi apidamo lun* (Abhidharmakośa-śāstra) states that it occurs in the [Saṃjīva] hell.
Between the Sañjīva and Kālasūtra hells, there is a hell named Mahāpatha (The Great Street).
There are certain sinners there whose skin is flayed and laid upon the ground, and their flesh is then sliced off and piled atop the skin.

This is due to the karmic retribution for having previously lived among humans as butchers or meat-sellers, sustaining their lives by killing sheep, pigs, oxen, and deer, or by catching fish, birds, and other creatures. Because of this karma, they [suffer] therein.
Rebirth. ○ Regarding the drinking of blood, according to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, it corresponds to the eighth distinct location of the hells, named Zhu-zhu Zhu-zhu (Cucucu).

If a person commits theft or sexual misconduct—such as with sheep, donkeys, or women who are not human—they will, because of such acts of lust, fall into this evil place, whether near a stupa or within a stupa.
Due to these evil karmas, they fall into this miserable state and dwell there constantly.
There are malevolent insects called *zhūzhū* that devour their flesh and drink their blood.
Having drunk the blood, they sever the tendons and drink the marrow. Or they cause the offenders to drink their own blood themselves.

As the sutras clarify regarding the eighteen locations of the hell of False Speech, the seventeenth is named "Drinking Blood and Marrow. In that place, there is a river named "Boiling Hot Blood Water. Therein...
The river boils with heat. Molten copper and tin are mixed within it (in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, this is called the Pus-Blood Hell, where pus and blood spontaneously emerge, boiling and surging forth;

the offenders run about and eat it themselves). ○ Such matters as having one's hands burned and one's feet burned constitute the sixth, the Hell of Scorching Heat, and the seventh, the Great Hell of Scorching Heat, wherein the entire body is burned and the skin and flesh are charred and putrefied. Now, following [the sequence]:

The Separate Karma Hell: Here one suffers only the burning of hands and feet. This is because, in previous lives, one slaughtered living beings by cutting off their hands and feet, roasting, burning, boiling, or broiling them;
therefore, one falls into this hell. The Inverted Thorns Hell: The *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra) states that the river of scum is twenty thousand li in length and breadth.
On both sides of the river stand iron trees. The *Lishi apidamo lun* (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya) states that these are *śāmbalī* trees with thorns pointing upward, all made of iron.
It blazes day and night. The tree is one yojana high, and its thorns are sixteen inches long.

The hell-wardens seize the arms of the offenders and drag them up the thorny tree, then drag them down again; as they are dragged up, the thorns point downward, and as they are dragged down, the thorns point upward.
His belly adheres to the tree; his skin and flesh are completely consumed, and it is the same for his back and ribs.

He undergoes this torment and injury because, in his former life among humans, he committed sexual misconduct with women or betrayed his husband, and furthermore, due to various other predominant karmic retributions.
They are born therein. The two hells of the Fire House and the Iron House are similar; each is named after its predominant feature.
The Fire House is composed entirely of iron, while the Iron House is ablaze with great fires. The *Sūtra on the Arising of the World* states:

"At that time, the hell-wardens seize those sentient beings and cast them into the chamber of the Iron House, which is fiercely burning and intensely hot, so oppressive and unbearable as to cause manifold afflictions."

They congregate together and then let out great cries of lamentation. Within that place there are further iron houses, iron carriages, iron pavilions, and iron towers. Inside them, glowing coals boil and surge, filling every space.
This is called the "Scorching and Roasting" hell in the *Dīrgha Āgama*; its circumstances are largely the same [as other accounts].

Regarding the "Fire Wolves," the *Loutan jing* (*Lokānuvartana-sūtra*) states: Having emerged from the *Nālā* River, they enter the wilds of wolves and jackals, which extend twenty thousand [yojanas] in length and breadth.

Li. The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states: "Due to the retribution of various unwholesome karmas, foxes and wolves are born within those hells—coarse, evil, and terrifying—who gnaw at the flesh of the sentient beings in those hells.
They trample them with their feet and pull them with their mouths, devouring them piece by piece" (and so forth). △ Second, the measurement of width.
In these hells, there are further various minor hells within each one— whether one, two, three, four,
or even up to a hundred thousand— each with its own distinct name.

The first phrase concludes the description of the various hells mentioned above. Regarding the phrase "within these," it means that within each of these hells, there are further minor hells acting as their satellites;
these may number one, two, three, or even up to hundreds and thousands, and their specific names and distinctions are beyond enumeration.
II. Answering regarding the evil matters of karmic retribution, in three parts: A. First, the direct demonstration of how evil karma brings about its retribution.

Second, the specific explanation of the distinctions in karmic retribution in the hells; third, the concluding summary revealing how karma evokes the instruments of suffering. The first part is divided into three sections. First, the indication of how karma evokes [retribution].
Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha addressed Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying: "O Benevolent One, all within this place belong to Jambudvīpa."
Such is the karmic retribution experienced by sentient beings who commit evil.
To single out the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa is because their dispositions are unsettled; having habitually created evil karma, they experience this hell.
The *Nāgasena Bhikṣu Sūtra* states: "The heat of the fires in the world is not like the fire within niraya (hell)."

Heat: Suppose one were to place a small stone in a worldly fire; it would not be consumed until evening. Yet if one were to take a large stone and place it in the fires of hell (*niraya*), it would be consumed instantly.
Similarly, there may be a person who commits evil deeds and dies to be reborn in hell, remaining there for many tens of millions of years without dying.
Both of these cases—being consumed or not being consumed—are brought about by the power of wholesome and unwholesome karma. Therefore, it is said:
The retribution of karma is thus. △ Second, explaining the greatness of the power of karma. Part one: the formal presentation.
The power of karma is exceedingly great; it can rival Mount Sumeru, it can deepen the vast ocean, and it can obstruct the Noble Path.
This explains the cause by which karma produces its results. The *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation) states: "That which invites a fruit is called a cause; it is also termed 'karma.
The karma of the ten dharma realms arises from the mind. As long as there is a mind, all karmas are fully present. Regarding "power," this refers to the capacity for functional efficacy.
The Buddha said: "Of all things that are formidable, none surpasses the mind. The mind is an enemy that constantly deceives and misleads people. The mind...
The mind takes up the hells; the mind takes up the hungry ghosts; the mind takes up the animals; the mind takes up humans and devas.

Those who fashion forms and appearances all act through the power of the mind, which possesses the greatest strength. It can withstand the height and breadth of Mount Sumeru; it can deepen the vast expanse of the ocean’s abysses;
and it can obstruct the empty penetration of the Noble Path. All these are the deeds of the multitude [of mental states].

It is caused by the power of the karma of birth; how could it be anything other than something extremely great? The two phrases concerning mountains and seas cite examples of that which can obstruct the Path of the Sages.
Defiled (sāsrava) karma can obstruct the Path of the Sages of the Three Vehicles, while undefiled (anāsrava) karma can obstruct the Middle Way of the Buddha-nature.
The *Wenju* (Text on Words and Phrases) states: "The three obstacles obstruct the Buddha; they are abandoned by those in the Heaven of Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-deva*).
Thus, one knows that the power of karma is both profound and vast. △ Second, the exhortation.
Therefore, sentient beings must not treat even minor evils lightly, thinking them to be without fault; for after death there is retribution, and one receives it down to the finest hair.
Though father and son share the deepest intimacy, they part ways at the crossroads of life; even if they should happen to meet again, neither will be willing to suffer in the other’s stead.

Continuing from above, because [these faults] are able to obstruct the Noble Path, they are thus cautioned against and exhorted to avoid. Within the human world, there are many who harbor such thoughts:
"Who would take account of such a trifling transgression? Yet, according to the *Wu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Absence of Samādhi), the Buddha told Ānanda:
"The reason why people in this world fail to attain the Way is simply because their contemplation is dominated by impure thoughts; it is due to these many defiled thoughts. A single thought...
Coming and going in a single thought-moment, within one day and one night, there are eighty-four million thoughts.
These thoughts ceaselessly succeed one another. A single virtuous thought yields a virtuous retribution; a single evil thought yields an evil retribution.

It is like an echo responding to a sound, or a shadow following a form. Therefore, virtue and evil, as well as sin and merit, are each distinct. This is as when King Yama proclaims the transgressions of the dead.
People say: "When a person lives in this world, their transgressions are small and light; yet when they die and fall into the subterranean hells (niraya), those transgressions become great and heavy.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Do not treat even a small evil lightly, thinking it will bring no calamity. Though a drop of water is minute," [it eventually fills a vessel].
The gradual filling of a great vessel is truly due to the fact that even the slightest evil does not perish throughout kalpas, while even a hair’s breadth of goodness endures for generations.
When merit is perfected, heaven arrives of its own accord; when sin accumulates, hell is reached.
This is an inevitable law, leaving no room for doubt. Now, the nature between father and son is intimately connected; it is the ultimate limit of kinship.
This is so. Yet, if the father cultivates goodness while the son commits evil, the father will be born in heaven while the son falls into suffering.

Since the paths have thus diverged, it is certain that they will find themselves on different courses; even if they were to happen upon one another by chance, how could the father willingly [exchange his state] for the bliss of paradise?
Would you rather exchange the sufferings of the hells with your child? If the child is virtuous and the father is evil, the principle of human emotion and reason is likewise the same.
As the *Ratthapala Sutta* states: "Goodness and evil follow a person like a shadow follows the body. A person is born alone, and they die alone."
The body performs good and evil deeds; the body alone must bear their consequences. There is no one who can take one’s place. Thus, the Buddha said in the *Catuḥsvabhāva-ātman-upaghāta-sūtra*:
"One does not contemplate impermanence, yet instead indulges in craving and attachment, saying, 'I have parents, brothers, wife, and children, as well as relatives both near and far.
Yet when old age, sickness, death, and the fruits of good and evil—suffering and joy—arrive, one must face them alone. There is no one to take one’s place."
Therefore, I urge you not to regard minor evils as insignificant and thus intentionally commit them. △ Third, the request that the Benevolent One listen to these words, in two parts:
First, Kṣitigarbha urges him to listen:
"I now rely upon the Buddha’s majestic power to briefly explain the matters of retribution for sins in the hells. I only pray that the Benevolent One will listen for a moment."
These words are as they appear in the text. △ Second, Samantabhadra explains his intention.
Samantabhadra replied: "I have long known the retributions of the three evil realms; I look to you, O Benevolent One, to speak [of them], so that future generations in the final age..."

"O Samantabhadra, you who teach all sentient beings who engage in evil conduct, please listen for a moment as I briefly explain the words regarding the retribution for sins, which you have spoken so that they may take refuge in the Buddha. How could I not know the suffering of the evil realms?
It is simply that you, O Benevolent One, have long transformed those in the dark gates and serve as the Teacher of the Hell Realms before this assembly."
If one preaches [the Dharma], people will surely believe it; only then can they be led to take refuge in the Buddha. The Verse on Impermanence says: "All who are born must die;
the karma one creates brings suffering to the very body. Only the Bodhi of the Buddha is the true place of reliance.
This exhortation to take refuge in the Buddha is the primary intent of Kṣitigarbha. Part Two: Specifically Clarifying the Differences in Rebirth in the Hells (2).
This is the initial general indication.
Kṣitigarbha said: "O Benevolent One, such are the matters regarding the retributions for sins in the hells.
This passage may be construed in two ways. If it serves as a conclusion to what precedes, it refers back to the names of the hells mentioned earlier, stating that "the matters thereof are thus."
"Rising from below" refers to the various hells and so forth. To say "in such and such a way" serves as a general indication for what follows in the text;
this interpretation is more appropriate. △ Second, the specific explanation.
There are some hells where they seize the tongues of the offenders and have oxen plow them. There are some hells where they seize the hearts of the offenders and yakṣas devour them.
There are some hells where cauldrons of boiling water seethe, cooking the bodies of the offenders. There are some hells...
There are hells where glowing copper pillars are made for the offenders to embrace; there are hells where various fires burn and pursue the offenders;
there are hells that are perpetually freezing ice; there are hells with limitless excrement and urine; and there are hells [of other kinds].
There are hells where one is struck by pure, whirling metal drills. There are hells where many fire-spears are thrust [into the body]. There are hells where only the chest and back are struck.
There are hells where only the hands and feet are burned. There are hells where one is coiled and bound by iron snakes. There are hells...
They are driven out by iron dogs. There are some hells where they are all mounted upon iron mules.

Regarding the first hell, as stated in the *Sūtra of the Eight Teachers*: those who engage in double-tongued speech, harsh words, false speech, and frivolous talk, and who slander others without cause [suffer here].
Those who slander the Triple Gem die and enter hell. There, the spirits within the prison pull out their tongues and plow them with oxen;
molten copper is poured into their mouths, yet they cannot seek death. ○ As for those whose hearts are taken and eaten by yakṣas, the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states:
"Various sinners are born amidst the rivers of ash and among the various sword-trees. There is a rākṣasa who..."
The yakṣas tear out their hearts and give them as food to the yakṣas.

Due to the causal conditions of their past sins of stealing from teachers, parents, and elders, they undergo five hundred billion births and deaths within a single day and night, suffering immeasurable pain.

○ Their bodies are boiled in cauldrons of boiling water. As the previous sutra states: "In the Hell of Boiling Cauldrons, there are eighteen cauldrons; each cauldron is four [yojanas] in length and breadth."
Ten *yojanas* [in extent], it is filled with boiling iron. Five hundred *rākṣasas* beat large lumps of charcoal, burning the copper cauldrons;

the flames overlap one another and do not extinguish for sixty days. While a day in Jambudvīpa lasts one hundred and thirty thousand years, the boiling cauldron becomes like a star and transforms into a wheel of fire.
This is due to violating the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, killing living beings for sacrificial offerings, and eating [the flesh].
Flesh and blood; they burn the mountains and wilds, and they scald living beings alive with fire.

They are cast into boiling cauldrons where they are quickly dissolved and rotted away until only bones remain. Iron forks lift them out, and iron dogs devour them; the dogs then vomit them onto the ground.
Soon they were revived again. The hell-wardens drove them back and forced them into the cauldrons. The red-hot copper pillars were as before. Flames pursued and overtook the sinners;
"chèn" (pronounced *chǔn*, with the second tone of *chēn*) means to pursue or to follow. The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) says:
In the Avīci Great Hell, various sentient beings, as a result of their unwholesome karma, spend immeasurable time there.
They see the eastern gate of the hell suddenly open; seeing and hearing the gate open, the inhabitants of the hell run toward it, running and running again.
They run with great speed, thinking, "We shall surely now attain liberation. As they run in this manner, all the limbs and joints of their bodies become even more intensely ablaze;
it is the same at the southern, western, and northern gates. ○ There is nothing but cold ice. The *Loutan jing* (Kāṭhāvatthu-sūtra) says:
"Emerging from the wilderness of wolves and jackals, they rush into the cold ice, which extends twenty thousand *li* in both length and breadth. All people..."
Upon entering therein, winds arise from the four directions. (The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "Between the two diamond mountains, there is a great wind named Saṃkha.

These winds blow against the skin, flesh, sinews, and bones of those people, penetrating into the marrow so that they die. Due to the retribution of their various unwholesome karmas, they are born within this place.
○ There is boundless excrement and filth. The *Niraya Sūtra* states that the Boiling Excrement Hell has ten [subdivisions].
There are eight partitions, each eight thousand yojanas in extent. There are eighteen iron cities, and within each one there are eighteen partitions.

Within these partitions, on the four walls, there are hundreds of billions of sword-trees, all of which breed iron insects that spit hot excrement from their mouths; sentient beings drink this excrement.
These worms gnaw at the tongue and devour the heart because, in previous lives, [the person] violated the eight precepts of the fast and committed impure, evil karma.
○ There are only flying *ji* (sharp) iron drills. The *Guanfo Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha) says:

"When the sinner falls into a place of darkness, there are iron crows with long, sharp talons that fly from the mountains and peck at the sinner. In their intense agony, the sinner runs swiftly; beneath his feet..."

The "metal spikes" (*jinji*) pierce through the bones and penetrate to the marrow. This lasts for five hundred million billion years. What is now called "pure flying" refers to the fact that the entire hell is filled with them.
This arises because in military camps, iron spikes are buried at the four corners to harm people; therefore, one is born here.
There are many "fire-spears" (*huoqiang*), which are the same as "through-spears" (*tongqiang*), differing only in that they possess fire. They only strike.
Regarding the chest and back: according to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, among the retributions for tactile contact, one experiences being struck and beaten;
thus, this fruit of tactile sensation is obtained through the cause of tactile sensation. As for the mere burning of hands and feet, the *Lokotpatti Sūtra* states:
"Having emerged from the minor hell of Grinding and Piling, one proceeds toward the minor hell of Measuring with Bushels, which is five hundred yojanas in extent. There, the hell-wardens..."
They seize those belonging to the hells and compel them to measure fire with hot iron measures; their hands and feet are burned, as are their ears, noses, limbs, and joints.
Because this is a distinct karmic action and a distinct retribution, only the hands and feet are burned. Iron snakes and iron dogs are as described previously.
[The Buddha] said, "He was riding an iron mule. As in the case of the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita, he saw a donkey whose body was being burned by fierce flames.
The Buddha said, "This is not actually a donkey. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was an ordained person who served as a kitchen overseer.

When distributing the food and drink for the Saṃgha, he would constantly take for himself the portions of two or three others. A bhikṣu who upheld the Vinaya reprimanded him according to the Dharma, to which he replied, 'I belong to the Saṃgha...'"
"In the kitchen, you underwent great toil and hardship. You were ungrateful and behaved like a donkey;
you cared only for your own body and did not remain silent. Because of this, you have entered hell and must now endure suffering as a donkey.

'Now it says you shall drive all' means that, roughly speaking, the sinner is mounted upon an iron donkey and its body is scorched by fire. △ Third, the conclusion which clarifies how karma evokes the instruments of suffering.

O Benevolent One, such retributions as these exist within each of the hells; there are hundreds of thousands of types of vessels for the paths of karma, none of which are not made of copper, iron, stone, or fire.
These four kinds of substances are the result of the induction of various karmic actions.
These and other such retributions collectively refer to the matters mentioned above.

Because all sentient beings constantly give rise to three kinds of unwholesome thoughts—thoughts of the five desires, thoughts of malice and harm, and thoughts of deceit—all of which arise with ignorance as their cause, they fall into the evil realms upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life. "The vessel" refers to the days of the sentient beings' lives.
The vessels used therein—now made of copper, iron, stone, or fire—are the instruments of suffering in hell. They are all produced by the karmic actions of the offenders;
they are not bestowed by gods or humans. Although karmic actions are manifold, they are fully subsumed within the ten non-virtues.

The three poisons act as the cause, and the seven branches of action act as the conditions. By performing evil deeds, one constructs these instruments of suffering, which one then returns to experience for oneself.
Regarding that which cannot be avoided, the *Guangji* states: "The mind that violates the precepts brings about the hells;
various instruments of suffering are prepared in advance and await [the offender]. Not a single thing arises from the outside. Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* says:
"Just as in the hells there is no lord of hell, yet the sentient beings in hell, by virtue of their natural karma, perceive the hell."
The Lord [bestows] various sufferings, and one gives rise to mental perceptions, thinking: "This is the place of hell; this is night, this is day.
Due to evil karma, one sees dogs, sees crows, or sees oneself being crushed by mountains. Based on these scriptural proofs, good and evil permeate the mind, causing it to easily perceive such things.
In reality, there is no hell. Nevertheless, although there is no hell external to the mind, because of evil karma—
At the time of its formation, one forcibly and falsely perceives it as such. Therefore, the *Vinaya-viniścaya* states: "I have spoken of the various sufferings of hell;
in reality, there is no evil realm to come or go to. There are no swords, staves, spears, or javelins, nor are there any who can create them.
It is through conceptual discrimination that they appear to exist. Immeasurable bitter poisons pervade the body, just as if one were [cut] into pieces."

It distinguishes these from illusions and mirages; that all such conceptualizations are entirely empty—this is precisely what is meant here. △ Third, the conclusion and indication of the extensive [explanation].
If one were to explain in detail the matters of retribution for sins in the hells, within each individual hell there are further hundreds of thousands of kinds of torment.
How much more so for many hells! Now, relying on the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and prompted by your inquiry, I have briefly explained it in this way;
if it were to be explained in detail, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
The retribution for transgressions consists of hundreds of thousands of agonies, all of which are produced by a single thought.
As stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*: "How is it that immeasurable and manifold evil karmas are all caused by the mind?

They flow on in succession like the seepage of a river, drifting sentient beings and causing them to fall into the realm of the retribution of evil karma, where they dwell in hell and undergo extreme suffering."

How is it that these sentient beings are thus deceived by their own minds and deceived by craving, such that they experience hundreds of thousands of kinds of retributions that inflict bitter torment upon their bodies?
How much more so for those who must pass through many hells, when we speak here of only the single Avīci hell?
There are already various kinds of painful retributions for sins; how much more so in many hells!
I now rely upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power to respectfully answer your question, yet I shall do no more than provide a brief explanation of such matters.

If one were to wish to explain in detail the names of the hells, the retributions for sins, and each individual instrument of suffering, even if one exhausted a full kalpa of life, one could not finish. Why is this?
The karmic power of sentient beings is inconceivable. For it is by the painter of mental karma that one’s own karma paints the various regions of the fruits of action;

with diverse minds, one undergoes suffering in different places. There are hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of terrifying and evil matters, none of which are similar or can be compared to one another, arising solely from the past contacts of sentient beings.

Attachment arises toward objects, giving rise to craving. Now, encountering these objects, one experiences revulsion and undergoes suffering. Therefore, the retributions of suffering, the conditions of suffering, and the vessels of suffering are exceedingly difficult to enumerate in their entirety.
This concludes the clarification of the capacities of those to be converted.
△ Third Major Chapter: Clarifying the Section on the Conditions for Deliverance. This is divided into two parts: first, the transformational master emits light and offers praise;
second, King Yama raises questions and praises [the teaching]. As stated in the *Ratnavarṣa Sūtra*: "How can a bodhisattva cause others to offer praise?
Good son, it is like the appearance of the moon, which enables people throughout the cities, towns, villages, and settlements to [honor] the kṣatriyas and brāhmaṇas..."
Whether they be men or women, all alike praise the Bodhisattva in this way, just as the moon appears and is praised by all the world—including devas, humans, asuras, and gandharvas.
This section has two parts: first, the World-Honored One’s praise of his meritorious virtues;
second, the benefits of Kṣitigarbha for both the living and the deceased. Regarding the first part, it begins with the title of the chapter.
Chapter Six: The Tathāgata’s Praise. Section Two:
The Text of the Two Chapters. Part One: The Tathāgata’s Praise of Compassion and Mercy. Part Two: Universal Wideness’s Request for Benefits.
Subsection One: The Narration of the Light, Sound, and Praise.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance from his entire body, which illuminated hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

He produced a great sound, universally proclaiming to all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others throughout all those Buddha-worlds: "Listen as I today extol and praise the Ground."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the [Buddha’s] treasury manifest great, inconceivable power of majestic virtue, compassion, and spiritual authority throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
rescuing and protecting all beings from their sinful suffering.

The preceding explanation of the transforming master and the sentient beings to be transformed is now complete. At this opportune moment, the World-Honored One offers praise to clarify the conditions for liberation;

thus it is said that "at that time, light was emitted from his entire body," which signifies that the great earth has become a ground of wisdom and that all living beings have entered the state of non-arising.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "From the thousand-spoked wheel-mark beneath his feet..."

He emitted six hundred trillion rays of light from his ten toes, both ankles, knees, calves, thighs, waist, abdomen, back, navel, heart, chest, shoulders, arms, fingers, neck, mouth, teeth, nostrils, eyes, ears, the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft, and the *uṣṇīṣa*.
From each of these, he emitted six hundred trillion rays of light. From all these lights, great radiance issued forth, illuminating the ten directions everywhere.
In as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, any sentient beings who encounter this light will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The light now emitted is likewise so; therefore, it is said that he emits a great radiance from his entire body, universally illuminating worlds as numerous as the sands of ten billion Ganges rivers.
This "great voice" refers to the Brahma-voice among the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*). (From the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*)

The *Śāstra* states: Within the throat-cavity of the Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice, there exists a wondrous primary element (*mahābhūta*) capable of producing a pleasing, harmonious, and sublime Brahma-sound, like that of the kalaviṅka bird, and a sound as deep and far-reaching as the roar of thunder, like the drum of Śakra.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Like the five kinds of sounds of the Brahmā King that issue from his mouth—the first being as profoundly deep as...
1. It is like thunder. 2. It is clear and heard from afar, bringing joy and delight to those who hear it. 3. It enters the heart, inspiring reverence and affection.
4. It is precise and easy to understand. 5. Listeners desire to hear it without weariness; therefore, it is said that he "emits a great sound" to address all the bodhisattvas.
In order to circulate this sutra, [the Buddha] addressed the devas, nāgas, and others to provide protection for it. Regarding the listener:

while the power of the eye is great—since people are more frequently led astray by external influences through sight—it does not match the ear in its ability to penetrate deeply into a person or benefit them so greatly.

Why is this? Because the gaze is scattered while the hearing is focused. The ancients perfectly realized this principle; thus, when creating characters, they derived the word for "ear" from the character for "to gather."
[The character for] "ear" (耳) is composed of "nine" (壬, an ancient form of 挺) and "virtue" (德). When the breath of the ear is raised once, that which is heard is governed by the mind of virtue.
Therefore, one must withdraw the gaze and turn the hearing inward to listen as I today extol and praise. "Manifest" (現) means to arise.
Although one knows that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, the seed of Buddhahood nevertheless arises from conditions; sentient beings take this as their cause.
"Response": Kṣitigarbha responds through these conditions. "Great" means that his nature is vast and expansive, capable of containing much;

his great lion’s roar brings immense benefit to both ordinary beings and sages. As for "inconceivable," it refers to the three aspects of essence, attribute, and function—all of which are beyond thought.
To merely wish to speak of them would wound their reality; to merely wish to contemplate them would lose their true nature.
True. Why is this? Since it is said that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is no longer any calculation of the four natures.

Furthermore, the Buddha-seed arises from conditions, enabling one to obtain the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*. This is the functioning arising from the essence; the functioning returns to merge with the principle.

The essence relies on functioning to be manifested, yet the essence is itself empty and quiescent. Thus, essence and functioning are non-dual; they spontaneously bestow and extract [benefit and harm], such that essence and functioning are not distinct.
As for essence and function: to bestow and to rescue is itself non-bestowing and non-rescuing; this is solely the benefit of the *siddhānta* of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Therefore it is said: "The great inconceivable power of majestic spiritual authority. Yet, the Way of compassion takes salvation as its priority;
the resolve of a Bodhisattva takes compassionate relief as its function. One should constantly travel throughout the hells to undergo suffering in their stead; hence it is called "rescue."
To protect against all matters of sin and suffering. △ Second, to cause the skillful means to protect this sutra:

"After my parinirvāṇa, you bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as well as devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and others, shall extensively employ skillful means to guard and protect this sutra, causing all sentient beings to realize the bliss of nirvana."
The Great Sūtra states that the Tathāgata does not, in reality, enter ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Why, then, is it said here, "After my parinirvāṇa"?
It is because when the fuel of the sentient beings' capacities is exhausted, the fire of the response ceases; thus, he manifests extinction in accordance with Pāpīyas.

To say that "expansive creation" is a skillful means (*upāya*)—skillful means is indeed the vessel for the Bodhisattva’s twofold benefit [of self and others], and it must never be abandoned for even a moment.
Because they are separated [from wisdom]. Thus, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says: "Wisdom without skillful means is bondage; wisdom with skillful means is liberation.
This means that one does not adorn the Buddha-lands or bring sentient beings to maturity with a mind of attachment or biased views.

Within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one disciplines oneself without weariness or fatigue; this is called "liberation through wisdom with skillful means. Otherwise, one is bound. [This is] the exhortation.
Those who protect this sutra serve as an excellent medicine for sentient beings.

Just as sandalwood can cure human ailments and is desired by all sentient beings without exception, suppose there were a person who obtained a great deal of sandalwood trees but instead bundled them with firewood to sell;
no one would buy them. This sutra can cause people to attain the Way, and there are none whom it does not deliver. I shall now enter parinirvāṇa.
After the *nirvāṇa*, if [this teaching] remains in the world without anyone to behold it, it will be like a bundle of sandalwood being sold as firewood, with no one to purchase it. Therefore,
one must extensively employ skillful means to protect and circulate it, so that all sentient beings suffering from transgressions may block the source of ignorance,
uproot the root of birth and death, emerge from the evil paths of the three miserable realms, and realize the three virtues.

[This leads to] the serene light [of ultimate reality]. I hope that this will not fail to repay the power of the Great Being’s majestic spirit and compassionate grace, nor his heart that seeks to rescue and protect those suffering from their karmic offenses.
△ Second, Universal Wideness requests the matters concerning benefits. Part One: The appropriate recipient requests the teaching.
When these words had been spoken, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Puguang. With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now see that the World-Honored One praises the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha for possessing such inconceivable and great majestic spiritual power.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for the sake of sentient beings in the future age of the Dharma’s decline, proclaim the teachings of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha."

This concerns the causes and effects of benefiting humans and devas, and so forth, so that the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, and sentient beings of future ages may receive the Buddha’s words upon their crowns.
The text is divided into two sections: first, the sūtra-master describes the majestic demeanor; second, from "Now I see" onwards, it recounts the praise, the request, and the benefits. Therein...
There was a bodhisattva who, having received this command, became the guardian of the sutra; his name was Puguang (Universal Extensiveness).

His wisdom arose from the mind, and as that wisdom pervaded the dharma-realm, it was called "Universal" (Pu). Guiding practice with wisdom, his conduct filled all of space, hence it was called "Extensive" (Guang).

The mind is the essence of the objective realm; "Universal" and "Extensive" are its functions. The mind is the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "Universal" is prajñā; "Extensive" is liberation (*vimukti*). It is for this reason [that he is so named].
O Great Being, you have long since realized the three virtues and extensively saved all living beings. Although function does not depart from essence, essence is manifested by means of function;
therefore, the name is established based on function. To explain this matter in detail would be identical to the ten "Universals" of Avalokiteśvara (and so forth).
Now, looking down, he first recounts the majestic virtue (mahā-tejas) previously praised. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "The Buddhas have emerged from the triple world;
they do not cling to the mundane, and they are without 'I' or 'mine. They regard non-Buddhists, evil persons, bodhisattvas, and arhats as equal and without distinction.
Why, then, is the bodhisattva praised? The answer is: "Although the Buddha is without self (*ātman*) and without [mine],..."
Regarding all phenomena, his mind is free from attachment to either aversion or affection. Out of compassion for sentient beings, he guides them all with a heart of great kindness and mercy;
thus, he distinguishes virtuous people and offers them praise. Furthermore, he seeks to shatter the aspirations of evil Māras by means of this praise from the Buddha.
Consequently, immeasurable sentient beings come to love and delight in the Bodhisattva, honoring and making offerings to him. Hereafter...
All have accomplished the Buddha-way; for this reason, the Buddhas praise the Bodhisattvas. How do they praise them?
Because the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, throughout kalpas long ago, has been able to contemplate all dharmas as ultimately empty, and has also possessed great compassion for sentient beings.

He practices the patience of enduring beings (*sattvakṣānti*) while not perceiving sentient beings; he practices the patience of enduring dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) while not clinging to any dharmas. Although...
Knowing that *nirvāṇa* is the unsurpassed, ultimate reality, they do not realize it for themselves.

Although they know that sentient beings are like illusions and magical transformations, they are nonetheless able to initiate the actions of body, speech, and mind. One may say that their aspirations are vast and expansive, and that they possess great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
To perform such deeds is truly rare. Now that we have seen this, the World-Honored One has praised its inconceivability.

Having deliberated upon his great majestic power and virtue, and considering the matters of cause and effect that benefit devas and humans, they further wished for these to be extended into the future;
therefore, they requested him to speak of them. When the World-Honored One preached the Dharma, it did not go beyond discourses on giving, discourses on morality, and discourses on rebirth in heaven.
Correct cultivation is called the cause; that which has already been attained is called the fruit. The subsequent sections clarify cause and effect by way of humans and devas.
If representing the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), there are the three stages of worthiness (*trayaḥ pūrvayogāḥ*) and the ten stages (*daśabhūmayaḥ*).

Examining the current scriptural divisions, regarding those capable of receiving [the teaching] upon their crowns—such as Buddhas, *devas*, and *nāgas*—the "receiving" (*pratigraha*) refers to taking the Buddha’s words into one's heart; it is so named because the human body uses the crown of the head [to receive].

[He] is the Honored One. Now, to say "received upon the crown" signifies the utmost respect and the deepest faith. If the Buddha’s words were not to be accepted, how could one speak of them being received?

△ Second, the World-Honored One provides the answer, which has two parts. First, the Tathāgata’s formal response, divided into three sections. First, the admonition to listen and the permission to speak.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Pukhang and the fourfold assembly, saying: "Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall briefly explain for you the matters concerning the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha’s bestowal of merit and blessings upon humans and devas."
The instruction to "listen attentively" refers to this inconceivable matter of majestic spiritual power and compassionate grace.

As for "blessing" (*fú*): it is the favor of the celestial way toward the virtuous. To be virtuous is to accord with Heaven; thus, harmonious vital energy daily gathers and settles. [The character] is composed of "to show" (*shì*) and "fullness" (*fǔ*); one should grasp its meaning through this synthesis.
As for "virtue" (*dé*): it is innate goodness. A straightforward mind constitutes virtue; it is the original rectitude of one's nature and destiny.
The merit of study lies in its ease and simplicity. The *Hongfan* enumerates the five blessings: longevity, wealth, nobility, peace and security, and the love of virtue;
it concludes with a peaceful death. The *Analects* demonstrates the five virtues: gentleness, kindness, respectfulness, frugality, and yielding.

Within our own teaching, according to the *Caturmahārājakāyika-sūtra*, on the six days of fasting, the messengers, the princes, and the heavenly kings diligently observe sentient beings to bestow auspiciousness upon those who practice [virtue].

Inauspicious. If on this day one purifies the mind and observes the fast, returning with reverence to worship and make offerings to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, the various devas will dispatch benevolent spirits to guard the gates and doors.
Malevolent epidemics and all manner of evil influences, as well as secret plots, shall be extinguished. There will be no evil dreams at night;
officials, thieves, bandits, floods, fires, and calamities shall ultimately fail to cause harm. At the time of approaching death, they shall welcome [the deceased]...

The spirit ascends to be born in the heavens. In the heavens, through the power of merit, all that is wished for manifests spontaneously. Within the palaces of the seven treasures, one dwells wherever the mind desires.
When their life ends, they descend to be born into the families of marquises and kings, with a radiant countenance that brings joy to the hearts of all who behold them.

Encountering the Buddha and meeting the Dharma, one will surely attain Nirvana; all this is brought about by the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Deeds, by the gathering of the mind and the restraining of desires, and by the Six Fasting Days.
These are the five benefits for humans and devas that produce merit. △ Second, receiving the instruction and requesting to hear it.
Puguang addressed [the Buddha], saying: “So be it, World-Honored One. We wish and desire to hear [it]. As written.
△ Third, the extensive explanation of the benefits, which has two parts: first, the Teacher of the Doctrine explains the benefits;

second, Puguang requests the name of the sutra. The first part further has two sections: first, the extensive explanation of the matters of the benefits; second, the summary of the power of majestic virtue.

Within the section on the benefits, there are again two parts: first, a general demonstration of the benefits of hearing the name and so forth; second, a specific demonstration of the benefits for those with chronic illnesses and others.
The first part also has two sections: first, obtaining merit through making offerings; second, receiving retribution for disparagement. Within the first of these, there are four sub-sections;
the first is the merit of hearing the name, praising, and prostrating.
The Buddha told Bodhisattva Puguang: "In future ages, if there are good men or good women who hear the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha—
whether they join their palms, praise him, prostrate to him, or cherish him with longing—
such persons shall transcend the retribution for sins spanning thirty kalpas."
Those who cultivate goodness are called good men and women; those who commit evil are called evil men and women. As King Yama instructs the offenders:
"Go now and become children in human households; you must be filial and obedient, repaying the kindness of your parents.
In the prime of your youth, you should endure evil and practice good, placing firm faith in the Triple Gem, observing the precepts, and honoring the Way."
Cultivate all manner of merit; do not commit evil again, lest you return here once more. Now, goodness is the natural, refined essence of human nature.
When it manifests, its excellence is beyond words; there is not a single instance that does not issue from within.

Therefore, following the character for "beauty" (美), one adds the radical for "mind" (心) to form "humanity" (仁), showing people the learning of the Heavenly Root. Furthermore, by adding two more strokes to the character for "man" (人), one forms "humanity" (仁).

What is this? It refers to the "mind" (citta). When one utters good words, others respond with goodness as well. Since the minds of people share a common ground, one can perceive the mind of Heaven (the divine) therein.
Now, it is said that by hearing the name of Kṣitigarbha and joining one’s palms, one obtains the merit of such goodness.
Indeed, the name of this Great Being (Mahāsattva) is adorned with myriads of practices and myriads of virtues; from his very first [vow]...

The filial thought of remembering to save one’s mother is the very source from which the resolve to rescue beings from suffering throughout the six realms arises; it is already profound, vast, and boundless.
Even were one to attempt to distinguish its manifestations over the eleven great kalpas that have passed until now, one would not reach their end even if an entire kalpa were exhausted.

Therefore, acts such as joining the palms all transcend the sins of kalpas. It is like Jīvaka grasping a blade of grass; there is nothing that is not medicine, capable of universally curing all ailments.
Possessing everything in full, it is like a wish-fulfilling jewel that completely fulfills all vows. Joining the palms symbolizes the oneness of the provisional and the real:
the nine realms are the provisional, while the Buddha-realm is the real. Now that this has been revealed and manifested, the living beings and the Buddha are of one essence. This...
There is the offering of physical action (*kāyakarman*). Or, one praises the subtle and wondrous marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), or extols the profound and vast merit;
this is the offering of verbal action (*vākkarman*). Bowing the head to the ground with all five limbs touching the earth, one realizes that their nature is empty and quiescent.

When the resonance of the practitioner meets the path of the Buddha, this constitutes the universal offering of the three actions (*trikarma*). With yearning and devotion, the mind remains uninterrupted from moment to moment, or one contemplates the majestic virtue of the Bodhisattva.
Or one may express one’s own grief; this is the offering of mental action (*manas-karman*).
Such a person—even by merely hearing the name [of the Buddha] and joining their palms as described above—is able to transcend the grave offenses of thirty *kalpas*.
Is this not the inconceivable power of majestic spiritual authority and compassionate grace? 2. The Merit of Sculpting and Painting Images.
Puguang, if there are good men or good women who, by means of colored paintings, or earth, stone, glue, lacquer,

gold, silver, copper, or iron, fashion the image of this Bodhisattva, and gaze upon it or prostrate before it even once— such persons shall be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three a hundred times,
never falling into the evil realms. Even should their heavenly merit be exhausted and they descend to be born among humans, they will still...
To act as a king is not to lose the great benefit.
Regarding the initial cultivation of causes, such as painting and so forth, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "If, for the sake of the Buddha, one establishes various images...
and so on. "Painting" (*cai*) refers to color; it means using the five colors to depict the marks of the hundred blessings. [This is done with] earth, stone, and glue...
Regarding lacquer: some are fashioned into images by molding pure clay, while others are crafted into forms by skillfully carving hard stone.

According to the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, the use of glue is not permitted (in this land, there are two types of glue: from ox-hide and from fish intestines); to use them would incur the offense of "loss of intent.

However, as for the use [of glue] mentioned in this sūtra, it refers to tree resin used in foreign lands (such as *baili* [polygonatum barbatum]). Some say it is soybean juice (the *Bencao* mentions black beans).
It may serve as a substitute for animal glue. Even if Guangzhai Monastery permits the use of ox-hide glue, it remains an impure substance that will ultimately yield impure karmic retribution.

This is because painted images without glue will have their colors flake off over time; and just as cloth without lacquer lacks durability, the physical form [of the image] will not be firm and stable.
Among these requisites for constructing an image, those that must never be omitted are gold, silver, copper, and iron.
Although their prices differ according to whether they are expensive or cheap, their substance is equally firm and hard. When cast into images, they provide eternal adornment.
*Vardhana* is translated as "gold. According to the *Mahā-śāstra*, it is said to be extracted from mountain stone, sand, and red copper. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states:
Gold has five colors, of which yellow gold is the foremost; it does not change even when buried for a long time, nor does it become light despite being smelted a hundred times.
*Ārūpa* is translated as "silver. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is produced from scorched stones. The *Erya* states that white metal is called silver. Copper is "red metal."
It is next in rank to silver. The *Ārūli jīng* (Arulika Sūtra) states: *duōlì lùhē*. The commentary notes that "the three metals" refers to gold, silver, and copper.
[The character for *tóng* (copper)] is composed of the radical for metal and the character for "same. Its color resembles gold, yet its qualities differ greatly.

Ancient scribes created characters based on the underlying meaning to demonstrate that one cannot judge a person by their outward appearance. *Tiě* (iron) means "black gold. It is composed of the character *yí*. To take...

One should always temper iron with intention. Just as iron, when tempered over a long period, attains its refined purity and remains undiminished even after a hundred smeltings—thereby being called "true steel"—iron is the lowest among the precious metals, yet it is most widely utilized; thus, the benefit to the people cannot be dispensed with.
The above clarifies the creation of images. According to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, impure money is unfit for the creation of images; it may be exchanged [for pure currency].
One should use pure money acquired in accordance with the Dharma to create an image. Furthermore, it is not permitted to create a half-body image;
such a form lacks auspicious characteristics and leads to falling back into the cycle of birth and death. Regarding the creation of this Bodhisattva:

for anyone who gazes upon or prostrates before it, others may use these various materials to fashion the sublime form of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. Should there be virtuous men or women who see it, or even those who merely gaze upon it...
Regarding prostration: there are those who gaze upon [an image] and prostrate. This clarifies that while the cultivation of causes may be minimal, the attainment of the fruit is exceedingly great.
Such persons—who create images and gaze upon them with prostration—all undergo one hundred rebirths in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and never again fall into the evil realms.
This is because the creation of images is fundamentally a celestial activity; therefore, it brings about rebirth in the heavens. As for creating...

The *Sūtra on the Merit of Image-Making* states: If a person, at the time of death, makes a vow to create an image—even one as small as a grain of barley (*yava*)—they can eliminate the sins of birth and death committed over eighty billion kalpas throughout the three periods of time. There are eleven merits [to this act].
1. One’s eyes shall be clear and pure in every lifetime. 2. One shall be born in places free from evil. 3. One shall always be born into noble families. 4.
One’s body shall be like the color of purple-polished gold. 5. One shall abound in rare treasures and playthings. 6. One shall be born into a family of the wise and virtuous.

7. One shall be born to become a king. 8. One shall become a Cakravartin King with a golden wheel. 9. One shall be born in the Brahma Heaven. 10. One shall not fall into the evil realms. 11. One shall be reborn hereafter.

△ Second: On the Merit of Reverently Paying Homage to the Image Out of Weariness with Ugliness and Illness.

"Ugly" (*chǒu*) means foul and filthy; "vulgar" (*lòu*) means base and wicked. In this region, during the time of the Yellow Emperor, there was Mǔmǔ; in the state of Qí, there was the Woman of Wúyán;

They oppress the virtuous and good. They construct their rhetoric from falsehoods and unleash their venom without cause. At first, they employ light words of mockery and incitement;

It is like the current of the Yangtze River, which overflows from a jar’s mouth; or like a tree reaching the heavens, whose sprout first emerges from a mere hair’s breadth.

They are discharged throughout the long night of existence, merely defiling one’s body and speech. When one considers this future retribution, how can one not be cautious? △ Second, revealing the censure and disparagement.
