Through ignorance and craving, one commits the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds of the middling grade, thereby inducing this rebirth in this realm. Within these two realms, one remains for vast eons before finally becoming a human being.
The word "even" (*zòng*) used here is not a term of absolute certainty. Even if one were to regain a human body, residual karma would still remain未尽 (unexhausted).
Because of having previously severed the wealth of the Dharma, one now experiences the retribution of poverty;

because of having formerly disparaged the honored countenance, this invites a lowly and base birth; furthermore, with the various sense faculties impaired and deficient, one is thereby bound by the nine fetters.
The mind proceeds from darkness into darkness, following suffering to further suffering. The *Mahāyāna-śāstra* states that the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati said:
"Those who slander the Mahāyāna teachings will certainly fall into the evil realms. They shall be scorched by extreme agony; such is the certainty of the retribution for their karmic offenses.
Even when they emerge from hell, they will again undergo other evil retributions: their faculties will always be deficient and deformed, and they will never hear the sound of the Dharma."
Even if they should hear it, they will again give rise to slander of the Dharma; by the causes and conditions of slandering the Dharma, they will fall back into hell.
Alas! Is it not necessary to be cautious? △ Second, the conclusion by way of comparison.
Therefore, Puguang, if even disparaging the offerings made by others results in such retribution, how much more so for those who give rise to perverse views and destroy them?

Thus, these two characters [“disparage” and “destroy”] lead directly to a perpetual fall into Avīci Hell, where one undergoes rebirths for immeasurable kalpas; what need is there to mention escaping from it? This is virtuous.
If one receives offerings from people yet reviles and slanders them, one will still incur calamity for many kalpas; how much more so for those who give rise to separate evil views?
For instance, the Mlecchas destroyed the Buddha-dharma, and their sin was even more severe than this. Thus, the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* says:
Those who slander are called fools; they fall into evil realms and undergo various sufferings and afflictions.
Furthermore, because they are held in contempt by all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—they should recognize the sin of slander.
It truly stands at the forefront of all transgressions. △ Second, specifically showing the benefits for those with chronic illnesses and so forth, in five parts.

First, from the evil signs of chronic illness up to the retribution felt through the recitation of the Five Fasts; this section is divided into three. First, showing the evil signs within the illness, which is further divided into two.
First, showing the signs.
Furthermore, Puguang, if in future ages there are men or women who have long lain upon their beds and pillows, seeking neither life nor death, yet finding neither possible;
or who see evil spirits and deceased relatives in their dreams at night; or who wander upon perilous paths, or suffer from frequent nightmares and travel with ghosts and spirits;
and as the days, months, and years pass, they become increasingly emaciated and ill, crying out in suffering amidst their sleep, filled with misery and grief.
Regarding "not delighting [in the body]":
the *Buddha-bhaiṣajya-sūtra* states that within the human body there are originally four diseases: first, earth; second, water; third, fire; and fourth, wind.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) constitute the body and are constantly mutually afflicting one another; within each of these four elements, there are one hundred and one diseases.

It arises thus: there are two hundred and two types of cold-natured illnesses, arising from the elements of water and wind; there are two hundred and two types of heat-natured illnesses, arising from the elements of earth and fire.
This is because the four great elements are difficult to harmonize and the six viscera become disordered. Thus, though possessing a retribution body, one suddenly becomes afflicted by disease.
Now, for years on end and for many months, one lies prostrate upon a bed and mat, unable to rise or move about. This is truly a matter of slaughter.
Due to the lingering effects of past transgressions, they suffer from chronic illness and distress. They long for life but lack the power to live;

they long for death but find it difficult to die. They dream of malevolent spirits and the like; their minds are clouded and disordered by the pressure of the disease, and they experience many nightmares at night.

The agitation and palpitations have increased further. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* elucidates four types of dreams: first, those arising from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance; second, those that are premonitions of good or evil;

third, those resulting from the imbalance of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); and fourth, those involving the roaming among former acquaintances. Your current dream of an evil spirit is a premonition of an evil omen.
Furthermore, seeing your family members is the roaming among former acquaintances. Wandering through perilous paths indicates an imbalance of the four great elements. As for the spirits...
"Roaming as a spirit" refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance. *Wusuman* (烏蘇慢) means "aversion. This is an inauspicious occurrence during sleep that accords with human sentiments.
The *Lunheng* states: "To lie down in aversion and fail to awaken is called 'yak-mei' (魘寐). To remain in deep sleep without waking for a long time, spirits and ghosts roam together;
as the years pass and the physical frame becomes exhausted and debilitated—*kwang* (尫, pronounced wāng)—it refers to weakness, that is, emaciation and illness."

"Human beings suffer from *rājayakṣman* (the 'royal consumption'), which refers to the five types of exhaustion and seven types of injury. As for those who cry out in pain during sleep, they take the body as an instrument of suffering;
internally it is like a fragile earthenware jar. The four great elements are unstable and hollow, mutually conflicting with one another.
Having received a physical form in the human realm during this age of defilement, they possess a counterfeit body and dwell in a state of dread within the immeasurable darkness."
Spirits and deities, as well as ancestral kin and their retinues—whether dwelling in houses or temples, or perched upon mountains and hills—all sentient beings alike respond with reverence.
Consequently, the spirits become obscured and darkened, and consciousness grows dim and confused; even in waking and sleeping, there is much terror.
Thus, one finds no peace within while asleep, crying out in suffering at dawn and dusk, and the heart is oppressed and distressed by constant agitation.
The stillness, the gloom, and the desolation are all manifestations of suffering within illness. △ Second, the explanation of the underlying meaning:

These are all matters addressed in the *Karmapatha-śāstra*, where the relative gravity [of the karma] has not yet been determined. Sometimes it is difficult to relinquish one’s life-span, or sometimes recovery is impossible.
To the eyes of ordinary men and women, such matters cannot be discerned.
This explains the ill omens of long-term illness; they arise from the karmic enmity of the paths of action. Therefore, the Buddha told King Ajātaśatru:
"All phenomena are characterized by conditions and oppositions. Whatever people do, each sees the results of their own conduct."
"Performing good brings a good retribution; performing evil brings an evil retribution. Therefore, Great King, you should abandon evil and follow good.
Now that the conditions of your karma have converged, it is likely that neither your life nor your person can escape.

However, as the lightness or gravity of the offense has not yet been determined, how could one immediately decide whether a person shall live or die? Thus, even those who ought to die may find it difficult to relinquish their life-span at once."
Those who ought not yet to die still linger in such a state, difficult to recover from;

this is likely due to curses cast through the five musical tones, or perhaps because the souls of karmic enemies from the three periods of time have been summoned, their spirits bound by the Yin authorities, causing calamity to arise in the world of Yang.
How could the vulgar and narrow eyes of worldly men discern such matters of karmic retribution? △ Second, explaining how cultivating merit brings liberation from sin (2).
First, the correct demonstration of the method; second, the illustration of the benefits. The first part is divided into three sections.
First, reciting the sutra before an image: one should simply recite this sutra once aloud before an image of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

If a person does not carefully regulate their lifestyle and diet, they may be afflicted by symptoms such as chills and fevers; in such cases, worldly physicians and medicinal prescriptions can provide a cure.
However, the illness that now arises from the retribution of evil karma must rely upon the power of the Dharma to be dispelled. For the mind of the Buddhas has compassion as its essence;
they act as the King of Physicians, skillfully healing the physical and mental ailments of sentient beings, and this sutra serves as the medicine of the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva is one who attends to the sick; therefore, one must recite the sutras before the image.
However, even a single recitation is like a single grain of elixir that transforms iron into gold, or a single word of ultimate truth that transforms the ordinary into the holy.
Why wait for many recitations? △ Second, relinquishing goods for the sake of the sick.
Alternatively, one may take objects dear to the sick person—whether clothing, precious gems, gardens, or dwellings—and before the sick person, proclaim in a loud voice:
"I, [Name], for the sake of this sick person, in the presence of the sutras and images, renounce these various items;
or I shall make offerings to the sutras and images, or fashion images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or construct stupas and temples, or light oil lamps."
Lamps. Or one may offer them for the support of the Sangha (chángzhù).
There are two kinds of illness among worldly people: the four great elements are the illnesses of the body, and the three poisons are the illnesses of the mind.

The illness of the body can be treated with medicine, but the illness of the mind requires the cultivation of merit. As the *Dharmapada* says: "When a person performs good or evil, calamity or blessing follows."
Although humans may undergo repeated cycles of birth and death, they cannot escape them; therefore, one must cultivate merit to ward them off.
As for those objects of affection that are beautiful, exquisite, and precious—now one must sever attachment to them, thereby cutting the very root of suffering.

Clothing is worn to adorn the body, jewels and treasures are amassed to achieve wealth, gardens and estates are provided for the pleasure of recreation, and houses and dwellings are established to settle one's children.
"Whatever belongs to my descendants shall all be for my own use; it must not be lacking. This clarifies the items to be relinquished. Regarding the recitation of the relinquishment of goods:

when addressed to a low-ranking patient, one proclaims the relinquishment of the goods; when addressed to a high-ranking patient, this is done so that they may know the merit of acting as a substitute donor, and thus remember and hold it in mind without forgetting.
As the Sūtra says: "All other things are entirely dispersed, yet this King of Vows alone remains."

This refers to "mutual abandonment. In the Sanskrit language it is *namaḥ*; here it is translated as "So-and-so" (*amuka*). "Jia" (甲) is the first of the Heavenly Stems (*tiangan*) and the number one;

it does not preclude the subsequent sequence of "Yi" (乙), "Bing" (丙), and so forth. Alternatively, regarding the method of cultivating merit through making offerings—such as offering to scriptures and images—the Dharma is the Mother of the Buddhas.
The Buddha arises from the Dharma; the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time all make offerings to the Dharma.

It is like the physical remains of the World-Honored One; though fashioned from clay or wood, those who behold them all conceive the thought that they are the Buddha, no different from the actual one.

Therefore, those who make offerings gain merit. Regarding those who create images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, according to the *Sūtra on the Merit of Making Images*, their virtue is exceedingly great.
Now, I shall briefly cite one or two points. The Sūtra says: "If the people of the world can make a Buddha..."
As for the physical image: in every place of birth throughout successive lifetimes, one’s eyes will be pure and clear, and one’s countenance upright and handsome.

One’s body, hands, and feet will always be exceptionally soft and supple. Even when born in the heavens, one will likewise be pure and clear, the most excellent among the devas, possessing the color of purple-polished gold and an incomparable beauty.
The merit of creating an image of a Bodhisattva is likewise so; as for stupas and temples, it is as described previously.
The *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states: "By constructing stūpas and temples, one will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven after death.
Regarding those who offer oil lamps, the *Dīpa-dāna-sūtra* records that the Buddha told Śāriputra: 'If there are people who offer lamps as an act of devotion before stūpas, temples, or images...'"
Even with as little as a small lamp-flame, such merit can only be known by a Buddha.
Becoming a single Buddha, one gives all beloved things and so forth in total to the world and makes offerings to the Sangha;

this statement refers to practicing even a single type of deed to evoke a superior retribution, rather than requiring that every single thing be performed. △ Third, liberation from sin and knowledge of the life-span.
In this manner, one should address the patient three times, ensuring they hear and understand.

Even if their various consciousnesses have dispersed and their life-force is about to end—whether it be for one day, two days, three days, four days, or up to seven days—one should recite with a loud voice and chant the scriptures aloud.
After such a person passes away, even their accumulated calamities and grave offenses, including those as severe as the five *ānantarya* sins, will be forever [extinguished].
One attains liberation. In whatever place one is born, one always knows one's past lives.

When giving away possessions on behalf of the sick, one must certainly recite the "Three White" [formula] so that those who hear it may understand clearly in their hearts, deeply realizing that I possess such merit.
"Hypothetically speaking" (jialing) means that by virtue of this merit from giving, the illness shall depart and the body shall find peace.

What could be more auspicious than this? Even if one’s great destiny is difficult to evade and worldly ties are forever severed, at the moment when the various consciousnesses disperse and breath ceases, one should for seven days chant aloud and recite the sutras.

That person will surely be liberated from heavy transgressions and ascend to a higher realm. Regarding the "dispersion of the various consciousnesses," the *Womb Sutra* (*Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*) states: At that time...

The World-Honored One, wishing to manifest the destinations toward which consciousness proceeds— consciousness of the path, consciousness of the mundane, conditioned consciousness, unconditioned consciousness, outflowing consciousness,
non-outflowing consciousness, consciousness of the flower, consciousness of the fruit, retributive consciousness, non-retributive consciousness, consciousness of devas,
consciousness of nāgas, and so forth, up to the consciousness of humans and non-humans, and reaching upward to the consciousness of the twenty-eighth heaven and downward to the ground of no refuge.

"Consciousness of the prison" (the text). This is a general reference. If one were to speak specifically of a single individual, it should refer to the eight consciousnesses as the "various consciousnesses.
"The vital breath is exhausted" means that what is called wind comes first and fire follows, and the soul-spirit departs;

the body becomes empty and cold, and the physical frame falls into desolation. The *Zongjing* asks: On the day the various sense organs perish and when consciousness migrates and leaves, one abandons this...
Therefore, the body separately receives other material forms. As for the characteristics of the consciousness that comes and goes, the answer is as stated in the *Vijñāna-pravṛtti-sūtra*:
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla, "The movement, transition, cessation, coming, and going of consciousness is like the element of wind (*vāyu-dhātu*):
it is without color and without form, and cannot be manifested; yet it can set all things in motion and manifest various shapes to the multitude... This person...

Below: This clarifies the transformation of obstacles and the taking of rebirth. One attains eternal liberation from past calamities, heavy sins, and the five crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).

This clearly demonstrates the extraordinary excellence of the merit of giving and the profound efficacy of the Triple Gem. Not only does one escape punishment and receive a favorable birth, but one can also constantly know past lives;
naturally gaining deep insight into cause and effect, with the distinction between sin and merit made manifest, one proceeds from light to light and will surely ascend to Buddhahood.
The fruits have been explained. △ Second, the benefits are further illustrated by way of comparison:
"How much more so, good sons and good daughters, for those who personally copy this sutra, or cause others to copy it;
or who personally mold or paint images of Bodhisattvas, even to the point of teaching others to mold or paint them—the karmic rewards they receive will surely result in great benefit."

The term "kuàng" (況) means "to compare" or "to illustrate. It implies that if the merit obtained by acting as a substitute for someone else in giving and practicing charity is already so great, how much more so when one practices it oneself—how can the former even be compared to the latter?
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra* clarifies that there are ten types of Mahāyāna practice, the first of which is transcribing [the scriptures].
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "In this degenerate age, one should transcribe the scriptural volumes and also encourage others to do the same."

To write [these teachings] is to be fully capable of understanding them and exhausting their profound meanings and flavors. Regarding the creation of images, the *Sūtra on the Making of Images* states:
"To fashion images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas brings forth immeasurable merit that is inexhaustible and beyond calculation.

Even the waters of the rivers and seas within the four continents could be measured in bushels, yet the merit of creating an image of a Buddha is so vast that it exceeds even that. It is exceedingly great.
The rivers, seas, and waters of the four continents are surpassed tenfold [by the merit of this]. Those born in future ages shall constantly protect the Buddha-way and fashion images of the Buddha;
after death, they shall no longer enter the various evil realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
Therefore, the retribution they obtain will surely result in great benefit. △ Third, the conclusion and exhortation to cultivate merit.
Therefore, Puguang, if you see anyone reading or reciting this sutra, or even praising it for a single thought-moment,
or showing it reverence, you must employ hundreds of thousands of skillful means to exhort such people to apply themselves with diligence and not retreat;
they will thereby attain inconceivable merits of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions in both the future and the present.
Building upon the preceding merits, it says "therefore. To read according to the title of the sutra is because one has not yet attained mastery;

to recite by way of the original text is because the phrasing has been mastered. Is there a distinction between sharp and dull faculties, or between long and short durations of time? This sutra is the *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra*.
The word "this" (*shi*) is used because the whole body is itself [the Buddha], with no duality whatsoever. Thus, the present school clarifies this through the six stages of realization (*liu ji*).
It is so. For the entire mind is this sutra; outside the sutra there is no mind. The entire sutra is the mind; outside the mind there is no sutra. Therefore it is said:

"If one praises this sutra for even a single thought-moment," whereas previously it was stated that disparaging or making offerings [to it] for a single thought-moment still incurs calamity for many kalpas, praising this sutra for a single thought-moment will surely evoke merit for many lifetimes. One should reverently read and recite it.
One who does so shall obtain merit equal to that of offering praise. You must descend. The Buddha exhorted Puguang:
"You should employ hundreds of thousands of skillful means to encourage those who read, recite, praise, and pay homage to this [sūtra]. As the Mahāvaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra says:
'After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if there is a Dharma master who skillfully accords with the inclinations and desires of others to preach the Dharma for them...'"

If one can cause Bodhisattvas who study the Mahāyāna, as well as the great assembly, to give rise to even a single hair’s breadth of a joyful heart, or even to shed but a single drop of tears, know that all of this is the Buddha’s spiritual power (*ṛddhibala*).

By this, one can verify that those who recite, praise, and pay homage [to this teaching] do so through the Buddha’s spiritual power; how then could one not know that this is the Buddha’s spiritual power? Therefore, it must be so.
He then exhorted him: "Be diligent in mind and do not retreat. As stated in the *Dṛḍhamati-sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there is a person of good heart and virtuous intent who hears the Buddha’s clear Dharma and listens with a single-minded focus—if they can do so for one day, or if they cannot for one day;
if they can do so for half a day, or if they cannot for half a day; if they can do so for one watch (muhūrta), or if they cannot for one watch; if they can do so for half a watch..."
It cannot last even half a moment; it may last but a brief instant. Yet its merit is immeasurable and beyond calculation.
You should explain this extensively to the assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and the lay populace.

If such is the case for merely listening to it briefly, how much more so for those who show reverence, how much more so for those who offer praise, and how much more so for those who read and recite it? Therefore, I exhort you.
Exert yourself with diligence and do not retreat, for you shall obtain inconceivable merit in both the present and the future.

△ Second, seeing ghosts in dreams and sleep, which is divided into three parts: first, dreaming of evil omens; second, being commanded to recite the sutras; third, the benefits gained by both the living and the deceased.
The first part is further divided into three sections, beginning with the manifestation of signs.
Furthermore, Puguang, if in future ages there are sentient beings who, whether in dreams or while asleep,
see various ghosts and spirits, as well as various forms, and experience grief or weeping, sorrow or sighing, or fear and terror;
The dreams within this context differ from those mentioned previously. The former were the karmic responses of one's own person;
these, however, are remotely associated with the entanglements of the *skandhas*. Both are indeed real dreams. The Real Man Sun said: "All dreams are conditioned by causes.

When the dream-soul is occupied with external objects, its spirit reaches the physical body and cannot circulate freely. Thus, at night, the soul and the dream engage in a hollow struggle, manifesting portents of what is to come."
Auspicious. To bring misfortune as a retribution for misfortune. Thus, Master Lü of Donglai said: "The engagement of forms constitutes affairs; the encounter of spirits constitutes dreams.
Now, because there is both the engagement of forms and the encounter of spirits, there are dreams of affairs. According to the *Zhouli*, one divines from six types of omens, including dreams.
Dreams are of six types: those of auspiciousness, those of misfortune, those of ordinary daily life, those of astonishment, those of joy upon awakening from a thought, and those of fear.
"Sleeping" (*mai*) means "obscurity"; it is the closing of the eyes and the withdrawal of the spirit. As Zhuangzi said: "In sleep, the *hun* souls commune.
To see ghosts and spirits therein refers to relatives from many lifetimes who manifest their forms by entrusting them to dreams; this is the dream of ordinary daily life.

This is the dream of one who dwells in rectitude. As for various forms—men and women, old and young being different, and the countenances of humans and ghosts being diverse—the sounds of lamentation and so forth are dreams of astonishment and terror.
According to medical texts, these arise because yin qi has taken possession; thus one sees ghosts and spirits.
When lung qi is excessive, one dreams of weeping and crying out, or of flying and soaring. When heart qi is excessive, one dreams of joy and laughter.
It is a state of fear and dread. This present situation is brought about by one's own kin; it has nothing to do with the reality or unreality of the Yin and Yang realms.
To wail, lament, and sigh in grief is the manner of a living person imploring the pity of a ghost. △ Second, the explanation of the underlying meaning.
These are all one's parents, sons, daughters, younger brothers, younger sisters, spouses, and kinsmen from one lifetime, ten lifetimes, a hundred lifetimes, or a thousand lifetimes past.
They remain in the evil realms, unable to escape, with no place where they can hope for rescue through the power of merit.
One should inform these former kin and have them employ skillful means, vowing to deliver them from the evil paths.
Because they give birth to many kinsmen, they manifest in various forms. Before the birth has even occurred, how could one possibly have thoughts of parents, sons, or daughters?

"Brother" (*di*) refers to a younger sibling; it signifies a sequence that follows upward. "Sister" (*mei*) means "dusk"; it is like the sun having just begun to set—having passed through but a short time, it is still dim.
"Husband and wife" (*fūqī*) carries the meaning of being a matched pair. Among the common people, the term for the female partner is simply "wife."
"Wife" signifies equality. Since the husband is of low status, he is insufficient for a respectful title; thus, "equal" (*qi*) refers to their parity.
Residing in the realms of evil, whether submerged in the underworld or fallen among the ranks of ghosts, they traverse a long journey with little aid toward liberation.
Having lost all hope of rescue through merit and blessings, they now cry out from afar to their kin of many lifetimes—this is the ultimate state of desolation for these spirits.

One contemplates the suffering of those seeking existence. Therefore, it is known that performing meritorious deeds for deceased parents and others is like sending provisions to someone in a distant land.

However, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "If one cultivates merit and practices giving on behalf of the deceased, those born into the realm of hungry ghosts may receive the benefit of that merit, because those ghosts are aware of their remorse for their previous stinginess and greed; thus, at the time of the offering, they..."
They were filled with joy. [The Master thought: "If they had been reborn in other realms, it would likely have been difficult for them to obtain this power.
Now these people seek to employ skillful means, wishing to escape the evil paths; I fear they may belong to the class of hungry ghosts. △ Second, the command to recite the sutra.
Puguang, by means of your supernatural powers, dispatch these attendants to stand before the images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
where they shall, with a sincere mind, read this sutra themselves three times or seven times, or request others to do so.
For what reason did Puguang employ his supernatural powers to dispatch his kinsmen to recite the sutra?

It is because among the foolish people of this world, those who recognize the debt of gratitude are few; even toward their own six types of relatives during their lifetime, they often show no regard, let alone toward relatives separated by several generations.
Even if there were those who did think of them, since they have never set eyes on them, even if they appear in dreams, their thoughts would not reach this point. Therefore—
An imperial decree was issued to Puguang to provide secret assistance through supernatural power, so that [the deceased] might quickly be enabled to recollect [their past lives].

They were to be made to reverently face images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, either reading the sutras themselves or requesting others to read them. As for why the number of recitations reaches three or seven:
these are all yang numbers. Three is the number of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity; by doubling the sequence from one, the Three Powers (sancai) are complete.
One becomes two: this is the generation of Yin from Yang. Two generates three: this is the harmonious blending of Yin and Yang.
Three generates the myriad things; their continuous production is inexhaustible. Seven is the number of the minor Yang. This is likewise a transformed manifestation of two and three:
two plus five makes seven. Advancing to nine constitutes the old Yang. It transforms the ghosts of the underworld into the Yin realm, giving birth to human beings.
This is the Yang world of Heaven; therefore, only the numbers three and seven are taken, while six and eight are not.
This is because even numbers represent the "Khan" hexagram’s state of entrapment, which is not the Way of transcending the dark. △ Third, the benefits gained through survival and extinction.
Thus, when the sound of this sutra has been heard for as many times as there are members of these evil realms, one shall attain liberation;
even in dreams, they shall never again be seen.
"Liberation" means being free from the evil realms. One will either be reborn among the heavens or humans, or advance upon the noble path of the Three Vehicles.
Once one's deceased kin have attained such transcendence, they will no longer manifest their forms within one's dreams or sleep. △ Third, seeking repentance from those of low station:
Part One, identifying the person capable of performing the repentance.
Furthermore, Puguang, if in future ages there are those of lowly station— whether slaves, servants,
or even those who lack personal freedom— who become aware of their past karma and desire to perform repentance:

Regarding those of lowly status and the like, the *Bianyi jing* (Sūtra on the Meaning of Discernment) states: "There are five things that constantly lead to birth in a base and lowly condition, becoming a servant or slave to others:
first, arrogance and lack of respect for one's parents; second, being stubborn and lacking a sense of reverence; third, negligence and failure to pay homage to the Triple Gem;
fourth, making theft one's livelihood; and fifth, fleeing from debt without repaying it. Thus, the lowly stand in contrast to the noble.

Regarding the term "slaves" (noble and base servants), there are differences when contrasted with the masters. If we speak in terms of the four continents, in Uttarakuru in the north, there is no distinction between servants and masters;
therefore, there is no nobility or baseness. In the other three continents, however, there is nobility and baseness because of the distinctions between rulers, ministers, and commoners.
Due to this difference between masters and servants, there are distinct classes of noble and base.
In total, encompassing both the noble and the humble, there are six classes: first, the most noble among the noble, such as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and the like;
second, the next in rank among the noble, such as minor kings (*kṣudrarāja*) and the like; third, the lowest among the noble, such as the various officials and the like;
fourth, the most humble among the humble, such as palace slaves and pageboys and the like; fifth, the next in rank among the humble, such as servants and the like; sixth...
The lowest of the low refers to concubines, handmaidens, and the like. Such is the general categorization; a detailed classification would be difficult to exhaust.
Those who lack autonomy are not merely of the class of lowly slaves, but include the ranks of menial servants and gatekeepers.
They receive monthly stipends and rely daily on these for their livelihood. They come when summoned and depart at the master’s command, living entirely dependent upon his very breath.
To receive their fame and glory yet fail to follow them in practice is not the way of a man of integrity. Regarding "past karma," the Buddha told King Prasenajit:
"When ordinary people dwell in this world, whether they are noble or base, high-born or lowly, rich or poor, suffering or happy—all these results are brought about by their past actions.
If there were those in the world who were ignorant, stubborn, and lacking in discernment, would they not surely find this bitter? Moreover, they claim to have attained [their status]..."
If one possesses even a modicum of cleverness and discernment, one would not only feel pity for them, but would truly wish to liberate them.

This is most difficult. If one does not believe this interpretation, how can these two characters be explained?
These three subsequent lines clarify the meaning of "this day. According to the *Fozu Tongji*, citing the *Tiwai Jing*, it clarifies the three long fasts.

Among the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa in the south, every movement and every thought is none other than karma; there is nothing that is not a transgression.

A single moment of goodness brings immeasurable rewards of goodness; a single moment of evil brings immeasurable retributions of evil.

If the mind is unwholesome, it can only harm things; if there is goodness within, one can only accord with merit.

This is far more detrimental than a lack of merit. How much more so, then, to indulge the six sense-faculties and allow the three types of karma to be created at will?

The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa have a great causal connection with this Great Being.
"Causal connection" is merely another name for "resonance and response. "Great" means that he desires to cause them all to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

This "great benefit" is what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* refers to as immeasurable treasures; attained without seeking, they are none other than Bodhi and Nirvana.
Such great causes and conditions have not begun only today, but extend back through immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Throughout kalpas, within Jambudvīpa, he has transformed sentient beings according to their capacities through the three stages of planting, ripening, and liberation, never ceasing at any time.
This is like parents who, when their child falls into water or fire, rush about to rescue them; or like parents whose hearts are especially moved by a child who is ill.
This is because the karmic offenses of the sentient beings in Jambudvīpa are particularly heavy. Therefore, the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa...

It is only toward this Great Being that my faith remains unshakable; therefore, whether high or low, noble or humble, monastic or lay, male or female, there is not one who does not follow the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha to seek rescue from water and fire or to cure illnesses.

It is like a magnet attracting iron—the response and the invocation occur simultaneously. There is a great causal connection here, which is deeply worthy of reflection and awakening. △ Second, the extensive explanation.
Regarding the benefit of hearing:
if these sentient beings hear the name of the Bodhisattva, see the image of the Bodhisattva, or even hear three characters, five characters,
or a single verse or line of this sutra, they will experience extraordinary and sublime peace and happiness in the present life, and in future worlds, hundreds of thousands of millions...
One will be born always handsome and into a noble family.
These words regarding "hearing the name and seeing the image" clarify the efficacy of the revolving [mantra]. To trace its origin: the Buddha and sentient beings share the same body of awakening.
The nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect; this perfectly limpid awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous. When one is unaware, the wind of ignorance arises.
In movement, one falsely differentiates seeing, hearing, and knowing, confining them to limited domains and creating obstructions through separation.
Consequently, seeing does not transcend form, and hearing does not go beyond sound. Now, by turning back that false hearing, one hears the name of the Bodhisattva;
by turning back that false seeing, one beholds the image of the Bodhisattva. This causes the names heard to accord with and enter the realm of true emptiness. Name.
There is also no name. The image that is perceived is identical to the body of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). How can an image be an image?
The name is nameless, yet true hearing is perfectly clear; the image is imageless, yet true seeing is brilliantly manifest.

Thus, by taking even three characters from any part of the sutras, one immediately destroys the three delusions, eliminates the three obstructions, accomplishes the three wisdoms, and realizes the three [bodies].

Virtue manifests the three bodies (*trikāya*). Alternatively, by taking up five characters, one may, according to circumstances, shatter the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*), emerge from the five paths (*pañca-gati*), establish the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), cultivate the five powers (*pañcabala*), and perfect the five branches (*pañcāṅga*).
One verse is the transcendence of a single gate; one phrase is the perfect luminosity of a single nature.
Thus, two, four, six, or eight [verses] increase in number according to practice. In the present life, one then attains the sublime and wondrous.
Peace and happiness. Moment by moment, one flows in harmony with the original vow; thought after thought, one manifests together with the Bodhisattvas.

In future ages, one shall always possess the marks and signs of excellence, being upright, dignified, and pure. Wherever one is born, one will always arise in a noble family. As the Buddha told King Prasenajit:
"One who is benevolent, compassionate, humble, and compliant, who respects elders and loves the young, shall become a person of nobility. (The wicked...)
Those who are wicked, violent, arrogant, and self-important are considered base persons. It is further said: within the cycle of the three realms, there is no fixed status.

By accumulating goodness and practicing benevolence and harmony, one is born into a noble and honored position; by habituating oneself to evil and indulging in license, one is born into a lowly and base station.
Observing this, one must not commit evil and should cultivate oneself. When the World-Honored One had finished speaking on these benefits, △
II. Universal Wideness (Puguang) Requests the Name of the Sūtra. Part One: A Summary to Clarify the Intent of the Request.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Universal Wideness had heard the Buddha-Tathāgata extol and praise the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, he knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One, for a long time I have known that this Great Being possesses such inconceivable..."

Considering the power of spiritual transformations and the power of great vows, and wishing to cause future sentient beings to understand the benefits [thereof], he questioned the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata then granted his assent, saying, "So be it," and [the questioner] received it upon the crown of his head.

First, the narrator of the sutra describes the ritual posture; second, he states the purpose of the request. Regarding "kneeling with one knee" (*hukuei*): the *Yinyi Zhigui* (Guide to Pronunciation and Meaning) states that it does not mean placing both knees on the ground.
This is likely a descendant of the Brahma world residing among the five regions of India, north of the Pamir Mountains, among various tribes such as the Rong and Qiang.
In current sutras and vinayas, this is frequently translated as "alternating kneeling," so called because three parts of the body are raised and held upright.
"Kneeling" means placing the right knee upon the ground. Because the right knee possesses strength, one can kneel for a long duration;
it is convenient for rising and sitting, and placing it on the ground provides stability. If a bhikṣuṇī is physically weak, the Buddha permitted her to remain in a full kneeling posture (long-kuei).
As for the phrase "one who knows for a long time," this refers to those such as Puguang and Dizang, who naturally possess inconceivable supernatural powers and great vows.

By the power of his vows, he is able to know this. Having already known it, he nevertheless asks because he sincerely hopes that the Tathāgata will proclaim it within this great assembly, so that future sentient beings may know that the benefits of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva are such as these; thus he asks.
"So be it" (*evam*) is a rapid expression of assent without doubt; it refers closely to the preceding text and, more distantly, reflects back upon the entire discourse.
The preceding passage states: "You bodhisattvas should take up this sutra and widely proclaim and disseminate it.
However, at that time, King Samādhi-vaśitā merely accepted the command to circulate it but did not request the name of the sutra;

this was because he knew with certainty that the matters concerning Kṣitigarbha’s spiritual power were not yet concluded—this is the first point. Furthermore, he anticipated in advance that Puguang would again request a detailed explanation of its benefits.

This is the second point. Thus, we know that the host and guest exchange verses, each proclaiming the other’s meaning, like the rhythmic striking of a mortar and pestle, where the upper and lower parts correspond perfectly.
Therefore, the disciple’s words of "solemn acceptance" follow. △ Second, the formal request for the name of the sutra, in two parts:
first, the request.
“World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named? How should I propagate it?
These questions all express doubt. Since the preaching of this sutra, the merits of Kṣitigarbha have been praised;
with the exception of the Buddha alone, no one can equal him. Now, the reason a name exists is to summon its reality.
This is so. Now, since the true virtue of Kṣitigarbha is said to be inconceivable, he cannot be designated by means of a name.
Therefore it was asked: "By what name should this sutra be called? Since no name can be established, we must ask:
by what dharma-gate should we propagate it? Thus it was asked: "How shall I propagate it? According to the *Zhou Li*, that which flows from a spring is called...
"Fu" (Spread) refers to the currency of the world, which flows and disperses like spring water. The circulation of this sutra is likewise so.
△ Second, the response, in two parts: first, the response regarding the name of the sutra.
The Buddha told Puguang: "This sutra has three names. One is named 'The Original Vows of Kṣitigarbha'; it is also named 'The Original Deeds of Kṣitigarbha';
and it is also named 'The Sutra on the Power of Kṣitigarbha’s Original Vows'."
The title of the sutra is like threads strung together. Furthermore, regarding the "original vow" (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*): that which the mind desires is called a "vow.

To regard desire as profound and single-minded is to direct the vow outwardly, which exhausts human desire. Only the principle of Heaven (*tianli*) constitutes the desire of one's nature; this is the original mind of humanity.
Following the source, the teaching leads people to seek back to their own foundation, desiring that they cultivate the goodness that is truly desirable. And so it proceeds.
[The character] "ye" (hú jié qiè). What does it mean? It means that the mind seeks to attain [the truth]. One must bow the head to pause in contemplation;

otherwise, one will surely fall into greed and surely fall into delusion. Although this concerns both Confucianism and Buddhism, how could the fundamental vow of Kṣitigarbha be anything other than this?
It is nothing but the desire for people to return to their original, fundamental enlightened nature and together enter the secret treasury. This is the Great Being’s [vow].
This is the vow of the original time; this is the practice of the original [time], that is, the practice of former times.
Therefore, I shall rely on this and, according to the ten wonders of the Original Gate in the *Miaoxuan*, clarify the ten inconceivable aspects of the Original Ground (*mūlabhūmi*).

Only when the meaning of the text is thus fully unfolded will the various inconceivable events accomplished in the interim—the provisional manifestation—be revealed as all being the vows and practices within the Trace. This is by the power of the Original Vow.
The term "者" (zhě) is *saṃnāha* in Sanskrit, which here means "great vow. One interpretation says *saṃnāha-mahā-pratijñā* (great vow of armor).

*Saṃnāha* refers to armor (*kavaca*), and *saṃnaddha* refers to donning it; thus, it is called "donning the great armor. The correct transliteration is *cīvara-khaḍga*, translated as "armor" (*kaṅka*).
[月*冊] (pronounced *sūyù*). Nātha. Translated as "worn" or "clothing. This refers to wearing armor; in the Guhyaka section, thirty-two types of armor are explained (*et cetera*).
This is precisely the Great Vehicle’s great vow-adornment. The Sanskrit name is *sāra*, which here means "power.
The *Śarīra-skandha-āyatana-sūtra* asks: "What is the meaning of that power? It answers: "That which cannot be destroyed is power."
Regarding the meaning of "power" (*bala*): to be beneficial is the meaning of power; to possess courage is the meaning of power; to be able to attain a reliance is the meaning of power.
Now, since Kṣitigarbha first resolved his mind toward enlightenment, he has not been thwarted or destroyed by celestial Māras—this is his first power.
To benefit sentient beings wherever they may be is his second power. To possess the courage to specifically transform those in the hells is his third power. He is able to...

The six realms of existence find their refuge; this is the fourth power. Because it is the power of the original vow made by Kṣitigarbha at the time [of his initial resolve], it is called the *Sūtra on the Power of the Original Vow*.
△ Second, the conclusion regarding its circulation.
Because this Bodhisattva, since the distant past for many kalpas, has made great and profound vows to benefit sentient beings, you all should propagate [this teaching] in accordance with those vows.
This reveals that the name "Kṣitigarbha" (Earth Store) was established from his original vow; it is because of these great vows that he benefits sentient beings.
Thus it was born. For this reason, you all should also propagate it in accordance with its original vow.
Therefore, there is profound significance in the fact that the *Sutra* is titled solely after the Original Vow. △ Second, Universal Good bows and withdraws.

Having heard this, Puguang joined his palms in reverence, prostrated, and withdrew. Regarding the two characters "reverence" (gōngjìng), I have often observed that commentators leave them unexplained, causing later students and beginners not to know what meaning they are intended to convey.

Here, I shall briefly clarify the original derivation of these characters to demonstrate that the study of the mind lies precisely therein. The character *gōng* (恭) is composed of the radical for "man" (*人*) on the left and "rice" (*米*) on the right. This signifies that when one is in the presence of others, one must be as humble and cautious as if treading upon rice grains, fearing lest one should tread upon them and cause them damage. The character *jìng* (敬) is composed of the radical for "heart" (*心*) on the left and "king" (*苟*) on the right. This signifies that when one is in the presence of others, one must maintain a state of solemnity and gravity, as if attending upon a sovereign. Thus, the essence of "reverence" consists in being humble and cautious toward others, while maintaining a solemn and grave demeanor. It is through this that one can truly realize the nature of the mind. Therefore, it is said: "If one knows how to be reverent, one will naturally attain peace. This is why the Buddha instructed Puguang to "join his palms in reverence" before withdrawing. It is because he understood that the path of the mind’s cultivation resides in this very practice. Thus, the principle of the mind’s learning is fully contained within these two characters.
The countenance expresses the virtue of reverence (*jing*). Since the demeanor of the hands primarily embodies reverence, the gesture of joining the two hands is taken as its symbolic meaning.

When a person is at leisure, they let their hands hang loose; their mind becomes dissipated, and their countenance consequently grows slack. By drawing the hands together, the mind is necessarily gathered within.

A dignified countenance results from this; it is the unification of the internal and external. Vulgar books do not realize that this [countenance] is itself the mind, and they further add the character "mind" (心) to create "respectful mind" (恭).
This implies that the mind has both an internal and an external aspect. It is the state of "focusing on one thing" (主一).

This was the art of the ancients for concentrating their essence and gathering their spirit. As for "manifesting respect through the countenance," if one merely forces it outward, it will secretly erupt from within.
Unable to maintain self-possession, those who say "I am reverent" will surely be lax in their conduct. How can empty words overcome actual evil? How, then, should one apply effort?
It is said: "Do not forget; do not assist growth. To "follow with urgency" (the character *jì*, pronounced as in *jí*) means to instruct them not to forget.
If one is slow, there will be no achievement; as soon as one perceives dullness or drowsiness, one must quickly call oneself back to attention.
Upon awakening, one perceives the distraction; one must immediately sever it oneself. As for "long-term practice," the teaching is that one must not assist growth prematurely.
If one is too hurried, one becomes constrained and pressured; something obstructs the chest, the blood and qi do not flow freely, and how could one possibly persist?
The mind is the master of my physical form. Reverence is nothing other than the mind itself acting as its own master. Why wait to borrow anything else?
The mind. Come, govern this mind. Though there be cause for fear, do not fear; though there be cause for rest, do not rest. Let it be continuous as if it were barely present.
The virtue of Heaven flows everywhere; let the mind be ever alive and never dead. *Song* (Sorrow) gives rise to reverence; *Jie* (Caution) maintains reverence;

*Wei* (Apprehension) overcomes reverence; *Su* (Solemnity) is the gravity of reverence; *Mu* (Harmony) is the profound reverence; *Qin* (Veneration) is the sagely reverence. Reverence is the source from which all virtues arise. Who could...?
This concerns the shallow and the deep. Herein lies the profound source of the sagely learning. By observing the heart-pictures of the ancients, one comes to know their heart-learning.
How could this be reduced to a mere study of written characters? [Such a study] obstructs the spiritual nature and blocks the gate of awakening; yet people fail to investigate it thoroughly.
How could they know that the true art of calligraphy can indeed liberate the spiritual nature and open the gate of awakening? Therefore, I have briefly indicated it here—do not [neglect it].
This means that I, the author, delight in searching out the obscure and investigating the hidden in order to display the extraordinary.
*Commentary on the Kuan-chu Scroll of the Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s Fundamental Vow Sūtra*, Scroll Three;
*Commentary on the Kuan-chu Scroll of the Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s Fundamental Vow Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Lingcheng of the Ancient Yan Kuang-an Qinglian Monastery, son of [Father] Ji.
Part Two: Benefits for the Living and the Deceased. Chapter One: Title.
Chapter Seven: Benefits for the Living and the Deceased.

△ Section Two: The Text of the Two Chapters, Part Three. First, Kṣitigarbha clearly elucidates; second, Mahāprajñā assists in manifestation; third, the spirits and deities resolve their minds. Part One of the first [section] has three parts:
first, a general demonstration that the goodness of sentient beings declines while evil increases; second, a specific demonstration that those who practice evil should be provided with merit;

third, a conclusion clarifying that one naturally receives results according to the amount of goodness cultivated. The first of these [three] further has three parts: first, the demonstration by means of the Dharma.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I observe that among the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa, every movement of thought and every stirring of the mind is without exception a transgression.

Even when they happen to obtain wholesome benefits, they mostly retreat from their initial resolve; yet when they encounter adverse conditions, these transgressions increase with every passing thought."

"Mind-thought" refers to the six consciousnesses; "movement" is their function. Through the conjunction of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, they turbidly disturb the master of the eight consciousnesses.
The eight consciousnesses, in turn, cause the first five consciousnesses to crave sounds, cling to forms, taste flavors, and smell fragrances.
The body touches what is soft and smooth; as it encounters these conditions everywhere, it is said that there is nothing that is not a cause for transgression.

Regarding the two phrases "if one obtains good benefit," this refers to a lack of firmness in maintaining the mind. The *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* states: "The people of Jambudvīpa are by nature difficult to inspire with faith.

Because they obtain benefit through the practice of goodness, they ought to advance in their efforts without interruption; yet, because they have obtained such benefit, they instead retreat from their initial resolve."

Therefore, the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states: "When a bodhisattva sees all sentient beings undergoing various sufferings and afflictions—even if they have accomplished even a slight root of virtue—it is but for a brief moment and not for long. This refers to cases where they encounter adverse conditions and the like.
This refers to the four great elements as poisonous vessels, filled with filth; the six thieves as mad masters, to whose objects one remains attached.
There is no longer any hope of reversing the current, only the force of cyclic progression. One stagnates in birth and death, clinging tenaciously to the conditioned.
For this reason, all Buddhas knit their brows in concern, and Bodhisattvas shed blood from their eyes in grief. This results from the mind’s failure to attain stability through its attachments.
This is evil. Therefore, the Great Master said: "One should know that all bodies are created by the mind;

it is like the great earth, which, being one, can produce various kinds of sprouts. This is so. (The *Jingdu sanmei jing* says: "Sins and blessings accumulate against one another, their heavy counts clearly distinct. Later, one shall receive the retribution of sin and blessing, not missing even a single instance.

One thought receives one body: through wholesome thoughts, one receives a body among gods or humans; through evil thoughts, one receives a body in the three evil realms. A hundred thoughts receive a hundred bodies; a thousand thoughts, a thousand bodies. In a single day and night, one plants the roots of birth and death. Hereafter, one shall... )

One has received eighty-five million bodies of various species. Within a single hundred-year span, the seeds for future existences planted are too numerous to count. The soul follows these seeds to receive form, pervading the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-systems;

the bones, marrow, skin, and hair of these bodies cover the ground of the great thousandfold world-system such that there is no empty space between them. Furthermore, the *Womb-Entry Sūtra* (*Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*) states: "Since immeasurable kalpas past, I have come and gone through the path of birth and death, discarding one body only to receive another, never escaping the law of the womb.

I have exclusively taken the form of a white dog; the accumulated bones would equal a hundred million Mount Sumerus, let alone those of dogs of various colors, whose number is immeasurable. Thus, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Kṣudrakavastu*) says: "A human body is difficult to obtain; yet when met with evil conditions, it is easily lost. This is because evil is abundant while goodness is scarce. Within a single day..."
There are hundreds of thousands of evil thoughts, yet not a single wholesome thought. Thus we know that for one who can subdue the mind to practice the Way, their power is greatest.

Yet what can be done about the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa? Their various anxieties fly about in confusion; they cannot maintain firm resolve. That goodness recedes while evil increases—is this not simply due to habitual conditioning?
△ Second, the illustration by analogy.
People of this sort are like those treading upon mud and carrying heavy stones; as they grow increasingly exhausted and burdened, their footsteps sink deeper.

This first analogy refers to the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, for whom goodness declines and evil increases. Like treading on a path of thick mire, they constantly dwell within the realm of birth and death, which is both deep and profound;
thus, it is difficult for them to seek escape. △ Third, the clarification through matters.
If one encounters a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they may take over part of the burden or bear it entirely;

for such a friend possesses great strength and thus provides mutual assistance, encouraging one to stand firm on one's feet. Once one has reached level ground, one must avoid the evil paths so as not to experience them again.

Regarding "if one obtains [such a friend]," this encompasses both fortunate and unfortunate aspects. That is to say, if that person happens to possess even a slight amount of merit and immediately encounters a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), how fortunate they are!
Yet, if they lack the conditions for merit, they will never encounter one; how deeply unfortunate! Spiritual friends may be categorized as near or distant.
"Near" refers to parents and relatives who assist one in performing meritorious deeds; "distant" refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

"Extinguishing their sins" means to replace them. "To bear" (fù) means to carry a load on one's back. There are partial and full [extinguishings] when discussing the merit of performing virtuous deeds;
causing the deceased to have their sins diminished is a partial bearing, while if the sins are completely extinguished, it is a full bearing.
The following explains the meaning of "being able to bear": it refers to this spiritual friend who...
Because of great power. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that based on the five powers of a person (the five powers of faith and so forth), there are the ten powers of the Buddha-fruit.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Bodhisattvas also possess the ten powers. Because they possess these powers, they do not merely bear the burden themselves;
they can further support and assist others, exhorting them to make their "heels" firm. For if one were to slip and fall into the mud, it would be difficult indeed to rise again. Furthermore...

Furthermore, he exhorted him that once he had reached a place of safety and stability, he must reflect upon and turn away from the evil paths he previously traversed, never again to pass through or tread them.
"Supporting one another" is a metaphor for teaching the ten wholesome actions; "firmly planting one's feet" is a metaphor for maintaining the mind without retreat.

"Level path" is a metaphor for ascending out of the realms of humans and devas. "Examining evil" is a metaphor for reflecting upon the sufferings of the three miserable destinies. "Passing through again" is a metaphor for not entering the realms of suffering once more.
△ Second, the actual instruction on how one who has practiced evil should establish merit; this has two parts, the first being the general indication.
World-Honored One, for sentient beings who habituate themselves to evil, it proceeds from a mere hair’s breadth to the immeasurable.

This corresponds to the preceding passage concerning "raising the mind" and "stirring thoughts," which asks: why does raising the mind and stirring thoughts—even encountering evil—lead to its increase?
It is because of the habituation to evil. "Evil habituation" (*akuśala-vāsanā*) refers to the seeds; "habituating to evil" refers to the active manifestation (*samudācāra*). By means of...
Because there are seeds of evil habits, they cause the manifestation of evil practices. Thus, it proceeds from a mere hair’s breadth to the immeasurable.
The *Sūtra on Examining and Discerning* states: "When seeking the form and nature of the mind, not a single distinct part can be found.
It is only due to the causes and conditions of the habitual perfuming of sentient beings' ignorance and deluded darkness that false objects appear, causing the mind to become attached to them."
Upon various phenomena, one falsely gives rise to various conceptualizations of phenomena—claiming they exist, claiming they do not;
claiming "that," claiming "this"; claiming "it is," claiming "it is not"; claiming "good," claiming "evil"—and thus falsely gives rise to immeasurable and boundless conceptualizations of phenomena.
Therefore, the *Guangming xuán* states: "Ascending is difficult, while falling is easy, because for the most part one relies upon evil bodies. The *Jì* states: "Precisely because the multitude..."

Born into this world, one is conditioned by beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), such that evil predominates and goodness is scarce. This causes the mind’s thoughts to frequently take recourse in unwholesome states.
Before the five vehicles can be mounted, one first wanders through the four miserable realms. It is easy to ascend to the higher paths but difficult to avoid falling back; who would say otherwise?

A practitioner cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* must constantly examine the minds of the ten realms; this is something they must not fail to know. It is for this reason that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are used to discern and eliminate non-virtuous states of mind.

△ Second, the detailed explanation of the two [sections]: First, establishing merit for the benefit of the living and the deceased; second, increasing the transgressions of a deceased person who has committed evil.
Part One: Establishing Merit at the Time of Death. This is divided into three sections. First, indicating the general intent.

These sentient beings have such habitual tendencies that at the time of their death, their parents and kinsmen should appropriately perform meritorious deeds on their behalf to provide for their journey ahead.
The first two lines demonstrate the intention behind cultivating merit and observing the precepts regarding killing.

Because sentient beings possess such evil habits, seeds and manifestations mutually perfume one another, and cause and effect resonate with each other. If one does not provide merit for their kinsmen, by what means shall they be sustained on the path ahead?
As the Verse on Impermanence says: "Constantly seeking the objects of desire, one does not perform virtuous deeds; the King of Death urges one on."
The Lord of Death awaits; relatives and kin merely stand guard together. All consciousnesses grow dark and obscured as one enters the perilous city and approaches King Yama.
One receives retribution according to one's karma: through superior causes one is born in the good realms, while through evil karma one falls into hell.
Only the Buddha’s Bodhi is the true place of refuge and reliance; therefore, one should provide virtuous merit to support the journey ahead. △
Second, the cultivation of merit:
either by suspending banners and canopies and lighting oil lamps; or by reciting and chanting the honored sutras; or by making offerings to images of the Buddha and various holy beings;
or even by reciting the names of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Pratyekabuddhas—even a single name or a single title—repeatedly and continuously.
Finally, regarding the human faculty of hearing, some maintain that it resides within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

Within this context, there are two types of fruits resulting from the cultivation of merit: first, the fruit of cultivating meritorious deeds, such as hanging banners, setting up canopies, and lighting lamps.
First, regarding the fruit of revering the Triple Gem: reciting sutras, making offerings to images, and invoking the names [of the Buddhas]. The *Puguang jing* (Universal Radiance Sutra) states:

"If members of the fourfold assembly, whether male or female, are at the point of death or have already passed away, on the day of their demise, one should create yellow banners and suspend them atop a stupa (*stūpa*) to cause them to obtain merit and virtue, leave behind the suffering of the eight difficulties, and attain rebirth in the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Regarding the banners:
Thus, through this offering, one’s wishes will be fulfilled until the attainment of Bodhi. As the banner turns with the wind, it is completely shattered and reduced to fine dust;
for every single turn of the banner, there is the merit of the rank of a Wheel-Turning King, down to the rank of a minor king when the dust is blown away—the retribution being immeasurable.
By making an offering of lamps, one illuminates all the dark realms, and sentient beings suffering in pain receive this [benefit].
Through this radiance, they are able to see one another. By virtue of this merit, those sentient beings are rescued and all attain rest.
Because there is such benefit and blessing, one should hang banners and light lamps. Making offerings to the image is as described before; recollecting the Buddha is as follows.
In the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, the King of the Yāma Heaven speaks a verse for the sake of the devas, saying:

"If a person’s mind recollects the Buddha, they are called one who possesses a virtuous life. Because they do not depart from the recollection of the Buddha, this is the life within life. It is the same for the recollection of the Dharma and the recollection of the Saṅgha.
To cause these names and titles to pass through the faculty of hearing and be received into the eight consciousnesses, so that they are never destroyed—this is like..."
When this vajra enters the belly, it does not decay for a long time; it must inevitably pass through the intestines and emerge.
Therefore, one must cultivate the seeds of Buddhahood through hearing—that is, the sound of the Dharma passing through the ears. Its merit and retribution extend across kalpas;
once it has passed through the faculty of hearing, it becomes forever a seed of the Way. Is it not so? △ Third, the benefits obtained.
Regarding the evil karma committed by these sentient beings, if one calculates the resulting retribution, they would certainly fall into the evil realms;
yet, because their kinsmen cultivate this sacred cause for them at the time of death, all such transgressions are entirely extinguished.

This combines with the preceding text: encountering a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is like gaining a full load. Since those who die have mostly practiced evil, they cannot escape the entanglements of karmic retribution;
as cause does not fail to meet its effect, evil inevitably brings calamity. If one does not cultivate the causes of noble merit, [one will suffer].
How can one avoid the fruits of the future? The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states: "Gati" (destiny/rebirth) means "to arrive," and it is also called a "path.
This is because the path of those causes—wholesome and unwholesome karma—can transport one to the place of birth.

Furthermore, it may refer to proceeding toward that place of birth according to the karma one has created. It also carries the sense of "tending toward," meaning that the karma one has created tends toward the heavens and...
This refers to the hells. As stated in the *Mahāyāna-samatā-nirdeśa-sūtra*, King Laṅkā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that sentient beings relinquish this lifespan and receive that lifespan; how do they relinquish this old body and receive that new body? The Buddha replied:
"Once sentient beings have relinquished this body, the power of the winds of karma blows their consciousness away. They then undergo the results of the karma they themselves have experienced."

Therefore, the Great Master Guifeng said: "If you wish to verify whether you will have mastery or lack mastery over your rebirth at the moment of death, simply verify whether your mind is free or unfree during your ordinary conduct.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, you must constantly examine yourself. How profound these words are!
Thus, having already created evil karma, one would inevitably fall into the evil realms; that one is now able to escape is due to [the protection of] one's kin."
Because one is currently cultivating various noble causes, these manifold transgressions are dispersed like clouds blown by a fierce wind or extinguished like a small fire by a great flood.
Thus, one knows that the total elimination of all transgressions is the great power of wisdom.
This is entirely due to their own transgressions. △ Second, performing good deeds after death:

If one can further perform extensive meritorious deeds within the seven periods of seven days following the person's death, it can cause these sentient beings to forever leave the evil realms and be reborn among humans or devas, experiencing supreme and wondrous bliss, thereby benefiting their current kinsmen.
"Immeasurable.
This refers to the five phrases beginning with "furthermore, they assist one another," which indicate a powerful spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Such a person not only bears the full weight of the heavy stone for another, but is also able to support them until they reach level ground; this specifically refers to performing [meritorious deeds] on their behalf after death.
It is auspicious. In the Sanskrit language it is *maraṇa*, which here means "death. As stated in the *Dvādaśamukha-śīrṣa-jāti-maraṇa-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Twelve Categories of Birth and Death):

"When a person dies, there are twelve categories [of consequences]" and so forth. Thus, the *Dharmapada* says: "Indeed, this body is the root of all suffering and the source of calamity and misfortune.
Being bound by the attachment to a self, birth and death do not cease—is this not all due to the body? Now, I wish to leave behind the suffering of the world."

Fundamentally, one ought to perform virtuous deeds for their sake. For seven weeks, as described below: it is like when a drought persists for a long time, one must think of the moisture of sweet rain;
or when calamities and pestilences are many, one must await the medicine of a skilled physician. When the sick obtain medicine, the body finds peace;
when the parched earth receives rain, the soil becomes moist. Thus, they shall forever leave the evil realms behind and attain birth among humans and devas.
Once one has reached level ground, having been born in the heavens, one dwells forever in halls of merit; or, remaining among humans, one enjoys perpetual wealth and nobility.

Even at such times of experiencing supreme and wondrous happiness, one must reflect upon those evil paths and firmly maintain this mind, ensuring that virtuous thoughts do not falter or be lost, lest one traverse the evil realms once again. As the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:

When one performs meritorious deeds on behalf of the deceased, even if the person has already passed away after the gift was given, that person’s merit will constantly arise in accordance with the object offered, for as long as that object remains functional.
This merit follows the person just as a shadow follows a form. Some may say that it is lost immediately upon death, but this is not the case.
Why? Because the object is lost at two times: when it is destroyed or when it is no longer used; it is not lost through death.
[They] lose everything [as described in the text]. Therefore, they obtain the means of subsistence in the realms of humans and devas and experience supreme, wondrous bliss.

Not only does the deceased obtain happiness and ascend, but the benefits obtained by those currently living are likewise immeasurable. △ Second, the increase of transgressions for deceased persons who have committed evil.

Part One: Instruction through Dharma. Part Two: Analogy and Application. Within the section on the Dharma, there are two subsections: first, following the previous [discussion], the formal exhortation.
Therefore, I now, before the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the assembly of devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, humans, and non-humans, exhort the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa:
on the day of their final passing, they must be careful not to commit acts of killing or create other evil conditions, nor should they perform sacrifices to ghosts and spirits.
Seeking among the *māra* spirits and *piśāca* demons:
this follows upon the previous discussion of cultivating merit at the time of death, wherein both the living and the deceased obtain benefit. These words of exhortation state:

"I shall now take the matter of benefiting both the living and the deceased upon my own shoulders. On the day of one's passing, there are four [points]: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "四自" (four self-...), suggesting the source material was incomplete.]
The *Qin jing* (Invasion Sutra) says: "The pleasures of the five desires cannot be obtained forever. When one is afflicted by illness and lies upon a bed, there is agitation and no peace.

When the decree of death suddenly arrives, the body shall perish; how could it endure long? Be careful—do not [be negligent]. Regarding "Be careful" (*shèn*): "Careful" means constant vigilance. The human mind has its deceptive aspects:
it cultivates itself when in the light of clarity, but runs wild in the darkness of obscurity. Only vigilance constitutes the true mind; therefore—
"From the heart and from truth. "Do not" is a prohibition. To be cautious and yet further prohibit [killing] means to resolutely vow never to commit slaughter.

"Evil conditions" refers to those things that assist in accomplishing the act of killing, such as performing sacrifices to spirits and deities. "To prostrate" (*bai*) means to bow down low in reverence.

When a person prostrates, they do so by bending their entire body; when one points specifically to the hands, it is because the appearance of the hands primarily expresses respect, according to the ritual codes (*li*).
This is why it is considered beautiful. The *Shuoyuan* states: "The term 'sacrifice' (*ji*) means 'to seek out' (*suo*). To "seek out" means "to exhaust.
This is how the filial son exhausts himself in service to his parents. Furthermore, sacrifice arises from the heart that seeks to repay the source of life.

With a heart full of trepidation, how could one bring [offerings] to them? Thus, one provides food through the path of the Way, hoping that they might perhaps partake; this is one manifestation of the teaching of single-minded sincerity.
Now, regarding these prostrations and sacrifices to ghosts, spirits, and *wangliang* demons—detailed in the *Rujiji* (the *Puyao jing* records that Kāśyapa said:

"Reflecting on my history of performing sacrifices, eighty years have already passed. I have served the deities of wind, water, and fire, as well as the sun, moon, and various mountains and rivers, never flagging day or night. My mind harbored no other thoughts, yet in the end I gained nothing. Only upon meeting the Buddha did I find peace and tranquility. This is it). △
The second part provides an explanatory interpretation of the reason for this, which consists of two sections; first is the direct explanation:
"Why is this so? All such acts of killing and slaughter, up to and including ritual sacrifices, possess not even a trace of power to benefit the deceased."
It is only that the conditions for the commission of offenses become increasingly grave and heavy.

The *Daśadig-dṛṣṭānta-sūtra* states: "The ghosts and spirits of the heavens above and the earth below know the lifespans, sins, and blessings of humans, as well as whether their time has arrived or not;
yet they cannot sustain a person's life, nor can they kill them, nor can they cause people to be wealthy or noble, or poor and lowly."

They merely wish to incite people to commit evil and violate the precept against killing; they seek to bring disorder by taking advantage of human decline and misfortune, speaking of calamities and blessings to induce people to establish shrines and offer sacrifices.
Thus, one knows that empty sacrifices to ghosts and spirits do not provide even a hair’s breadth of benefit to the deceased.
The *Guanding jing* (Consecration Sutra) also says: "The spirits of miscellaneous objects wander among human villages; once they have [entered],..."

There are those who consume no food and perform various strange transformations to incite the minds of people. Or there are drought-demons (*pāpa*), malevolent spirits (*māyā*), and heterodox teachers who rely on such practices as blessings, seeking all manner of auspicious protection and desiring eternal life. Driven by ignorance and false views, they slaughter living beings for sacrificial offerings;
