upon death, they enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, from which there is no time of escape. How can one not be cautious? Therefore, these acts merely create the conditions for further transgression.
[Their suffering] increases ever more deeply and heavily. Thus, the *Sūtra on Self-Inflicted Harm* states:

"Those who rely upon heaven and earth, water and fire, the sun and moon, mountains and rivers, or various ghosts and spirits will derive no lasting benefit. Consequently, they remain within the cycle of birth and death, unable to escape the nets and prisons [of saṃsāra].
Various sūtras explain this matter in detail; it is a pity that people of the world cannot believe it.
△ Second, the further elaboration on the two [types of karma]. First, regarding those who should receive good but instead obtain evil:
even if they were to attain the factors of the noble ones (*ārya-bhāga*) in a future life or in the present existence, being born among humans or devas, because of this, at the time of their death—
Because his kinsmen have created these evil causes, they cause this deceased person to face the retribution of their transgressions; yet, [the deceased] will eventually be reborn in a good realm.

This passage is divided into two sections: first, the conditions for being reborn in a good realm; second, the obstacles caused by evil that prevent such rebirth. The section on the Noble Ones consists of seven types of bodhisattvas.

The factors of enlightenment, the factors of the Noble Eightfold Path, and the factors of the Bodhisattva’s fruition—these very factors, such as those in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, we too should possess.

The character "part" (*fen*) is the same [in all cases]. This means that while the deceased possessed their own wholesome causes during life and thus ought to have attained a portion of wholesome fruit, leading to rebirth among humans or devas, it was solely because at the time of death they were subjected to the causal karma of killing by their relatives that they [fell into an evil state].

The killer seeks his life; he must inevitably pass through the offices of the underworld to undergo interrogation. Although the karmic retribution may be cleared, his rebirth will be delayed. Master Daoshi said:

"When parents pass away, if one extensively slaughters living beings, the father who died shall suffer this heavy agony, while the mother whose life ended shall especially increase her torment in boiling water and burning coals.
Consequently, one wanders through the three realms and passes through the six paths for a long time; it is easy to fall back into the four miserable destinies."
Difficult to open [the gates of heaven] for ten thousand kalpas—this truly describes the grieving spirit of the compassionate mother and the lamentable requital of poison by the rebellious son.
How can one not feel sorrow? △ Second, those who deserve to receive evil further increase their karma.

How much more so for one who is at the point of death? Having never cultivated even a small root of goodness during their life, they must each undergo rebirth in the evil realms according to their own fundamental karma.
How can one bear to have their kinsmen further increase that karma?

In this context, the intended meaning is as follows: if even those who possess wholesome karma and ought to be reborn in a favorable realm are still dragged down by unwholesome karma and only reach that favorable realm late, how much more so for one who lacks roots of virtue and is destined for the miserable realms?

If such a person is now further subjected to killing and harm, will their unwholesome karma not increase all the more? It is like a person who is already clutching a stone and sinking into a deep abyss, yet is further...
If one throws an object on top of it to press it down, it will be difficult to emerge from there. Therefore, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:

"If a father has passed away and fallen among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), and the son performs meritorious deeds on his behalf, one should know that [the father] will immediately obtain [the benefit].

To say that one obtains merit by killing living beings for sacrificial offerings is not correct. Why is this? One does not see people in the world planting *eranda* seeds and producing *candana* [sandalwood].
[The text states that] one may obtain merit by taking the lives of sentient beings [as in the case of the *candana* tree].

If one wishes to perform a sacrifice, one should use incense, flowers, milk, curd, ghee, and fruit to cultivate merit for the deceased (the text). Therefore, the two characters "how could one bear" (*hěrěn*) at the end signify that the heart of such forbearance is extreme.
The increase in karma is great indeed. △ Second, the analogy and its application:
Suppose there is a person who has come from a distant land; having been without food for three days, the burden he carries on his back exceeds a hundred catties.
Suddenly encountering a neighbor, he further received a small amount of goods; for this reason, he became even more exhausted and heavy.

Someone used the analogy of sentient beings in Jambudvīpa coming from a distant land, etc., which is a metaphor for those who, since the vast eons of beginningless birth and death, have long lacked the provisions of the three roots of goodness; it can be known that their bellies are empty and their strength is feeble.

Furthermore, the heavy burden of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) they carry exceeds even one hundred *jin* (catty). This means that within the phenomena of the five aggregates, they fail to understand their fundamental emptiness;
they falsely calculate a self and others, fully committing the ten non-virtues, each complete with all the others, like a burden of one hundred *jin*.
This precisely corresponds to the aforementioned person at the point of death who lacks roots of goodness themselves. "Suddenly encountering," below—

Each case should be judged according to the relevant scriptural passages concerning one’s own karma and so forth. Those who are like neighbors include their kinsmen; those who possess a sincere heart are like close friends, while those who lack a sincere heart are like neighbors.

If one further attaches small items [to the corpse], it is as if one were to inflict additional killing at the moment of death, thereby increasing the gravity of the suffering and augmenting the resulting karma.
△ Third, the conclusion clarifies that the amount of good one attains depends on the extent of one’s cultivation of virtue.

World-Honored One, I observe the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa; they are able, within the teachings of all Buddhas, to obtain for themselves every benefit, even as small as a single hair, a single drop, a single grain of sand, or a single speck of dust, down to such minor good deeds.
This statement concerns the wholesome deeds cultivated within the Buddha-dharma; even such things as a hair-tip or a drop of water are likewise attained by oneself. As the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* says:

"If there are sentient beings who, in the presence of the Buddhas, give rise to a single thought of faith, such roots of goodness shall never perish. It is like a person who splits a single hair into one hundred parts, takes one part of that hair, and dips it into a single drop of water, then entrusts it to me, saying:

'Do not let this water increase or decrease. The Tathāgata accepts that entrustment and places it in the Ganges River. Thus, that drop of water neither increases nor decreases; together with the great mass of water, it gradually enters the great ocean. Even if..."

"Suppose there were a person who remained in the world for one kalpa, and I likewise remained for one kalpa. When that person reached the end of the kalpa, he would come to me and say: 'I originally deposited water with you; does it still exist now?

At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that drop of water within the great ocean, perceives that it remains in the water, neither increasing nor decreasing, remaining as it was, equal and unchanged. He then returns it to that person. Ānanda, the Tathāgata possesses great supernormal powers; among those who receive deposits, he is the most honored and supreme.

If one were to entrust such a minute drop of water to the Buddha, it would not diminish or be lost even after a vast period of time. The fine hair is a metaphor for the mind, consciousness, and mentation (*citta-vijñāna-manas*); the Ganges is a metaphor for the flow of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); and a single drop of water is a metaphor for a single thought of awakening, a minute amount of wholesome merit."

The roots [of faith]. The great ocean is a metaphor for the Tathāgata; those to whom he entrusts [the water] are metaphors for the pure-faithed and others; dwelling for one kalpa is a metaphor for the Tathāgata receiving that entrusted water, which he never allows to diminish or be lost. Thus it is, Ānanda:

if one gives rise to even a single thought of faith toward the Buddha, the roots of goodness will not be lost, let alone other various superior and wondrous roots of goodness. I say that all such people are entirely those who proceed toward the fruit of nirvāṇa. Part Two: Great Eloquence Aids in Manifestation. 1. Great Eloquence Raises the Question.
When these words were spoken, there was in the assembly an elder named Mahāpratibhāna.

This elder had long since realized the non-arising of phenomena and manifested in the body of an elder to transform and deliver beings throughout the ten directions. With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, saying:
"O Great Being, after the lives of sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa have ended, their small and large kinsmen perform meritorious deeds on their behalf."
...up to the point where they provide a vegetarian feast and create various roots of goodness. Will this person who has ended their life obtain great benefit and liberation?
First, the narrator provides a preface and praise; second, the elder’s formal inquiry. As before, the elder—whose name in the Sanskrit language is *Bhadrika*—[asks].

This is called *pratibhāna* (eloquence). "Bian" (辯) means to speak. Because it proceeds without obstruction and distinguishes things with clarity, it is called "unimpeded eloquence" (*pratibhānāsaṅga*).
There are four kinds: first, meaning (*artha*); second, phenomena (*dharma*); third, terminology (*nirukti*); and fourth, joyful exposition (*pratibhāna*).

An elder who possesses these four virtues is therefore named "Great Eloquence. As for why the eloquence is called "great": within a single meaning, one expounds immeasurable meanings; within a single phenomenon...

He expounds immeasurable dharmas; within a single word, he expounds immeasurable words. Because he delights in preaching these three dharma-gates until the end of the future, this auspicious title was established.
This concludes the mention of his name; what follows is the praise of his virtues. "One who has long realized non-arising" means that there is no [arising].
It is taught as "non-being. That which is called the non-arising of all phenomena and the non-arising of Prajñā—this non-arising of non-arising is named Great Nirvāṇa.
Such Nirvāṇa has been realized since long ago; his stage is lofty and vast, and he belongs to the class of those on the level of Equal Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbuddha).

Because he wishes to transform and deliver beings throughout the ten directions, he manifests in the body of an elder. Within the context of this direct inquiry, this refers to Jambudvīpa in the south.

[The text] begins with “etc. Because the preceding passage extensively explained that one ought to cultivate merit after death at the time of passing away, [the author] follows up by inquiring about it.
“Merit” refers to such acts as hanging banners; “providing a feast” refers to feeding the Sangha and so forth; and “wholesome causes” refer to giving alms, creating images, and the like.
"Regarding 'at the end of life' below: this is the core of the inquiry. Life (ming) is the inner sincerity bestowed by Heaven;
it is the celestial root of one's nature. A student must realize it through self-attainment. Furthermore, the vital breath (qi) received from Heaven is also called fate (ming);

according to its differences in clarity or turbidity and thickness or thinness, the distinction between the wise and the foolish, the worthy and the unworthy, is determined. The numerical allotment of Heaven is also called fate; this applies to all that has life."
Longevity or early death, poverty or wealth, nobility or meanness—all these are predetermined. These are all metaphorical extensions of the meaning of "ming" (fate).

When the ruler issues a great decree, it is called "ming. It is composed of the radical "person" (亻) and the semantic component "mouth" (口), forming a compound ideograph. The ruler is as venerable as Heaven; all things receive their mandate from Heaven.
All matters are ordained by the Lord; therefore, it is called "fate" (*ming*). Thus, Master Zhu Wen-gong said: "Fate is like a command.
This is the refined and subtle meaning of the Confucian tradition. However, one may not yet know the reason why fate is as it is:

it is because when one mounts upon the karmic causes and conditions of previous lives, at the moment of entrusting oneself to a womb, the eighth consciousness enters therein, and for a single breath, one follows the mother in her inhalation and exhalation.
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is established at this time; thus, consciousness (vijñāna) relies upon the body and abides therein, with life residing within it.

Therefore, it is said that the continuous, uninterrupted connection between form (rūpa) and mind (citta) constitutes life. If even a single breath does not return, the physical substance decays and the soul-spirit departs;
this is called the end of life. This, then, is birth. It is not that Heaven ordains one to be born, nor does it ordain one’s end.
It is not that Heaven seizes one at the end; rather, it arises through the convergence of conditions and ends when those conditions are exhausted.
"To create" means to construct. In the performance of any virtuous deed, one must rely upon the sevenfold paths of body and speech to plan and carry it out;
yet, it must invariably originate from the mind. Regarding "attaining benefit and liberation," this refers to how practicing merit in the world of the living can enable—
Does the deceased truly obtain benefit and thereby attain liberation from birth and death? Or does he fail to obtain benefit and remain unliberated from birth and death?
△ Second, Kṣitigarbha’s response in two parts: first, the promise to speak.
Kṣitigarbha replied, "O Householder, I have now, for the sake of all sentient beings of the future and the present, and by the majestic power of the Buddha,
briefly explained this matter."
As stated in the text. △ Second, the response and demonstration, in two parts. First, demonstrating that hearing the names at the time of death leads to universal liberation:
"Elder, all sentient beings of the future and present, on the day their lives come to an end, shall hear the name of one Buddha, the name of one Bodhisattva, or the name of one Pratyekabuddha.
Regardless of whether they have committed offenses or not, they shall all attain liberation."
Since it is said that one may hear [the name] at the moment of death, it can be known that one does not recite it during ordinary times.
Furthermore, since it is said that hearing even a single name is sufficient and that others need not be reached, this can also be understood.

Yet, as for how those who do so—regardless of whether they have committed offenses or not—all attain liberation, how marvelous must the power of its efficacy be! This is truly because the situation is urgent and the mind is single-minded, just as...
Some may face execution, some are confined in prison; some are pursued by vengeful enemies, while others are beset by water or fire.

With a single-minded resolve to escape such suffering, the practice of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is thereby accomplished. This is distinct from the mindfulness practiced during ordinary times.
It may be that one’s words do not accord with one’s actions, or that the power of one’s faith is slight and weak; lacking a continuous resolve, one possesses an interrupted intention.
Consequently, the merit accumulated during ordinary life is delayed, while the thought at the moment of death is swiftly realized.

As it was said when a king once asked the śramaṇa Nāgasena: "If a person commits evil throughout their life in the world, yet at the time of death, for a hundred years, they maintain a [virtuous] thought..."
"Buddha, after death one may be reborn in a Buddha-land; I do not believe these words. Nāgasena said, "It is like placing a hundred large stones upon a boat;
because of the boat, they do not sink. Although a person may have inherent evil, if they once mindfully recollect the Buddha,"
One does not enter the hells. As for those small stones that sink, they are like people who commit evil and do not know to recite the Buddha’s name;

they then enter the hells. Is this not because when the situation is urgent, the mind becomes single-minded, and thus the merit surpasses that of ordinary times? It is like a person entering the ranks of battle.
One who does not spare their own body or life is called a "valiant person. Thus we know that good and evil have no fixed nature;

while the essence of causes and conditions is empty, their traces involve rising and sinking, and their manifestations are distinguished by superiority and inferiority. A single *liang* of pure gold surpasses a hundred *liang* of layered flowers;
the faint light of a torch consumes a mass of grass thousands of *zhang* high. This is immediately seen in the case of Zhang Zhong (also known as Shanhe, also known as Kui) at the time of his death.
Matter. Thus, one comes to believe the words of this sutra regarding liberation. △ Second, showing that after death one creates merit and attains two [results].
First, a brief explanation; second, a detailed demonstration. The first [section] further has two parts: first, directly explaining the attainment of one result after death.
If there are men or women who, during their lives, did not cultivate roots of goodness but committed many transgressions, after their deaths, when their kinsmen— both great and small—
perform meritorious deeds and all manner of sacred rites on their behalf, they shall obtain but one-seventh of the benefit.
The sixfold merit is such that the living beings gain self-benefit.

When our Buddha preaches the Dharma for the laity, he invariably begins with a discourse on morality (*śīla*), a discourse on generosity (*dāna*), and a discourse on rebirth in heaven (*svarga-kathā*), because generosity and morality are the virtuous causes for birth in heaven.
Alas, all sentient beings fail to understand what truly exists within this world.
When one returns solely to emptiness and non-existence, it is a time of peace and security. Yet, amidst myriad affairs and a thousand complications, one fails to plan for the welfare of the self;

thus, ten thousand offenses are summoned, and calamities respond like echoes. When impermanence arrives face-to-face, one is bound and pursued by attachments, never escaping the prison of the five aggregates and the six sense-decays.
Therefore it is said: "If one does not cultivate wholesome causes but creates many offenses, at the end of life one will fall low. To remedy this, one should cultivate merit and benefit.
Hanging banners, setting up canopies, and lighting lamps are all meritorious deeds.

By dedicating these merits toward rebirth in the blessed halls of the heavens or the fortunate realms of the human world, they are called "beneficial merit. As for "sacred matters," the sacred teachings are considered correct;

reciting sutras, making offerings to images, and mindfulness of the Buddha are all authentic practices of the Dharma-gate that enable one to transcend the world and attain the holy fruits of the Three Vehicles.
Therefore, it is called a "sacred matter" (śāstṛ-kārya). One receives one-seventh of the merit; what is obtained is extremely small.
Nevertheless, the effort is not in vain: the living person naturally obtains six-sevenths. Thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states:

"If one performs meritorious deeds after the death [of another], the deceased receives one-seventh of the merit, while the remainder belongs to the living. These two scriptures are in agreement. △ Second, the negative illustration of self-cultivation.
They all obtain it.
For this reason, good men and women of the future and present who hear [this teaching] should cultivate themselves while they are healthy; they will each obtain their share of the benefits.
This follows the preceding text to show by contrast that those who cultivate themselves fully obtain the benefit. "Hearing while healthy" means having keen hearing.

"At the time of vigor and strength. "Vigor" (*jian*) means "to establish" (*jian*). It signifies being able to establish and carry out something. This is an exhortation for people to act as early as possible.
For "vigor" is the essence of pure Yang, the virtue of *Qian*. It is composed of the radicals for "person" and "to establish," signifying that one models oneself after Heaven to set one's will.
Once the will is established, the vital energy (*qi*) follows of its own accord. The *Yijing* says: "The movement of Heaven is vigorous; the superior man, accordingly, exerts himself with strength."
It is so. Therefore, in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (The Sutra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows), the Bodhisattva Puguang addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If good men or women, before their death, proactively perform the 'Seven-Day Rite for the Living,' lighting lamps, hanging banners, and inviting monks to recite the sutras—will they obtain much merit?
The Buddha said: "Their merit shall be immeasurable. He further said: "When parents and kinsmen have passed away and are undergoing suffering..."

"If one cultivates merit on their behalf, will they obtain much merit? The Buddha said, "They shall obtain but one-seventh of it, because in a previous life they did not believe in the Way and its Virtue (Dharma).
However, if one uses the deceased's personal ornaments, houses, gardens, and groves to make offerings to the Triple Gem, one may extricate them from the suffering of hell.
(Text). According to the *Yijian zhi*, it records that Wang Ao of E-zhu established a "deposited treasury" (*jiku*) and ordered...
Regarding my own practice of signing the name [of the deceased]: one must cultivate oneself while in good health; this cannot be left undone.

There are those in the present age who perform the "Seven Days of Life" (shìqī) rites, and there are those who entrust their affairs to the monastic treasury in advance. Do not dismiss these as the idle fancies of foolish old women or village matrons, nor treat them with contempt or negligence.
△ Part Two: Detailed Explanation, in two sections: First, showing how the deceased looks for rescue; Second, exhorting the relatives.

The first part of the practice of the *zhāi* (fast) is divided into two sections: first, the uncertainty of sin and merit; second, the definitive determination of receiving retribution. The first section is further divided into two parts. First, the intent of seeking salvation:
the great ghost of impermanence arrives unexpectedly; the spirit wanders in the darkness, yet remains unaware of its sins or merits within the seven-times-seven days.
They are like the ignorant and the deaf. Sometimes they are in various offices, debating the fruits of karma; once the judgment has been finalized, they must undergo rebirth according to their karma.
While this is not yet understood, there are tens of millions of sorrows and sufferings—how much more so when one falls into the various evil realms?

In the Sanskrit language, *satkāya* means "the impermanent" (*asat*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are entirely subject to causes and conditions;

because they arise and perish anew at every moment, they are called 'impermanent. There are two types of impermanence: first, the impermanence of the destruction of continuous phenomena (*saṃtānadharma*);

second, the impermanence of arising and ceasing in every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*). The *Zongjinglu* clarifies two sets of four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): the first is explained in terms of coarse karmic retribution (*vipāka*).

This refers to birth, old age, sickness, and death. Second, it is explained in terms of subtle afflictions and karma; that is, arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, which is identical to the two types of impermanence in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding the "Great Ghost" (*Daiguī*): according to the *Xiaojing Yuanshenqi*, Mount Tai is the grandson of the Heavenly Emperor and presides over summoning the souls of humans.

(In the Eastern Peak Office, there is the Great Protector [Taibao]; the General E summons and captures living souls, while the General Meng summons and captures dead souls. There is also the Nine-Curved Soul-Summoner and Ghost-Slayer Wei Yuan-shuai of Fengdu.)

Therefore, the *Qingling jing* (Scripture of the Azure Spirit) states: "The death of both humans and things alike involves ghosts," as recorded in the *Mingbao ji* (Records of Miraculous Retribution). During the Wude era, Li Shanlong, a cavalry officer from Fengyi, died suddenly. His heart did not grow cold, and before his family had completed the enshrouding, he revived after seven days.

He recounted that he had been collected by the underworld authorities and led up the steps of the King’s hall. The King ordered him to ascend the seat and recite the *Lotus Sūtra*. When Shanlong opened the title of the scripture, a thousand people who shared his karmic offenses were spared from their misfortune.

The King then commanded his officials to release him. As he was leaving, three individuals said to Shanlong, "The King has released you; might you not leave us a small gift? The official replied, "These were those who previously collected you: one is the Master of the Rope, who bound you with red cords; the other is the Master of the Staff, who struck you with a staff."

"Your head" refers to the owner of the sack. Because the one who was sucking your breath from the sack saw you and returned, he merely begged for goods, and so forth. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "When a person is about to die, they see the signs of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
If they have performed evil deeds, they see Yama holding various weapons and leading them away in captivity;
therefore, it is called the 'Great Ghost of Impermanence. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says: "There are those who die within the womb, and there are..."

At the time of birth and at the end of life, there are those who perish while only just beginning to walk, and those who die suddenly while still able to run; thus it is said that death arrives without appointment.

The *Neide lun* (Treatise on Inner Virtue) states: "A hundred years easily come to an end, yet the five blessings are difficult to maintain forever. Life flows like a river and passes away like a flash of lightning."
"The karma-ground is long and the heavens are eternal"—this is what that refers to. Regarding the "spirit" (*shen*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Ordinary people, through recollection, imagination, and conceptual discrimination, grasp at signs according to their own minds; thus they reckon there is a spirit, which is precisely the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*).
As the celestial being Lu Xuanchang said: 'Humans receive the seven consciousnesses, and each consciousness has its own spirit. The mental consciousness is the sovereign. In...
Wandering through the void amidst darkness— namely, the three miserable realms that are most treacherous and profound,
and the four currents that are boundless and vast— it is said that one's spirit roams in obscurity. Since the soul does not yet know the nature of its own merits and demerits—
namely, the ten unwholesome and ten wholesome actions— it remains like one who is deluded and insane within the seven seven-day periods.
"Understood. It is like being deaf and hearing nothing; this is precisely at the moment of initial death. Or, it may be below, clarifying the post-mortem examination.

The various offices follow the *Daozang* (Canon of the Dao): there are those who summon souls and pursue spirits, seize the living and dispatch the dead, reward the good and punish the evil, and investigate transgressions and rectify wrongs.
Among them is the Manifest Response Tai Bao, General Zhu, who summons souls. Furthermore, there are the officials for summoning, recording, and investigating.

The Investigating Officials (*kanpan-guan*) are those who manage the pursuit of criminals and verify the evidence according to the case records. According to the *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Pure Passage), beneath King Yama there are five officials:
first, the Fresh Official (*xian-guan*), who prohibits killing; second, the Water Official (*shui-guan*), who prohibits theft; third, the Iron Official (*tie-guan*), who prohibits sexual misconduct;
fourth, the Earth Official (*tu-guan*), who prohibits double-tongued speech; and fifth, the Heaven Official (*tian-guan*), who prohibits alcohol. These are all the various bureaus of the Netherworld.

Furthermore, when debating the karmic fruits of good and evil, there are three grades for each. Since the state of mind at the time of committing an act differs, one receives retribution according to what was done.
Heaven is without partiality or excess; it is impartial and consistent, without duality. Heaven’s net governs according to what has been done;
therefore, it is necessary to debate this. Once the matter has been thoroughly determined, those who receive rebirth according to their karma are as follows:
The Treatise states: "All unwholesome [karma] are causes for the hells; the remnants of this unwholesomeness lead to birth among animals and hungry ghosts.
According to the *Mingxiang ji*, when Zhao Tai died, the Lord of the Underworld appointed him as the Commander-in-Chief of the Water Office to oversee the affairs of the various hells.
There he saw a city measuring more than two hundred li on each side, called the City of Receiving Transformational Bodies.
Those whose punishments in hell have already been completed shall undergo further retributive transformations within this city.
Tai entered the city and saw several hundred officials of the bureau examining documents. They said: "Those who killed living beings shall become mayflies, born in the morning and dying at dusk.
Those who committed robbery and theft shall become pigs and sheep, to be slaughtered by others. Those who were lewd and dissolute shall become cranes and wild ducks."

Deer and elk [are the retribution for killing]. Those who engage in double-tongued speech become owls, hawks, and screech-owls. Those who refuse to repay debts become donkeys, mules, oxen, and horses;

thus it is said that one receives birth according to one's karma. According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, this is simply the evil karma of the sinner permeating the mind, causing the mind to undergo transformation and leading to false perceptions where there is nothing. In reality, there is no Yama presiding therein to judge all beings.
They are sinners. Yet, because they have been permeated by their karma, they falsely perceive those realms as real; thus, the sinners believe them to be actual rather than illusory.

Consequently, from the moment after death until they have gained certainty—before they can fathom the extent of their own merit or demerit—they undergo thousands of thoughts and ten thousand anxieties, such that their grief and suffering are beyond description.
How much more so when they fall into the various evil destinies, where this suffering becomes even more extreme.
Indeed it is so. △ Second, the time of seeking rescue:

This refers to the person whose life has ended but who has not yet received rebirth; during the interval of seven seven-day periods, in every moment of thought, they look toward their kinsmen and relatives to provide the power of merit for their rescue and deliverance.

The *Tongji* (Comprehensive Record) clarifies this in the section on the seven-day funeral rites (*qijīzái*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that when a person dies, if the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) has not yet obtained the conditions for rebirth, it remains for a maximum of seven days;
having died, it is born again, and in this manner it undergoes repeated death and birth for up to seven weeks.
Birth is certain [to occur]. However, if there are conditions for birth, it is not fixed. Now, seeking the intent of the sutras:

regarding the utmost good and evil, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*—also called *antarāśarīra*). The utmost good leads to birth in a Pure Land; the next level leads to birth among humans or devas; the utmost evil leads to entry into hell. One dies on that very day and does not pass through the intermediate state. Furthermore, citing the *Shishi yaolan*:
"Nowadays, when someone passes away, one must invariably prepare a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*) every seven days to cultivate merit for their pursuit. This is called a 'feast'..."
Seventh, it prevents the seeds within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) from being transmigrated into the evil realms (*durgati*).

This is precisely why those in the present world perform meritorious deeds during the seven periods of seven days: it is for the purpose of comforting the deceased and rescuing them. △ Second, determining the reception of retribution.
After this period has passed, one receives retribution according to one's karma. If it is a person of sin, they will pass through many hundreds or thousands of years without a day of liberation.
If it is a crime of the five immediate retributions (*ānantarya*), one falls into the great hells and shall eternally undergo various sufferings for a thousand or ten thousand kalpas.
One receives retribution in accordance with one's karma; cause and effect are never forgotten. The *Fayuan* states: "Where there is form, a shadow appears; where there is sound, an echo responds.
One does not see a form persist while its shadow perishes, nor a sound continuing while its echo deviates. Thus, good and evil are reciprocated."
The logical principle is indeed so. I hope you will believe this deeply and not harbor suspicions about its resemblance [to the truth].

According to the sūtras, there are differences between retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*), retribution in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), and retribution in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*). In the sixth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the Buddha said: "Now, unwholesome conduct brings about unwholesome retribution;
being dark and obscure conduct, it results in dark and obscure retribution. Now, practicing wholesome dharmas must result in wholesome retribution; practicing pure and bright conduct..."
Wholesome actions will inevitably yield white retribution; these sinful persons, however, receive dark and gloomy retribution.

These belong to the middle or lower grades, and they may fall into peripheral or minor hells, as well as among hungry ghosts and animals, wandering through the three miserable realms for thousands or hundreds of years, with no day of liberation in sight.
The five crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) are the highest grade of the ten non-virtuous actions; therefore, [their retribution is eternal].

There is no time of emergence [from suffering]. As the *Sishijing* (Sūtra on the Four Beginnings) says: "If one practices unwholesome deeds of body, unwholesome deeds of speech, and unwholesome deeds of mind, then at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one will undergo the retribution of extreme suffering.
This is it. II. Exhorting one's kinsmen to practice the *zhāi* (fast/retreat). Part One: First, showing the method for organizing the *zhāi*.

Furthermore, householder, when such beings who have committed these sinful karmas pass away, their kinsmen and relatives shall prepare and offer vegetarian feasts (*śrāddha*) to assist them on their path of karma.
Before the meal is finished, while the feast is being prepared, or during the course of its preparation, one must not discard the rice-water or vegetable leaves upon the ground;
nor, until all the food has been offered to the Buddha and the Sangha, should one eat beforehand.
The initial exhortation to prepare the *zhāi* (fasting meal) clarifies that this refers to honoring the Three Jewels through the observance of the fast;

it does not refer to the practice of abstaining from food after noon. As for rice-water and vegetable leaves, these must not be discarded on the ground but should be collected in a vessel to be given to animals after the meal.
According to the *Buddhabhāṣita-rakṣāśuci-sūtra*, one must wash the rice and vegetables with clean hands; one must never use unclean hands.
Regarding the consumption of pure food, such as that which has not yet been offered and so forth, this demonstrates the rules for the *upavāsa* (fasting) ceremony.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites a sutra stating that although the Buddha possesses a vajra-body and does not rely upon or require food, he manifests the act of eating in order to deliver sentient beings; in reality, he does not eat.

When food is prepared for the Buddha, if the Buddha has not yet eaten it, humans cannot digest it. Therefore, one must not eat beforehand what has not yet been offered to the Buddha and the Sangha. Thus says the *Hujing* (Protecting Purity).
All the worthy ones establish this merit assembly (*puṇya-pariṣad*). Yet, those who taste this food beforehand leave much of it as leftovers;
such an assembly is performed in vain—it would be better not to hold it at all. Why? Because the devas do not rejoice and the spirits (*bhūta*) do not delight.
This person who tastes it first shall suffer the torments of a hungry ghost (*preta*) for five hundred lifetimes. Therefore, one should be cautioned to refrain from eating before others.
△ Second, explaining the power of making offerings.
If one has violated dietary precepts or lacked diligent effort, such a person at the end of life will not obtain the benefit of these powers.
However, if one diligently maintains purity and makes offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha, such a person at the end of life will obtain one-seventh of the merit.

First, it clarifies what is not in accordance with the Dharma; next, it clarifies that which is in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding the *Jingqin hujing* (Sutra on Diligent Protection and Purity), it says:
"In all places where food is prepared, one must perform the ritual meal in accordance with the Dharma; one must not fail to be careful. From this day forward..."
Those who wish to obtain blessings should prepare vegetarian offerings according to the Dharma; thus they may gain merit and virtue.

The various devas will rejoice, the hundred deities will celebrate, and celestial spirits will provide protection. The sutras do not speak falsely; the retribution of blessings follows like a shadow or an echo.
The scriptural texts clearly demonstrate this, yet it is a pity that people of the world do not know to believe it. △ Third, concluding with the benefits for both the living and the deceased.
Therefore, Elder, if the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa can, for the sake of their parents or even their kinsmen after death,
establish a vegetarian feast and make offerings with sincere and earnest devotion, such people will benefit both while living and after passing away.
"Sincere mind and diligent earnestness" refers to the intent of zealous application and maintaining purity. It is through diligence alone that one can maintain a sincere mind;

"diligence" (jing) signifies the perfection of one's cultivation. As for the character composed of "grain" (mi) and "green" (qing): initially, when the grain is husked, it is yellow and still coarse. Once the grain is pounded, it approaches the heart [of the rice];
its color becomes slightly greenish, signifying that which is contained within the vital life-force (*shengyi*)—the ultimate refinement of Heaven and Truth (*zhentian*). It is like...
This was earnest and sincere; thus he himself attained benefit regardless of life or death. The assistance of Mahāprajñā in manifesting [the truth] is complete.
△ Third, the spirits and deities resolve their minds.
While these words were being spoken, there were thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of *yāma* spirits from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven palace, all of whom...
They gave rise to the immeasurable mind of bodhicitta.
Why did these spirits and deities come here to resolve their minds upon enlightenment? The preceding section clarified that making offerings to spirits and deities is of no benefit;

it merely causes people to create karma for themselves. Yet even spirits possess goodness; how can they not feel shame? Therefore, they resolved their minds upon enlightenment to become spirits who protect the Dharma.

[The Master] listened. [The questioner] asked: "Does the spirit awaken the aspiration for enlightenment on its own, or does the Buddha and Kṣitigarbha instruct it to awaken the aspiration? [The Master] answered:

"It cannot be said that it is through self, other, or both together; rather, one speaks of awakening the aspiration in terms of the mutual resonance between the response and the stimulus. △ Third, the Elder bows and withdraws.
The Elder Mahāpratibhāna prostrated and withdrew.
Since he was already present in the assembly, where would he go? When asking about the Dharma, he rose from his seat to prostrate;
once the exchange of questions and answers was concluded, he prostrated again and withdrew to his own place. This simply signifies that each individual abides in their own samādhi.
△ Second, the Questions and Praises of King Yama. Part Two: First, the Title of the Chapter. "Chapter Eight:
The Questions and Praises of the Assembly of King Yama.

△ Second, the Text of the Chapter. Part One: First, the Narration by the Sūtra Master. Part Two: The Actual Presentation of the Questions. Within the Narration, there are three sections. First, the Principal and Retinue.

They arrived with majestic deportment. At that time, within Mount Cakravāḍa, there were immeasurable kings of ghosts who, together with the Son of Heaven, Yama, proceeded to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and came to where the Buddha was.
The location of King Yama’s palace has already been detailed in the preceding text. Yama is the supreme sovereign over the ghost-officials, under whose command countless kings of ghosts serve.
When the king arrives, his ministers must follow him; when the master reaches his destination, his attendants must surely guard him. Thus it is.
They all proceeded together to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and arrived at the place where the Buddha was.

This was because they had received the light and sound of the World-Honored One and the majestic spiritual power of Kṣitigarbha (according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, all mountains, rivers, trees, lands, cities, and walls, as well as all ghosts and spirits, are under the jurisdiction of the Four Heavenly Kings; therefore, they all followed along and came together).
△ Second, listing the names of the ghost kings.
These are known as the Ghost-King of Malicious Poison, the Ghost-King of Many Evils, the Ghost-King of Great Strife, the Ghost-King of the White Tiger,
the Ghost-King of the Blood Tiger, the Ghost-King of the Red Tiger, the Ghost-King of Scattering Calamity, the Ghost-King of Flying Bodies,

the Ghost-King of Lightning Light, the Ghost-King of Wolf Fangs, the Ghost-King of a Thousand Eyes, the Ghost-King of Devouring Beasts, the Ghost-King of Carrying Stones, the Ghost-King Who Governs Waste, and the Ghost-King Who Governs Misfortune.

The King of Ghosts; the King of Ghosts Who Presides over Food; the King of Ghosts Who Presides over Wealth; the King of Ghosts Who Presides over Livestock; the King of Ghosts Who Presides over Birds; the King of Ghosts Who Presides over Beasts;
the King of Ghosts Who Presides over Demons; the King of Ghosts Who Presides over Childbirth; the King of Ghosts Who Presides over Life; the King of Ghosts Who Presides over Illness;
the King of Ghosts Who Presides over Peril; the Three-Eyed King of Ghosts; the Four-Eyed King of Ghosts; the Five-Eyed King of Ghosts; the King Qili; and the Great Qili.
King Li-shi, King Qi-li-cha, Great Qi-li-cha, King A-na-ta, and Great A-na-ta.
Because E-du (Evil Poison) is the foremost among the kings of ghosts, he is listed at the head. "Evil Poison" refers to the ten evils and the three poisons. Since...
"Evil and poisonous," thus they established this defiled designation. The three poisons reside in the mind and serve as the root of the seven evils of body and speech;
because both the root and the branches are clearly revealed, they are called "evil poisons. Nevertheless, these ghost kings are all inconceivable bodhisattvas.
Through the great power of responsive transformation, one uses evil to strike evil and poison to expel poison.

The intent is to cause people to realize that cultivated evil is itself inherent evil (*xing-è*), and that phenomenal poison is itself ultimate poison (*li-dú*). Therefore, evil and poison are employed as gateways for conversion;

this is the metaphor of the "poisonous drum" from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and also accords with the meaning of "nurturing and poisoning" found in non-Buddhist texts. As the *Liezi* says: "To give life and to foster growth."
"Make them grow and nourish them" (*ting zhi du zhi*). "Ting" means to shape their forms; "du" means to bring their substance to completion.

Later generations know only that "du" signifies something profoundly evil, yet they fail to realize that it carries the meaning of "du" (to be earnest or sincere)—which is, in fact, a great good. Regarding those who commit many evils:

even a single thought possesses all manner of evils, which expand and multiply until they become immeasurable. They manifest outwardly the evil appearance of anger, while inwardly [they give rise to...]
The virtuous mind of compassion. ○ Great Contention. "Contention" refers to strife and quarreling. In the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the Buddha told Śakra:
"The arising of enmity and resentment is entirely due to greed and jealousy; it causes sentient beings to strike one another with blades and staves.
Śakra replied: "It is indeed so. From what cause does the arising of greed and jealousy originate? The Buddha said: "The arising of greed and jealousy is entirely..."
Due to love and hatred, the Patriarch said: "Simply leave behind love and hatred, and all will be transparently clear.
Yet worldly people do not realize that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally empty; thus they struggle over the breath in their throats—a matter of no urgency.

This is what Zhuangzi called "the clash between mother-in-law and daughter-in-law," arising because the mind is the master of poison and the mouth is the vessel of calamity. No dispute or litigation has ever occurred without first violating the physical form.
Thus, those who preserve the Great Transformation employ the Dharma-gate of Great Contention to transform people toward non-contention.
○ The White Tiger, the Blood Tiger, and the Red Tiger—these tigers are mountain beasts, also called "great insects" (*dàchóng*). They are fierce and majestic, arrogant and prone to violence.
The White Tiger is the beast of the Western Quarter. The Blood Tiger has a mouth like a basin of blood. The Red Tiger’s fur is like... [text fragment]
The Fire [Deity] is red. The head of the Ghost is like that of a tiger; thus each is named after the tiger. ○ *Sanyang* (Dispersing Calamity). *Yang* means fault or misfortune.
The Scripture of the Eastern Peak says: "The sentient beings of the world do not believe in the causal conditions of good and evil retribution.

They do not revere Heaven and Earth, they are unfilial toward their parents, they do not honor their teachers and elders, they deceive the divine principle, they act one way in front and another behind, and their mouths are..."

The mind is not at peace. It has already been subjected to constant morning and evening interrogation by the officials and holy assemblies of the Yuezhou Prefecture, with their transgressions being recorded.
Consequently, calamities and misfortunes arise crosswise; one remains in the prisons of government offices for many years and seasons, unable to find stability.

The household is filled with clamor, meeting only with misfortune and decline; thieves and robbers encroach and deceive, making it rare to see an era of great peace. For these reasons, the King of Ghosts has appeared.

To stand at the gate of one's house [to do harm] is the business of those who bring calamity and misfortune. ○ *Feishen* (Flying Body): This refers to the class of *kumbhāṇḍa* or *yakṣa* spirits who travel through the air.
○ *Dianguang* (Lightning Eye): Their eyes flash like lightning, causing terror in those who behold them. ○ *Langya* (Wolf Teeth):
The wolf is as large as a dog, blue in color, and skilled at chasing game. In ancient times, when fashioning ritual implements, the wood used was the knotted heartwood of the *huai* tree.
The *zǎoliú* (date-fruit gall) uses wolf fangs as its pillars; because it is taken for its spiritual intelligence, its character is composed of the radical for "good" (*liáng*).
These ghost-fangs are sharp and point outward like the fangs of a wolf. According to the *Báizé tú*, the essence of burial mounds is called the "Wolf Ghost," which excels at fighting with humans.

To strike it, one uses the *táoshǐ* (peach-headed arrow) and the feathers of an owl. It then transforms into a whirlwind; one must take off one's shoes and seize it. If not [seized], [it will cause harm].

[He] is able to manifest transformations. ○ Regarding the "Thousand-Eyed": The Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara has a thousand eyes upon his hands; the Sixty-Four-Eyed Hell-Warden has them on his corners.

As for these ghosts with a thousand eyes, it is unclear how they are established [anatomically]. ○ Regarding the "Beast-Eaters": These ghosts take beasts as their food. However, ghosts are themselves merely beasts.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* clarifies that the physical forms of the realm of ghosts (*preta-gati*) are for the most part like those of humans. Furthermore...
There are those whose faces resemble pigs or other malevolent birds and beasts. ○ "Carrying stones" refers to such acts as carrying stones and hauling sand to fill up rivers and block off seas.
○ "Presiding over waste" and "presiding over calamity"—these two matters are interdependent; therefore, the Most High said: "Heaven and Earth have deities who oversee transgressions.
According to the lightness or gravity of a person's offenses, they subtract from that person’s life-span (*suan*). When the life-span is diminished, [the person’s years are shortened]."
One will suffer poverty and depletion. One will frequently encounter sorrow and calamity. All people will detest one. Punishment and misfortune will follow;

auspicious celebrations will avoid one; and malevolent stars will bring disaster upon one. This is so. (Formerly, Guo Xin, the Magistrate of Lueyang, could not find a promotion in his official post. He was uniquely crippled and beset by adversity; wherever he went, he clashed with others.

Even his closest relatives and intimate friends gradually distanced themselves and rejected him. He constantly had two creatures, shaped like monkeys, that leaped about beside him, following him in and out. One night, while sleeping in distress, they suddenly came to bid him farewell, saying: "We are the spirits who preside over worldly depletion. Because you harbored hidden malice, you incurred sin. By divine command, we must follow our master. )

"Your term of misfortune has ended; as your allotted span is now complete, you shall depart. You may enjoy peace and prosperity. (Regarding food: food is the providence for the livelihood of the people. Only the virtuous partake of it.)
Evil is diminished by this. Therefore, the Most High detests those who scatter and discard the five grains; he withholds their flowers and vital essence, so that many in the world suffer from famine.

Furthermore, those who recklessly waste the products of nature often die of cold and hunger. ○ Regarding the Mastery of Wealth: In the Bureau of the Peaks, there is the Office of the Master of Wealth.
Its presiding deity is the *Buddhamani* bowl, which masters and protects the wealth and goods of human beings. Thus it is said:
If one does not give away wealth, ghosts will gaze upon it from the side and envy it. Furthermore, the Supreme Being strictly forbids the wrongful seizure of others' property;
therefore, one's wife, children, and household members will gradually meet with death and loss.
If they do not die, there will be calamities such as floods, fires, thieves, the loss of belongings, illnesses, and disputes—all of which serve as the price for one’s reckless taking of wealth.
Each has its presiding deity. ○ The deity presides over animals (*chù*). Animals have four modes of birth (*sìshēng*), and their habitats comprise three locations.

Within the Bureau of Mountains (*Yuèfǔ*), there is an official who oversees cases concerning those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation, as well as aquatic creatures. ○ The deity presides over birds. The deities who preside over birds and beasts are all spirits of the Bureau of Mountains.

Those that fly are called "birds" (*qín*); this is the general name for the feathered tribes. They are called "birds" because they are subject to human control. Those that run are called... [text fragment ends]
"Beast" (*shòu*) is the general name for hairy insects. It is so called because they possess great strength and are difficult to capture; they can only be obtained by surrounding and guarding them.
Each of these birds and beasts has a king of ghosts (*guǐwáng*) presiding over them. Regarding the "beasts of the twelve hours" cited from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* in the *Zhiguan*:
the *Fuxing* commentary states that among the five elements, they are called the "twelve similitudes" (*shí'èr xiào*). "Similitude" (*xiào*) means resemblance. These twelve deities resemble...
It is for that reason. According to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, on the lapis lazuli mountain in the eastern ocean there are a tiger, a rabbit, and a dragon;

on the crystal mountain in the southern ocean there are a snake, a horse, and a sheep; on the white silver mountain in the western ocean there are a monkey, a rooster, and a dog; and on the golden mountain in the northern ocean...
There are caves inhabited by pigs, mice, and oxen (each having its own specific name in the sutras). In each direction there are two rākṣasī women who make offerings to three deities.
These caves are all dwelling places of bodhisattvas. Each of these animals practices the compassion of a śrāvaka;
they once made vows before past Buddhas. One animal, every day and night, travels throughout Jambudvīpa, while the others remain settled in peace.

Cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Beginning from the first day of the seventh month, the rat is the first; on the second day, the ox; and so on until the thirteenth day, when it returns to beginning with the rat.

This is the Bodhisattva Beast King (*mṛgarāja*), and for this reason he is venerated by others. [The deity] presides over *mei* (possessing spirits). *Mei* refers to *chimei* (goblins and sprites); these are aged, refined entities.
See the *Xiangru ji* (Record of Fragrant Milk) for details. [The deity] presides over childbirth. The *Dongyue chan* (Repentance Rite of the Eastern Peak) says: "To form..."

The formation of the fetus receives the creative transformation of the Two Polarities (Heaven and Earth). The rites for sending forth the child and protecting the birth are the fundamental principles of the Two Sages.
For universal salvation and deliverance, there is the Nine Heavens’ Overseer of Birth, Lord Ming-su Zhenjun;
for many sons and daughters, there is the Nine Heavens’ Guardian of the Chamber, the Holy Mother Yuanjun; and furthermore, the Sister of Guizi-mu, named Zhinü, who also presides over childbirth.
The presiding deity of life. According to the scriptures, Vaiśravaṇa presides over the protection of the lives of those under the four heavens.

Within the Bureau of Mountains, there are the Judge of Records who governs the cases of birth and death throughout the world, as well as the Perfected Man Who Preserves Life (Baosheng Zhenren) and the Primordial Lady of Azure Clouds (Bixia Yuanjun). They preside over illnesses.

As before. ○ Regarding the Lord of Perilous Places: high mountains and steep ridges, the vast oceans and deep abysses—wherever there is danger and hardship, and where life itself is at stake—he records those who are destined to die and protects those who are not. This refers merely to minor instances of peril.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are two divisions of hell: first, the Cold Ice; second, the Blazing Fire. In both, one undergoes punishment through physical contact with these elements.

These great kṣetrapati kings, each accompanied by hundreds of thousands of minor kṣetrapati kings, all reside within Jambudvīpa;

The thirty-four positions listed above are all great ghost-kings. Beneath each king, there are subordinate minor kings with retinues numbering in the hundreds of thousands.

The mind lacks the [seal] dot; even one's own body cannot be governed by it, so how could one govern the world?
Now, each of the various ghost kings possesses the dot within themselves; therefore, they are able to preside over the myriad things.

For instance, there are those who seize humans and bind ghosts, who oversee spirits and deities, who summon souls and sever spirits, who arrest the living and cast down the dead, as well as the presiding officials of various cases and the various judicial recorders. Therefore...
The phrase "each having its own adherence" refers to that which each presides over. The following passage clarifies the purpose of the coming [of the King].

How could a ghost-king from the dark and obscure realms ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven? This is solely due to the majestic spiritual power of our Buddha and Kṣitigarbha. Regarding the term "one foot" (*yī-mian*):
"foot" (*yi*) refers to the name for standing firm. A person is born with two feet; thus, one stands firmly upon heaven and treads upon the earth, remaining solemn and upright.

The appearance of "zhí" (straight) is thus derived from "dà" (great). When placed upon the earth, it becomes "yì" (intention/thought). Because one reveres the Buddha and honors the sovereign, one remains standing and does not sit.
△ Second, the formal raising of the question, in two parts: First, Yama raises the question and offers formal praise; second, the King of Ghosts protects the Dharma and assists in its propagation.
This section is divided into five parts: First, the narrator introduces the scene.

At that time, the Prince Yama knelt with palms joined and recorded the Ten Court Kings of the Netherworld as transmitted by the Venerable Master Daoming. Regarding the Prince Yama’s presence in the Fifth Court, the *Tongji* states:
"The names of the Ten Kings can be verified through the scriptural canons and biographical records; six are extant: Yama and Wuguan (two names)."

Regarding the Three Long Fasting Periods (*Sanzhāngzhāi*), see the *Tieweijing* (Tiwei Sūtra). Regarding Pingdeng: according to the *Huayan Ganyingzhuan* (Biographies of Miraculous Responses of the Avataṃsaka), when Guo Shenliang was serving as a messenger, he pursued [the king] to the abode of King Pingdeng; by reciting the verse beginning with "If a person wishes to fully understand," he obtained permission to return. Regarding Taishan:

according to the *Yijing Tuji* (Record of the Illustrations of Translating Scriptures), Dharmakṣema translated the *Jingu Taishan Shuzu Jing* (Sūtra on the Golden Offering for Expiation at Mount Tai). Regarding Chujiang: according to the *Yijianzhi*, Mr. Guo dreamed that he entered the underworld; the King greeted him and invited him to sit, saying:

I am Wang Lang of Ximen. Because the Underworld Registry recorded my loyalty, filial piety, and integrity, and that I did not harm living beings, I have been appointed as the First King of the River for one *jì* (twelve years).

Regarding Qin Guang: according to the *Yijian Zhi*, after Chen Sheng of Nanjian died, his younger brother’s daughter saw two ghosts lead her to a palace, saying it was the residence of King Qin Guang. The King said to the girl, "If you wish to save your elder brother, you may recite the scriptures. When the girl awoke, her family arrived with the scriptures; they invited a monk to recite them a thousand times.

Her brother then appeared in a dream to thank her, saying, "He has already attained rebirth in heaven. As for why only King Yama is currently asked about [the deceased], it is generally because he presides over the Fifth Court.
This is the position of the central sovereign, presiding over all kings; therefore, he is specifically bestowed with the title of "Son of Heaven" (*Tianzi*).
With Śakra-devānām-indra as his father-king, he appoints Yama as the Son of Heaven, charged with governing the netherworld—the so-called *Vairocana* (縛囉呬) deity of the underworld.
△ Second, the intent of the Son of Heaven is described.

They addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we and all the kings of ghosts have now, by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and the strength of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, been able to attend this great assembly in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. This is also because we have obtained excellent benefit.
We now have a minor matter of doubt and venture to ask the World-Honored One about it; we only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately explain it."
First, the intention of the introduction is stated. Regarding the word "etcetera" (*ādi*): it does not mean that he is equal to the other nine kings of the hells.

According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, there is one King Yama for every small chiliocosm; how much more so for a trichiliocosm, and how much more so for the kings of Yama across the trichiliocosms of the sands of the ten directions?
Nevertheless, since the Buddha appeared in this Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa), it is the King of Darkness of this very realm [who is addressed].

This is correct; it is also an expression of congratulation. This is because King Yama and the other spirits all experience retribution according to their karmic conditions, suffering through the three periods of time, as described in the *Disciple’s Death and Rebirth Sūtra*. An official said to the King:
"Great King, do you uphold the pure precepts of the Buddha? The King replied: "It is because I did not uphold the Buddha's teachings that my transgressions have now come to haunt me."
"O King of Hells, you have now reached the celestial palace, where you have seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma, naturally attaining supreme and excellent benefit.
Therefore, I send down these words of celebration. Now that I have descended, I inquire and request: although what I call 'minor doubt' may seem small, its obstruction of faith is great;
thus it must be clarified through questioning. I pray only that, out of great compassion, you will proclaim this meaning for me, bestowing happiness and uprooting suffering."
...the causal conditions thereof. △ Third, granting the question and providing the explanation.
The Buddha addressed the Devaputra Yama: "Ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you. *Zi* (恣) means to allow freely.
This indicates that regarding any doubts one may have, there is no need for concealment; let your mind be free to ask, and there is nothing I shall not [answer].
"To explain for you" is like a great bell suspended on its frame: it rings in accordance with every strike, symbolizing that the Buddha’s compassionate mind is without limit or boundary.
△ Fourth, the expression of doubt and the request for instruction has three parts; first, the description of the ritual protocol.
At that time, the Devaputra Yama paid homage to the World-Honored One and then turned his gaze toward Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva to pay homage.
Paying homage is the ritual for revering the Buddha and seeking the Dharma; turning one’s gaze signifies having a specific object of focus. Why did he turn his gaze [toward the Bodhisattva]?
According to the ritual for inquiring about the Dharma, one must face the Buddha while paying homage. Since the Buddha was at the center, the Bodhisattva was by his side.
Therefore, he turned his head to look at him. △ Second, the formal request, in two parts: first, directly praising his supernatural powers.

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I observe that Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, within the six realms of existence, employs hundreds of thousands of skillful means to deliver sentient beings from their suffering and retribution.
Without declining even through weariness and fatigue, this Great Bodhisattva possesses such inconceivable [powers]."

Regarding the matter of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), [the Buddha] dwells within the six realms of existence and so forth. The *Zhan-cha jing* (Sūtra on Divination and Observation) states: "By virtue of the power of sovereign mastery resulting from his original vows, he manifests transformations through skillful means, appearing like reflections throughout the ten directions.
Yet, within this world of the five turbidities and evil ages, his transformative benefit is particularly profound; he skillfully expounds the Dharma and is able to..."
He skillfully provides guidance; all of these are the power of his expedient means (*upāya*).

His primary aim is to manifest as Brahmā to eliminate arrogance, to transform human beings so they may cultivate generosity and precepts, to undergo suffering in place of those in hell, to satisfy the hungry ghosts, to subdue the evil minds of the asuras, and to grant wisdom to animals—causing them all to emerge together from the wheel of suffering and arrive at the same destination.
The Ground of Wisdom. Throughout immeasurable kalpas, he has never declined from his tirelessness; this is the inconceivable supernormal power of courageous wisdom.

As for the character "Lou" (婁), it represents that which is performed by people. Its upper part follows the "zhi" (之) radical, and its lower part follows the "you" (又, ancient form of 右) radical, with the "zhong" (中) radical held between them.
Why is this? It is said: "All myriad affairs in the world are fundamentally rooted in the mind; there is nothing else."
The human mind possesses a natural standard. When events arise, it maintains its center as it proceeds, penetrating the myriad things as if they were one, without excess or deficiency;
this is called the Heavenly Law (*tiantze*). Now, Kṣitigarbha, through hundreds of thousands of skillful means, manifests various supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

All are fundamentally based on the Middle Way and the One Mind, yet they respond to the myriad occasions of sentient beings to deliver those suffering from afflictions, leading them all back to the Middle Way.
How could the causal conditions for this Great Matter be conceivable? △ Second, the further articulation of the matter of doubt, in two parts:
first, the formal presentation of the basis of the doubt.
However, as for sentient beings, even after they have escaped the retribution of their offenses, before long they fall again into the evil realms.
Regarding the phrase "before long": for example, in the Saṃjīva Hell, compared to the lifespan of the Four Heavenly Kings, fifty years of the human realm [constitutes one day].
What constitutes one day and night for the heavens above is but two days for the Netherworld Offices, even if it spans a hundred years on earth.
Is this not because they come as soon as one departs? They deeply loathe those who do not shrink from such tediousness. △ Second, restating the matter of doubt.
World-Honored One, since this Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha possesses such inconceivable supernormal powers,
why do sentient beings not rely upon the wholesome path to eternally attain liberation?
In this context, the intent of the question raises two points of doubt. First, it asks:
since the Bodhisattva possesses such supernormal powers, he should himself cause those beings to rely upon the wholesome path and attain liberation forever. Second, it asks:

since the beings of the six realms have already received the transformation of the Great Being, they too should have long relied upon the wholesome path and attained liberation forever. Yet, this is not the case.
Is it because the spiritual power of Kṣitigarbha has not reached them? Or is it because the mental power of sentient beings is insufficient?
The Sanskrit term *ni-ti* translates here as "reliance. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: "The ten wholesome paths of action are the pure land of a bodhisattva;
if sentient beings can rely upon these ten wholesome paths, they will naturally be liberated from birth and death. △ Third, the vow to speak.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me.
△ Fifth, the response showing and manifesting his virtues, in two parts: first, a general indication of the difficulty of transforming beings.
The Buddha told the Devaputra Yama: "The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa in the south are of a stubborn and fierce nature; they are difficult to harmonize and difficult to subdue."
As for their nature, it is their habitual nature; hence they are called "stern and violent. If this were the *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena), it would have been gentle from the beginning.

Here, "stern" (*gāng*) means "hard and rigid. This is not the "Qian" hexagram of central, correct, pure, and refined strength (pronounced *gāng*), but rather a stern ferocity arising from blood and breath.
It is like a wicked elephant or a sluggish horse, difficult to tame and subdue. △ Second, a specific praise of the region.

This section consists of three parts: first, a direct demonstration of the Dharma; second, an elucidation through parables; and third, an illustration by applying the Dharma to the case at hand. The first part [the direct demonstration] further has two sub-sections.
First, regarding the skillful means of Kṣitigarbha to rescue and deliver:
this Great Bodhisattva, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, has repeatedly rescued and delivered such sentient beings as these, seeking to bring them to liberation at an early date.
Such a person is one who bears the retribution of these sins, even to the point of falling into the great evil realms.
The Bodhisattva, through the power of skillful means, extracts the root karmic conditions and causes them to awaken to the events of their past lives.

Although the nature of sentient beings is stubborn and difficult to subdue, Kṣitigarbha does not abandon his great compassion, rescuing and uplifting them everywhere—“everywhere” meaning in every single place, that is, in thousands and tens of thousands of places.
This phrase regarding “such sentient beings” specifically points to those who are difficult to subdue: he teaches the rigid through gentleness and the aggressive through harmony.

Those who are difficult to subdue must necessarily be brought under discipline. Just as the kings’ charioteers, Liang and Cao Fu, were skilled at taming the nature of horses and would certainly bring them into the proper path before ceasing their efforts;
so too, regarding the Three Jewels, giving, and the precepts, one must certainly cause them to be practiced and maintained.

When pure precepts arise, one attains pure liberation. Therefore, those whose retribution for offenses is light and small are immediately rescued and delivered, even if they have committed transgressions.

Regarding those who have committed the highest offenses and would otherwise fall into the great evil destinies of Avīci, he likewise employs the power of skillful means to uproot the karmic conditions of their fundamental transgressions.
This is called *āpohaṇa* in the Sanskrit language, which here translates as "the extraction of the roots of sin. One must understand that all evils [are thus removed].
One receives retribution according to one's karma, yet the three poisons serve as its foundation. Among these three poisons, craving is the root.
It is like grasping one end of a cloth: the rest follows along entirely. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one does not sever craving, craving will moisten and sustain rebirth."
Therefore, the four modes of birth all arise from craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"Just as a tree continues to grow if its roots are not pulled out, so too does the tree of suffering persist if the root of greed is not uprooted. From this we know that craving is the fundamental basis of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The cessation of craving is called the Third Noble Truth. The *Daśacakra-sūtra* states: "To eliminate all afflictive obscurations and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)."
It is like the scorching midday sun dissolving light ice. Thus, a verse on impermanence says: "For those with clear vision, nothing surpasses wisdom;
for those in darkness, nothing surpasses delusion. Now that the fundamental karmic conditions have been uprooted, one spontaneously awakens to the nature of past lives.
This is like an ancient mirror being polished again; its constant radiance manifests of itself. △ Second, regarding the difficulty of sentient beings' evil habits.
They were liberated.

From that time forth, the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa have heavy karmic bonds and habitual tendencies; they emerge and re-enter [the cycle] repeatedly, causing this Bodhisattva to labor for many kalpas to bring them across and deliver them.
"Self" refers to the fact that through such skillful means of rescue and deliverance, one ought to achieve liberation for oneself in every instance.

That one is currently unable to do so is because sentient beings have created their own evil karma and bind themselves with it; it is not the fault of the Bodhisattva. Their evil habits are heavy and firmly bound—this is a crucial statement.

To speak briefly of the root source of birth and death, there are three fetters (*saṃyojana*): the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). A detailed explanation follows.

The eighty-eight afflictions (and so forth). Due to these fetters, one commits evil and creates the ten habitual causes (the habits of lust, greed, pride, anger, deception, fraud, resentment, false views, injustice, and litigation).
One then undergoes the sixfold retributions for their intersections. Consequently, as soon as they emerge from the three miserable realms, they immediately enter even more grievous places.

This exhausts the efforts of Kṣitigarbha, who must pass through countless kalpas of dust, employing immeasurable skillful means to create the conditions for their deliverance. Is this not the case for sentient beings?
Evil habits entangle one another, causing the gates of transformation to remain closed for a long time; can they not be shut? △ Second, explaining through analogy in three parts:
First, entering the perilous path through delusion.
It is like a person who, having lost their way home, mistakenly enters a perilous path. Within that perilous path, there are many yakṣas.
Furthermore, such deluded people encounter tigers, wolves, lions, vipers, snakes, and scorpions; while in the midst of these perilous paths, they are struck by various poisons in an instant.
The text is divided into three sections. First: "Deluded regarding the source, one enters the perilous. "There is a person" is a metaphor for sentient beings in the evil realms.

"Having existence" (*yu*) means that cause and effect are not forgotten. "Person" (*ren*) means patience; it refers to the ability to endure the sufferings of the five turbidities. The Land of Constant Quiescent Light is one's original home.
Sentient beings who commit the ten evils are originally children of the Tathāgata. The places of suffering in the three miserable paths are nothing but [the manifestations of] the eternal.
The House of Quiescence: Because they do not know that the Dharma of True Suchness is one, they fail to awaken to the movement of the wind of ignorance.
They drift to foreign lands and fall into alien regions; having forgotten their original home, they lose the way back. Wandering and pursuing sensory objects, they arrive at perilous paths.
This textual commentary on the "perilous and evil paths" of the *Lotus Sūtra* uses a comprehensive metaphor for the causes and effects of birth and death within the nine realms.

Therefore, it is said that *pariccheda* (segmented existence) and *pariṇāma* (transformative existence) constitute the perils of the result; while the five stages of delusion (*pañca-vāsana-sthāna*)—namely, the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*cetanā*)—constitute the perils of the cause.
For these reasons, they are called "evil paths. However, according to the subsequent passage, [the practitioner] is born among humans and devas, causing them to experience sublime bliss.

One regards only the three miserable realms as perilous paths because, by failing to rely on the discourse that practicing giving and precepts leads to rebirth in the heavens, one falls erroneously into the three evil destinies.
Second, these perilous paths abound in evils because they are filled with yakṣas and the like. Yakṣas possess wisdom and supernatural powers, flying with great swiftness;
they are like those with sharp faculties who hold false views, slandering the existence of cause and effect, and whose intellectual sophistry is swift and rapid.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "The mind is like a yakṣa; it can devour all kinds of meritorious dharmas.
Thus, beasts such as tigers and wolves—which are ignorant and stubborn—are used as metaphors for the dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*).

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, because of the abundance of pride (*māna*), one is born among lions, tigers, and wolves; because of the abundance of hatred (*dveṣa*), one is born among vipers, snakes, and scorpions. Thus, the tiger...

The wolf and the lion should both serve as metaphors for the latent tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*). However, since we are currently discussing the three poisons as the root of body and speech, the tiger is used as a metaphor for the latent tendency of pride.
