This is as stated in the *Vibhaṅga-kuśalākuśala-sūtra*: "One who is arrogant and constantly haughty will be reborn later as a fierce tiger.

The wolf serves as a metaphor for the latent tendency of greed (*lobha-anuśaya*); because a wolf seeks food without ceasing until its desire is satisfied, it is called "greedy and wolfish" (*tṛṣṇā-vṛka*).

The lion symbolizes the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*). Although one may have strictly observed the precepts in the past, if one lacks pure wisdom and becomes arrogant toward others due to attachment to those precepts, one falls among the animal species.
Yet, by the power of those precepts, one attains the status of the king of beasts. Since the absence of wisdom is precisely delusion, it is used as a metaphor for this.

The vipers, snakes, and scorpions symbolize the latent tendency of hatred (*dveṣa-anuśaya*). A "viper" (*uraga*) is known as a *śatapadī* (centipede); on a wall it is called a *yǎntián* (lizard), and on an island...
It is said to be the lizard (*śīrṣaka*). Because its venom is so potent, it stings even without being touched; this is analogous to anger that is contrary to principle.
Yangzi said: "The *yuán* (viper) runs wild. The *fù* is the *táo-yán*. If it stings the hand, one cuts off the hand; if it stings the foot, one cuts off the foot—because it causes harm to the body.
The scorpion and the tiger are poisonous insects that sting people, yet they sting only when provoked; this is analogous to adhering to principle.

Regarding "anger": the scorpion is not used as a metaphor for anger arising from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), because there is no conceptual proliferation in the three miserable realms (*apāya*).

Third, "encountering poison in a perilous place" refers to those who are deluded; because their delusion regarding the Truth is profound, they fail to recognize the Four Noble Truths and consequently wander lost within the treacherous path of the ten afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Encountering poison in an instant" means that within a single thought-moment there are ninety *kṣaṇas*.
In a single kṣaṇa, there are nine hundred births and cessations; moment by moment, they diminish and never increase.
They are like a mountain torrent that cannot be made to stay still, or like the morning dew whose power does not endure for long. Therefore it is said: "Encountering poison occurs in but a moment.
Regarding these various poisons, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, snakes have four types of poison: the poison of sight, the poison of touch, the poison of the bite, and [the poison of breath].
Stinging venom. Tigers, wolves, lions, bears, brown bears, wildcats, foxes, hawks, and falcons—these and their like possess every kind of poison.
How could this be anything other than a perilous path? △ Second, the guide who points out the way.
There was a friend who was highly skilled in great arts and well-versed in the prohibitions against poisons, including those of yakṣas and other malevolent toxins.
He happened to encounter a person who was lost and about to enter a perilous path, and spoke to him, saying: "Alas, man! For what purpose are you going?"
And enters this path. What extraordinary skill does he possess that is able to subdue all poisons?
His spiritual friend points to Kṣitigarbha, saying: "It is I alone who can provide protection and rescue. Therefore, it is called "one. The *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* (Siyi jing) says:
"Toward sentient beings who have fallen into deviant paths, one generates the mind of great compassion, causing them to enter the right path, without seeking [anything in return]."

Because he repays kindness, he is called a "Guide" (*śāstṛ*), which is to say a "Kinsman" (*kalyāṇamitra*). Because he possesses extensive knowledge of great arts and is skilled in restraining poisons, he is called a "Kinsman.

Because he employs wondrous skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to guide others according to their capacities—extensively preaching discourses on generosity, morality, and rebirth in the heavens, and universally demonstrating the gates of the Truths, Dependent Origination, and the Factors of Enlightenment—he is named "Extensively Learned" (*bahu-śruta*); his wisdom is vast and profound, and his skillful means are ingenious.
The "Exquisite" (*miao*) refers to the Great Artifice (*mahā-vidyā*). It is skilled at neutralizing poisons;

that is to say, the various categories of the Path (*mārga-satya*) serve as antidotes to the poison of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) for those with excessive greed, and so forth. (According to the *Shanxin jing*: There is a divine medicinal tree named King Mālādharāja, which suppresses all the myriad poisons under heaven. There is a divine serpent, one hundred and twenty feet in length.)

A snake crawls about seeking food. There is a black-headed insect, five feet in length, which encounters the snake. Just as the snake raises its head to bite the insect, it perceives the fragrance of the medicinal herb; it bends its head to flee, but its body is ensnared by the medicinal tree, which severs it into two pieces. The half of the head remains alive and flees, while the tail immediately becomes putrid and rotten.

When the various poisons smell this stench of the snake, all their malignant poisonous vapors are completely extinguished. Suddenly encountering [the path below], the Great Being points out the three miserable realms (trāya). One does not know how one has encountered it; thus it is called "suddenly encountering" (*hu-feng*).
Having reached the point of entry but not yet having entered, it is called "about to advance" (*yu-jin*). This is precisely...
This corresponds to the preceding "erroneous entry. To "speak" is to show the Way.

It is because [the being] was previously transformed and made to emerge from suffering, yet, unable to stabilize their disposition, they again committed evil karma and re-entered the three miserable realms;

therefore, he speaks to them with words of sorrow and alarm. "Alas! (*duḥ*) is a term for calling one to wakefulness. "Man" (*puruṣa*) conveys a sense of caution and alertness. A "man" is named a "great man" (*mahāpuruṣa*).

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "One who is able to see the Buddha-nature is called a 'great man' (*puruṣa*). Since one is currently deluded regarding the Buddha-nature, the term 'man' is used here to awaken one to what is originally possessed.
The *Daśacakra Sūtra* says: "It is like one who has lost their way meeting a guide. This is the meaning. The phrase "What is this matter? is an expression of startled inquiry.
"This path" refers to the three miserable realms (*trividha-durgati*). The Buddha said that sentient beings take the three evil paths as...
Therefore, it refers to this. By means of this path, two kinds of people arrive—namely, those with supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and those through the power of karma (*karmabala*).
Without these two things, one can never arrive; thus, he asks in astonishment: "Have you entered here to rescue us from suffering through supernatural power?"
"Have you come here because of the retribution for karma created in this life? What extraordinary arts do you possess? and so forth—these are words of rigorous inquiry. They ask:
"What kind of marvelous and extraordinary magical arts (*ṛddhi-vidyā*) do you have, by the power of which you are able to subdue all poisons?

"Extraordinary arts" (*i-shu*) signifies extraordinary expedient means (*upāya*), that is, the various Dharma-gates that counteract all evil phenomena and assist in manifesting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). △ Second, seeking liberation from delusion.
At the beginning of the second path, one who is lost hears [the instruction] to retreat in order to seek the way;
this is the lost traveler. Suddenly hearing these words, he finally realizes it is an evil path and immediately retreats, seeking to exit this road.
"Suddenly hearing" refers to hearing the Four Noble Truths; it means that what was previously unheard is now suddenly heard.

This is analogous to Sudatta, who at first heard the Buddha’s name and felt his body hair stand on end upon suddenly seeing the radiance. "Knowing the evil realms" refers to fearing suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*).
The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) says: "In every thought-moment one constantly discriminates between right and wrong; even if a wrong thought arises, one should [counteract it] with the appropriate..."
The teaching is that which extinguishes this mind; it is not the mind itself, for that is the perilous path. The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states:
"Sentient beings dwelling in the world are possessed of perversions and fall onto dangerous and evil paths, following what is not the proper place.
I shall now cause those sentient beings to enter the path of reality. For this reason, the Tathāgata, for the sake of all sentient beings, gives rise to...
This is Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā). Thus, one takes a step back, ceasing the ten unwholesome actions and cultivating the ten wholesome ones.

One seeks an exit, departing from the three miserable realms (triyapatha) to seek rebirth among humans and devas. △ Second, the guidance and instruction of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), in two parts: first, the guidance.

These spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) take one by the hand and lead one out of the perilous path, sparing one from all evils and poisons, and bringing one to the excellent path so that one may attain peace and happiness.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they cause one to fulfill the pure conduct (brahmacarya), personally cultivate various wholesome dharmas, and lead all students to gradually [attain realization].
To distance oneself from unwholesome dharmas and increase wholesome dharmas is called being "supported and led by a virtuous friend. Just as described before, they provide mutual assistance;

they support one, lead one, take one by the hand, and pull one along. They draw one out from perilous paths, causing one to leave behind the sufferings of the three miserable realms and escape all evil poisons.
They sever the fetters of habitual evil and give rise to the auspicious paths of humans and devas, leading to the attainment of Nirvana.
It is the peace and happiness of the *paryaṅka* (cross-legged posture). The *Daśacakra-sūtra* says:

"For example, just as the bright moon, in the middle of the night, can show the level and correct path to all sentient beings who have lost their way, enabling them to reach wherever they wish to go; so too is this son of good family.
In the night of ignorance, he can show [the way] to all those who are迷失 (lost/confused) regarding the paths of the Three Vehicles. He causes them to... run [toward the goal].

Sentient beings gallop through the vast wilderness of birth and death. According to their respective capacities, they are established through skillful means upon the true path of the Three Vehicles, enabling them to attain liberation.
Based on this, one should also explain the perilous road in terms of the causes and effects of the nine realms;

only upon reaching the treasure-trove of Nirvāṇa, five hundred *yojanas* away, does one find true security. For now, however, we shall consider only those in the three miserable realms and those among humans and devas.

The *She-ti lun* (Śatashāstra) is the essential treatise for transforming those lost in the current of the five turbidities. It first employs the Small Vehicle to receive them, and subsequently leads them into the Great Vehicle;
its skillful means are adapted with precision, providing wondrous transformation according to individual capacities. Do not say that this scripture merely produces rebirth among humans or devas.
Having pointed this out here, apply it to previous and subsequent cases as well. II. The Instructional Address, in two parts: 1. Directly addressing the deluded.
Then he spoke to him, saying: "Alas! Deluded man, from this day forward, do not tread upon this path.
Those who enter this road find it extremely difficult to escape and further lose their lives. At these words, the deluded traveler was deeply moved.
"Speech" refers to exhorting one to cultivate the path of goodness. "Alas! is a solemn warning intended to bring about awakening.
Because the power of skillful means has been exhausted, one has barely managed to escape the evil realms; therefore, there is this repeated warning: "You must contemplate this suffering deeply;
you must not again commit evil karma that would cause you to be cast into the three miserable paths. The reason for this admonition is to lament [the presence of] evil wisdom.

Regarding such perverse cultivation, they willingly accept it as their own path through treacherous ways. Encountering such a state, how could one remain silent? Considering their ignorance, how could one bear to sit idly by?
Furthermore, the World-Honored One, out of his compassionate heart, entrusted this task; he left behind great vows to universally rescue those lost at the ford.
Thus, the Bodhisattva, following the teachings, practices them accordingly, manifesting the same activities to transform others and lead them to Buddhahood. As for what is seen...
To lose one's way and fail to point out the correct path—where is compassion? To behold those drowning and not think of rescuing them—wherein lies skillful means?
Therefore, I say to you: this path of birth and death is difficult to exit once entered; it further harms the Dharma-body and the life-force of wisdom.
It is a truly perilous place. That the deluded person feels such heavy regret is because they were previously ignorant and led astray.
Having entered the perilous realms of birth and death, one has now suddenly been awakened and once again ascends to the land of peace and bliss.
It is like a drifting wanderer suddenly returning home, or one submerged in a deep abyss suddenly reaching the shore. How could this not be felt as a profound and most weighty realization?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One should first perceive the Path with the eye and then proceed. While proceeding, one should be diligent.

When practicing with diligence, one should constantly keep in mind what the Guide has taught. Having so recollected, one should advance along the road with single-minded focus, not following wrong paths."
This is precisely what is meant. △ Second, the instruction to pass on the message.
At the time of parting, the spiritual friend spoke again: "If you see acquaintances or any travelers—whether men or women—"
It is said that on this path there are many poisons and evils that cause the loss of life; do not let this assembly bring death upon themselves.
At the time of parting, one should transform others through teaching, so that they may successively transmit the transformation and the process of transformation continues without end.

"Relatives and acquaintances" refers to those who follow the inner Way (Buddhism) but have not yet attained liberation; "wayfarers" refers to those who have not yet received the Way and remain within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
"Those" refers to men and women. "Bestowing concentration and wisdom" means that regarding this path, one further uses the truths of suffering and its origin to instruct those before them, saying:
"This path is full of many evils and poisons; you will surely lose your lives. Therefore, you must know suffering and sever its origin; you must aspire to cessation and cultivate the path."
Do not allow yourself to lose the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body. The above constitutes the formal instruction for transmission; the following shows the intent of that transmission.
To speak of "this multitude" is no different from speaking of one's own kinsmen; to speak of "seeking death" is truly a matter that cuts deeply into my own thoughts.
Regarding the phrase "deliberately seeking death," the *Wukuzhangju jing* states: "In the past, King Yama possessed a vast and universal compassion."
To those who have fallen into hell, he appears in person and asks them, "Why are you here?
The sinners reply, "When we were dying, we did not realize that we had committed various evils; they pursued us naturally and brought us here."
The King said, "What you have done yourself, you must now receive the consequences of. I do not wrong you (text). Is this not merely seeking death for yourself?
It is like embracing a stone and throwing it into a deep abyss; one sinks and falls by one's own hand. Or like a moth flying into a flame;

it is scorched and consumed by itself. It is not that Heaven or another person bestows [this fate] upon you. Part Three: Manifesting the Convergence with the Dharma, in Two Sections. First, the convergence with the skillful means of rescue.
First, regarding the extraction of the difficult-to-liberate evil habits, there are two parts; first, directly applying the Dharma:
For this reason, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, endowed with great compassion, rescues sentient beings suffering from their karmic offenses and delivers them to birth among humans and devas.
It causes them to receive sublime bliss. These multitudes of transgressors, knowing the suffering of the paths of karma, shall be liberated and escape, never again to traverse it.
This is an analogy for the perilous path, explained by applying it to the Dharma. Possessing great compassion—because they share the same essence, they are said to "possess" it;

bestowing bliss is itself the extraction of suffering, and the extraction of suffering is itself the bestowal of bliss; therefore, it is called "great. This is because the essence is realized through principle.

The preceding section describes the manifestation of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) for the purpose of rescuing and delivering [beings]. Producing rebirth in the human and celestial realms (*deva-manuṣya*) specifically demonstrates the practical application of compassion.
Humans and celestials are the vessels for receiving the Path; therefore, it is necessary first to produce them in the human and celestial realms so that they may experience various pleasures.
This precisely accords with the previous passage concerning how a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) provides guidance and support, even leading one to attain peace and happiness. This is it.

"Various lower [realms]," etc., clarifies that the assembly of those with offenses knows their transgressions and repents. This assembly of those with offenses consists of those who are to be converted;

they know the suffering of karma as something experienced firsthand, and therefore they vow to attain liberation and never again undergo such experiences. *Qishi jing* (Sutra on the Arising of the World).
After King Yama had endured the suffering of having molten copper poured into his mouth, he made this vow:
"From now on, after I have cast off this body, whenever I receive another body, may I be reborn only among human beings.

Within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, may I develop faith and understanding, shave my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and once I have gone forth, may I attain the realization of the Path and never again [return to such states]."
If even King Yama undergoes such rebirth in the world, how much more so others?
Thus, in the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*, the various bodhisattvas rebuke the hungry ghosts, saying: "In immeasurable past lives, you committed limitless sins."
Having slandered [the Dharma] and lacked faith, they fell into the Avīci Hell, where they undergo various sufferings that cannot be fully described.

You should now give rise to a heart of compassion. Upon hearing this, all the hungry ghosts cried out, "Namo Buddha," and immediately at the end of their lives, they were reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
They repented and reproached themselves, giving rise to the bodhicitta. The light from the hearts of the Buddhas does not abandon such beings as these.
He gathers in these people just as he did Rāhula, teaching them to avoid hell as one would cherish one's own eyes and ears; now Kṣitigarbha is likewise.
Therefore, sentient beings suffering from their transgressions give rise to this mind of repentance. This precisely accords with the passage beginning with "Alas!
The deluded person," up to "even bringing about his own death. Part Two: Explaining through the Conjunction of Dharma and Parable. Subsection One: Conjoining the Deluded Person’s Entry.
Perilous, like a lost traveler who mistakenly enters a dangerous path.
This corresponds to the preceding passage from "Suppose there were a person" up to "immediately encounters various poisons. △ Second, the correspondence with the wise guide.
Pointing out the Deluded: Part One. The deluded person emerges on their own;
meeting a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they are guided and received so that they emerge and never enter [delusion] again.

This corresponds to the passage above beginning with "There was a spiritual friend" and continuing through the text regarding the arising of profound gratitude. △ Part Two: Turning [the teaching] to inform others.
When people encounter others, they further advise them not to enter. They say that because they were deluded by this, once they have attained liberation,
they shall never enter again.
When combining the sections on the time of parting, including the passage up to "do not allow this assembly to take their own death," the skillful means for rescue and deliverance are concluded.
△ Second, combining the section on the difficulty of escaping evil habits: First, the combined metaphor.

If one were to step upon it, one would still be deluded and mistaken, unaware of the perilous path previously traversed, which might even lead to the loss of life—just like falling into the evil realms.

This directly corresponds to the aforementioned difficulty of being hard to tame and hard to subdue; with heavy, accumulated evil habits, one repeatedly emerges and repeatedly enters, as described in the text. Thus, since...
Having emerged from the three miserable realms and been born among humans or devas, one ought naturally to apply oneself with diligence to cultivation.
Yet, alas, because habitual evils have not been eliminated, one creates further evil karma and enters the three miserable realms once more.

Still deluded regarding the source, one erroneously enters perilous paths, ultimately failing to realize the dangerous and evil realms where one had previously fallen. Some may even fall into such perils without losing their lives.
Because of their meager past roots of goodness, they emerge from the peril swiftly; yet some enter the peril and lose their lives, which is similar to falling into the evil destinies (*durgati*).
Not only do they fail to uproot the fundamental karmic conditions, but they are also utterly deluded regarding the affairs of their past lives.
△ Second, the application to the Dharma.
By the power of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s skillful means, they are caused to attain liberation and be reborn among humans or devas; yet they are soon carried back again.
If their karmic fetters are heavy, they will dwell forever in hell with no time of liberation.

The three phrases beginning with "Kṣitigarbha" correspond remotely to the preceding passage on how Bodhisattvas, through the power of skillful means, even cause [beings] to awaken to the events of their past lives;
they correspond proximately to the passage concerning Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s possession of great compassion, even to the text stating that he causes them to receive sublime bliss.
Furthermore, these phrases are integrated to correspond to the preceding section: "It is because these sentient beings have heavy karmic habits of evil," and so forth.
Thus, he composed this text for the purpose of liberation. Therefore, the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* says:

"I am not like a debtor, such as Śreṇika, who goes swiftly and returns swiftly" (Śreṇika was a foreign illusionist who performed the feat of flying, coming and going through the air with extreme speed).
As for those whose karmic fetters are heavy, they commit a category of the ten grave evils; having already bound themselves with such karma...
"How could one hope for liberation? For within the dharma of non-self, one clings to the existence of a creator of karma;
having thus become deluded regarding the ultimate truth, one naturally contravenes the principle of quiescence. Therefore it is said: 'Bondage arises from oneself; liberation arises from oneself.

If one seeks emptiness within every phenomenon, then naturally, through every gate, one attains liberation. After King Yama had finished his lamentation, [the second section follows]: "2. The Demon King’s Protection and Assistance."

First, the protection by the malevolent poison-demon; second, the assistance in cultivating the first stage of the two lords' lives. This section has two parts: first, the world-protecting ghost king’s protection;
second, the Tathāgata’s praise and joy. The first of these also has two parts: first, describing the places where one practices.
At that time, the King of Ghosts of Evil Poison joined his palms in reverent salutation and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we ghost kings are infinite in number. Within Jambudvīpa, some benefit people while others harm them; each of us is different."
However, this is due to karmic retribution. It has caused my retinue to wander through the worlds, where evil is prevalent and goodness is scarce.
Because I am the leader of a multitude of evil-omened ghost kings, I have come forward first to present this report. First, I shall enumerate the number and dwellings of these ghosts.

As for those whose numbers are immeasurable, they include the spirits of the ancestral shrines and temples throughout the nine provinces, the numinous beings of the ten thousand nations, the deities of the water realms and mountain essences, and the masters of the wind.
The Rain Lord has three thousand attendants and five hundred followers; their number is beyond measure.
As for their dwelling places, there are differences between the primary and peripheral locations. The primary location is five hundred *yojanas* beneath Jambudvīpa, under the jurisdiction of Yama.
The peripheral locations are not fixed; those possessing majesty and virtue dwell in mountain valleys, in the air, or upon the ocean.
On the perimeters, there are palaces. Those lacking majesty and virtue rely upon impure filth, excrement, grass, wood, burial mounds, latrines, and ditches;
they all lack dwellings and reside within Jambudvīpa, or below it. This clarifies the karmic activities of ghosts.
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "When all men and women are born, they are all accompanied by ghosts and spirits."
[The Buddhas] follow and protect them. Why is it that among people today, some are afflicted by ghosts and spirits while others are not?
It is because worldly people act contrary to the Dharma, practice wrong views, and commit the ten unwholesome deeds.

Thus, among a hundred thousand people, there may be but a single deity who protects them. However, if one cultivates wholesome dharmas, possesses right faith, and practices the ten virtuous actions, such a person will have a hundred thousand deities as protectors.
For this reason, some are afflicted by ghosts and spirits while others are not. Thus, those who are good bring benefit to many, whereas those who are evil cause harm to many. Indeed...
Discussing the laws of ghosts and spirits, they particularly delight in the midst of the demonic and the obscurely hidden. Sometimes they dwell in secluded crags;

at other times they rely upon high ridges. Within deep ravines and dense thickets, amidst desolate outskirts and wild brush, they produce strange sounds and assume most peculiar forms, shaking the ordinary consciousness and terrifying the ignorant mind.
Even their majestic radiance and their false,怪异 (strange) appearances [serve this end].
They arrogantly exercise power and authority, recklessly causing harm or bestowing benefits; their actions differ in ten thousand ways and a thousand variations, being unequal.

This section clarifies the retribution experienced by ghosts. According to the *Saddharma-smṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, it clarifies that their causal conduct arises from greed, envy, wickedness, flattery, deceit, and the accumulation of wealth without practicing charity.
Driven by these karmic causes, they are reborn in the realm of ghosts with malevolent minds.

The seeds of habitual perfuming are extremely difficult to reform. Therefore, among my own retinue wandering through the world, there are many who are evil and few who are virtuous. An external text states:
"As for ghosts and spirits, they are the manifest evidence of the retribution for calamity or fortune in the world. (Master Yi asked the celestial being Lu Xuanchang, saying:

"Regarding the ancient site of Xiangsi Monastery in Fuzhou, it is said that during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the mountain deity Luo Ziming was a disciple of that Buddha. He harbored a deep hatred for those who violated the precepts and made a vow to become an evil ghost to devour those who broke them...")

This mountain deity was a person who, due to his vows, took birth as such. He presides over a territory of more than seven thousand *li* and used to devour more than ten thousand people per year. Kāśyapa converted and subdued him, causing him to receive the five precepts; because of this, he ceased eating humans.

Fearing that his mind might change later, the Buddha left behind a footprint. Furthermore, at Lingkan Temple on the northern mountains of Xunzhou in Nanhai, within the borders of Xingning County, there are many miraculous traces. This [deity] was originally a disciple of Mañjuśrī who served as the mountain deity for this area, but he had committed many evil deeds. Mañjuśrī then compassionately transformed him.

He then recognized his past lives and requested that [the traces] be left so he might pay them homage and thereby escape all evils. Mañjuśrī manifested them for him; these are the ones seen today. In the third year of the Zhenguan era, the mountain deity passed away and was reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.

Another ghost came to dwell there, who was a close relative of the former deity and committed many great evils. Out of pity for this being, the former deity requested Mañjuśrī to manifest small traces. Later, the deity again followed the True Dharma; thus, both large and small traces were manifested. Part Two:
Protecting People’s Practice, divided into two sections. First, the virtuous places visited.
In noble families, or in cities, towns, villages, estates, and houses; or among men and women who perform even minor virtuous deeds—
such as hanging a single banner or a single parasol, offering a small amount of incense or flowers to the images of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas,
or reciting the honored sutras and burning incense as an offering— even for a single phrase or a single verse.

The first section clarifies the dwelling places of ghosts and spirits. I have privately investigated how worldly people perform good deeds in the hidden realm and receive retribution in the manifest world;

this is what the world calls "hidden virtue" (*yin-de*), and everyone believes it. Conversely, when one commits evil in the manifest world and receives retribution in the hidden realm, this principle is all the more evident.
How could one not believe this? Therefore, the Sages set forth blessings to encourage goodness and manifest calamities to warn against evil.
Now, misfortune and fortune surely have their roots; they cannot be brought about arbitrarily without cause. Good and evil must reap their retributions;
it is certainly not the case that there is no response and they simply end in vain. This is based on the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 20, where the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "All..."
"The dwellings where people reside all have spirits and deities; there are none that are empty (and so forth).

How much more so for the various heavens that traverse the void and the multitude of ghosts who roam the world. The *Mingxiang ji* records the case of Zhao Tai (style name Wenhé, a native of Beiqiu in Qinghe), who died from a heart ailment.
Two men led him to Mount Tai and entered through the Black Gate in the south. There sat a man in crimson robes upon a great throne.
Beneath the eaves, they called out the names one by one and questioned them regarding the sins and merits committed during their lifetimes: "Speak the truth!
We constantly dispatch messengers from the Six Ministries who always dwell among humanity, recording good and evil in detailed registers; these cannot be falsified.
Therefore, the Most High said: 'Heaven and Earth have spirits who oversee transgressions,' and there are also the Three Enclosures and the Northern Dipper."
The Lord of the Spirits, the Three Corpses (Sānpíshén), and the Hearth God (Zàoshén) all monitor human transgressions. For major offenses, they strip away one’s *jì* (a cycle of years);
for minor ones, they strip away one’s *suàn* (a unit of days). Therefore, one must not fail to be cautious. Next, clarify the virtuous deeds to be cultivated, regardless of their quantity.

Even the smallest good deed—whether as minute as a hair or as fine as a strand of silk—is significant. Furthermore, this includes the construction of monasteries and the furnishing [of sacred objects].
To mold sacred images, or even to suspend a single banner or a single parasol, and to burn or scatter a small amount of incense or flowers as an offering to the images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—
this is illustrated by the case of Zhao Tai, who, while inspecting the hells, emerged from a prison gate and saw two men carrying official documents who said to the jailers:
"There are three people whose families have suspended banners at stupas and monasteries on their behalf."
Incense was burned to redeem him from his transgressions, and he was permitted to leave the House of Blessings. Suddenly, three men were seen emerging from the prison;
they were already wearing natural, complete garments upon their bodies. They headed south toward the Great Hall of Radiant Light, and Sengtai also followed them inside.
Upon a bed of gold and jade, he beheld a divine being of extraordinary and peerless beauty. The Prefect respectfully prostrated himself. Tai asked, "Who are you?

The official replied, "He is named the World-Honored One (Śākyamuni), the Teacher who delivers sentient beings. He has made a vow that those within the evil realms shall all emerge to hear the sutras.
At that time, one million and nine thousand people emerged from hell. Thus it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin).
It is said: "If one scatters a single flower into the air, its merit will not be exhausted until the end of suffering.

The *Śāstra* states: "The phrase 'until the end of suffering' refers to the exhaustion of the two types of death. This means that even the merit from scattering flowers upon attaining Buddhahood is still not exhausted (text).
There are indeed many such examples regarding the merit of burning incense. Alternatively, one may recite the *Original Sūtra of Kṣitigarbha* and various Mahāyāna sūtras.
Burn incense as an offering; it matters not whether it be the whole work or the entire volume, even down to a single phrase or a single verse.
Jingxi said: "A single phrase or a single verse advances one toward Bodhi; a single form or a single fragrance ensures that one never regresses. Is this not precisely what he meant?
△ Second, causing [the Dharma] to protect against evil matters.
"We, the kings of ghosts, pay homage to this person as we do to the Buddhas of the past, present, and future.
We shall command all the minor spirits who possess great power, as well as those belonging to the local territories, to provide protection so that no evil deeds,
untimely calamities, malignant diseases, or sudden illnesses— even down to any disagreeable occurrences— shall approach this house or its vicinity, much less enter its gates."
The phrase "We" indicates that the king of ghosts reveres the good. The command to "all subordinates" indicates the dispatching of protection to repel evil. Question: Ghosts are a wicked breed;
how can they perform even the slightest bit of good, such as paying homage as if to a Buddha of the three periods?

Answer: That which is called a "Buddha" is attained by cultivating all wholesome dharmas. Now, when men and women cultivate various virtuous deeds, the seed of the fruit of Buddhahood is planted therein.

Therefore, ghosts and spirits revere them. They are of one essence and no different from the thousand Buddhas of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*, the thousand Buddhas of the present *Bhadrakalpa*, and the thousand Buddhas of the future *Nakṣatrakalpa*. Furthermore, how could they not be revered and paid homage as Buddhas?
By their mere presence, they can now repel all evils; for this reason, the various kings have issued commands to the minor spirits, each of whom—
Those of great strength and those assigned to specific territories were then ordered to guard the gates and protect the lands under their jurisdiction;

these are what are called "land-division" (tǔdìfēn). This refers to the local deities of the quarters and districts (sèlìng) found today. Regarding evil and calamitous events, as stated in the *Rāhula-kṣānti-sūtra*:
"May [misfortune] oppose one's blessings; may there be constant evil dreams at night; may demons and portents follow one from beginning to end; may calamities fly upon one."
"Transverse calamities. Now that you have cultivated merit, there will be no such transverse misfortunes; wherever you are born, you shall always be at peace, and all calamities will be extinguished.
As for "evil diseases and transverse illnesses," in Sanskrit this is *kāmalā*, which here means jaundice, or "evil filth," and also leprosy.
*Śaṇḍhapa* means "paralyzing wind-disease," which once it breaks out does not arise again. *Asaja* means... [text ends]
These are incurable diseases. The *Hongming ji* states: "A disease that must end in death cannot be dispelled even by a sage;

an ailment that can be treated will only be cured through medical prescriptions. The aforementioned are all malignant, incurable diseases. Furthermore, there are also pestilential calamities and epidemic vapors.
They defile and encroach upon one another; they may squander family wealth or even cause the loss of life. For example, Sima Wenxuan of the Song dynasty was quite devoted to the Buddha-dharma.
Less than a month after his younger brother’s death, a ghost suddenly possessed his spirit-seat.

At that time, monks from the two monasteries of Nanlin and Lingwei engaged in detailed conversation with the ghost. The ghost said: "In the past, I was of noble status, yet because I committed many evils—"
Having received this ghostly body, four hundred classes of ghosts have been spreading a great pestilence since the Year of the Tiger.

Those who were destined to suffer calamity did not offend the practitioners of the Way; rather, those who committed transgressions were extremely numerous, and many innocent, virtuous people were wrongly implicated.
Therefore, I have come to act as a supervisor. Thus, those struck by this sudden illness all failed to cultivate goodness. Now that you have cultivated merit, [your body...]
One will be strong and have few ailments; wealth, fortune, honor, and dignity will increase.

As for that which is contrary to one's wishes—such as the decline and depletion of family affairs, the failure of undertakings to harmonize, and a lack of peace in one’s dwelling—these shall no longer occur.

With the mind constantly filled with terror, now that one has cultivated merit, spirits and deities will provide protection, not even allowing various evils to approach one’s residence, much less permitting them to enter the gate. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s Praise.
The Buddha praised the King of Ghosts, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! You and Yama are able to protect virtuous men and women in this way.
I shall also inform Brahmā and Śakra, commanding them to guard and protect you."
For what reason does the Tathāgata praise joy? It is because the kings of ghosts are for the most part fierce and evil. For example, the King Mother of Ghosts has a thousand sons;
five hundred roam in the heavens harassing the devas, while five hundred roam in the world harassing the people.
They are extremely jealous, harmful, and wicked, causing people to perform sacrifices by slaughtering animals for them, thereby leading those people into hell. Now, these kings of ghosts and Yama—

The Devaputra Rāva, being thus able to protect men and women who cultivate goodness, ensuring they are free from untimely death, malignant diseases, and unfavorable circumstances, and not permitting such things to approach their homes—this may indeed be called the height of goodness.
Therefore, one aspect of his goodness lies in reforming evil to protect the world, and another lies in warding off calamities to increase auspiciousness; hence, he is praised for both. Now, I...
He also addressed the Great Brahmā Lord who governs a small chiliocosm and Śakra, the Ruler of the Desire Realm, saying: "By means of your celestial powers, protect you all alike.
Turn back the immediate calamities of the iron bed and boiling copper, and liberate you from the karmic conditions under which you were once governed by the Lord of the Netherworld.
All this is brought about through the protection of the Dharma and the defense of the virtuous. △ Second, the Lord commands his assistants.

The first section, "Cultivation," has two parts: (1) The recipient of the teaching addresses the matter; (2) The Tathāgata reveals the original intent. The first part [of the second] has two sections:
(A) The Lord commands and states his intention; (B) The World-Honored One praises and exhorts. The third part, "The King of Ghosts Accepts the Command," also has two sections:

(A) He recounts his own karmic conditions as the Lord commands him; (B) He turns to explain why others do not understand the meaning. This latter section is further divided into two: (i) The sūtra narrator records the name.
When these words were spoken, there was a king of ghosts in the assembly named Zhujing (Lord of Life).
Having finished recounting his wicked and poisonous deeds, Zhujing broke ranks and said: "What is it that I have done?

Indeed, when people of the world are born, they possess nothing but their destiny (*ming*). Those who cultivate goodness are said to be 'preserving their life' (*wei sheng*); those who commit evil..."
This is what is called "injuring life. The *Chunqiu*, in the section on Duke Cheng, states: "The people receive the centrality of Heaven and Earth to live;
this is what is called 'destiny' (*ming*). Therefore, there are rules for movement, ritual propriety, righteousness, and dignified demeanor, by which one stabilizes destiny."

Those capable nourish themselves with blessings; those incapable bring about their own ruin and incur calamity. Now, the people of this world do not understand the King of Ghosts’ intent to protect humanity;
they merely follow evil and pursue poison. This can be called self-destruction of one’s life, which is a profound transgression against Heaven.
Yet, what the life-force values most lies in the interval between birth and death: when there is life, the life-force exists; when there is death, the life-force is extinguished.

The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states: "Just as the power of the wind causes inhalation and exhalation, which sustain the lives of all sentient beings, yet the birth and death of life are like the rising and setting of the sun and moon, and the good and evil of karma follow one like a shadow follows a form;
therefore, at the threshold of birth and death, one must surely cultivate goodness to preserve one's life. This is from the *Shouming Bai* (Prayer for Longevity).
The matter lies in this very point. However, when we speak of the "Lord," it refers at most to the one who oversees life and death;
he is not able to grant or take away human lives, nor can he cause one to live or die. It is merely the duty of the Lord of the Underworld to oversee the registers of the dead and the living.
△ Second, the King of Ghosts recounts his affairs in two parts. First, he recounts the matters over which he presides.

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, by virtue of my original karmic conditions, I preside over the lives of those in Jambudvīpa. Whether at birth or at death, I preside over them all."
First, regarding the conditions of karma: all sentient beings revolve according to their own karma.

If they commit superior misdeeds of body, speech, and mind characterized by stinginess and greed, they will be reborn in the realm of Yama, where they experience the karmic retribution of hunger and thirst for hundreds of thousands of years.
There, they do not even hear the name of water; how could they see it, let alone touch it? This is the most extreme state among the hungry ghosts.
As for the inferior: if one possesses a cause of generosity alongside evil deeds, one will be born among the hungry ghosts (preta) with great majesty and power, becoming a king of the ghosts.
Although they possess the majesty and power of a king, they are constantly driven into service by the various devas—acting as gatekeepers, sentries, guides, attendants, and messengers.
This too is bound by past karma; even the office of their lord’s command is performed in accordance with that karma. Therefore it is said:

"By the karmic conditions of my original vocation, I am the master over the life spans of those in the Southern Continent. Their times of birth and death are my exclusive domain, and I cannot contravene them.
△ Second, clarifying that people do not understand the underlying meaning.
It was my original vow that I most deeply desired to benefit [all beings]. Yet, these sentient beings have failed to understand my intent, resulting in neither life nor death finding peace.
"Intent" (yi) is a term for deliberation; it means that my mind deliberated that things must be thus, yet there was nothing one could do as people failed to grasp my meaning.
This mind has defied my will. Once it has touched my heart, I can no longer restrain it; thus, it causes both the living and the dead to find no peace.
This is a calamity brought upon oneself by others, not my own fault. △ Second, the further explanation that people do not understand the meaning, divided into two parts:
1. Prohibiting killing at the time of birth; 2. Encouraging the cultivation of goodness at the time of death.
Furthermore, there are two initial points regarding how practicing virtue leads to happiness.
Why is this? When people of Jambudvīpa are first born—whether male or female—at the very moment they are about to be born, [they experience pleasure].

Simply perform virtuous deeds to increase the prosperity of your home; this will cause the local deities to be immeasurably joyful, providing protection for both mother and child, securing great peace and happiness, and bringing benefit to your kin.

What is the intent behind this further explanation? Generally, when a person is conceived in a womb, it is always due to the force of past karma. The *Xiuxing daodi jing* (Sutra on the Stages of Cultivating the Path) states:
"When a person’s conduct is not uniform—whether good or evil—and they are destined for the human realm, the parents come together and their vital essences do not miss their proper timing;
the child then arrives ready to be born. The mother’s womb is open and unobstructed, and she harbors a heart of joy. The father...

At that time, when the semen descends, one immediately loses the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and enters the womb. Therefore, it is advised that at this moment one should perform only wholesome deeds;
this will augment the majestic radiance of the dwelling and increase the joy of the land. "Dwelling" (*śaya*) refers to resting within it; "house" (*gṛha*)—

"Selection" means to select an auspicious location and construct [a dwelling] there. "Earth" (tǔ) means "to emit" (tù); it emits and gives birth to the myriad things. "Ground" (dì) means "reality" (dì);

that which is produced by the five types of soil is all truly real and trustworthy. According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, when humans were first born, they disputed with one another over right and wrong, and the "skin of the earth" (the natural crust) no longer appeared.
They collectively gathered non-glutinous rice to eat, and their bodies became coarse and ugly; among them, there were males...
The two, being of female form, gazed at one another and subsequently gave rise to lustful thoughts. They went together to a secluded place and engaged in impure conduct.
Others rebuked them, whereupon they repented their transgression, saying, "What we have done is wrong. They immediately cast their bodies to the ground.
When the women saw that they had fallen to the ground and did not rise, they brought food to them; thus, there arose in the world the designation of "unvirtuous husbands" (*asat-pati*).
Because she brought food to her husband, she was subsequently named "wife" (*bhāryā*). Thereafter, sentient beings became licentious;
to conceal themselves, they began to construct houses. Due to these causes and conditions, the name "house" first came into being. As licentiousness increased further, they became husbands and wives.
Other sentient beings, whose lifespan, karma, and merit were exhausted, passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and were reborn [here].
Because [the child] is here within the mother’s womb, this world has the designation "womb-dwelling" (*garbha*). This house where the husband and wife reside is the source of childbirth;
the local deity (*sthānapati*) is the master who protects the dwelling and the person.

Having been pleased, he will come of his own accord to provide protection, ensuring that both mother and child attain great peace and security, while also benefiting their kinsmen. There are two kinds of benefit: [benefit for the present life and benefit for future lives].

At the time of birth, both mother and child are free from harm; at first, it causes the entire family to rejoice. Once the child has increased in prosperity and virtue, they will later cause the household to flourish.
For those who have practiced goodness in their youth, their fortune and longevity increase further; for those who have practiced evil in their youth, even their transgressions are extinguished.
△ Second, receiving calamity for committing evil, part one: Directly instructing against killing.

If a child has already been born, take care not to kill or harm it. To provide fresh delicacies for the mother who has given birth, and to assemble a vast circle of kinsmen to drink wine, eat meat, and enjoy songs, music, and stringed instruments, will prevent both mother and child from attaining peace and happiness.

The act of killing has been lamented alike by the ancients and the moderns; it is nothing other than a failure to embody the Way’s Heaven-endowed compassion for life and to preserve the precious life of a human being.
How could one, for the sake of nourishing one's own mouth and body or celebrating the birth of a child, injure living beings and truncate their lives?
To disembowel them or scrape off their scales is to violate the benevolence of Heaven and provoke the wrath of the Spirits. Thus, Yunqi Da... [text ends]
The Master said: "When a child is born, it is improper to kill living beings. People grieve when they have no children, yet rejoice when they do.

One should reflect that all birds and beasts likewise cherish their own offspring. To celebrate the birth of one's own child while causing the death of another's child—is this truly at peace with the heart?
Now, when an infant is first born, it has not accumulated merit; instead, to kill for its sake is to create karma. This is indeed excessive."
How foolish! Formerly, the scholar Zhou Yu was once boiling eels. He observed that they curled their bodies upward while directing their heads and tails toward the hot water.
Upon cutting one open, he saw that there were young within its belly; he then realized that the reason the eel had curled its body to avoid the heat was out of love for its offspring.
Alas! Although humans and animals differ, the heart of parental love is one and the same. How can you [claim] joy?

I, mother and child, were born to cause that mother and child to embrace suffering until their end, to face their finality with grief, and once subjected to slaughter and dismemberment, further to endure the torment of cauldrons and pans. This agony is beyond words; it pierces the bones and enters the marrow.
At such a time, my single point of benevolent heart would have long since perished, while their inexhaustible resentment would remain forever. I sought not to seek [retribution].
"I do not believe in retribution in future lives. [The reason for] gathering a vast assembly of kinsmen and so forth is to celebrate the birth of one's own child.
The reason the ruler issues a decree prohibiting killing is to increase the child's merit, fortune, and longevity. As it was said of old:
Wine is the medicine that harmonizes the spirit; meat is the meal that satisfies hunger. This flavor has been the same throughout antiquity and the present; why do you now look down upon it?
It is simply because meat comes from the taking of life, while wine can disorder the spirit. Since not eating [meat] is the correct principle, how could one possibly act contrary to it?
In the Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra, the Buddha said: "All sentient beings, as they revolve through the cycle of birth and death, have been none other than our parents, brothers, sisters, or other kin.
Like actors, they change and are impermanent; thus, one's own flesh and the flesh of others are but the same flesh.
For this reason, all Buddhas abstain from eating meat. Moreover, drinking alcohol cuts off the seed of wisdom, while eating meat cuts off compassion."
If even the seeds of past karma are severed, how can one ensure that present seeds do not likewise cease?

If you follow the instructions of our Lord’s command, you will not only eliminate calamities and expiate transgressions, but will also be able to accumulate merit and prolong your lifespan. Please reflect upon this carefully; do not remain mired in worldly customs.
As for singing and music—both the sounds of strings, pipes, silk, and bamboo—instruments such as these are also cautioned against, for they involve the drinking of wine.
Eating meat confuses one's nature and harms compassion; singing, music, pipes, and strings distract the emotions and cause the will to stray.

This violates the benevolent virtue of Heaven and Earth and greatly contradicts the compassionate mind of the Lord’s mandate. It diminishes the majestic light of one's dwelling and offends the protective intent of the local deities.
That mother and child may not find peace and happiness—whom shall we hold responsible for this transgression? △ Second, the turning [of the wheel].
To explain its meaning: first, at the time of birth, evil spirits consume the blood.
Why is this? Because during the time of difficult childbirth, there are countless evil spirits, as well as *wangliang* demons and malevolent ghosts, who desire to eat the raw, bloody flesh.
The meaning of this further explanation is as follows: there are malevolent spirits who desire to consume raw flesh and blood.

Because of the blood shed upon the ground during life, the foul-smelling secretions, and the presence of pestilential vapors, demons and specters come to harass them; they are struck by epilepsy and demonic possession, or touched by corpses.
Those practicing sorcery and wandering ghosts each lie in wait to violate them, just as when a piece of meat falls at a crossroads, crows, ravens, eagles, and wolves [each vie for it].
They come to contend [with her]. Various malevolent spirits and demons, seeking an opportunity to seize the child, likewise surround her on all sides.
The *Huìjīng* (Sūtra on Protecting Purity) states: "Hungry ghosts constantly guard and capture women during childbirth, taking the blood and impurities as their food and drink.
A verse from the *Fēnbiè shàn'è jīng* (Sūtra on Distinguishing Good and Evil) says: "They delight in harassing the elderly and children, beggars and the sick... [The text continues: "Later..."
They become stinking hungry ghosts who feed on the foul impurities of childbirth. The evil karma of such ghosts is truly pitiable.
△ Second, I cause the local deities to bear responsibility for their protection. Part one: Protecting them so they may dwell in peace and happiness.
I have already commanded the spirits and deities of this dwelling and its land to protect you, mother and child, so that you may enjoy peace and security and obtain benefit.
As for the Master of Life, he considers himself the one in charge of human life; since a person’s birth depends upon him, he [claims] it is his responsibility. Therefore...

First, it causes the earth to "bear and protect" (ho-go) its children and mothers; this is like carrying an object on one's back so that it may not be dropped or lost, hence the term "bearing and protecting.
*Himavata* translates as "householder"; it is likely the name of a deity who protects the dwelling.
Regarding peace, happiness, and benefit: may they be born in safety and well-being. Hearing the sound of their first cries brings joy to the father at the birth of a son;
the household is freed from the anxiety of extinguishing the ancestral fire. This is truly the protection bestowed by the Earth Deity and the command dispatched by the Lord of Life.
According to the *Daozang*, when a male or female child is born in the human realm, the Nine Heavens’ Mysterious Woman dispatches celestial deities into the void.
In the middle [of the rite], one chants "Bengong" (Feng-gong). For the birth of a boy, chant "Beng" (Feng) one thousand six hundred times;
this is to ensure that he will serve his parents at home and serve his sovereign when entering official service. For the birth of a girl, chant "Gong" one thousand six hundred times;

this is to ensure that when she returns to her husband's family, she will show reverence to her parents-in-law and her husband. One may wish to chant both "Beng" and "Gong," but for auspicious or inauspicious occasions, only one is used.
This refers to what occurs in a brief moment. △ Second, not knowing how to bestow merit:
Such a person, seeing [only] peace and security, ought to bestow merit; yet instead, they respond to the local deities by committing acts of slaughter.
Gathering one's kinsmen constitutes the first point.
When seeing that the children born into the household have been raised in peace and happiness, one should reflect on the cause of this well-being.
Since its merit derives from the land, it is appropriate to establish meritorious and virtuous deeds to repay the kindness of the master of the estate. Now, [this is] reversed.
They slaughter living beings, gather their kin and followers, drink wine, eat meat, and indulge in song, music, and stringed instruments, thereby provoking the wrath of the deities;

their loss of mindfulness is extreme. To clarify this first: in the thirty-third year of the Wanli era, when Lord Cai (styled Huaiting, courtesy name Chengzhi) was serving as Governor of Jiaxing, he issued prohibitions and exhortations against sacrificing animals to the deities.
The gist of his decree stated: "The offerings enjoyed by ghosts and spirits are no different from those of the human world..."

They are not the same. Humans who are fond of wine and meat offer wine and meat to the deities; this is like maggots that feed on excrement and then present excrement as an offering to humans—would they not thereby incur the displeasure of those people? For the deities are pure and clear;

when they hear of the filth of human wine and meat, they are so overcome by loathing that they have no leisure even to consider it, much less deign to examine or taste it. Therefore, those who perform sacrifices at the suburban altars use only plain wine.

As for those who preside over sacrifices, they must abstain from alcohol and pungent vegetables; the intent is clear. As for hungry ghosts, who cannot even drink water, how could they possibly eat meat?

The story of Maudgalyāyana rescuing his mother serves as a warning. Whenever sacrificing to the deities, one should burn incense, prepare a vegetarian feast, and recite one scroll of the Diamond Sūtra.
The spirits will naturally accept this with discernment, for the underworld authorities hold this sūtra in the highest regard.
If one continues as before to slaughter livestock to defile the gods, not only will it be of no benefit, but one will also incur sin and retribution.
I say that Magistrate Cai has truly manifested the body of a lay official to preach the Dharma for the myriad ghosts and the myriad people.
It is a pity that the people of this world do not know to believe and take refuge in him; they bring this fault upon themselves. What can be done about it?
△ Third, the indication of calamities and injuries.
For this reason, one who commits an offense receives the retribution themselves; both mother and child are harmed.
Regarding those equal in their offenses, the Sūtra says: "There are yakṣas and rākṣasas who always delight in devouring human fetuses, and they can cause people..."

[Those who] have no children, those who harm the fetus in the womb, or those who take life at the time of birth, and who inflict such afflictions upon them, will cause their offspring to die prematurely.
This results from being killed by humans themselves; it is not because the local deity fails to protect them.

△ Second, exhorting [the people] to cultivate goodness at the time of death, in two parts: first, stating one’s own original intention; second, showing that others do not understand. The first part has two sub-sections. First:
This demonstrates that both the virtuous and the non-virtuous may transcend [suffering].

Furthermore, regarding those in Jambudvīpa who are approaching the end of their lives—regardless of whether they are virtuous or non-virtuous—I desire that these dying persons not fall into the evil realms;
how much more so for those who cultivate roots of virtue themselves, as this increases my power.
The *Dharmapada* says: "Life is like the ripening of flowers and fruit; one always fears they will fall away. All that is born possesses suffering;
who can attain immortality? An ancient saying goes: "In life, one is sustained by the eight consciousnesses; in death, the four elements disperse."
Swift indeed is the hundred-year lifespan; it ultimately ends in extinction. One wanders through the three realms, its revolutions never ceasing.
Thus the Sūtra says: "There is a beginning and there is an end; once born, one must perish. Who can prevent this from being so?
However, at the moment of death, the karmic deeds of good and evil performed throughout one's life all manifest simultaneously. According to one's karma, one proceeds to a subsequent birth.
The *Dharmapada* states: "When a person performs good or evil, calamity or blessing follows that person. Although one undergoes birth and death, it cannot be avoided.

Yet, according to my original intention, regardless of whether someone performed good or evil throughout their life, I shall cause them all to be reborn in a favorable realm and not fall into the evil paths; how much more so for those who originally did no evil and cultivated themselves?
Through giving and precepts, once those roots of goodness have been cultivated and perfected, they shall cause my own majestic power to increase and blaze forth.
When the retribution for these deeds is received, one will surely be reborn among the heavens or the human realm. △ Second, explaining the transformation of ghosts and spirits into evil.

Even for those who practice virtue in this Jambudvīpa, at the time of their death, hundreds of thousands of malevolent spirits from the evil realms may transform themselves into parents or even various kinsmen to lead the deceased away and cause them to fall into the evil realms;
how much more so for those who have originally committed evil?

The *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Pure Deliverance) states: "If a person performs good or evil deeds and is destined to be born in heaven or fall into hell, there are messengers who come to welcome them.

When they are near death, they will see these messengers coming before their eyes. Those who are to be born in heaven will see celestial deities arrive bearing heavenly garments and music to welcome them.
Those who are to be born in other realms will see venerable persons appearing before their eyes and speaking wondrous words to them."
Those who fall into hell due to their evil deeds see themselves surrounded by soldiers bearing swords, shields, spears, halberds, and nooses;
what they see differs for each, yet none can speak, as each receives the fruit corresponding to their own actions.
Thus we know that at the time of death, there truly are malevolent spirits who cause such turmoil; even for those who have practiced goodness in their lives, it is difficult to repel them.
He will torment them, or transform himself into the appearance of their parents, brothers, uncles, or aunts, causing the mind to become attached to love and the spirit to fall into confusion.
The ghost then uses a body resembling that of the parents and others to lead them into the evil realms; how much more so for those who have originally committed evil?
For when a person of the world is about to die, the Heavenly Emperor dispatches a written decree; yet if the time of death has not yet arrived, the ghosts of Mount Tai [will intervene].
The gods incite them to commit sins and cause them to fall into the evil realms; one should know that it is precisely these [gods] who manipulate them—who else could it be?
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* quotes the *Vibhaṅga-karma-sūtra*, in which the Buddha told Ānanda: "A person who practices evil may be born in a good place."
"A person who practices goodness may be born in an evil place. Ānanda asked, "How can this be?

The Buddha said, "For such a person, the karmic retribution for their evil deeds in this life has not yet ripened, while the wholesome karma from past lives has already ripened; therefore, although they currently perform evil, they are born in a good place."
Or, at the time of death, wholesome mental states and their concomitants arise, and one is likewise born in a good realm.

As for those who practice wholesome deeds yet are born in an evil realm, it is because the wholesome karma of this life has not yet ripened, while the unwholesome karma of the past has already ripened; thus, although they perform wholesome deeds now, they are born in an evil realm.
Or, at the time of death, unwholesome mental states and their concomitants arise, and one is likewise born in an evil realm. Therefore, in both cases...
Sheshun said: "If a person, at the time of death, gives rise to a mind of false views, that person will fall into hell because of the conditions of their prior unwholesome deeds.

Thus, even if there were no spirits to lead them away, it would still be difficult to guarantee that the virtuous would certainly be born in a good realm and the wicked would certainly be born in an evil one;
how much more so for those who have fundamentally committed evil, who are naturally led into evil."
It is so. △ Second, showing that people do not understand this, in two parts: first, the spiritual consciousness of the deceased is in a state of confusion.
"World-Honored One, when men and women of this Jambudvīpa approach the end of their lives, their spiritual consciousness is confused and darkened;
they cannot distinguish between good and evil, and even their eyes and ears no longer possess the capacity for seeing and hearing."

Regarding those whose consciousness becomes昏沉 (muddled) at the moment of death: among the various consciousnesses within the human body, they may depart all at once, or they may depart one after another;
it is only the eighth consciousness that departs last. At that time, how could there still be cognition? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"When a person is casting off their life and undergoing great suffering, surrounded by kinsmen who wail and lament in distress, that person is terrified and knows no refuge or salvation."
Although they possess the five sensory faculties, there is no longer any cognition or awareness. Their limbs tremble and quiver, unable to be sustained;

their bodies are cold and hollow, and the warmth of life is about to be extinguished. They behold the signs of the retribution for the good and evil deeds previously cultivated, like the sun about to set.

Just as the shadows of mountains, hills, and mounds appear to shift eastward—since it is logically impossible for them to travel west—the karmic fruits of sentient beings are likewise thus. Therefore...
At the time of death, the faculties grow dim and consciousness is unable to discern; though the eyes and ears remain, how can one see or hear?
△ Second, regarding the kinsmen’s duty to cultivate merit: first, through many virtuous conditions, one departs from the suffering of the evil realms.
For these kinsmen and attendants, one must provide great offerings, recite the honored sutras, and chant the names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Through such virtuous conditions, one can cause the deceased to leave all evil realms, and cause all demons, ghosts, and spirits to retreat and disperse.
When it is necessary to provide offerings, this is the essential point of the matter. It is like a boat traveling through dangerous waters; one must exert effort with urgency.
If there is even a slight lapse, both person and boat will be lost. This is because the previous *antarābhava* (intermediate state) is about to cease and the intermediate body arises.
There are two kinds of intermediate bodies: those resulting from wholesome karma and those resulting from unwholesome karma. Due to wholesome karma, one attains wholesome perceptions.
Contemplation. Due to evil karma, one acquires evil thoughts and observations; following the causes and conditions of that karma, one proceeds toward the place of rebirth.

The *Sūtra on the Five Precepts* states: "The perils of birth and death are truly terrifying; therefore, one must arrange a great offering, recite the scriptures, and invoke the names [of the Buddhas].
Regarding what is called a "great" offering, it means exhausting one's own resources and exerting all one's strength in its preparation. However, concerning this offering—
At this juncture, one must depart from what is called the "substantial mind. Whether it be incense or flowers, their substance is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

The offering and the recipient of the offering are by nature fundamentally empty and tranquil. They arise through weighing and measuring, yet they abide eternally in accordance with their true nature.

Widely presented to the Triple Gem and equally offered to the ten directions, although these are called the giving of material wealth, they are the true Dharma-offering; therefore, they are termed "Great. When recollecting the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, if there is light...

The *Ming shu* states: "Since the contemplation of the mind is thus, the contemplation of the Buddha is likewise; therefore, it is called 'recollection of the Buddha' (*nianfo*). This refers to the contemplation of principle (*li guan*);

now, however, we merely recite the name. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If there is a person who recites 'Namo Buddha,' their merit shall not be exhausted until they reach the end of suffering.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "How can one merely by empty recitation of the name attain the end of suffering?"
The merit thereof is inexhaustible. The answer is: This refers to having heard of the Buddha’s merits, which can deliver people from the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death;
whether making offerings much or little, or even merely reciting the Buddha’s name, one obtains immeasurable merit (text).
Thus, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* says: "If one can sincerely recollect the Buddha’s merits, even scattering a single flower into the air..."
In future lives, one shall become a celestial Brahma King; his merit will be inexhaustible. Because it is inexhaustible, he will ultimately attain Nirvana.

Now, as this has been provided as a virtuous condition for reciting the name of the sutra, it can naturally cause the deceased to leave the three miserable realms and evil paths, so that shape-shifting devils and ghosts will retreat and disperse of their own accord without being driven away. II. Eliminating [Obstacles] through Minor Virtuous Conditions.

"World-Honored One, regarding those who have committed the five sins of immediate retribution: when all sentient beings approach the end of their lives, if they should hear the name of a single Buddha, the name of a single bodhisattva,
or even a single phrase or verse from a Mahāyāna sūtra— I observe that such persons shall be exempted from the [retribution for] killing among the five sins of immediate retribution."
As for the sin of causing harm, even minor evil karmas that would otherwise lead to rebirth in the evil realms are immediately liberated.

The aforementioned three kinds of merit—making offerings, reciting scriptures, and invoking the name—sustain blessings in the afterlife, bring one away from the evil paths, and repel malevolent spirits;
such is the power of great merit. Now, regarding the Buddha and Bodhisattvas, it is sufficient to have but a single name. Regarding...
A single phrase or a single verse from the sūtras alone is sufficient to eliminate even the most grievous offenses of the five ānantarya crimes.
In India, a verse consists of merely thirty-two syllables; it is termed an *anuṣṭubh* or a *śloka*.
There is a profound reason for this: thus, one may hear it at the moment of death and attain the highest grade [of rebirth].

Once the great offenses have been eliminated, those minor, middling, and lower evil karmas that would otherwise cause one to fall into the peripheral hells shall be immediately liberated and transcended, just as the blazing sun melts frost;
how could there remain any further transgressions? Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"It is better to undergo the sufferings of hell than to hear the names of the Buddhas; it is not better to enjoy immeasurable bliss while failing to hear the names of the Buddhas."
This is because in the past, throughout countless kalpas, they suffered and transmigrated within birth and death without hearing the name of the Buddha.

Question: How is it that merely hearing the name of the Buddha leads one to attain the Way? Answer: There are sentient beings whose merit and virtue have fully matured and whose afflictions and mental fetters are thin;
if they hear the name of the Buddha, they immediately attain the Way. It is like a newly cleaned white felt cloth, which is easily [dyed].

"To receive this teaching on the merit of hearing the Buddha’s name is a deed whose merit is immeasurable. Having finished explaining his intention, Wuliu addressed the World-Honored One. △ Second, the World-Honored One’s praise and exhortation:
The Buddha told the Ghost King Wuliu, "Because of your great compassion, you have been able to give rise to such a great vow amidst the cycle of birth and death."

Protect all sentient beings. If, in future ages, there are men or women who reach the time of their death, do not withdraw from this vow, but ensure that they all attain liberation and forever find peace and happiness.
This is the text of the Tathāgata’s praise and exhortation. To speak of "great compassion" is to share the same mind as all Buddhas;
to "give rise to great vows" is to share the same resolve as all Bodhisattvas. Now that you have taken the Buddha-mind as your own mind, you are able to give rise to such great vows.
These are indeed the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. For this reason, I now exhort you: whenever men or women in future ages approach the time of death, do not withdraw from your vow to provide protection;
do so regardless of whether they have committed sins or are free of them, whether their transgressions are great or small.
"May you ensure that all are liberated from the three miserable realms and attain peace and happiness among humans and devas; thus you shall truly not fail my instructions today.
△ Third, the King of Ghosts receives the command, in two parts: first, explaining that he has already provided protection.
The King of Ghosts addressed the Buddha, saying: "I pray that you have no concern. Until this form perishes, I shall protect the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa in every thought-moment.
Whether at birth or at death, may they all attain peace and happiness."
As stated in the text. △ Second, the vow for beings to believe and accept:
"I only pray that all sentient beings, at the time of birth and death, will believe and accept my words; may there be none who do not attain liberation and obtain great benefit."
In the *Lokasthāna-sūtra*, the Buddha said: "All men and women, from the very moment of their birth, are followed and protected by spirits and deities.
When they die, those guardian spirits withdraw their vital essence (*ojas*), and the person then dies.
Therefore, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others' lives, one must be careful not to kill or harm; rather, one should cultivate roots of virtue. Great!

The *Jiyun* states: "If one cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*), at the time of relinquishing body and life, one will behold the Buddhas of the ten directions rubbing the crown of one's head with their hands.
By virtue of being touched by those hands, the mind becomes peaceful and joyful, and one shall immediately attain rebirth in a pure Buddha-land.

Thus, Yunqi [Zhuhong] maintained that it is improper to kill living beings during ancestral sacrifices to provide for the posthumous blessings of the deceased. Now, when the eight delicacies are laid out before one, how could one possibly...
To raise the remains from the nine springs of the underworld and cause them to eat [this] would be beneficial in no way and harmful; the wise do not do such a thing.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s manifestation of his original state, part one: manifesting the distant origin.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva: "This great king of ghosts, the lord of life, has already undergone hundreds of thousands of births as a great king of ghosts.
Throughout the cycle of birth and death, he has protected sentient beings by virtue of this Great Being’s compassionate vows."
He manifests the body of a great ghost, yet in reality he is not a ghost.

Generally speaking, when discussing the fundamental and the manifest, the fundamental is identical while the manifestations differ. It is because the manifest is suspended from the fundamental that the manifestation does not differ from the fundamental;
