it is because the fundamental is revealed through the manifestation that the fundamental is not separate from the manifestation. Although the fundamental and the manifest are distinct, they are one in their inconceivability. Therefore, [the text] cites hundreds of thousands.
The kalpa prior to this is the fundamental basis; this is the non-dual path shared with the Buddha. This present ghostly body is manifested through the power of compassionate vows.
It is like the single moon in the sky, its reflection appearing upon all waters. If one grasps at the reflection as real, one loses the source.
Therefore, it is said that while he manifests the body of a great ghost, in reality, he is not a ghost. Long ago, when Master Daosheng preached the Dharma, tigers [appeared].
A ghost appeared before Master Qiu, coming daily to listen to the Dharma. Master Sheng invited it to take rebirth as a human being, to which the ghost replied with a verse:
"Having been a ghost for five hundred autumns now, I have neither affliction nor sorrow.
Master Sheng exhorts me to become a man, Yet I fear that being a man may not reach its end. It is said that this great king of ghosts has passed through hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
Is this not because he has come by the power of his vows, manifesting in the form of a ghost to preach the Dharma? △ Second, the prediction regarding the kalpa and the land:
One hundred and seventy kalpas hence, he shall attain Buddhahood, titled the Tathāgata Formless (Amūrti).
The kalpa shall be named Peaceful Bliss (Sukhāvatī), and the world shall be named Pure Abode (Vimalāvāsa). The lifespan of that Buddha shall be incalculable kalpas.
Regarding "one who shall attain Buddhahood": this refers to one who, upon first dwelling [in the stage of Bodhisattva], becomes a Buddha within the hundred realms.

Regarding "formless" (*animitta*): it is not only that there are no marks of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing; even the mark of being "formless" is absent, and for this reason it is called "formless.

Nevertheless, it is through the very appearance of a ghost that one achieves formlessness; it is not a dull insentience identical to the great void where nothing exists. Formlessness is itself form. This is because... [of what follows].
One contemplates the form of a ghost within the signless (*animitta*). This is not something fierce or malevolent; rather, the manifestation of various terrifying forms is itself the signless.
The form of the ghost today is the inconceivable wondrous existence (*prajñapti-satya*); the signlessness of other worlds is the inconceivable true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Because existence is emptiness, existence cannot be apprehended; because emptiness is existence, emptiness [cannot be apprehended].
It is ineffable. Since both emptiness and existence have vanished, the Middle Way cannot be established. Whether as ghosts or Buddhas, where could their names possibly reside?
Whether as marks or marklessness, how could their substance persist? If this is the case for names and titles, it is likewise for kalpas and realms.
Who would say that ghosts and spirits are constantly driven about and lack peace and happiness? Kalpa after kalpa, they are fundamentally peaceful and happy. Who would say that ghosts and spirits...
To be subsumed under the offices of the netherworld is to dwell in impurity; yet, from the very beginning, every realm dwells in purity.
Who could say that the lifespan of a ghost consists of only five hundred years? The lifespan of a Buddha cannot be measured in kalpas.

Thus we know that by examining the traces through the fundamental source, the traces return to the source; by looking at the fruit through the cause, the fruit does not differ from the cause. This is to manifest the intent of the source.
Is it not marvelous? △ Third, the conclusion on saving sentient beings:
Kṣitigarbha is a great king of ghosts; his deeds are thus inconceivable. The celestial and human beings he saves are likewise beyond measure.
That their deeds are inconceivable refers to praising their manifest traces (*traces*) by way of their fundamental nature (*essence*).
As stated in the *Ānāpūrṇa-yakṣa-mukha-paritrāṇa-sūtra*: "Among them, those who act as sovereigns and leaders are all bodhisattvas dwelling in inconceivable liberation.
Through their compassionate vows, they divide their forms and spread their shadows, manifesting transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*)."

Within the six realms, those who undergo suffering as members of the same class may, through skillful means, act as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to bring all sentient beings to maturity, benefit, and happiness, and thereby realize Great Nirvāṇa. (Text).

If this is so, how could the Lord of the Ghost Kings of Life and others, as well as the Son of Heaven Yama, truly be born from their own karma and undergo suffering during the three periods? Furthermore, one should know that—
All things are merely floating dust and various illusory transformations. They arise where they are and perish where they are;

they are called "characteristics" due to illusory falsehood, yet their nature is truly the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity. If one understands this principle, then more than half of the understanding regarding the provisional and ultimate gates of transformation of all the sages will have been attained.

△ The Fourth Major Chapter: Clarifying the Causes for Attaining Buddhahood. This section has two parts: first, showing the primary practice for attaining Buddhahood; second, revealing the auxiliary path for attaining Buddhahood.
Now, the first part: the title of the chapter is "The Ninth Chapter: Invoking the Names of the Buddhas."

△ Section Two: The Text of the Two Chapters is Divided into Three Parts. First, Kṣitigarbha explains the benefits; second, the Tathāgata grants permission to save them from the suffering of their transgressions;
third, the Great Being correctly invokes the names of the Buddhas. Now, the first part.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I now wish to expound for the sake of future sentient beings matters of benefit, so that they may obtain great benefit within the cycle of birth and death. I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me leave to speak."

The Great Being specifically expounds this "Chapter on the Names of Buddhas" because, as previously stated in numerous instances, the recitation of the names of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—regardless of whether one has committed offenses or not—completely eliminates all transgressions, enabling rebirth among humans or devas, and ultimately leading to the end of suffering.
Therefore, ten names are now briefly set forth as a standard or model; subsequently, many Buddhas will be revealed, culminating in the section on Śākyamuni.
This is the River. It serves two purposes for future sentient beings: first, it is the heart of entrustment from the celestial palaces of the Dharma-body Buddhas;
second, it manifests my own resolve to rescue and deliver those in the Southern Continent. The Buddha’s compassion knows no end, and my vow is inexhaustible.

This is truly because those of the past have already transcended the cycle of birth and death, and those of the present are now bathed in this supreme transformation; it concerns only the future multitudes.

Beings are born ignorant of the path to liberation and exclusively create conditions for evil. If you do not bestow upon them the method of transcendence, they will willingly suffer the misery of sinking together with the world.
Just as one bequeaths a legacy to their descendants, your concern is profound and far-reaching; thus it is said that you expound beneficial matters for the sake of future sentient beings.
These benefits differ according to the mundane and the supramundane, as well as the *pitaka* (Tripitaka) and the *āgama* (Shared/Universal).
The inequality between the Separate and Perfect [Teachings]. This is now the supramundane benefit, the fruit-benefit of the Perfect Teaching.
However, regarding the statement that one attains great benefit within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*): as for birth-and-death, it is indeed the great affliction of sentient beings.
As the Buddha says in the *Catuḥpratisaraṇa-sūtra*, the Buddha stated: "There are four things in the world that cannot be avoided: first, age..."
In youth, one's complexion is radiant, and all people love and respect them. Yet, in a single day, they suddenly become senile; their hair turns white and their teeth fall out.
To wish that one remains eternally young and does not grow old is ultimately impossible. Second, when the body is strong and healthy, one considers oneself powerful and influential.
Sickness arrives suddenly; its manifold afflictions are beyond comparison. If one wishes to avoid it and remain forever peaceful and free from illness, this can ultimately never be attained.
Third, as for the desire to seek long life and the eternal preservation of the five desires: when the impermanence that opposes them arrives, it is like the wind blowing away the clouds.

Though one hopes for longevity, it can ultimately never be attained. Fourth, as for parents, brothers, and the joys and pleasures of affectionate bonds: these are the karmic retributions of past lives that arrive suddenly.
It is like hot water melting snow; if one seeks immortality, it can ultimately never be attained.

From antiquity to the present, since the establishment of heaven and earth, no one has been exempt from the calamities of these four hardships. Because of these four sufferings, the Buddha appeared in the world.
Now, if one wishes to escape these four sufferings, nothing surpasses the benefit of reciting the Buddha’s name. As the Great Sutra says: "Suppose that..."

To constantly provide clothing and food as offerings to all sentient beings for an entire month is not equal to even one-sixteenth of the merit obtained by someone who recites the Buddha’s name with a single thought-moment.
Even if one were to fashion figures of people out of gold, transport them by means of chariots and horses,
and offer up hundreds of each kind of precious jewel as a gift, it would still not equal the merit of giving rise to a single mind directed toward [the Buddha].
The merit obtained by the Buddha taking a single step is immeasurable and boundless (as the text states). For this reason, the tradition was first initiated in the Eastern Land by Master Yuan;
it flourished greatly in the Western Capital through Shandao. Our Patriarch [Zhiyi] annotated the *Contemplation Sūtra* and discussed the Ten Doubts;

Siming [Zhipan] copied the *Miaozong chao* and practiced the Great Compassion [Repentance]. Yongming [Yanshou] taught that all good deeds return to the same source, and Ciyun [Zongjing] [composed the *Fahua xuanyi shiqian* and the *Wanshan tonggui ji*].
This essential practice has been transmitted through successive generations without interruption. Reaching the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, the Venerable Master Yunqi emerged;

his virtue and deeds were fully realized, and his reputation spread far and wide. He exclusively promoted the Pure Land method until it was understood by every household and passed down from generation to generation.
This is because this Dharma gate can cut across the evil realms and lead directly to the original source; thus, throughout India and China, [it has been revered].
All praise this extraordinary and wondrous skillful means; its merit is inconceivable and truly beyond the reach of other practices.

Yet, one must believe it with earnest conviction and without doubt, practicing with diligent and uninterrupted effort. Amidst walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, and throughout the seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter, one must wash away defiled thoughts and maintain a continuous stream of pure mindfulness.
If there were anyone who, despite this, did not escape suffering and ascend [to liberation], then the Buddhas and Patriarchs would be deceiving us.
All such [teachings] are but deceptive words. Therefore, Kṣitigarbha now proclaims this wondrous Dharma for saving the world, so that future sentient beings may have a means to emerge from suffering.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s Granting of Permission to Rescue from the Suffering of Sin. Part One: Urging Him to Speak Swiftly.

The Buddha addressed Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva: "Now you wish to give rise to compassion and rescue all sentient beings of the six realms who suffer from their karmic offenses, and you seek to expound inconceivable matters.
This is precisely the right time; you should speak of them swiftly."

First, I shall set forth the matter to be explained: that you wish to rescue the sentient beings of the six realms by giving rise to this non-referential, coessential compassion (*anālambana-sahaja-karuṇā*).

This is truly the essential gateway for uprooting suffering and the wondrous artifice for benefiting living beings. Like a divine elixir that transforms iron into gold, the ultimate principle transmutes the mundane;
its merit is so towering it is truly difficult to conceive. Since you wish to speak of this, now is precisely the right time.
The Tathāgata’s conditions for transformation are about to cease; his entry into parinirvāṇa is not permanent. If we do not offer this plea for salvation now, when shall we wait for another time?
Therefore, he earnestly urges him to speak quickly. △ Second, praising and consoling him to dispel sorrow.
"I shall enter *nirvāṇa* so that you may fulfill this vow early. I have no anxiety regarding any sentient beings of the present or future.

This demonstrates the intent of earnest exhortation. *Nirvāṇa*: Tripitaka Master Xuanzang translated it as "perfect stillness" (*yuánjì*). It is so called because its virtues are complete and lacking nothing.

Perfect. Because there is no obstruction that is not exhausted, it is called "quiescence" (*śānti*). Master Zhao said: "Nirvana as the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*)—how could it merely be the exhaustion of fetters?
It is called 'cessation' because birth and death are forever quiescently extinguished. Thus, I take this very phrase to be Nirvana.
People could not bear to hear it. As stated in the *Cankrama-sūtra*, gods, humans, and others all sighed, saying:
"How swift is the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata! How rapid is the passing of the World-Honored One! How quickly has the Great Dharma been eclipsed!"
The multitude of living beings shall forever decline; the Eye of the World is extinguished. It is like a great tree whose roots have been uprooted, its branches and twigs shattered;
or like a severed snake, writhing and turning in confusion, not knowing where it will go.
At that time, the various devas likewise all hovered and agitated in the air, wailing in grief and leaping about in distress. Yet, once the fuel of the karmic mechanism is exhausted, who can—?

"Should I not remain to preserve this so that it does not perish? Even if I were to grant your request for you to complete this vow early, how could the vow of a Great Being (Mahāsattva) ever be completed so soon?
This is said to emphasize the marvelous nature of this Dharma; even if I were to enter Nirvana immediately,"
Even if you were to fulfill this vow early, I would still have no anxiety regarding all sentient beings of the present and future. Why?

Because there exists this Dharma of invoking the Name; every person can thereby avoid falling into suffering and collectively proceed toward the human and celestial realms to practice, until they undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
They will be able to embody the Buddha’s mind, realize the Buddha’s intent, and excellently continue his resolve.
As for those who recount these matters, none surpass my Lord Kṣitigarbha, the Compassionate Honored One. Therefore, [the Buddha] permitted him to speak quickly, praising and consoling him.
△ Section Three: The Great Being Properly Invokes the Buddha’s Name. Part Two: First, Invoking the Name; Second, Concluding the Benefits.
The first part is divided into two: first, specifically enumerating the ten names, from the first, Infinite Body Buddha, to the tenth.
The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū now first [explains] for the second time: first, the invocation of the name; second, the manifestation of benefits. The following nine sections follow this pattern.
The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Anantatanu Tathāgata.
If there are men or women who hear this Buddha’s name and briefly give rise to reverence..."

Because the Tathāgata cultivated ten thousand practices to achieve this fruit of wondrous adornment, when men and women hear his name, they immediately transcend the sins of birth and death for a hundred kalpas. △ Ten Great [Vows] (or Ten Great [Qualities]).
Regarding the Buddha Great Pervasive Mountain King (*Mahāvyūha-śailarāja*): furthermore, in the past, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Tathāgata Great Pervasive Mountain King.

If there are men or women who hear this Buddha’s name, those persons will encounter Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who will extensively preach the Dharma for them, and they will certainly attain accomplishment.
"Bodhi" refers to the King of Mountains, namely Mount Sumeru. It is uniquely called "King" because it stands towering in the midst of the ocean, surrounded by seven golden rings.
"Great" means its height is eighty-four thousand yojanas. "Pervasive" means its radiance shines and reflects in the four directions; this is a metaphor for *vipāka* (retribution).
This is the Buddha-body. The *Shorter Prajñāpāramitā* says: "Suppose there were a person whose body was like Sumeru, the king of mountains.
Would this body be large? Subhūti replied, "It would be very large. The Great Master said: "This is precisely 'non-fruit yet fruit. Because the cause is great, the fruit is great.
One attains the five aggregates of the Dharma and accomplishes the Dharmakāya; therefore, it is said to be as large as Sumeru. Thus it is.
It is like the nature of form (*rūpa*). Because form is great, Prajñā is great; as the mountain is great, the deity is also great.
Since the fruit of cultivation is perfected and the fruit of retribution is fulfilled, it is called the "Great Body.

Thus, the Great Penetration is the cause of Prajñā, while the Mountain King is the fruit of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), adorned by the ultimate perfection of the four wisdoms. Regarding the benefits revealed therein: whoever hears this Buddha’s name...
Having encountered Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who preached the Dharma for him, he was able to hear the Prajñāpāramitā of Great Pervasion;

thus, moved by this, the Buddhas preached the Prajñāpāramitā for him, enabling him to give rise to cultivation based on the perfection of his nature. Having already heard of the resultant essence of the Mountain King, [he now proceeds to practice].
Thus, they receive the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas, enabling them to proceed from cause to fruition.
By hearing the name of a single Buddha, one attains the identity of the cultivated and the innate natures, thereby perfecting both cause and fruit. The power of the Buddhas is inconceivable;
their karmic retribution is likewise inconceivable. △ Third, a general reference to all Buddhas.
Furthermore, in the past there were Buddhas such as Pure Moon Buddha, Mountain King Buddha, Victorious Wisdom Buddha, Pure Name King Buddha, Accomplished Wisdom Buddha,
Unsurpassed Buddha, Wondrous Sound Buddha, Full Moon Buddha, and Moon Face Buddha. There were unspeakably many Buddhas such as these.
"Pure Moon" refers to the Buddha’s true Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is like empty space. It manifests forms in response to sentient beings, like the moon reflected in water.

The moon serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s body; the Dharma-body is like space, while the radiance of the mind is pure and bright. Emanating from the Truth, it appears as reflections in the water.
This clarifies that the three bodies (*trikāya*) are one essence. "Mountain King. The Sanskrit name is *Śailendra-rāja*. This...
Mount Yunshan King. In the *Mahāvaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Flower-Cluster (*Puṣpasaṃcaya*) praises the Buddha, saying:
"The World-Honored One’s golden body is like a mountain of gold; he is like the light of the sun illuminating the world, able to uproot all suffering and affliction."
I now prostrate to the Great Dharma King. (Same as above. ○ *Ji-sheng* (Victorious Wisdom). This is precisely the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"The wisdom of *sarvajña* (all-knowing)—in the Qin language, the 'aspect of all-knowledge'—is the wisdom of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. The wisdom of the *mārgākārajñatā* (knowledge of the aspects of the path) is the wisdom of the bodhisattvas.
The wisdom of *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience) is the wisdom of the Buddhas, because they know all things through every kind of aspect and characteristic."

He is praised as supreme among all wisdoms. [He is] the King Vimalakīrti (Pure Name). Because he has purified and exhausted the five abodes and two deaths, and because he possesses mastery, this supreme title is established (*The Samādhi of Gathering All Merit* states:

thirty-two lands to the east of here, there is a land named Universal Purity; the Buddha’s name is King Vimalakīrti. In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, Śākyamuni was the Most Victorious Rishi;
having heard the *Samādhi of Gathering All Merit*, he was later reborn in that land and has now attained Buddhahood). [He is] the accomplishment of wisdom through skillful means.
This is because both types of wisdom are fully accomplished. Regarding "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*): it is a title for the ultimate in honor.
Those who have something yet to be severed are called "surpassable persons" (*sottarapudgala*); since there is nothing further to be severed, one is called "unsurpassed.
As the *Anuttara-sthāna-sūtra* says: "If sentient beings give rise to a mind of faith and inclination toward the unsurpassed state of the Buddha, among gods and humans..."

They attain the unsurpassed fruit. ○ Regarding "Exquisite Sound": The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that in mountains, valleys, and wildernesses, there are many *kalaviṅka* birds which produce exquisite sounds.
Such beautiful voices are [unmatched] by those of devas, humans, *kiṃnaras*, and others.
There is none who can equal it, except for the voice of the Tathāgata; therefore, it is called "wondrous sound.
Regarding the two Buddhas, Pūrṇacandra and Candrānana, their general meaning is the same. As the sutra says:
"Just as the moon on the fifteenth day is perfectly full, the king among all the stars, most supreme and most excellent; so too is the Buddha’s face pure and perfect, just like the moon. Thus it is.
Regarding these unspeakable numbers of Buddhas, their kalpa counts and the benefits of hearing their names are no longer detailed;

therefore, they are summarized here. Thus one should know that from the time Kṣitigarbha first resolved his mind until this day, every Buddha he encountered—such as Śākyamuni—entrusted him with the task of delivering and liberating beings, just as it is today in the celestial palace, such that [the number] cannot be fully grasped.
This is inconceivable. The recitation of the name is concluded. II. Conclusion on the Benefits, in two parts: A. The benefit of reciting the name at the time of birth, in two parts:
1. The benefit illustrated by comparing one with many.
"World-Honored One, if all sentient beings of the present and future—whether gods or humans, whether men or women—merely keep [the Buddha] in mind..."
The merit of obtaining the name of a single Buddha is immeasurable; how much more so for many names!
Now, the Way is contrary to the mundane, and names often diverge from reality. Those who grasp its essential principle will mysteriously harmonize with the profound truth.
Why is this so? It is because, in the secular world, one is not permitted to recite the names of one's ancestors, whereas in the Dharma-gate, the names of Buddhas are invoked.

One shall receive immeasurable blessings. This is truly because the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, out of great compassion for all beings, manifest their spiritual descent into the mundane world with the primary aim of delivering them.
Those who harbor a heart of aspiration will, without exception, receive benefit—whether by invoking them with speech, contemplating them with the mind, or paying homage with the body.
By adding reverence through these three karmas, the three poisons are cooled, the roots of existence are gradually uprooted, and one emerges from [saṃsāra].
Regarding the realms of existence (*dhātu-bandhana*), there are those of great virtue; those who praise them obtain merit. Those who follow worldly conventions are the opposite of the former.
The *Daśacakra-sūtra* states: "If one contemplates a single Buddha, one sees a single Buddha; if one contemplates many Buddhas, one sees many Buddhas.
If one contemplates a Buddha with a small body, one sees a Buddha with a small body; if one contemplates a Buddha with a large body, one sees a Buddha with a large body."
If one contemplates immeasurable Buddhas, one then perceives immeasurable Buddhas and so forth; therefore, by means of a single Buddha, one may infer the many.
△ Second, the benefit gained in relation to birth and death.
These sentient beings, at the time of birth and at the time of death, naturally attain great benefit and never fall into the evil realms.
Master Yuancheng said: "The ordinary beings of the six paths and the worthy sages of the three vehicles each possess the jewel-light of the awakened nature in its full perfection.
Originally, they are neither called Buddhas nor called sentient beings; it is only because this mind does not maintain its own nature."

According to the conditions of delusion or awakening, one performs karma and undergoes suffering; this is called a "sentient being" (*sattva*). By cultivating the path and realizing the Truth, one is then named a "Buddha.

Out of compassion for sentient beings who fail to realize it due to their false conceptualizations and attachments, the Buddha—while remaining identical to the nature of the *dharmadhātu*—proclaims the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).
If one attains this gate, one becomes equal to all Buddhas in a single morning; if one does not attain it...
If one does not enter this gate, one will merely cultivate causes throughout vast eons.

Therefore, whenever sentient beings are in the midst of birth and death, if they are able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha—whether it be of a single Buddha or many Buddhas—they will each obtain great benefits and shall ultimately never fall into the evil realms.
However, this is the Buddha encountered by a Mahāsattva, whom he personally served and made offerings to, thereby attaining all manner of benefits.
Yet, among the various sūtras and śāstras, only Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter is praised for his reception of beings from the Sahā world; his power of aspiration is particularly weighty.
Therefore, among all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, Amitābha alone is pointed out as the ultimate.
If, at the time of birth and death, one can truly and sincerely invoke his name, the response will be even more abundant. This is what is meant by returning to the Pure Land without moving a step;
why wait for gradual stages? To realize Amitābha without conceptual deliberation—how could there be any lingering words or thoughts? Awakening or delusion depends solely upon oneself.
The mind transcends the deep abyss; how could this be due to other dharmas? Through sincere faith and diligent practice, one shall personally witness the progress of one's own merit.
△ Second, the benefit of reciting the Name at the time of death, in three parts: first, showing that reciting the Name extinguishes transgressions.
If, at the time of death, even a single member of one's family or circle of relatives should loudly recite the name of a single Buddha for the sake of that sick person,
that person who has passed away will be cleared of the five sins of immediate retribution, and all other karmic retributions will be entirely extinguished.
"Even down to a single person who recollects the name of a single Buddha"—this is a condensation from the case of many people and many Buddhas down to the absolute minimum.
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "One who utters the name 'Namo Buddha' even once, by this root of goodness, shall enter the realm of nirvāṇa;
it is inexhaustible. How much more so, then, could one doubt that the five sins of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) would not be dissolved? These are the most grievous transgressions.

Once the transgressions have been eliminated, how could the remaining middle and lower karmic retributions not be entirely extinguished? (To "eliminate" means to remove them; it does not mean that they are permitted to remain while failing to be extinguished).
Formerly, the Vinaya Master of Great Wisdom made a vow to always be reborn in Sahā [World] to act as a great guide.
Furthermore, he said upon seeing Dharma Master Huibù: "Although this land is pure, it is not what I desire. For this reason, regarding the gate of the Pure Land, he was brief...
Having no place of refuge, he saw those who cultivated pure karma and again gave rise to disparaging slander. Later, he suffered a grave illness;

his consciousness became clouded and confused, whereupon he suddenly realized his former errors and deeply reproached himself. He then consulted the *Ten Doubts* treatise by Tiantai for the sake of bodhisattvas at the initial stage of resolve.
Without having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), one must constantly remain inseparable from the Buddha. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"It is impossible for an ordinary person bound by all fetters to possess a heart of great compassion and vow to be born in an evil age to save suffering sentient beings.

It is like an infant who cannot be separated from its mother, or like a fledgling with weak wings that can only cling to a branch. From this point on, [the practitioner] completely abandons their former life.
In his studies, he focused exclusively on the teachings of the Pure Land school, never abandoning them for even a moment over the course of more than ten years.
Furthermore, the Great Master Fazhao of the Tang dynasty went to Zhulin Temple on Mount Wutai and saw Mañjuśrī to the west and Samantabhadra to the east, preaching the Dharma to the assembly.
Fazhao prostrated himself and asked: "Ordinary beings of the final age possess shallow and inferior wisdom and knowledge; regarding their Buddha-nature and mind—"
The ground has no means of manifesting itself. I do not yet know which dharma-gate one should cultivate as being most essential. Mañjuśrī said:

"Among all gates of practice, none is like the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti). It is because I recollect the Buddha that I have attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). He asked again:
"How should one practice mindfulness? Mañjuśrī replied, "To the west of this world lies Amitābha, whose power of vows is inconceivable.

You should fix your mindfulness upon him without interruption; then, at the end of your life, you will certainly attain rebirth there. Having spoken thus, he stroked the crown of Huìrì’s head with his hand and withdrew.
Dharma Master Huìrì sought the Black Avalokiteśvara and was moved by the manifestation of a radiant sign; what he recounted was largely the same as above.
Therefore, one must by all means believe in the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha. △ Second, resolving doubts regarding the extinction of the five immediate transgressions:

Although these five immediate sins are extremely grave—such that even after passing through billions of kalpas one still finds no way out—if, at the moment of death, another person recites the name of the Buddha for them, then even within those sins they will gradually be extinguished.
A doubt arises: "The karma of the uninterrupted [ānantarya] offenses is heavy; how can the mere recitation of the name of a single Buddha cause it to be extinguished?

As the *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "If sentient beings have committed evils through the three karmas, yet at the time of death they recollect the merits of the Tathāgata, they will certainly leave the realms of evil destinies and attain rebirth in the heavens. This applies even to those who are extremely wicked; by means of mindfulness of the Buddha..."

Therefore, one may also attain rebirth in heaven. Thus we know that although the karma of an *ānantarya* offense is heavy and difficult to escape from for an eon, by relying on the power of mindfulness of the Buddha at the moment of death, inverted delusions will not arise;
the *dharmatā* (nature of reality) will manifest before one, and thus [the offense] can be extinguished.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Even if one hears the name of the Tathāgata and the Dharma he has taught, yet does not give rise to faith and understanding..."
If even those who have merely planted the seeds of merit can achieve such results, how much more so for those of your current retinue who invoke the Buddha’s name with sincere faith;
how could they possibly fail to attain extinction? It is like using a lion’s sinew as a lute string: once it is plucked, all other strings snap.
It is also like placing the milk of cattle, sheep, donkeys, and horses together in a single vessel; if a single drop of a lion’s milk is poured into it, [it causes them all to turn sour].
It was transformed into water. Now that you have already cultivated the bodhicitta and practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, your grave offenses will be extinguished;
why wait to harbor doubts? △ Third, furthermore, regarding the self-claiming of merit and sin:
How much more so for sentient beings who recite and contemplate [the name] themselves; they will obtain immeasurable merit and extinguish immeasurable sins.
This is even more so for those who form the resolve [to do so]. It is precisely to exhort people that self-contemplation is superior:

if the extinction of sin through having another recite on one's behalf is already such as this, how much more so for one who contemplates it oneself! Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 24, asks: "At the time of death, for a brief moment..."
Question: How can the mind at that moment overcome the power of a lifetime of practice? Answer: Although this mind is small, its power is fierce and sharp.
Just as fire or poison, though small, can accomplish great things, so too is the mind at the time of approaching death decisively fierce and powerful.
Therefore, it surpasses the power of practicing for a hundred years; this subsequent mind is called the "Great Mind.

Because the matter of relinquishing the body and the sense faculties is urgent, at the time of recollecting the Buddha, all transgressions are transformed into merit. It is like Jīvaka grasping grass—there is none that is not medicinal, capable of universally curing diseases.
Or like the sand and pebbles held by Śreṇika Bimbisāra’s son, Mānava—all were transformed into jewels, as his entire mind was filled [with faith].
Every day is nothing other than the realm of the Buddha. The offenses and merits one contemplates are themselves the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Since everything is purely the true mark, offenses and merits cannot be found at all when sought; how, then, can one discuss whether they are finite or infinite?

For now, however, we follow worldly convention and say that by self-proclaiming and self-reflecting, one obtains merit and extinguishes offenses, which is many times more superior than what was mentioned before.

△ Second, revealing the aids to the path for attaining Buddhahood: Since it has already been stated that the Buddha’s name signifies that right practice is perfected, why is it necessary to further clarify giving (*dāna*) as an aid to the path?
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, among the karmas that benefit others within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), none surpasses giving.
Why is this so? Because the reputation of one who is fond of giving spreads throughout the eight directions, inspiring faith.
I shall have no lack of love or respect; I shall be without fear or difficulty when amidst the great assembly; I shall have no regrets at the time of death.

By planting my wealth and goods in a fertile field of merit, I shall surely attain the bliss of humans and devas, as well as the gateway to Nirvana—not merely opening these three joys, but being able to open the place of immeasurable Buddha-ways through the six pāramitās.
Honey is the Buddha-way, and generosity (*dāna*) is its initial gateway; all other practices follow from it.
Because such acts of giving possess immeasurable merit, the Buddha taught that generosity is the primary causal condition for assisting the path.
Since human life is impermanent and wealth is like a flash of lightning, one should give even to those who do not ask, let alone to those who do.
Because giving should be practiced as a causal condition that aids the Path, one must weigh the conditions for giving in order to assist in the opening of the Buddha-way. Chapter Title:
Chapter Ten: Weighing the Conditions for the Merit of Giving.
△ Section Two: The Text of the Second Chapter. This section has two parts: first, Kṣitigarbha requests a comparison with the merit of giving; second, the Tathāgata compares them before the assembly.
The first part has two sub-sections: first, the sūtra narrator describes the ritual setting.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, rose from his seat, knelt on his right knee, and joined his palms.
[The hand gesture] is as described in the text. △ Second, Kṣitigarbha’s inquiry and request.

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I observe that among sentient beings on the path of karma, when comparing their acts of giving, there are those that are light and those that are heavy."
"One receives blessings for a single lifetime; there are those who receive blessings for ten lifetimes; and there are those who receive great benefit and merit for a hundred or a thousand lifetimes.
How is this so? I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this to me."
Regarding the paths of action (*karmapatha*): sinful actions such as killing are called "black-black" karma and are unwholesome karma.
Meritorious actions such as giving are called "white-white" karma and are wholesome karma. Now, within the context of wholesome karma, one specific instance—the merit of giving—is clarified;
thus it says, "I observe," and so forth. Giving is of many kinds: the gift of material wealth, the gift of the Dharma, the worldly gift, and the supramundane gift. [The latter] is light...
To weigh this again: like threads strung together, the two characters for "receiving blessings" are the most essential matters in both the mundane and supramundane realms;
all are obtained through giving. This question of yours, Great Being, is truly a sublime remedy for escaping suffering and the very root of the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding this matter, what are the phrases? One rightly doubts why the causes for giving are equal, yet the resulting blessings are not the same.
Question: Is it that Kṣitigarbha truly does not know, or is it that sentient beings have doubts? Answer: He truly knows; he does not truly know. This is beyond the measurement of ordinary minds.
According to the *Saṃyukta Āgama* (Zá zàng jīng), in the past, there was a person who went to the Pratimokṣa Monastery and obtained...
There was an *āmra* tree flower, its color like gold. He took it into a Buddhist stūpa and beheld the marks and signs of the Buddha Śākyamuni’s image.
As he continued to recollect the Buddha’s merits, his heart grew fervent and his hair stood on end. He immediately offered the flower to the Buddha and went out to ask a certain practitioner:
"How much merit does one obtain by scattering a single flower upon the Buddha? He replied, "Such a profound matter as this, I am unable to know."
He asked those who recited the scriptures, and they went to question them. They said, "We do not possess the supernormal power of the divine eye; we cannot perceive the retribution of karmic results.
You should ask an Arhat who possesses the six supernormal powers and practices seated meditation. They immediately went to question him.
The Arhat then observed for them and saw the sequence of his discarding of bodies, as well as the meritorious blessings he received among devas and humans, up until the eighth [life].
Even after ten thousand great kalpas, his merit would still not be exhausted; beyond that, it could no longer be known.
He then dispatched a manifested person to the place of Maitreya to ask how much karmic fruit he had obtained. Maitreya replied, "It cannot be known.

Even if Bodhisattvas bound for their final birth before Buddhahood were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they still could not know it, let alone I alone. The Buddha possesses the immeasurable."
"Such merit! Such a most excellent field of blessings! Its various fruits and rewards are inexhaustible; I shall only be able to know this when I have attained Buddhahood in the future.
Based on this, it is clear that he does not truly know [the nature of the field]. Who would say otherwise?

Therefore, I respectfully pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me, so that those of future generations may know that the blessings of giving are indeed such as these. △ Second, the Tathāgata [responds].
Having first exhorted the assembly to listen and granted permission to speak, the Buddha then addressed the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha:

"I shall now, in this assembly of all beings within the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven palace, discourse upon the relative lightness and heaviness of the merit of giving in Jambudvīpa. Listen attentively; I shall explain it for you."

The direct answer to this question lies in the context of the inquiry itself. Since those among the people of Jambudvīpa who are able to practice generosity will surely be reborn in the heavens, [the Buddha] spoke before the assembly in the celestial palace regarding the relative weight of the merits of giving; you should listen attentively.
Now, the practice of giving is the source of all virtuous deeds. Furthermore, wealth and possessions are impermanent; the five families vie for them.

The foolish and ignorant are stingy and possess no heart of renunciation. Consequently, wives and children glare at one another with hostile eyes, brothers quarrel within the walls of their home, kinsmen fall apart, and friends are severed. Such transgressions truly have avarice as their root; therefore, it is necessary—
Listen attentively as I proclaim the merit of giving. △ Second, the aspiration to hear due to doubt:
Kṣitigarbha addressed the Buddha, saying, "I have doubts regarding this matter; I wish most earnestly to hear [your explanation]."

The first part of the "Merit of the Wife" is divided into two sections. The first clarifies the person to whom one gives offerings, which is further divided into two parts, beginning with the donor.
The Buddha addressed Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva: "In Jambudvīpa, there are various kings, ministers, high officials, great elders, great kṣatriyas, and great brāhmaṇas."

The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to householders (*gṛhapati*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 32, states: "If a person, by virtue of practicing generosity and maintaining the precepts, is born into a family of the kṣatriya caste;

or if, while being attached to wisdom and sacred scriptures, they do not afflict sentient beings, then through that practice of generosity and maintaining the precepts, they are born into a family of the brāhmaṇa caste.
As for the householder: though a person of humble status, they possess great wealth. This is due to...
The former was the merit of giving; now it has resulted in the retribution of wealth and nobility. △ Second, the field of recipients:

if one encounters those who are most lowly and impoverished, even down to those who are crippled, mute, deaf, mentally deficient, or blind—those of such various kinds who are incomplete in their faculties.
This refers to the field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*). It is especially appropriate to plant merit therein.

Even those who are most destitute and impoverished, the lowest and most inferior among men, are the very embodiments of those who committed evil and failed to practice giving in their previous lives. Thus, the Mahāmāyūrī Sūtra states: "If one possesses wealth but does not give."
One suffers poverty from lifetime to lifetime because, in a previous life, one perhaps gave alms to the poor to make them joyful, but later regretted not having given.
Consequently, one incurs the retribution of being among the most wretched of the poor. Regarding "lun" (癃) and "can" (殘): "lun" refers to chronic illness.

According to the *Píngyuán chuán* (Biographies from the Píngyuán Era), a minister lamented, "I am unfortunately afflicted with the disease of chronic exhaustion. Furthermore, a protruding back is called "lun," such as when the Duke of Zhou had his back "lun" (protruded). Additionally...
Impaired bladder function is also called *long* (retention) or *can* (deficiency). When the limbs and body are incomplete, one is crippled;
when mute, one cannot speak; when deaf, one does not hear; when foolish, one lacks discernment; and when sightless, one cannot perceive objects—these are the most pitiable among humanity.
This results from having seen beggars in previous lives and frowning one's face, speaking harsh words, and reviling them.

At times they whip or beat others; at times they themselves lack faith in giving; seeing others practicing generosity, they cannot rejoice in it, but instead give rise to disparagement, causing others to lose their faith;
or the wealth and property within their households are shared with their wives and children, such that many people have a share in them.

To be stingy alone in this regard and to employ [resources] exclusively with fault, refusing to practice generosity and obstructing others from cultivating merit, constitutes deep evil and heavy transgression;
therefore, one receives this retribution. As the Sūtra says: "If you wish to observe the causes of past lives, look at what is received in this life;
if you wish to know the causes of future lives, look at what is created in this life. Meritorious retribution follows like a shadow or an echo; it must not be ignored.
△ Second, manifesting the superiority of the merit of giving, in two parts. First, the actual explanation of the compassion of the donor:

When such great kings and others wish to practice giving, if they can possess great compassion, lower their minds with a smile, and personally bestow gifts everywhere, or have others give while consoling them with gentle words, then the benefit and merit obtained by these kings and others will be as follows.
The merit and benefit of practicing giving toward as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in a hundred Ganges Rivers is such that one possesses great compassion.
"Possessing" (具) refers to the foundation of giving, consisting of both bestowing and rescuing; "capable" (能) refers to the actual practice of virtuous giving;
and "great" (大) means not discriminating between the high and the low. The *Sudatta Sūtra* states: "Even toward a single sentient being, one practices..."

Loving-kindness and compassion. Even for the duration of a cow's lowing, this brings great merit (as the text says). This is able to discipline the mind; through loving-kindness and compassion, one takes pity on all beings.

Whatever one performs as an act of giving will all become great goodness. If one observes external signs while cultivating merit, being coarse within and meticulous without, one will only produce mixed karma.
"A humble mind" and so forth reveal the true locus of compassion. A humble mind means lowering one’s own nobility to accord with the lowly and inferior.
A smiling countenance demonstrates joyful relinquishment and a lack of parsimony. The *Bhūmivastu* states: "If one gives to those of low status..."

It is this: not giving rise to thoughts of contempt. Regarding "with one's own hands" and so forth: setting aside one's own wealth and status, one takes pity on others who are poor and lowly and bestows gifts upon them equally.
As the Buddha told Sudatta: "One should give with a focused mind, give with faith, give at the appropriate time, give with one's own hands, and give according to the Dharma.
The phrase "with gentle words to comfort and console" contains two meanings. First, when having someone else give on one's behalf, one uses gentle [words]...

One should speak words of consolation and encouragement, saying: "Please practice giving for my sake; do not be negligent or disrespectful. Second, whether giving oneself or causing others to give, one should always use gentle speech to console and encourage the person before one, saying:
"I only pray that you, O virtuous one, will not give rise to a heart of resentment. The *Womb Sutra* (*Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*) says:

"When making offerings to various fields of merit, one need not select them, for one will surely encounter the Noble Ones. When practicing giving and performing meritorious deeds, one need not select [the recipient]."
Discerning between high and low—this merit is praised by the sages as the most supreme and foremost.
Therefore, the benefit obtained is like the merit of giving to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of a hundred Ganges Rivers, because the mind is impartial and free from discrimination.
As the layman Vimalakīrti said to the elder Sudatta: "If a donor gives with an equal mind even to a single person of the lowest station..."
The beggar is like the Tathāgata’s field of merit (puṇyakṣetra): free from discrimination, equal to great compassion (mahākaruṇā), and seeking no karmic reward.

This is what is called being fully endowed with the gift of Dharma (dharmadāna); it precisely accords with the present text. 2. Second, the secondary explanation concerning the inferiority of the recipient of the gift.
Why is this? Because these kings and others have given rise to great compassion toward those who are most poor and lowly, as well as those who are incomplete in their faculties;

therefore, such is the reward for their merit and benefit: that throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, they shall always possess the seven treasures in abundance, let alone the enjoyment of food and clothing.
The first section clarifies that the object given is in accordance with the Dharma. The following passage demonstrates that the resulting retribution is particularly sublime.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "A bodhisattva, having personally assessed the quantity of his wealth and possessions, practices giving according to what is appropriate.
He perceives those who come to seek [gifts] as being of two kinds: first, those who are not poor or lowly, but are solitary and have no one to rely upon; second, those who are poor."
Suffering from solitude and being lowly and base, having no one to rely upon, he thought to himself: "If I had abundant wealth, I would ensure that all were fully provided for;
if my wealth were meager, I would first distribute it to those who are poor, suffering, lowly, base, and without support. (Text)
This loving-kindness specifically takes as its object sentient beings who are suffering; it is the spirit of providing relief in times of urgency through the gate of giving (*dāna*).

Therefore, regarding the karmic rewards obtained, even those who possess the seven treasures and are noble throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes can still constantly attain full abundance—how much more so for ordinary food, clothing, and enjoyments?
This is truly because there is a distinction between the wise and the foolish among those capable of giving. As for the objects given...
Regarding the objects of giving, there is a distinction between compassion (*karuṇā*) and reverence (*gaurava*). Compassion refers to the poor; reverence refers to the Triple Gem.

Compassion involves an inferior field but a superior mind; reverence involves a superior field but an inferior mind. If one prioritizes the superiority of the mind, then giving to a Buddha is not as [meritorious] as giving to the poor.
Thus, the *Sūtra on Resolving Doubts during the Semblance Dharma* states: "There are sentient beings who, seeing others gathering together to perform various..."

Regarding meritorious deeds: to seek only fame and reputation, exhausting one's family wealth and possessions for the sake of giving, yet upon seeing those who are poor, suffering, or destitute, to revile and drive them away without providing even a single hair’s breadth of relief—this is called performing good deeds perversely and creating merit improperly.
Such people as these are truly to be pitied; they expend vast amounts of wealth yet obtain but meager merit.
Now, since this heart of compassion has arisen toward the field of the wretched, the karmic reward for such giving will naturally be obtained in future lives.
△ Second, the merit of making offerings to stupas, temples, and sacred images. Part One: Clarifying the donor and the object of offering.

Furthermore, Kṣitigarbha, if in future ages there are kings, up to and including brahmins, who encounter Buddhist stupas and temples, or images of the Buddha, or even images of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas, and personally provide for them with offerings...
Cultivating the Merit of Giving:

First, regarding the person who is able to give; second, the field to which the gift is directed—namely, stupas enshrining relics, monasteries providing for sacred images, and the merit of molding and sculpting them.
These matters are explained extensively in the sutras and śāstras. Now, encountering the flourishing of sacred images, one plants the roots of merit through reverent offerings.

Section on Fields. (Tao Kan, a renowned minister of the Eastern Jin dynasty, styled Shixing, served as the Governor of Nanhai. A fisherman frequently saw a light along the seashore at night and reported it to Kan, who dispatched him to investigate. Suddenly, he beheld a golden image gliding over the waves toward his boat. Upon examining the inscription on its back...)

This is an image of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva created by King Aśoka. In the past, after King Aśoka had unified this continent, he studied the methods of the demon kings for constructing prisons; his cruelty and toxicity were particularly extreme. Mañjuśrī manifested himself within a cauldron; though the fire blazed fiercely, the water remained clear, and blue lotuses grew therein.

The king’s heart was moved by realization, and on that very day he demolished the prisons and constructed eighty-four thousand stūpas and erected sacred images—this is one of them. The śramaṇa Huiyuan welcomed it and enshrined it in the upper pavilion of Donglin. Toward the end of the Sui dynasty, bandits broke in.

An elderly monk took leave of the image, and the image said, "You are old; simply stay here. When the rebels entered the mountain searching for gold, the monk said there was none. They then attempted to scorch him with fire. [The image] said, "If the monk dies from being scorched, the foul stench will fill the monastery; how would that compare to being outside the temple? As the rebel leader was about to go out and kill him, [the monk remained].

He said, "I am seventy years of age; I have not betrayed the Buddha's teachings. When my mindfulness is firm and I stretch out my neck, you may strike. When the bandits saw him stretch out his neck, they struck immediately. The blade pierced back into his heart, the hilt protruding from his own back. The bandits fled in all directions until they reached the tomb of Master Yuan.

At that time, the sky was clear and bright, but suddenly clouds gathered like a black mass and spread below; thunder and lightning swirled about, striking six of the bandits dead. From this, the bandit horde did not dare enter the mountain. How majestic is the spiritual resonance of this sacred image!
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, a bhikṣu asked the Buddha about the matter of Sundarananda’s renunciation and realization of the fruit. The Buddha told the bhikṣu: "In the past..."
After the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, Nanda was at that time a great elder.

Within a stūpa dedicated to a pratyekabuddha, he applied blue indigo to the walls and painted an image of a pratyekabuddha. Thereupon, he made a vow: "May I be born into a noble family in every lifetime;
may my body be golden in color; and may I encounter a Buddha and attain the Way. From then on, for ninety-one kalpas, he did not fall into the evil realms.
The Way: Among gods and humans, one’s physical form is upright and possesses thirty marks of excellence; noble, honored, wealthy, and prosperous, today you have been born as my companion.
Having left the household life, you have attained the Way (text). Such is the merit of making offerings and support to a Pratyekabuddha;

how much more so for the likeness of a Bodhisattva, and how much more so for the likeness of a Tathāgata! As a rhinoceros develops patterns on its horn by gazing at the moon, so too does the elephant [manifest its virtues].

When a flower struck by lightning enters the tusks [of an elephant], such is the way of spiritual resonance; the principles of nature are thus. If you should encounter a field of merit, do not let it pass in vain.
△ Second, revealing the blessings of the gift, in two parts: first, receiving the bliss of Śakra for three kalpas.
These kings and others shall obtain the body of Śakra for three kalpas and experience supreme, wondrous bliss.

As for kings and others who encounter stupas, temples, Buddha images, and so forth, and through making offerings to them, are moved to be born as Śakras or Brahmā kings—this is as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:

"If a person, regarding the text concerning stupas, temples, and painted images, makes offerings to the Great Master [the Buddha] by means of various sensory objects (*viṣaya*), it clarifies the heavenly realms."
Because of such karma, he was reborn as Śakra and Brahmā. In the *Madhyama Āgama*, a bhikṣu asked the Buddha: "By what causes and conditions is he named Śakradevendra?

The Buddha told the bhikṣu: "In his former life as a human, when śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas were poor and suffering, he gave them food, drink, wealth, lamps, and so forth. Because of this capacity for generosity, he is named Śakradevendra."

Now, since one has already made offerings and gifts to the physical images of the Buddha and so forth, there is no doubt that one will experience rebirth for three *kalpas*—that is, three small *kalpas*.
According to the causes from which this result is induced, only a Buddha can know them. One will receive supreme and wondrous bliss.

As detailed in the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter on the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "The gods of the Thirty-three Heavens enjoy the pleasures of the five senses; these are like the pleasures enjoyed by a Golden Wheel-turning King. Compared to the heavenly bliss, they do not equal even one-sixteenth part," and so forth).
For twenty kalpas, he shall be a Great Brahmā King.
If one can take the merit of such giving and dedicate it to the Dharma-realm, that great king and others shall constantly serve as Great Brahmā Kings for ten kalpas.

In all practice, one must necessarily perform dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). It is like an echo entering a horn; the sound then becomes great. It is like a cup of water cast into the ocean; it does not dry up.
When a small object is offered to a king, the reward obtained is great. Therefore, dedication is necessary. There are three meanings: first, dedicating phenomena toward principle.
Originally, it is because principle is fully present that there can be the function of phenomena. Now, one turns this mind toward the reality [of principle].
1. Turning [merit] toward the ultimate. 2. Turning from oneself toward others: formerly, while deluded regarding the pervasive principle, one adorned one's own person;

now, in accordance with the original nature, one dedicates it to sentient beings. 3. Turning causes toward the fruit: every minute good deed of the three karmas becomes both the contributing and the direct cause;
these causes must manifest their fruits, all returning together to the ultimate Three Virtues. The Sanskrit name is *dharmadhātu*, which here means "Dharma-realm."
Regarding the dedication of my cultivation toward the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), as the Sūtra says:
"I humbly reflect that all the roots of goodness I have cultivated, such as giving and the rest, flow from the Dharma-realm; they are the practice of all Buddhas.

According to the *Miaoxuan*, these are the ten Dharma-realms, whose essence is the three truths. Since the number ten is entirely based upon the Dharma-realm, there is no further phenomenon apart from the Dharma-realm.

The subject and object are spoken of in combination; thus, they are called the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). To turn phenomena toward principle is the realm of emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), for all ten dharma-realms are empty.
To turn oneself toward others is the realm of conventionality of the relative truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), for all ten dharma-realms are conventional.
To turn cause toward fruit is the realm of the mean of the middle truth (*madhyamasatya*), for all ten dharma-realms are the mean. Therefore, one should know this.
Tenth: All are the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which encompasses all phenomena. That which is called the "cool" Dharma-realm is the fundamental substance of the body and mind of all sentient beings.
It is emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; it is without one, two, or three. It universally includes all that exists and is thus the One Mind.
Therefore, one must dedicate [merit] to the Dharma-realm. Below, the great kingdom where the fruit is received is clarified, as indicated by the King and others.
One who is able to give is one who has skillfully cultivated generosity and does not cling to the act of giving.

Therefore, although the act of giving may be the same, the retribution for that giving differs based on whether it is dedicated toward enlightenment (*pariṇāmanā*) or not. [The phrase] "becoming a Great Brahmā Heaven deity for ten kalpas" refers to this.

According to the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, the lifespan in the Brahmakāyika heaven is half a kalpa; the lifespan in the Brahma-purohita heaven is one kalpa; and the lifespan in the Mahābrahmā heaven is half a kalpa.

According to the *Fayuan zhulin*, within the desire realm, a lifespan of one kalpa refers to a small kalpa (*antarakalpa*); in the three heavens of the first dhyāna, a lifespan of one kalpa refers to a medium kalpa (*madhyama-kalpa*);
and from the second dhyāna upward, a lifespan of one kalpa refers to a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). Based on this, the present ten...
This kalpa is, in fact, an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*). It is through this successive process that one receives the merit of Brahmā in the Rūpadhātu heavens.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because of the first pure mind, one is born in the Mahābrahmā heaven. The *Madhyama Āgama* clarifies the four merits of Brahmā (*brāhma-puṇya*):
if a person with faith is able to erect a stūpa (a *stūpa*), this is the first reception of the merit of Brahmā; if one repairs an old temple...
This is the second Brahma-merit. If one is able to bring together the noble Saṃgha, this is the third Brahma-merit.
If, when the Buddha first turns the wheel of Dharma, the devas and people of the world offer exhortations and requests, this is the fourth Brahma-merit.
A bhikṣu asked: "How much, in total, is the merit of Brahmā? The Buddha said: "It is as much as the [merit] of all sentient beings on the land of Jambudvīpa..."

There is merit. Thus, proceeding by successive stages from the merit of the four continents up to that of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), it does not equal the merit of a single Brahmā heaven.
Therefore, one should know that dedicating the merit of giving is entirely distinct from what precedes it.

If one can realize that the three wheels are fundamentally quiescent and the four marks are originally empty, such that the mind arises without abiding and abides without arising, then one is in accord with Prajñā and can fully perfect the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). Therefore it is said:

"There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm, and there is nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm. One will certainly attain Buddhahood without doubt. △ Third, the Cultivation of Giving as a Remedy.

Regarding the two sections on the merit of scriptures and images, the first clarifies the cultivation of causes, and the second reveals the merit of giving. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, personally repairing scriptures and images;
second, furthermore, Kṣitigarbha, if in future ages there are kings, up to and including Brahmins, who encounter the teachings of former Buddhas...
Regarding stupas and shrines: when even the scriptures or images have become ruined or dilapidated, one is able to resolve to repair them.

The Sanskrit name is *stūpa*, which here is translated as "shrine" (*miào*). A shrine (*miào*) refers to appearance; it is a representation of the physical forms of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others.
There are three purposes for establishing these stupas and shrines: first, to manifest the excellence of the person [who established them]; second, to inspire faith in others; and third, for...
To repay their kindness, precious stupas store its radiant light and monasteries depict its sacred forms.

It serves as a vessel for crossing the sea of suffering and acts as the trunk and branches of the faculty of faith. To behold it awakens the resolve for enlightenment; upon seeing it, one forgets all worldly attachments.
It increases merit and gives rise to goodness—this alone is the foremost priority. That which is now ruined and dilapidated is due to the vast passage of time and the decline of the Dharma teachings.

The [Dharma] has declined. Although the temple and its images remain standing, those who revere them and cultivate merit are rare. If they are not repaired and adorned, they will daily fall into ruin and decay;

therefore, one must resolve to do so and with sincerity undertake their restoration. The *Xiangfa jueyi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma) states: "Creating something new is not as good as repairing what is old."
It is better to avoid misfortune than to perform meritorious deeds. However, if one wishes to engage in construction or creation, it must necessarily accord with the Dharma.
Even if the work performed is small, the merit obtained will be immeasurable; yet if one does not follow the Dharma, even great effort will be of no benefit.

The *Śatapañcāśatkakṣudrakasūtra* records the case of a very wealthy elder who had a son of exceptionally handsome and wondrous appearance, beloved and respected by devas and humans. As the boy grew up, he encountered the Buddha and attained the state of an Arhat.
In the Han period, because the stupa containing the relics of the past Buddha Vipaśyin had slightly fallen into disrepair, a young boy entered the stupa and saw this damaged spot.
With a serene and joyful countenance, he gathered and called together a crowd of people to jointly plaster and repair the stupa; having made his vow, he departed.
By virtue of this merit, for ninety-one kalpas he did not fall into the three miserable realms, but instead received blessings among the devas and humans.

Infinite [merit]. Now, having encountered me, he has left the household life and attained the Way. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, while the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala, a brahmin was plowing his field.
Seeing the World-Honored One passing by, he leaned his ox-goad against the ground and paid homage to the Buddha.
When the Buddha saw this, he smiled. The bhikṣus asked the Buddha, "For what reason do you smile? The Buddha said, "This man is now paying homage to two Buddhas;
he is paying homage to me, and beneath my staff is a stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha. The bhikṣus wished to see it.
The Buddha ordered him to ask a brahmin for some land and gave it to him. The Buddha then manifested a stūpa made of the seven treasures, one yojana in height and half a yojana in width.
When the brahmin Byañjana saw this, he addressed the Buddha, saying, "I am of the Kāśyapa clan; this is my Kāśyapa mound.
May the Buddha erect a Kāśyapa stūpa there. The bhikṣus then asked the Buddha, "May we receive the clay?"

The Buddha said, "One may receive [the precepts]. He then spoke this verse: "Even if one were to take hundreds of thousands of loads of pure gold and use it to practice giving, it would not equal taking a single lump of clay and, with a respectful heart, repairing a stūpa of the Buddha. At that time, people of the world revered the Buddhas of the past;

they would prostrate themselves, and the bhikṣus likewise prostrated. The Buddha said, "Even if one were to take hundreds of thousands of pieces of gold and use them to practice giving, it would not equal..."

First, with a virtuous mind, one should reverently pay homage to the Buddha’s stūpas (the *Kusuma-hasta-sūtra* states: "If one sees that a stūpa or temple is dilapidated, one should restore and repair it, whether using mud, clods of earth, or even a single brick").
One shall never regress from unsurpassed bodhi. Thus, one should know that the merit of repairing Buddhist stupas, sutras, and images is inconceivable.
△ Second, exhorting almsgiving to establish karmic connections.
These kings and others, whether arranging matters themselves or exhorting others—even those numbering in the hundreds or thousands—make offerings to establish karmic connections.
That these kings cultivate merit themselves and encourage others to do so can be called a profound understanding of sin and merit, as the Buddha taught in the *Ātmavatsa-sūtra*. Thus said the Buddha.
He addressed the King of Śrāvastī, saying: "As a king, one ought to provide enlightened guidance, leading the people by means of the Way and seeking future blessings.
The King replied: "It is indeed as the Buddha teaches. For if one does not plant the seed, there is no way to obtain its fruit. Thus, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"If there are sentient beings who recognize fields of merit, and see a Buddhist stūpa [endangered] by wind or rain..."

If one repairs, paints, adorns, or mends a ruined monastic dwelling with a mind of merit, and further instructs others to repair ancient stupas, upon the end of life, one will be reborn among the Śuklodana-devas (White-Body Devas).
One’s body will be fresh and white; entering a coral grove, one will enjoy the five desires with various celestial maidens.
When that karma is exhausted, one will descend and, if born among humans, one’s body will be fresh and white, and [one will achieve...]
The *Lun tong miao xuan* states: "The fourth [heaven], the Vīṇā-devas, has ten abodes; the fifth is named 'White Body' (*Bai-shen*).

The *Qian* says: 'The merit of the stupas is greatest here. White is the fundamental color. Now, as the kings and others practice superior wholesome karma, the wind of their virtue bends everything below.
Ruler and subjects together cultivate the ten wholesome paths, and self and others together receive the retribution for a thousand lifetimes. Thus we know that this is the result of giving."
The Retribution: It is like taking goods according to a contract; there is not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy. △ Second, manifesting the merit of giving, in two parts:
First, being kings for a thousand lifetimes of oneself and others.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, one constantly takes the form of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); likewise, others equally [attain this].
Regarding the donor: throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, they have constantly been the body of a minor king.

Since kings and others who practice giving naturally ascend [to higher realms], why would they receive retribution as a human king? As the *Wudao zui fu jing* (Sūtra on the Merits and Faults of the Five Realms) says:
"Those among humans who are noble and wealthy—kings, ministers, and elders—come from having performed acts of worship and service toward the Triple Gem."

He became a person of great wealth with limitless possessions, all of which arose from his practice of giving. Thus, one knows that if one does not practice generosity within the Buddha-dharma, one can never obtain such superior retribution.
Now, by virtue of being a minor king, he has received the reward of becoming a Wheel-Turning Sage King;
by virtue of his ministers and subjects, he has transformed from the body of a minor king into one of high station. Since his rank is so exalted, his merit is likewise vast.

This is most profound and substantial. Miaoxuan states: "These were all instances of maintaining the precepts with a distracted mind, combined with the compassionate exhortation of others to perform meritorious deeds.
Therefore, as his retribution, he became a sovereign, a *cakravartin* (Flying Emperor), to whom the four quarters submitted their virtue, and divine treasures appeared spontaneously.
The Shiqian states: "As for a *cakravartin*, he first practices seven dharmas: first, providing gifts to the poor; second, showing respect..."

1. The people practice filial piety and support their parents. 2. Three: At the four seasons and the eight festivals, they offer sacrifices to the Four Seas. 3. Four: At the [four] times, they cultivate patience (*kṣānti*). 4. Five, Six, Seven: They eliminate the three poisons (*triviṣa*).
Thereafter, they bathe, observe the fast (*upavāsa*), and make vows; then the divine jewels will respond spontaneously. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
Among all humans, the Wheel-Turning Sage King is the foremost. Lesser kings are like scattered grains of millet spread across the four quarters, all brought under the governance of the Golden Wheel.
Thus, those who exhort others become great kings, while those exhorted become lesser kings. Past deeds follow the person;
the retribution of merit is like a shadow or an echo. △ Second, the dedication that brings everything to completion.
The Buddha-way.
Furthermore, if one can generate the mind of dedication before a stupa or temple, such kings as well as all other people will all attain the Buddha-way;
by this karmic fruit, it shall be immeasurable and boundless.
What is meant by dedicating the merit of providing funds for the repair of stupas and temples? One must understand that the practices mentioned above are all merely material giving;
they bring retribution in the realms of humans and devas, but are not the cause for *nirvāṇa*. For example, when Master Bodhidharma first arrived in the Great Liang...
Emperor Wu asked, "Since my accession to the throne, I have built monasteries and ordained monks; what merit and virtue do these bring? Huiming replied, "In truth, there is no merit or virtue.
These are but the minor fruits of the realms of humans and devas, causes characterized by outflows (*āsrava*). The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit and virtue?
Huiming replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and tranquil. Such merit and virtue do not..."
Regarding worldly pursuits, according to this profound intent, one must necessarily turn affairs toward principle (*li*) before they can correspond with the true wisdom of *prajñā*.

Therefore, it is known that the repair of stupas and temples, when further accompanied by dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), will all transcend the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) and fully realize the five wisdoms (*pañcajñāna*).
The retribution induced by such dedication is immeasurable and boundless; it is precisely for this reason that dedication is said to be of great benefit.
△ Fourth, the merit of giving to the elderly, the sick, and women in childbirth. Part one: the giver and the recipient of the gift.
Furthermore, Kṣitigarbha, in future ages there will be various kings, brahmins, and others who see those who are aged and infirm,
as well as women in childbirth.
The Sūtra on Impermanence. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "There are three things in the world that are unlovely, lack luster, are not to be longed for, and are disagreeable. What are these three?
They are old age, sickness, and death. If old age, sickness, and death did not exist in the world, the Tathāgata would not appear in the world for the sake of all beings."

The Buddha taught that one should explain the Dharma realized and matters of discipline; therefore, the elderly, the sick, and women who have recently given birth are the most compassionate fields for planting merit.

When old, the faculties mature and one gasps for breath, requiring others for food and drink; when old and childless, one is termed a "solitary man. In the West, King Bimbisāra was the first to provide for them;
in the East, King Wen was the first to feel compassion for them, because they have no place to turn. As for the sick...
Then the hundred bones ache and pain, and one’s life hangs by a single thread. If there were no one to attend to them, who could refuse to wait for their death?
Therefore, our Buddha instructed that nursing the sick is the foremost field of merit. During his lifetime, he himself would tour the monastic quarters to visit the ill, out of compassion for them.
When a woman first gives birth, foul secretions cover her body; if [she is not cared for]...
At that time, they provide food and drink; yet mother and child perish together because their suffering is so extreme.

Therefore, these three classes of beings are those for whom the benevolent person should especially be moved to feel compassion and provide for them with generosity. △ Second, the causes and effects of what is bestowed, in two parts:
first, cultivating the cause.

If, in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), one possesses a mind of great compassion and bestows medicine, food and drink, and bedding to bring about peace and happiness—according to the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*, which clarifies the divisions of time, there are twelve such layers.

The first is named *kṣaṇa*, translated as "one thought-moment" (*nien*), which may be called the shortest unit of time. To possess great compassion within this [moment] refers to the aspect of bestowing happiness.
