Treatise: Because happiness is that which all sentient beings love and cherish, one should give rise to great compassion (mahākaruṇā) upon encountering a field of suffering;

why then speak of "great loving-kindness" (mahāmaitrī)? As the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states: "If one speaks of loving-kindness, then compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity have already been spoken of."
Furthermore, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is truly immeasurable. Loving-kindness is like a king; the others are like the common people. Why is this?
First, with a mind of loving-kindness, one desires to cause sentient beings to obtain happiness. Seeing those who do not obtain happiness, one consequently gives rise to compassion (*karuṇā*).

Because compassion can be fully realized through loving-kindness, it is called "Great. Since it is said to be "in a single thought-moment," this refers to the compassion of same essence (*samatā-kāya*).
Regarding medicine, food, clothing, and shelter—the four requisites for human life—these are urgent necessities for daily use. For the sick, there is no cure without medicinal herbs;

for the body and life, there is no subsistence without food and drink. Furthermore, items such as bedding, quilts, covers, and cushions are especially vital for the elderly, the infirm, and women in childbirth.
Essential items such as clothing are included within bedding and requisites; giving in this manner ensures that both body and mind are at peace and happy.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one provides sufficient food and drink to those who are hungry and thirsty, their gratitude will be profound.

The Buddha taught that giving to travelers, those coming from afar, the sick, and those nursing the sick, as well as giving during times of wind, cold, and various hardships, constitutes 'timely' giving."

By giving alms; by giving medicine to the sick; by providing food and drink to those who are hungry and thirsty, one creates the karmic causes and conditions for having few illnesses, and thus attains the mark of fullness beneath both armpits and the mark of the supreme sense of taste.

By giving fine clothing, bedding, gold, silver, and precious jewels, one attains the golden-colored body and the mark of thin skin. Thus, one knows that the marks of the Tathāgata are all obtained through the practice of giving.
△ Second, the attainment of the fruit:
Such merit and benefit are most inconceivable. For one hundred kalpas, one shall constantly be the Lord of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven;
for two hundred kalpas, one shall constantly be the Lord of the Six Desire Heavens. Ultimately attaining Buddhahood, one shall never again fall into the evil realms, even for a hundred [kalpas].
Throughout a thousand lifetimes, one shall not hear the sound of suffering.
Giving is called merit; it necessarily yields three benefits, hence it is termed "beneficial merit. Regarding that which is most inconceivable: "foremost" (*jue*) refers to being at the front;
it means the foremost person of the vanguard. This signifies that among all things inconceivable, this is the first and most inconceivable.
This is indeed a matter for deliberation. However, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Dwellings, bedding, food, and medicine are worldly dharmas;
they are not supramundane dharmas that are difficult to obtain. (Text). How can it now be said that these are most inconceivable?
This is because when one correctly practices giving, a single thought-moment endowed with great compassion becomes the very root of attaining Buddhahood. Thus we know...

They are born among the gods of the desire and form realms; they first experience worldly happiness as a karmic retribution, and only when they finally attain Buddhahood does the merit of their giving reach its consummation.

Thus, one knows it is most inconceivable that they "should ultimately attain Buddhahood. Regarding the statement that those who have purified themselves for a hundred kalpas become gods of the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) heavens, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"With a mind of loving-kindness, they are fond of cultivating goodness and cultivating merit, reaching the Subhakṛtsna (Utterly Pure) Heaven; within the three realms, the Subhakṛtsna is the most [pure]."

Because it is blissful, it is called "Utmost Pervasive Purity" (*Śubhakṛtsna*). According to this principle, it should be situated among the three "Pure" heavens (*Śuddhāvāsa*) within the Realm of Form (*Rūpadhātu*).

Why, then, is it here designated as the "Lord of the Pure Abodes"? It is because this [state] is the giving of a pure mind through a heart of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Within this context, there are one hundred eons (*kalpa*).

Regarding the statement that two hundred *kalpas* are required to become a lord of the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this refers to the "compassion based on sentient beings" (*sattvālambana-maitrī*).
Because this is *sāsrava* (with outflows) and takes only the desire realm as its object, its retribution is birth within the six heavens of the desire realm.

The mention of "two hundred *kalpas*" is calculated according to *antarakalpas*. Question: Since the heavens of the desire realm are frequently ravaged by the fires of the kalpa, how can one enjoy the six heavens eternally?
"Is this merit? He replied, "According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, when the world is destroyed by the three calamities, human beings are not destroyed.

They cultivate dhyāna in succession and are reborn in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Once they have attained birth in the Desire Heavens (*kāmadhātu*), they return once more to experience pleasure in turn. Question:

"If one practices giving with the same mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), why do the resulting retributions differ so vastly? Answer: "At the time of practicing giving, there is [a difference in] the loving-kindness..."
Whether one is victorious or not, the mind may be pure or impure; thus, the resulting rebirths in the two realms of desire and form differ, and there are variations in the length of one's lifespan.

As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 33: "If one gives alms without having abandoned desire, one will be born among humans as wealthy and noble, or within the six heavens of the desire realm.
If one gives alms with a mind free from desire, one will be born in the Brahma-world, and so on, up to..."

The Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*). If one gives alms apart from form and mind, one is reborn among the gods of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). If one gives alms apart from the three realms for the sake of *nirvāṇa*, one attains the path of the *śrāvaka*.
If, at the time of giving alms, one feels aversion toward bustle and delights in solitude and stillness, one attains the state of a *pratyekabuddha*.
If, at the time of giving alms, one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) with the desire to deliver all beings, this is the foremost and most profound [perfection].
Ultimately, through pure wisdom, one attains the Buddha-way. The Dharma of all Buddhas is inconceivable; they speak in such ways according to those among sentient beings who are ready to be saved.

Yet, as the momentum of a thousand mountains ceases at the edge of a peak and the sound of ten thousand streams vanishes upon the sea, the true intent lies solely in the ultimate attainment of Buddhahood. Thus, while practicing giving prior to becoming a Buddha, [one must never...]

They do not fall into the three evil realms, but constantly receive blessings among humans and devas. For hundreds of thousands of years, they do not even hear the sound of suffering, let alone experience it with their own bodies in the evil realms.

(The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "If one sees someone afflicted by illness whose life has not yet ended, and provides them with drink or bestows wealth to sustain that life, upon death they will be born in the Heaven of Deep Waters, enjoying pleasures like those of Śakra.

When their life in that heaven ends, they will not fall into the three paths, but will obtain a human body; from birth to birth, they will not encounter the suffering of illness, nor will they suffer any affliction or disturbance. △
Second, the dedication toward the stage of Buddhahood, which has two parts. First, the dedication of the merit of the offering.
Furthermore, Kṣitigarbha, if in future ages there are kings, brahmins, and others who are able to perform such acts of giving, they shall obtain immeasurable merit.
If they can further dedicate this merit, regardless of its magnitude, they will ultimately attain Buddhahood.
How much more so the retributions of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Wheel-Turning King.

The text is divided into two sections. First, "concluding the merit of the aforementioned giving. Then, "furthermore," and so forth, concludes the preceding dedication, stating "one can perform," and so on.
This is like saying that one must practice giving; it is as described in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*.
When the elder Sudatta and Śāriputra were measuring the ground for the vihāra with a cord, Śāriputra smiled joyfully. Sudatta asked, "Why do you smile?

He replied, "As you have just begun to measure the ground here, the palaces of the six heavens of the desire realm have already been completed. He then immediately lent him the divine eye, through which [Sudatta] saw all six [heavens].
The celestial palace was magnificently adorned and purified. Then, the cord was moved once more. Śāriputra looked distressed with a sorrowful expression.
[The Buddha] asked, "Why do you have such a sorrowful expression? He replied, "Do you see these ants in this ground? (Their Sanskrit name is *Pipīlikā*). [The Buddha] said, "I have seen them.
Śāriputra said, "In the past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, you also built a vihāra upon this very spot, yet these ants—"
Born here, even as far back as the time of the seven Buddhas, you have built monasteries for each of those Buddhas;
yet this ant was also born therein. To this day, for ninety-one kalpas, it has received only one kind of body and has not attained liberation.
Saṃsāra is long and distant; merit alone is essential—it must be planted. This [merit] pertains only to humans and devas.

If one still remains within the cycle of birth and death, yet does not seek for oneself the rewards of human or celestial fortune, but instead dedicates all merit toward the sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, then regardless of how much was given, one will ultimately attain Buddhahood. How much more so, then, for those who practice the six perfections!

This is a reductio ad absurdum (paryudāsa). It means that if even the fruit of Buddhahood can be realized, how could there be anyone who fails to achieve the minor fruits of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Wheel-Turning King among humans and devas?
The *Miaoxuan* (4b) states: "The Wheel-Turning King is the rank of a lord of men; Śakra and Brahmā are the ranks of lords of devas.

These are all positions defined according to their karmic fruition. Since there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority in the meaning of these fruits, the cultivation of the causes must [necessarily differ]."
There are degrees of depth. The *Sūtra on the Merit and Demerit of the Five Paths* states: "The worthy one who delights in giving is supported by the celestial deities themselves.
By giving once, one obtains ten thousandfold; peace, joy, and longevity shall be long. Today’s great act of giving brings forth merit beyond measure;
all shall attain the Way of the Buddha and deliver beings throughout the ten directions. Its retribution is inconceivable. △
Second, the command to universally exhort study.
For this reason, Kṣitigarbha universally exhorts all sentient beings: "You should study in this manner.
This "should be so" expresses the intent of admonishing, encouraging, and urging them forward; it means that one must certainly and universally exhort sentient beings to rely upon [this teaching].
The foregoing constitutes the practice of giving and its dedication, as taught in the *Dṛḍhamati-sūtra*. In that sūtra, the Buddha told Ānanda: "I have extensively explained giving;
it plants the provisions for birth and death. It is like planting grain: according to what is sown, so shall it grow. There has never been a case where one reaps fruit without having planted.
By planting goodness, one obtains blessings; these blessings naturally return to oneself. Therefore, he commanded Kṣitigarbha to universally exhort others.
Sentient beings should train themselves in this manner. This concludes the comparison of the merit of giving by kings and ministers. II. The Merit of Giving by Men and Women.
Part One: First, the general indication of the benefits and merits within the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, Kṣitigarbha, in future ages, if any son of good family or daughter of good family plants even a small root of merit within the Buddha-dharma—
be it as slight as a hair, a speck of dust, or a grain of sand— the benefit and merit they shall receive will be beyond compare.
Why is it that within the Buddha-dharma, even a small amount of merit planted yields great results? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Although there are various fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), the Buddha is the foremost field of merit. Because he is fully endowed with immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, one speaks specifically of planting seeds in the Buddha-field.
The Buddha-field can yield immeasurable retributive fruits; while other fields are also said to be immeasurable, they possess distinctions."
[From] the *Dīrgha Āgama*. The Buddha addressed the Brahmin Kūṭadanta: "Among gods and humans in the world, only the Buddha is supreme.
Those who wish to seek great merit should make offerings to the Three Buddhas.

This is because sentient beings, throughout the beginningless world, have not known how to practice giving toward the Triple Gem; therefore, [their merits] are all exhausted and extinguished. These are the Three Jewels."
There are immeasurable dharmas; therefore, giving is likewise inexhaustible, and one will certainly attain nirvana. Thus, the Great Sūtra says:
"If one makes an offering of even a single incense stick or lamp to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, or even presents a single flower, one shall be reborn in the Land of Immovability."

This is precisely the eternal adornment of the Pure Land, unmoved by the three calamities. Miaole states: "The virtues of humans and devas can all be opened up as contributory causes (*pratyaya-hetu*).
This sutra intends to encompass even the subtle virtues from beginningless time, so that they all tend toward Bodhi.

If one has already resolved their mind [for enlightenment], then whatever virtue exists, even as slight as a hair, is none other than a contributory cause. Now, the original vow of Kṣitigarbha specifically opens up those who have not yet [resolved their minds].

Coming to the Buddha-field brings about the attainment of merit. That which cannot be compared is this: because the Buddhas have accomplished inexhaustible merit, planting merit within them results in merit that is likewise inexhaustible.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha-field is pure; it has uprooted the weeds of afflictions such as craving.
Pure precepts serve as its level ground, and great compassion serves as its fertile soil. It eliminates all evil and heterodoxy."
The saline soil is the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the ditches and ridges are the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
It is able to produce the fruits and rewards of the three vehicles and nirvana.
To plant seeds here in this unsurpassed and peerless field, its merit is inexhaustible (as the text says). Therefore, the benefits and blessings received there are beyond all analogy. △
Second, comparing the merit and benefit within the Buddha-dharma, there are three parts: first, the merit of making offerings to sacred images; second, the merit of making offerings to the Mahāyāna;
third, the merit of making offerings to the cultivation of the sūtras. Now, for the first [part], there are two sections: first, directly clarifying the merit of giving.
Furthermore, Kṣitigarbha, in future ages, if there are good men or good women who encounter images of the Buddha,
images of bodhisattvas, images of pratyekabuddhas, or images of wheel-turning kings, and offer them gifts and worship,
they shall obtain immeasurable merit. They will constantly dwell among gods and humans, experiencing supreme and wondrous bliss.

First, the donor who bestows is indicated; next, the field of merit to whom one gives is clarified. By practicing the cause of giving and making offerings, one constantly receives the subtle and wondrous fruits among humans and devas.
Since Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others teach people how to escape suffering, they are the "field of respect" for sentient beings.
Although a Wheel-Turning King has not yet transcended birth and death, he transforms the world through the ten wholesome paths and possesses [these qualities] as well.

Land and water are the fields of merit for the common people; therefore, through acts of giving and making offerings, all equally obtain immeasurable blessings. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Wealth is a causal condition for an evil mind and should always be renounced by oneself; how much more so when giving it away brings about great blessings."
Yet one does not practice giving. Stinginess is a sign of misfortune and decline; it gives rise to sorrow and fear. To wash this away with the water of giving is to produce merit and benefit.
Thus, one attains immeasurable blessings and dwells constantly among humans and devas—precisely the places where blessings are found.
Why, then, do the preceding and following sections of the sutra necessarily speak of humans and devas receiving joy? According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, regarding the human realm...
The fetters and latent tendencies are thin, and the mind of renunciation arises easily; because wisdom is sharp among the devas, it is easy to attain the Path in these two realms.
It is not so in other realms. Furthermore, when one speaks of "devas," all celestial beings are included; when one speaks of "humans," all those born on the earth are included. Why is this?
Because in the heavens, the devas are predominant, while on the earth, humans are predominant. Therefore, [the former...]

The subsequent "raising of persons" refers to devas (*deva*). On one level, they receive pleasure among humans and among devas; ultimately, it points toward *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, the bliss of the awakening to the cessation of all phenomena.

Therefore, the *Guangming shu* (Commentary on the Light) uses "human" to represent the thirty stages of the worthy ones (*śaikṣa*) and "deva" to represent the ten stages of the noble ones (*ārya*), receiving the bliss of the ultimate heaven of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Humans practice..."
The one who practices giving shall have their fame fill the ten directions; they will be loved and respected by the wise; they will enter assemblies without fear;
at the end of life, they will be reborn in the heavens; and after a long time, they will surely attain nirvana. This is it. △ Second, the incomparable dedication.
If one can dedicate [the merit] to the Dharma-realm, the benefit and merit of such a person is beyond comparison.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Among the two kinds of giving taught by the Buddha, the gift of Dharma is foremost. This is because the retribution for the gift of material wealth is finite, whereas the retribution for the gift of Dharma is infinite.
The gift of material wealth yields retribution within the desire realm; the gift of Dharma yields retribution throughout the three realms. It also says:

It transcends the retribution of the triple world. If one does not seek fame, wealth, profit, or power, but instead studies the Buddha-way solely to propagate great compassion and deliver sentient beings from the suffering of old age, sickness, and death, this is called the pure gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
If it is otherwise, it is merely trading for the sake of profit. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva knows the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena to be like *nirvāṇa*.
It is exhausted because the merit enters into the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; yet it is also not exhausted. Therefore, its benefits and blessings are beyond comparison.
△ Second, the merit of making offerings to the Mahāyāna, part one: directly clarifying the merit of giving.
Furthermore, Kṣitigarbha, in future ages, if there are good men or good women who encounter Mahāyāna sūtras,
or hear even a single verse or a single phrase, and give rise to a heart of profound sincerity, praising and revering them, and making offerings through giving;
This person shall obtain a great fruit and reward, immeasurable and boundless.
"To encounter" (*yuè*) means to meet; it is a word of celebration and good fortune.

Since the Buddha-dharma is difficult to hear and difficult to encounter, to encounter it now all at once is like a hungry person encountering a royal feast—beating their belly and singing—or like parched seedlings encountering sweet rain.
It arises with a sudden surge. What is its joy like? The Mahāyāna refers to the various Vaipulya sūtras. According to the *Awakening of Faith*, there are three aspects:
first, the Greatness of Essence (*tathatā*), meaning that all phenomena are the equality of true suchness, neither increasing nor decreasing;
second, the Greatness of Characteristic, meaning that the Tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with immeasurable inherent merits; third, the Greatness of Function.
Because it can give rise to all mundane and supramundane wholesome causes and effects; because it is that which all Buddhas have fundamentally mounted;
and because all Bodhisattvas mount this Dharma to reach the stage of the Tathāgata—it is called the "Great Vehicle" (*Mahāyāna*) since it is mounted by great beings who have transcended the world.
Regarding "listening and so forth," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Listening to the Dharma is the cause..."
By this condition, one draws near to Great Parinirvāṇa because the Dharma-eye has been opened. There are three types of people in the world:

first, those who are sightless, who represent ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who never hear the Dharma; second, those with one eye, who represent the Śrāvakas who, though they briefly listen to the Dharma, do not abide in it with their minds;
third, those with two eyes, who represent the Bodhisattvas who listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion and practice according to what they have heard.

It is by listening to the Dharma that one comes to know the world. These three types of persons, having now heard these scriptural passages, possess pure faith and thus give rise to the Dharma-eye of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Even a single verse or a single line further advances them toward Bodhi;
therefore, one must develop a heart of earnest respect, praising and revering both the person and the Dharma.
One should make offerings by bestowing the Dharma upon such people; thus it is said in the *Sūtra on Skillful Reverence*. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If someone hears a single four-line verse from another, or writes it down on bamboo or silk, and for many eons carries the names of all those associated with it—such as their preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and teachers (*ācārya*)—upon their shoulders, or bears them on their backs, or wears them upon their heads..."
Even if one were to offer all manner of musical instruments as an offering to this teacher, one still could not fully repay the teacher’s kindness.

If, however, one conceives a disrespectful mind toward the *upādhyāya*, constantly speaks of his faults, and I declare such a person to be foolish, they will undergo extreme suffering and will certainly fall into the evil realms in future lives. Therefore, I instruct you all to always practice respect.
With a heart of reverence, one who cherishes the profound Dharma of the Triple Gem will surely obtain immeasurable and boundless great fruits.
△ Second, the dedication beyond analogy.
If one can dedicate [this merit] to the Dharma-realm, its blessings are beyond comparison.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-sūtra* (Fu fazang jing) states: "All sentient beings who wish to emerge from the great ocean of birth and death within the triple world must rely upon the Dharma-boat to attain deliverance.
The Dharma is the true spiritual friend of sentient beings; it performs great benefit and provides salvation."
All these sufferings arise because the dispositions of all sentient beings are not fixed; they follow whatever they are conditioned by. If one associates with the good, one becomes good;
if one associates with the evil, one becomes evil. If one draws near to evil friends, one will create evil karma and transmigrate through birth and death without end.
If one draws near to virtuous friends, one will give rise to a mind of reverence, listen to and receive the sublime Dharma, and will certainly be able to...
May they be freed from the suffering and afflictions of the three miserable realms. By virtue of this merit, may they experience the most supreme bliss.
It is like the story of a brahmin who once went to the city of Pāṭaliputra to sell skulls. The upāsakas would pierce the ear-holes with copper needles;
those that were pierced all the way through fetched a high price, those half-pierced fetched a low price, and those that did not penetrate at all were not given any value. The brahmin asked:
Therefore, the answer is as follows: "The 'pierced' (che) refers to those who, while alive, listened to the Dharma with superior wisdom; thus they were given a high price.
The 'half' (ban) refers to those who, although they listened to the sutras and teachings, did not yet skillfully discern them; therefore, they were given a small amount.

Those who were entirely unpenetrated (quan) did not listen to the Dharma at all; therefore, no price was given. By taking these skulls—whether fully pierced or otherwise—and erecting stupas to make offerings to them, one may still attain [merit]."
They will be reborn in the heavens; how much more so those who are able to listen to and receive the Dharma with a sincere heart, and who offer worship and respect to those who uphold the sutras?
The karmic reward for this is truly difficult to exhaust; in the future, they will certainly attain the Unsurpassed Way.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke the *Dṛḍhamati Sūtra*. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If there are persons of good heart and virtuous intent who hear the Buddha’s luminous Dharma—even for a single moment—"
Listen with a focused mind. If you cannot do so for a full day, half a day will suffice; if not for half a day, one hour will suffice;
if not for an hour, half an hour will suffice; if not for half an hour, even a brief moment will suffice.
The merit of this is immeasurable and beyond praise. Therefore, the wise who desire unsurpassed peace and happiness [should practice it].

One should listen to the sutras and Dharma with a sincere and diligent mind. Having now personally listened to the Mahāyāna sūtras, one further praises, reveres, and makes offerings to those who uphold the Mahāyāna, people and the Dharma alike, dedicating all of this universally to the Dharmadhātu.
The merit thus obtained shall be equal in measure to the empty space of the ten directions; therefore, it is beyond all analogy. △ Third: Cultivating the Practice of Bestowing Sūtras.
Section Two: First, the Cultivation of Merit by Oneself and Others.

Furthermore, Kṣitigarbha, if in future ages there are good men or good women who encounter Buddha-stūpas, monasteries, or Mahāyāna sūtras—whether new or old—and offer them gifts, worship, circumambulation, and praise; who pay homage with palms joined; or if they encounter...

Regarding "old" or "dilapidated," it refers to those that have been repaired and maintained, or for which one has personally resolved to do so, or encouraged many others to collectively resolve to do so.
As for Mahāyāna sūtras— whether they be yellow scrolls with red bindings in precious caskets or crystal cases, or those that have been newly bound and restored— then:
When one makes offerings to others by giving them [these texts], causing them to gaze upon, venerate, praise, and pay respect with palms joined, this is called the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*).
If one encounters those that are damaged or destroyed, one should immediately repair and restore them, managing and maintaining them.

As the sages of old said: "Whether opening or closing boxes and chests, [one finds] insects have eaten through them or they are decayed and rotten; or [the texts] are torn, missing, or erroneous on paper."

If ink blots have appeared and one does not repair them oneself, nor is willing to circulate [the text], one cannot avoid incurring an offense against the Dharma-treasure and violating the Buddha’s regulations.
If one is unable to restore it, one must not burn it. As stated in the *Five Hundred Questions*: "If the precepts and Vinaya are no longer used and have fallen into disrepair, may they be burned?

Answer: "They must not be burned. If one burns them unknowingly, there is the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (forfeiture and confession); if one burns them knowingly, [the offense is more severe].
It is a transgression; therefore, one should burn it. This constitutes a violation of a definitive rule, equivalent to the preparatory act (*prayoga*) of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.

It is also like burning one's parents. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyama-ekottarika* (or *Muktaka*) states: "If other leaves or paper upon which the Buddha’s sūtras are written become worn out, one should wipe the old ones and write new ones over them, so that the text is clear and distinct.
Do not commit this grave offense again. This clarifies that one should personally resolve to repair [the texts]; what follows is an exhortation.
People all set out together. If one acts in this manner, one is indeed a Bodhisattva. △ Second, the rewards obtained by oneself and others:
Such individuals as these will, for thirty lifetimes, constantly serve as minor kings and patrons (*dānapati*).
They will also constantly become universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), using wholesome dharmas to transform and instruct those minor kings.

Regarding those who accept exhortation, they become minor kings through the influence of conversion; regarding those who are able to exhort, they become wheel-turning monarchs (*cakravartin*) and exercise sovereign rule.
The *Sūtra on the Four Self-Injuries* states: "Those who are able to practice giving shall long obtain peace and security in both this life and future lives.

It serves as provisions for birth and death; in every generation they will be noble and wealthy, and all shall receive peace. Where there is one who practices giving, people from the borderlands will rejoice in their aid, and they shall obtain merit."

It is immeasurable; how much more so when the donor personally serves the food. In future lives, the merit produced follows the person as its retribution, like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound.
Regarding the term *dānapati*: the *Nei zhuan* (Inner Tradition) states that the Sanskrit is *dānapati*, translated as "donor" (*shizhu*).
*Dāna* means "giving," and *pati* means "lord. As for the term *tanyue* (檀越), it is originally...
This is not a literal translation; it omits the character "na" (那) and takes the sound "da" (陀) from the preceding term, transposing it to form "dāna" (檀).

Furthermore, the character "yue" (越) is added, intending to convey that through the practice of giving (*dāna*), one can transcend poverty. Although this is a clever interpretation, it ultimately deviates from the original source.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, *dāna* has many names: worldly *dāna* (the giving of ordinary persons and the giving performed by noble ones with a mind associated with outflows) and supramundane [giving].

Generosity of the sages (though they may give with a mind still subject to outflows, it is supramundane because their fetters have been severed); generosity praised by the sages (supramundane, pure generosity); generosity not praised by the sages (that is, mundane generosity);
the generosity of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas (they give because they know the true nature of all phenomena); the generosity of Śrāvakas (their merit is incomplete; they obtain only a small portion).
Among these, there is both the pure and the impure (and so forth). [The Buddha] further uses wholesome dharmas to transform and teach them.
When a king of a small country transforms the world through the Golden Wheel, he must take the practice of the ten virtuous deeds as his foundation.
For example, in the past there were five kings who maintained friendly relations with one another. The eldest was named King Puan (Universal Peace), who practiced the conduct of a Bodhisattva;
the other four minor kings, however, constantly practiced unwholesome deeds. The Great King, wishing to deliver them, summoned them to the palace and entertained them for seven days.
The Four Kings took their leave. Out of compassion, the Great King spoke to the minor kings, saying: "Each of you speak of the pleasures that bring you joy.
One king wished for the trees to flourish with blossoms during the spring months, finding delight in wandering through the fields and wilds.

Another king wished to always be a king, finding delight in coming and going on his travels. Another king wished for his wife and children to be beautiful, finding delight in the height of sensual passion.
They find pleasure in the gratification of their desires. One king wished that his parents and retinue might always enjoy fine food and the music of the zither as their delight.
The Great King said, "This is not a lasting pleasure. The four kings asked, "What is the king’s pleasure? The Great King replied, "My pleasure is neither birth nor death;
it is neither suffering nor joy; it is neither hunger nor thirst; it is neither cold nor heat; it is independent of existence or non-existence."
"This is my pleasure," he said. The Four Kings asked, "Where is this pleasure? The Great King replied, "My teacher is named Buddha; he is currently nearby at Jetavana.
The kings were filled with joy and went together to the Buddha's dwelling. They paid their respects and withdrew to sit. The Great King knelt and addressed him:
"We have now attained human birth, yet we are dull-witted and ignorant. We are deeply attached to worldly pleasures and do not understand the nature of sin and merit."
"We pray that you will explain the Truth of Suffering for us. The Buddha then expounded upon the eight types of suffering in detail.
Upon hearing this, the Four Kings' minds were opened and their understanding awakened; they immediately attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. They addressed King Universal Peace, saying:

"Great King, you are truly a Bodhisattva of Great Expedient Means (*mahopāya-kauśalya*), who has transformed and guided us, enabling us to attain the tracks of the Path. Your grace is such that we originally observed all..."
Regarding the palace, his heart was filled with attachment and he could not bear to leave it; yet now, beholding the palace, he views it as a foul latrine, finding nothing in it that is pleasurable.
He immediately abdicates the throne to his younger brother, and both go forth to lead the life of a seeker of the Way.

This is the precedent for a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) converting minor kings, as detailed in the *Dīrgha Āgama*. A Golden Wheel-Turning King governs and transforms the four continents by means of the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala*).
△ Section Three: The Merit of Directing Toward the Dharma-realm (2). First, pointing to the practice of virtuous deeds:

Furthermore, Kṣitigarbha, in future ages, if there are good men or good women who plant roots of goodness within the Buddha-dharma—whether by practicing giving and making offerings, repairing stupas and temples, or restoring and arranging the scriptures—then...
"Down to a single hair, a single speck of dust, a single grain of sand, and a single drop of water"—these all conclude the preceding passage.
Now, whenever it is said "within the Buddha-dharma," it is because serving other paths does not lead one out of birth and death;
such efforts are merely self-inflicted toil and are not the cause for *nirvāṇa*. In the *Puṇyakṣetra-sūtra*, the Buddha told Śakra Devendra:
Among the ninety-six kinds of paths, the Buddha-way is the most honored. Among the ninety-six kinds of teachings, the Buddha-dharma is the most true.
Among the ninety-six kinds of Sanghas, the Buddha’s Sangha is the most upright. Why is this?

Because since the Tathāgata, from incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, made vows with sincere truth, sacrificed his life to accumulate merit, and vowed for the sake of sentient beings, [he perfected] the six perfections and the four...
Thus, all virtues are universally perfected, and wisdom is attained in full measure. He is the World-Honored One of the three realms, whom none can equal.

Should there be any sentient being who gives rise to even a single thought of reverence toward the Tathāgata, they shall obtain a merit superior to that of bestowing the precious treasures of a great trichiliocosm.
This is the most honored and unsurpassed path; therefore, I instruct good men and women that they must [take refuge] in the Buddha.
This refers to planting roots of goodness within the Dharma. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three roots of goodness: non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
All wholesome dharmas arise from and grow through these three roots of goodness. What is now called the "causes and conditions of the roots of goodness" refers to this.
The requisites for making offerings consist of flowers, incense, lamps, and light, as well as the offering of the Dharma, such as maintaining the precepts and reciting the sutras.

Because one offers with a virtuous mind, these are called "roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla*). Giving itself is not identical to merit; rather, it is able to destroy stinginess and greed and open the gateway to wholesome dharmas.
Since roots of goodness are what constitute merit, there is nothing—be it as small as a hair, a speck of dust, a grain of sand, or a drop of water—that is excluded. All [of these] are...
It depends on the mind. If the mind is great, [the merit] is great; if the mind is small, it is small. If the mind merges with the *dharmadhātu*, then the merit is equal to empty space.

As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: Once, when the Buddha and Ānanda were begging for food in the city of Śrāvastī, a Brahmin king had established a decree stating that if anyone gave food to the Buddha or spoke with him, they should be fined five hundred gold coins. The Buddha and...

Ānanda came out with an empty bowl. He saw an old maidservant carrying a broken earthenware vessel filled with foul-smelling rice-water (the upper character *pan* means the water used for rinsing rice;
the lower character *dian* means shallow water, implying there was not much rice-water). As she was about to go out and discard it, she saw that the Buddha’s bowl was empty.

Thinking of making an offering, and knowing her thoughts, the Buddha extended his bowl to beg from her. The maidservant immediately purified her mind and gave it to the Buddha. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "This..."
Because of this gift to a maidservant, for fifteen kalpas he experienced happiness and bliss among gods and humans, never falling into the evil realms.
Later, he obtained a male body, left the household life, and became a pratyekabuddha.
At that time, a certain brāhmaṇa standing beside the Buddha said, "You are the crown prince of King Śuddhodana; why have you uttered a falsehood for the sake of food? The Buddha then—
He extended his tongue, covering his face up to the hairline, and said to him: "Have you ever seen a person with such a tongue as this tell a lie?
He immediately conceived faith and said: "I do not understand how a small gift can yield such a great reward. The Buddha said: [This is the case.]
“Have you ever seen anything rare? He replied, “I once saw a nyagrodha tree whose shade covered five hundred chariots.
The Buddha asked about the size of the seed from which the tree grew. He said, “It was as large as one-third of a mustard seed.”

The Buddha asked, "Who would believe you? He replied, "It is truly so. The Buddha said, "I see that this woman, having offered with a pure mind to the Buddha, has obtained a great fruit of retribution, just like this tree:
from a small cause, a great reward arises. At that time, the Brahmin’s mind was opened and his understanding awakened; he turned toward the Buddha to repent.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. He then cried out in a loud voice, saying:
"The gate of ambrosia has opened for all people; why do you not come forth?
When the people heard this, they each offered five hundred pieces of gold to the king, requesting that he provide offerings for the Buddha. The king and his ministers also took refuge in the Buddha.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained the fruits of the Path. Thus, the Sūtra says: "That which can be given as an offering is not limited by quantity. This is precisely what it means.
△ Second, showing the method of dedication. Part one: dedicating toward principle so as to receive happiness for a thousand births.
If such virtuous deeds can be dedicated solely to the Dharma-realm, the merit of that person will cause them to experience supreme and wondrous happiness throughout a hundred thousand births.

The first phrase refers generally to all the virtuous deeds cultivated above. Although these are distinguished as superior, middling, or inferior, once they are dedicated to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), how could there be any distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles?
Therefore, throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, the cultivation of causes never falters and the merit of giving remains ever-present.
By supporting the *dharmakāya*, the five fruits are all made eternal; by benefiting the life of wisdom, the four virtues are fully manifested.

The supreme and wondrous joy of the Dharma is enjoyed without end. As described in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Maudgalyāyana saw a celestial maiden seated upon a single lotus flower one hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth. This flower alone was exquisite, surpassing all others.
Whatever requisites for life she desired—palaces, food, drink, and so forth—appeared from the flower at her mere thought. Her every movement followed [the flower].
Śāriputra asked, "What meritorious deeds did you perform to receive such a retribution as this?
He replied, "After the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, his remaining relics were enshrined by his disciples in a stūpa made of the seven precious gems, forty *li* in height and breadth."
At that time, I was a woman. Upon coming out and seeing the Buddha image in the stupa, a feeling of faith and reverence arose within me.

Recalling the merit of the Buddha, I removed the flowers from my head and offered them to the image. By virtue of these causes and conditions, I have received such an exceptionally wondrous retribution as this.

Thus, even with a small good deed rooted in flowers, one may obtain such a reward; how much more so for those who repair stupas and temples and dedicate the merit to the Dharma-realm! This is but natural.
For one hundred thousand lifetimes, they shall experience supreme and wondrous bliss. △ Second, regarding the merit received after three lifetimes of dedication:
if one dedicates [the merit] solely for the benefit of one's own family members or for one's own personal gain, such a result will lead to the experience of happiness for three lifetimes;
by relinquishing one [selfish aim], one obtains ten thousandfold rewards.
The first two phrases reverse the mind that is unable to dedicate [merit], causing the fruits of merit to be limited and finite.
As for "relatives," they are those who love one another by nature and mutually serve and obey one another. As soon as one speaks of "one's own family," one is unable to extend thought to others;
thus, the principle of universal kinship (*baoyu*) is violated. Regarding "one's own relatives," the *Wukuzhangju jing* states:
It is said: between father and son, husband and wife, brothers, family members, acquaintances, and servants, there are five causes and conditions:
first, the enemy (father and son killing one another); second, the creditor (the parents' wealth being dissipated by the son); third, the debtor (the son’s wealth being provided for the parents);

fourth, the original vow (vows made in previous lives with a joyful and virtuous mind); and fifth, the true friend (serving one another through the Way in previous lives). Now, ordinary people do not recognize these [past lives].

The source [of suffering] is that one does not contemplate impermanence, yet instead clings with greedy attachment. One speaks of having parents, brothers, wives, children, and relatives both near and far.
When illness suddenly arrives and one is so debilitated as to be confined to bed, one addresses the relatives at dawn, saying, "Share my pain.
They all reply, "We cannot. Only then does the sick person realize that these five kinds of kin, whom they thought would benefit them, will not assist them.
Toiling to provide for one's livelihood, one satisfies the needs of the moment; yet this causes the body to follow after greed, binding and encroaching upon itself.

One becomes anxious for the nine branches of the clan, neglecting and abandoning virtuous conduct, and corrupting the wholesome mind. When old age, sickness, death, and the fruits of good and evil—suffering and joy—arrive, one must face them alone;
there is no one to take their place. All who have not yet attained the Way harbor these thoughts, and thus they are unable to practice giving or maintain their vows.
The Way is virtue. Alas! That people of the present age, even at the moment of death, still linger on without realization, moves the Tathāgata to profound pity;
thus he specifically provides these words to cause them to redirect their merit. Therefore he says:

"Whether for the sake of one's kin or oneself, one may only obtain three lifetimes of receiving the fruits of blessings in the human or heavenly realms; once that merit is exhausted, one falls back again."
Therefore, Yongjia said: "Giving while dwelling in signs produces the merit of rebirth in heaven; it is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void.
Once its momentum is exhausted, it falls back to earth, bringing about an unfavorable rebirth in the next life. The Sūtra speaks of giving while dwelling in signs.

This refers precisely to what is called "the third type of enemy, born of one's own kin. Regarding the phrase "forsaking one to obtain ten thousandfold retribution," it is as stated in the *Old Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra*:
"Formerly, outside the city of Śrāvastī, there was a woman of pure faith. The Buddha himself went to her door to beg for alms."
The wife placed rice into the Buddha’s bowl and, stepping back, prostrated herself. The Buddha said: "Planting one yields ten; planting ten yields a hundred; planting a hundred yields a thousand;
planting a thousand yields ten thousand; planting ten thousand yields a hundred million. One shall attain the Path of Seeing the Truths.
Her husband did not believe this, yet he silently listened from behind as the Buddha offered his blessing. The husband said: "How excessive are these words! She has given but a single bowl."
"By eating this meal, you have obtained such merit and have further realized the Path of Seeing (satyadarśana-mārga). The Buddha asked, "Do you see the Nyagrodha tree? How high is it?
He replied, "It is four or five *li* high and yields tens of thousands of *hu* of fruit each year. The Buddha asked, "How large is its seed? He replied, "It is like a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*).
The Buddha said, "Your words are far too exaggerated. How could a single mustard seed grow into something as tall as four or five *li*?"
He gave birth to several hundred thousand sons. He replied, "It is indeed so. The Buddha said, "The earth is insentient; yet its power of karmic retribution is such as this.
How much more so for a human being, who is a sentient being capable of joy? To offer a single bowl of rice to the Buddha brings forth exceedingly great merit."

The husband and wife had their minds opened and their intentions liberated; they immediately attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. This has issued from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata—how could one not believe it?
Nevertheless, because they had not yet turned back toward the *dharmadhātu* to attain the ultimate fruit, they were limited to three more births and ten thousand karmic retributions.
The comparison is concluded. △ Second, the summary and demonstration.
"Therefore, Kṣitigarbha, such are the matters concerning the causes and conditions of giving.
This concludes by demonstrating the cause and effect, praising them exhaustively to complete the comparison of the karmic paths and the merit of giving.
Therefore, this inquiry collectively points to the causes practiced by kings, ministers, men, and women, as well as the fruits they obtain;
thus it says, "The matter is such. Alas, among the people of the world, those who believe do not exert themselves fully in their practice, while those who do not believe are entirely unable to act.
Now, let us cite an event as proof. The *Piyū jīng* (Sutra of Parables) states: Long ago, there were two bhikṣus who both attained [realization].
Regarding the fruit of *srotāpanna*: one person constantly practiced teaching and begging for alms in order to cultivate merit;

the other simply sat in meditation to maintain himself, taking no pleasure in cultivating merit. He spoke to the beggar, saying, "Why do you not sit in meditation? You toil in vain by cultivating merit.
The cultivator of merit replied, "The Buddha has always said that a bhikṣu should practice giving. Subsequently, they both passed away.

Those who perform meritorious deeds are born into the families of elders as sons of elders; their servants and slaves attend to them, food and clothing come to them naturally, and their happiness is boundless.
Those who practice dhyāna are born as the children of female slaves; they sit alone upon the ground, weeping from hunger and thirst.

They both possessed the knowledge of their past lives. At that time, the son of the elder said to the servant’s son, "I told you before that you should practice giving, yet you refused to follow my words;
this was your own fault. Why do you weep? Later, they both sought and attained ordination, and both became arhats.
The son of the elder always sat upright and composed, and people vied with one another to bring him food and clothing.
As for that maidservant’s child, he went outside to beg for alms, but no one gave him anything; he constantly suffered from hunger and thirst.
For this reason, those who practice the Way should not merely observe the precepts, practice meditation, and recite sutras, but should also practice giving and cultivate merit.

The *Mahāprajāpatī Sūtra* says: "In this life one extinguishes transgressions, and in future lives one attains fulfillment. If one has wealth but does not give it away, one will suffer poverty life after life."
Therefore, entering the Way must take wisdom as its foundation; wisdom must take merit and virtue as its basis.

It is like a bird equipped with two wings soaring ten thousand fathoms, or a chariot with two wheels galloping a thousand li. The resources of the conditional and the ultimate establish the perfect cause;
the assistance of the practices and the perfections opens the Buddha-nature. One cannot but believe this. The formal exposition is concluded.
△ Third Major Chapter: Circulation, divided into two parts: first, specific circulation; second, general circulation. The first part is further divided into three:

first, the circulation concerning the earth goddess’s protection of the Dharma; second, the circulation concerning the benefits of seeing and hearing [the teaching]; third, the circulation consisting of the entrustment to humans and devas.
"Circulation" (liú) means to flow downward; "penetration" (tōng) means to be unobstructed. This is intended so that the waters of the True Dharma may flow from this time forward.
The commentary states: The scriptures of the Holy Teaching must not be obstructed in future ages;

for while the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma benefits only those with karmic capacity present at that time, it must rely upon compilation and transmission to serve as a model for practice for all sentient beings—like being instructed by ear or taught face-to-face—so that they may realize the fruits of the path without exception.
Thus we see that our Buddha’s compassion flourishes in the present world and extends its pity to future kalpas.
It must be circulated. Now, first, we protect the Dharma and circulate the title of the first chapter:
"The Earth Deity Protects the Dharma," Chapter Eleven.

Part Two: The Text of the Chapter has two sections: First, the Firm Resolve praises the virtues; Second, the Teacher and Master recounts and confirms the praise of those virtues. Within this, there are two [sub-sections].
First, to briefly clarify their previous encounters:
At that time, the Earth Deity Sthāvarā addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, since ancient times, I have gazed upon and prostrated before immeasurable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas;
they all possess inconceivable supernatural powers and wisdom, and extensively deliver sentient beings."
"Born. At that time refers to when the exposition of the four chapters has been completed. The Sanskrit name is *Nṛcu*, which translates here as "Firm" (*kṣāra*).

It has two meanings: first, in terms of its physical substance, it takes on the power to support, generate, nourish, and sustain the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*). Second, in terms of its function, it nurtures...

It establishes the myriad people and sustains all classes of beings. Second, in terms of its attributes (*dharma*): through the gateway of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it is eternally unchanging—this is its "constancy" (*nitya*).
It can support mountains and rivers—this is its "joy" (*sukha*). It can give birth to the myriad things—this is its "purity" (*śubha*). Its power is sovereign—this is its "self" (*ātman*).
Possessing these four virtues, she is called the "Divine" (referring to the *Shenyu Gong*, where "attaining success" [*diji*] refers to the land itself, as in "attaining success at Qintai and Huai").

Because she fully embodies both the meanings of "substance" (*shi*) and "dharma" (*fa*), she is named the Earth Deity of Firmness (*Kṣitigarbha*). Question: Is this Earth Deity male or female? Answer: She is a goddess.
According to the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There are four great deities: first, the Earth Deity; second, the Water [Deity]..."

The deity [asked]: "First is the earth deity; second, the water deity; third, the wind deity; fourth, the fire deity. Previously, the earth deity held a mistaken view, claiming that within the earth there are no water, fire, or wind.
The Buddha said: 'Within the earth there are indeed water, fire, and wind. However, because the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is predominant, it receives the name 'earth.

I shall now teach the Dharma in its proper sequence. When the Buddha had spoken thus, the earth deity rejoiced. The Buddha then preached the Four Noble Truths for her, and the earth deity immediately became free from dust and defilement (*vīta-rajo-vigata-mala*).
She attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and said: "I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. For as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, nor shall I drink alcohol, and so forth.
Grant me permission to be a laywoman (*upāsikā*) within the True Dharma; the same applies to the deities of water, fire, and wind. Thus we know she was a goddess.
In the explanation of the title, the Mother (*Kun*) is paired with the Lord (*Fu*), and the Father (*Ch'en*) with the Master (*Chu*); this is not [the case here].
Is this not a speculative assertion? As for his addressing the Buddha: the intention was that the propagation of the Sūtra must rely upon land, and the turning of the Dharma requires sustenance.
Since the land is certainly under my jurisdiction and food is likewise produced by me, if I do not protect and maintain it, how can it be circulated?
Therefore, prior to the great assembly in the celestial palace, amidst the countless earth deities, he resolutely...
Bearing the heavy responsibility of protecting the Dharma, I have thus bypassed the formal order of precedence to present this petition.
First, I shall indicate that from ancient times, I have manifested my resolve; that for days and nights, I have gazed upon and prostrated before [the Buddhas];

and so forth, thereby demonstrating the great number of holy lineages I have encountered—all of whom were no ordinary persons, but possessed of great inconceivability and the praise-worthy excellence of divine wisdom and penetrating insight.
This is the vessel for delivering sentient beings; it is the wondrous wheel of the three mysteries (*triguhyacakram*).
As the Great General Saṃjñeya said: "I personally behold the inconceivable realm of wisdom. The *Guangshu* (Commentary on the Light) states:

"If this realm could be known by wisdom or expressed in words, then the realm would not be secret (*guhya*). It cannot be known by wisdom, it cannot be cognized by consciousness, it cannot be named, and it cannot be spoken."
This is called the inconceivable secret realm. Now, all bodhisattvas extensively deliver sentient beings by means of the three secrets;
therefore, they all possess great, inconceivable supernormal wisdom. II. Specific Praise of What Is Heard Now.
Part One: Praising Kṣitigarbha’s Virtue. Section One: Extolling the Profundity of His Vows.
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha has made profound and weighty vows among all bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha possesses great karmic affinity with Jambudvīpa.
This is a general statement of Kṣitigarbha’s vows, which specifically indicate that he has a particular affinity with Jambudvīpa; all of these points appear in the subsequent text.

△ Second, citing the Great Being as an example to clarify [his nature]: Just as Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and Maitreya also manifest hundreds of thousands of physical forms to deliver beings within the six realms. His...
May there still be an ultimate [attainment].

Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya are as before; Avalokiteśvara is as after. According to the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, with the exception of Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and other great bodhisattvas, all others fall short of Kṣitigarbha. Now, the Earth Goddess, combined...

This means that Mañjuśrī and the others all yielded a single tally [in the counting of their vows], not because there was any superiority or inferiority in their merits, but precisely because their vows were either ultimate or non-ultimate. It is also like the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which says:
"From every single pore of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, worlds of Buddhas, as well as Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, constantly emerge, filling the ten directions."
To transform sentient beings, Mañjuśrī manifests emanations and enters among the five realms of existence;
he may appear as a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, or he may manifest in the body of a Buddha, as described in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*.

According to that sūtra, in the past Mañjuśrī was the Buddha Nāga-vaṃśa-guru, and seventy-two billion times he appeared as a pratyekabuddha (*Bhadrapāla-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-sūtra*). In the *Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:

This Mañjuśrī possesses great compassion. He will be born in this land, in the village of Tālā, into the family of the Brahmin Brahmadeva. At the time of his birth, his dwelling will transform into a lotus flower, and he will emerge from his mother’s right side with a body the color of purple gold.

Upon touching the ground, he will be able to speak, and a jeweled canopy will follow him to provide shade. He will leave the household life under the Buddha and abide in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Four hundred and fifty years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he will go to the Snowy Mountains and proclaim the twelve divisions of the scriptures to five hundred rishis.

Having transformed them so that they abide in non-retrogression, he returned to his birthplace at the empty wilderness lake, beneath a nyagrodha tree, and entered the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. From his pores issued golden light that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, delivering all those with whom he had a karmic connection.

His body was like a mountain of purple gold; he was exactly sixteen feet tall, and his halo was magnificent and radiant, each side measuring one fathom. Within his halo were five hundred transformation Buddhas, and each transformation Buddha had five transformation Bodhisattvas serving as attendants.

This was Mañjuśrī, who possessed immeasurable supernatural powers and manifestations that cannot be fully described. Furthermore, when Wentai Biancong entered the capital, an elderly monk sent him a letter, instructing him to seek out Bohe at the north of the city and entrust it to him. Upon arriving at the banks of the Guangci River, he found him there.

Hearing a child calling out "Borhe," he threw his book at him; the child immediately ate it and suddenly stood up as a man and vanished. Only then did he realize that the old monk was Mañjuśrī and Borhe was Samantabhadra. This butcher, surnamed Zhao, had kept [the image] for fifteen years and fed it only Borhe, hence its name.

(Han-shan and Shi-qi were of this same category). As for Avalokiteśvara, there are the thirty-two manifestations described in the *Pumen pin* (Universal Gate Chapter), as well as many more accounts recorded in various biographies.
As for Maitreya, there are examples such as Master Fu and the Cloth Bag Monk (*Po-tu seng*). This is based on...

This refers to what was said recently (the *Huishang pusa jing* states: "In the past, during the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, there was a bhikṣu named Vimala who dwelt in seclusion in a mountain cave.

Nearby were five immortals. A woman encountered rain and entered the cave; when the rain cleared, she departed. When the five immortals saw her, each declared that the bhikṣu had committed lewd misconduct. Upon hearing this, Vimala immediately leaped into the void, causing the five immortals to prostrate themselves on the ground in confession of their fault—this was none other than Maitreya).

Because the great bodhisattvas manifest their presence without fixed form, it is stated generally that they "also transform into hundreds of thousands of physical forms," and so forth. However, its...
All vows and thoughts have a time when they come to an end; it is not that they do not reach ultimate completion. △ Third, revealing that his teaching and transformation are immeasurable:

This Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha has made vows for kalpas as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of Ganges Rivers to teach and transform all sentient beings throughout the six realms.
As before. △ Second, protecting those who make offerings, in two parts: first, obtaining benefits through molding images and making offerings with praise;
second, eliminating calamities by reciting scriptures and making offerings to images. The first part is divided into three sections; first, cultivating the causes.

“World-Honored One, I observe that among the sentient beings of the future and the present, in their places of residence, they shall construct small shrines from earth, stone, bamboo, or wood in clean locations to the south.
Within these, they will be able to fashion images of Kṣitigarbha by molding, painting, or even casting them in gold, silver, copper, or iron;
they will then burn incense as offerings, gaze upon them with reverence, and offer praise.”
True wisdom has no fixed direction; it is not confined to the east, west, south, or north. The Dharma-body has no form; how could it require copper, iron, gold, or silver?
Nevertheless, the earth serves as the locus for images, and images serve as the gateway for generating reverence.

While following worldly conventions, one does not destroy conventional designations while discussing the true nature (*dharmatā*). To expound the Dharma of the [Buddha-]nature, one must necessarily realize the true countenance through conventional appearances. Therefore, relying on...
It is by dwelling therein that signs are produced. However, when one speaks of the "place of abiding," this is merely the terminology used by earth spirits regarding their traces.

If one were to discuss its fundamental nature, what place could possibly be discussed? The four wisdoms have no means to discern its beginning, and the five eyes are utterly unable to peer into its profundity.
As stated in the *Daśacakra Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Paripṛcchaka addressed the Buddha, saying: "This son of good family, from..."

"From where have you come? In which Buddha-field do you dwell? How far is it from here? The Buddha replied, "Great Being, such as you are, wherever you may reside in various Buddha-fields, and whichever samādhis you may abide in...
(and so forth). According to this, how could [the Buddha] be restricted to a single direction or a single location?
As for the current mention of building a chamber in the south, according to the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Origin of the World), it corresponds to Jambudvīpa...
To the south of Mount Pūrvavideha, outside the second Iron Ring Mountain (Cakravāṇa), lies the palace and dwelling place of King Yama.

Because Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva specifically manifests his body within the hells to serve as the Teacher of the Netherworld, he established a chamber to the south at the very spot where he assumes this form.
This refers to the intention of manifesting from the world of the south within the Great Assembly, appearing as clouds of fragrant rain and flowers.
This is because the hour of noon represents the Middle Way; the south corresponds to the trigram Li, which signifies correctness, the sun, and brilliant clarity.

Because the center of Li is empty, it is luminous; this symbolizes the emptiness of all phenomena. Thus, when the sun of wisdom shines forth, it illuminates the entire world. Therefore, this is established according to its outward manifestation.

To construct a chamber and provide offerings for the image is precisely to cause every person to emerge from the dark paths of the pit and ascend to the sunny ground of *li* (the hexagram of separation).
This is because the Yin governs death while the Yang governs life. Regarding the purification of the site:

according to the ritual manuals of the Secret Mantra (*Guhyamantra*) for constructing mandalas, one must excavate away the impure soil and take up the pure earth beneath it, [establishing the site] within a secluded and tranquil forest.
Alternatively, it may be made by a clean spot beside a river; only then can it be said to accord with the Dharma. Therefore, it is also said today: "In a clean place.
*Kān* (pronounced *kūhán*) means a dragon’s cave. It is composed of the radical for "to join" (*hé*), taking the sense of hibernating and sealing the entrance—a state of ultimate stillness.
The dragon is the quintessence of pure Yang; therein the transformations of the Way of Heaven are fully realized.
Why is it that the dragon with its yang head remains hidden, achieving virtue through invisibility? It is precisely because the Way of Heaven is vast and profound, without sound or scent.

Whether the dragon remains hidden or does not remain hidden, the primordial chaos is neither pierced nor leaked. Thus, one may perceive that which appears yet does not appear, and that which is concealed yet is not concealed, thereby attaining the Yin.

Yang (the active) and Yi (the unitary) are one; by merging cultivated nature with innate nature, they share a single source. This is precisely the contemplation of non-differentiation, the dharma-gate of transcending study.
The remainder is as in the text. △ Second, the benefits obtained, in two parts: first, the presentation of the ten benefits.
Those who dwell in such a place shall immediately obtain ten kinds of benefits.

This demonstrates the excellence of the noble abode of humans. For once they have heard of the inconceivable vows, majestic power, and spiritual authority of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, they are able to believe and understand;
furthermore, they construct shrines, fashion images, and offer worship, praise, and veneration. At the very first thought-moment—

Faith and understanding. Next, one concurrently practices the six perfections. Since this is the dwelling place of a respected disciple, whatever land it occupies is universally named "Auspicious" (Śrī).
Therefore, it constantly gathers auspicious omens and possesses ten kinds of benefits. △ Second, the enumeration of the ten names.
What are the ten? First, the land shall be fertile and rich. Second, the household shall enjoy perpetual peace and security. Third, those who have passed away shall be reborn in the heavens.
Fourth, those currently living shall have their lifespans increased. Fifth, all that is sought shall be fulfilled according to one's wishes. Sixth, there shall be no calamities from fire or water.

Seventh, the expulsion of wasting and depletion; eighth, the blocking off of evil dreams; ninth, divine protection when entering or departing; tenth, frequently encountering auspicious causes for attaining the holy.

The first phrase poses the inquiry. From "First" onwards, the successive stages of mutual generation are enumerated; thus, there are ten benefits. First, one establishes a residence by selecting the land.

Next, one clarifies the household to settle the body. This continues until the protection and assistance of spirits and deities, which ultimately leads to encountering the causes for attaining the Sages.
Regarding "fertile soil": "feng" (豐) means grand and flourishing. When things are flourishing, sacrifices must be fully provided with all necessary items; therefore, [this term] is taken.
The beans are large and full, signifying abundance. The character [甡/(廾-一)] (pronounced *fúróng*; meaning "the vitality of life is overflowing") denotes being filled to the brim again and again.

According to the *Yùgōng* ( Tribute of Yu): "Its soil is white and soft (*báirǎng*). The commentary states: "Soil without clods is called *rǎng* (soft earth). 'White' indicates the purity of its color;
'soft' (*rǎng*) indicates the excellence of its nature. The *Zhouguān Dàsītǔ* (Great Minister of the Land of the Zhou Officialdom) distinguishes twelve types of soil.
One knows the species [of plants] and thereby teaches the cultivation of crops and the planting of trees. However, there are two ways to discern the suitability of the soil:
by its color and by its nature. Generally, soils of five colors are all fertile grounds for planting and cultivation, as it is said: "Its soil is black and rich," or "Its soil is red and rich.
Thus, the commentary on the *Dili Guan* (Office of Geography) in the *Zhouli* states that "rich" (*rang*) refers to red soil, because all things [thrive] from it.
When it comes into existence, it is called "earth" (*tǔ*). That which is ploughed and cultivated by people is called "loam" (*rǎng*). *Rǎng* means harmonious and settled.
The *Yìyǎ* explains *rǎng* as being synonymous with *láng*, capturing the sense of being fertile and moist. The *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"All the lands within Jambudvīpa are called 'fertile loam' (*wòrǎng*), prosperous and joyful, producing much precious treasure, and possessing pure forests and waters. (This accords with the *Dīrghāgama*, which describes the land of Jambudvīpa as narrow in the south and broad in the north.)
It is seven thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth (the human face is shaped like this terrain). Having obtained such fertile land, one’s household and dwelling may enjoy eternal peace.
The character for "household" (*jiā*) consists of *mián* (roof) and *yún* (the character for "multitude"); thus, fathers, sons, brothers, and wives dwell together in harmony and joy.

The character for "dwelling" (*zhái*) consists of *mián* (roof) and *tuō* (the character for "to entrust"); thus, one selects an auspicious place to settle, whereby signs of prosperity manifest and calamities are eliminated.
Thus, those who are living find peace; their merit also benefits their ancestors and parents, enabling them to receive the fruits of wholesome karma and be reborn together in the heavens.

If this is true even for those who have already passed away, how much more so for one who builds a dwelling and venerates sacred images? As it says in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*: "If there are sentient beings..."
For the sake of making offerings to the sūtras, they adorn their dwellings, even hanging up a single banner or a single parasol, or offering a single garment.
Although the six heavens of the desire realm already possess natural palaces made of the seven treasures, when such a person’s life comes to an end, [they will be reborn there].
They immediately attain rebirth there, where each naturally has seven celestial maidens with whom they enjoy themselves, constantly experiencing inconceivable and subtle bliss day and night;
it is even so now, not only for those who have passed away who are reborn in heaven.
It also causes those in the present to increase their lifespan. The *Cloud of Radiance* (*Prabhāsa-megha*) says:
"Within Jambudvīpa, medicinal herbs, trees, roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits flourish and grow lush. They are fully endowed with beautiful color, fragrance, and flavor.

When sentient beings have consumed them, their lifespan, physical appearance, strength, eloquence, and tranquility increase. Their six sense faculties and various organs become complete and sharp. This is it. Since there is already longevity...
Furthermore, since all worldly affairs fail to harmonize, how can they be considered worthy of esteem? Now, whatever one prays for, there is nothing that does not accord with one's intent;

"to follow one's will" is termed "fulfillment," which is also a synonym for "accordance. This refers to being able to use things according to one's desire and receiving happiness—namely, various foods and drinks, clothing, bedding, palaces, houses, trees, groves, gardens, rivers, ponds, wells, and springs—all of these.
All are fully provided for; this is what it means to have no unfulfilled intentions. Fulfillment of intention lies within, while calamity and fortune lie without.
As for what are called water and fire, they are things that human life cannot do without for even a single day. For water flows toward moisture and nourishes the myriad things;
thus it occupies the northern position of *kan*. Fire seeks out dryness and parches the myriad things; thus it occupies the southern position.

Regarding the state of separation: when fire and water are in mutual completion (*jì*), all things are generated and sustained. Should fire and water not be timely, then all things will be scorched and rotted;
how much more so when the *shāngyáng* bird appears to dance and the god Huílù (the Fire God) secretly approaches—then the calamities will not be slight.

(According to the *Báizé tú*, the essence of fire is named Bìfāng; its form is like a bird with one leg. If one calls it by its name, it departs. The essence of water is named Wǎngxiàng; its form is like a small child with red eyes, black skin, large ears, and long claws. It is [captured] with a rope...)
Bind it; then you may cook it (it will be auspicious). Although internal and external peace has been attained, one must still ward off empty depletion (*hào*).
Regarding "depletion," the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a type of grain. The *Lüshi Chunqiu* says, "Among the finest grains are those from Mount Xuan and the *hào* of the South Sea.
If one follows the *Xunzi*, which defines "depletion" as being "abundant yet chaotic," this refers to reduction and empty waste. [Dong...]*
Zhongshu’s memorial states: "To examine the increase and decrease of the world. This is correct. (Note: *Xi* means growth; *hao* means depletion.
In common parlance, the sixteenth day of the first month is called the Day of Depletion (*Haomo*), on which government offices do not open their granaries. Guangming said:
"If in this land there are various depletions and all manner of hardships, by our power we shall cause all such hundreds of thousands of matters of decline and loss to be entirely [eliminated]."
It is thus: since all conditions have been favorable during the day, one must sleep peacefully and dream serenely at night.
Now, all manner of evil dreams are like the roots and bark of wood—blocked and not extended; they are like the fibers of hemp—severed and not continued.
As the days pass and the months roll on, you sit and enjoy constant auspiciousness. From day out and night in, I especially hope for your peace.
"May you now cultivate merit and goodness; your every movement shall be protected by the divine. Guangming said:

"We, the Four Heavenly Kings and the spirits of the twenty-eight divisions, along with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of other spirits, constantly observe and protect this Jambudvīpa with our pure celestial eyes, which surpass those of humans. These nine items above are all mundane benefits.

"Benefit. The tenth is the "Noble Cause" (*ārya-hetu*). This refers to supramundane benefit. "Noble" (*ārya*) means correct; it refers to the causes for cultivation that lead to the supramundane, the true nobility.
These include such acts as hearing the Dharma and awakening to the Way, practicing the fast, giving alms, molding images, repairing stupas, and restoring scriptures and icons.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "A virtuous friend causes one to gradually distance oneself from unwholesome dharmas and increases..."

Regarding wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*): where there was originally no concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), or the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*), these now come to exist;
and where they were not yet complete, they are increased and expanded. Thus, one constantly encounters many such noble causes.
If it were not for making offerings to the Great Being (*mahāsattva*), how could one attain these ten benefits? △ Third, the conclusion.
