World-Honored One, in future ages and among present sentient beings, if they can perform such offerings in the direction where [this teaching] resides, they shall obtain such benefits.
This concludes the two sections on cultivating the causes and attaining the benefits. The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* states:

"O son of good family, suppose there were someone who, for a hundred kalpas, with a sincere mind, took refuge in and invoked the names of Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, Samantabhadra, and others as their leaders, along with as many great bodhisattvas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."

This is called recitation. To perform prostrations and offerings while seeking various desires is not as effective as for someone who, for the duration of a single meal, takes refuge with a sincere mind in the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha.
This causes the wishes of all sentient beings to be fulfilled, like a wish-fulfilling jewel or a hidden treasure.
Such a Great Being has long cultivated [these practices] for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to spiritual maturity.
With firm great vows and great compassion, and with courageous diligence that surpasses all other bodhisattvas, you should therefore make offerings to him.
As the verse says: "Even if one were to praise and describe his merits for a hundred kalpas, one would still not be able to exhaust them;
therefore, all should make offerings. The reason for making offerings is that one thereby attains such benefits as these.
△ Second, reading the sutras, making offerings to the images, and eliminating transverse obstacles.

Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in future ages, if there are good men or good women who have this sutra and an image of a Bodhisattva in their place of residence, and these people are further able to recite the sutra and make offerings [to it]..."
Bodhisattva, I shall constantly, day and night, protect this person with my original spiritual power, so that even water, fire, thieves,
and great or small calamities— all such evil matters— shall be entirely extinguished.
First, the locations where the sutras and images are to be enshrined are clarified; next, the protection by power that extinguishes evil is clarified.
This reflects the spirit of the earth deities (*pṛthivī-devatā*) protecting the Dharma, which is identical to the vow made in the *Prabhāsa* assembly to protect the sutra. As it says there:
"Wherever this sutra circulates, I shall always remain therein to provide constant watch and guard. This refers to the [destruction by] water and fire mentioned above.

The six, seven, eight, and three matters are great calamities, as described in the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*. The nine untimely deaths are minor calamities, as described in the *Sūtra on the Nine Untimely Deaths*.

All evil matters are as stated in the *Prabhāsa Sūtra*. By means of this sūtra, all evil dreams, sorcery, the five planets and various lunar mansions, portents, disasters, and all other evil matters shall be extinguished without remainder. So too shall immeasurable ghosts and spirits [be subdued].

Together with the various Great Beings (mahāsattvas), they shall diligently exert themselves day and night to protect the four directions, ensuring that no calamities or misfortunes occur and that all beings are forever freed from suffering.

May their hearts be content and their minds at ease, according to whatever they desire. Is this not the case where evil matters are eliminated and good matters gather, where disasters and transgressions are extinguished and auspicious signs assemble?
Yet there are people in the world who, being faithless, claim this is merely a means of inducement.

As for speech: Have you not heard that in a family where goodness accumulates, there will surely be an abundance of blessings; and in a family where non-goodness accumulates, there will surely be an abundance of calamities?
Furthermore, have you not heard that when one utters good words, they are responded to even a thousand li away; when one utters ungood words, they are rejected even a thousand li away?
Words and deeds are the pivot and trigger of the gentleman; they move heaven and earth and stir the ghosts and spirits.
Should you not therefore attain reverence and caution? △ Second, the Teacher’s confirmation in two parts: First, praising his virtues, further divided into two;
first, directly praising his supernatural power.
The Buddha addressed the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā: "Your great supernatural power is such that few among the various deities can approach it."
"Great supernatural power" refers to what follows in the text. "Various deities" refers to those of the same class;
for example, when Sudhana visited the Earth Goddess Anala, one million earth goddesses each emitted light, signifying that none of these earth goddesses could equal her supernatural power.
△ Second, the further explanation of the presiding deity over objects.

Why is this? The entire land of Jambudvīpa receives your protection; even down to the grasses, trees, sand, stones, rice, hemp, bamboo, reeds, grains, and precious gems that exist upon the earth—all are due to your power.
The first two lines provide a general explanation; "down to" [the end] provides a detailed explanation. In the *Prabhāsa-parivarta*, the Earth Deity herself says:
"This great earth is sixteen thousand eight hundred yojanas deep, from the adamantine foundation up to the surface of the sea."
All flavors were fully developed and abundant; the soil was rich and fertile, surpassing that of today.
Regarding the grasses, trees, rice, hemp, and other seeds, from where did they originate after the world was first formed?
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, there was a great chaotic wind that blew seeds from the indestructible world (*asaṃvarta-loka*) to bring them forth into this land.

First, the single-rooted; second, the stalked; third, the jointed; fourth, the peduncled (the character *dì* has the same pronunciation as *dì*; for dates and plums, one says "to remove the peduncle"); fifth, the seed-podded—these constitute the five types of seeds.
This is due both to the majestic power of the earth deities and to the karmic retribution of sentient beings.
According to the *Yèbào Chābié Jīng* (Sūtra on the Differentiation of Karmic Retribution), there are further ten types of karma that cause sentient beings to receive external evil retributions. If...
There are sentient beings who, because they have extensively practiced the ten unwholesome karmas, cause all external things to be entirely incomplete (and so forth).
If one practices the ten wholesome karmas, it is the opposite of the above.

This is because when the evil karma of sentient beings is rampant, it causes the earth deities to fail in their protection, thereby diminishing all things; if one extensively cultivates virtue, their majestic power increases.
All things become more beautiful. Therefore, the Earth Deity said: "This is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.

If it is explained in detail, the merit obtained by myself and my retinue will be twice that of usual times; our physical strength will increase, and our minds will become courageous and sharp. World-Honored One!"
Having partaken of the flavor of the unsurpassed Dharma-nectar, the soil of Jambudvīpa has become twice as fertile as usual.

This great earth, which is the support for all sentient beings, is now able to increase all necessary provisions, allowing all beings to use them according to their wishes and experience happiness. Therefore, it is now praised, saying: "The land of Jambudvīpa," and so forth.

"O Treasure! All that belongs to the earth is brought about by your power. (The "bao" [treasure] refers to the sea shell; its substance is minute, yet its texture is naturally patterned. Its back is convex and rounded, representing the Yang of Heaven;

its belly is flat and open, representing the Yin of Earth. It moves by means of its belly, like the people of antiquity. Ancient people were simple; they used shells as currency and valued tortoises. Thus, when characters were first formed, they took "shell" (*bei*) as the radical.

This was done to accommodate the convenience of the people. Later generations began to cast coins (*quan*). Once coins circulated, the shell was discarded, and authority over currency passed to the ruler. Nevertheless, in terms of benefiting the people's livelihood, virtue has further declined. Paper money was created to oppress the people, and in the end, none...)
...that they are able to practice it). △ Second, the description of the events, in two parts: First, the description of the accomplishment of praising the matters of benefit.
Furthermore, one should constantly praise the deeds of benefit performed by Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, as well as your own merits and supernatural powers.
A hundred thousand times greater than the usual portion, the Earth Deity extols and praises [the merit].
This is the second gate among the Ten Vows of Samantabhadra. Indeed, by extolling it for even a single thought-moment, the ten thousand virtues are spontaneously possessed;
therefore, whenever the sons of the Buddha come to a Dharma assembly, they first see and long hear the chanting of the Brahma-songs being proclaimed and spread.
Now, this earth deity is not merely able to preside over the things of Jambudvīpa; furthermore, she extols the deeds of Kṣitigarbha’s benefits.

Thus, she becomes an earth deity who protects the Dharma. Her karma of merit and her karma of wisdom naturally become profound and vast, and her virtues and supernormal powers are likewise inconceivable.
Compared to other earth deities, she surpasses them ten thousandfold. Why is this? It is truly because of the Great [Bodhisattva].
The spiritual power and supernatural penetrations of this person are inconceivable. It is like the nectar of the devas:
regardless of whether one is noble or humble, old or young, if there is anyone who tastes it, there is none who does not attain longevity and immortality. II.
Describing the Accomplishment of Reciting, Making Offerings, and Receiving Protection. A. Men and Women Making Offerings to the Image and Reciting the Sutra.
If, in future ages, there are good men or good women who make offerings to Bodhisattvas and recite this sutra,
practicing even according to a single matter from the *Kṣitigarbha-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra*, [they shall attain liberation].

The first section clarifies the person and the Dharma. It simply relies on what follows below to cause one to practice with single-minded devotion; that is, to restrain the mind to a single point, where there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.

The Sanskrit term *niśraya* is translated here as "reliance" (*yi*). It means to rely upon or depend upon. By relying on the merit of this sutra, one departs from the ocean of suffering. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* elucidates the four reliances;
this refers specifically to relying on sutras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not relying on sutras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
It is said in ancient proverbs: "The skins of a thousand sheep are not worth the armpit fur of a single fox. Thus we know that the myriad scriptures do not equal this sūtra.
For among people there are those with discursive thought and those beyond discursive thought; among sūtras there are those that reveal and those that have not yet revealed.

Now, by specializing in the study of sūtras that are beyond discursive thought and fully revealed, one's transgressions are instantly eliminated and merit is swiftly accomplished. Why trouble oneself with many?
To seek while the mind and will are distracted and confused—this is precisely the "peaceful and happy practice with signs" (sanimitta-sukha-vihāra) of Mount Nanyue.

As for what is called "practice," it means acting according to what one has taught. If one hears but does not act, it is like counting another's jewels while eating; how could this relieve hunger or poverty?
The proverb says: "To speak for ten feet is not as good as to practice for one inch. This is truly a teaching for the world.
△ Second, protecting against calamities and attaining the fruit, in two parts: first, the earth deities protect and eliminate calamities.
By means of your original spiritual power, protect them so that no calamities or undesirable events may ever reach their ears, let alone cause them to suffer.
Regarding the imperial decree to enjoin the Earth Deity to provide protection: by virtue of this wholesome faith, if the Buddha were present, it would suffice as the fourth of the four faiths;

now that he has entered parinirvāṇa, it corresponds to the fifth of the five grades. Since reading the sutras constitutes the second grade, and making offerings constitutes the fourth—furthermore encompassing the practice of the six perfections—one should know that this begins from a single thought of faith and understanding, and culminates in the perfection of profound faith and contemplation.

Because the practices of the five stages of contemplation are like those of a Buddha, they cause [the deities] to provide protection. Regarding "original spiritual power" (*mūla-ṛddhi*): in terms of phenomena (*vastu*), it refers to the Lord of the Earth as the basis;
in terms of the Dharma (*dharma*), it refers to the four virtues as the basis. Because of this basis, their spiritual power is double that of other protectors.
As when the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhādrdhavajra addressed the Buddha: "When a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma sits upon the Dharma-seat..."
I shall constantly guard and protect you day and night, never departing from your side. Concealing my form, I shall remain beneath the Dharma seat, supporting your feet upon my head.
Once all calamities and misfortunes—namely those caused by us kings and various spirits and ghosts—have been cast away, that kingdom shall experience various disasters and anomalies:
comets shall appear as portents, meteors shall fall, and the five planets [shall be disturbed].
The laws of order are lost; both sun and moon appear simultaneously; the sun and moon undergo eclipses; ominous rainbows appear frequently; the earth shakes violently;
and fierce winds and torrential rains arise. Once these calamities have begun, they afflict the people; therefore, they are called "disasters.

Furthermore, it is said that grain and rice soar in price; there is famine and freezing hunger; enemies and bandits plunder; and the people suffer greatly. In such a land, there is nothing [to be found].

This place of love and joy is now a matter of what is not as one wishes. Since you are now making offerings to the images and reciting the sutras, practicing solely in accordance with your original vows, even such calamities and matters of what is not as one wishes shall not suddenly reach your ears, let alone be seen by the eyes or experienced by the body.
Part Two: The Testimony of Protection by the Various Devas and the Realization of Joy. 1. First, showing those who provide protection.
It is not only you alone who protect this person; there are also Śakra and Brahmā, along with their retinues and the hosts of devas, who provide protection for this person.
The first phrase means that it is not only you, the earth deity, who protect [them] alone. If one practices as described above, there will also be Brahmā.
The retinues of all the devas have come to provide protection. As the Four Heavenly Kings said to the Buddha:
"If this person should hear this sutra, they will be able to attain various immeasurable merits of both the future and the present.
For the sake of hearing the Dharma, we shall conceal ourselves and remain invisible, yet we shall go to wherever they dwell and where the Dharma is being preached."
Mahābrahmā Deva-rāja, Śakra-devendra, Mahāprajñā Devī, Guṇarāja Deva, Vaiśravaṇa the Great General,
and the great generals of the twenty-eight divisions of spirits; Maheśvara, Maṇibhadra the Great General of Spirits,
Haritī with her five hundred sons, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions [of others].

Billions of nayutas of spirits, ghosts, and devas—such multitudes as these—all concealed themselves and did not manifest their bodies in order to hear the Dharma, arriving at the place where this person dwells and expounds the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the Vaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Completeness.
If even the devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts provide such protection for it, how much more so for this most supreme scripture now being revealed and elucidated? Its...
As for the power of the protection afforded by Brahmā, Śakra, and the other devas, what need is there for further words? △ Second, explaining the intent of this protection:

Why is it that one receives such protection from the sages and worthies? It is entirely because of reverently beholding and making offerings to the image of Kṣitigarbha, as well as reciting and transcribing this Sūtra of His Original Vow.
By these means, one will naturally and ultimately transcend the sea of suffering and realize the bliss of Nirvāṇa. For this reason—
Therefore, one obtains great protection. The first phrase poses the inquiry.
"Sage" (ārya) refers to the truly authentic; "worthy" (bhadra) means virtuous and upright. Furthermore, the leader is called a sage, while the retinue is called worthy.
Those who are upright serve as devas and spirits. All that follows is the explanation. Within this explanation, there are three points. First:
The two lines [of verse] provide the formal explanation of the meaning. The following two lines demonstrate the benefits obtained.
Regarding the term "ocean of suffering," according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the waters of the four great oceans are salty and bitter due to three causes and conditions:

first, there are natural clouds that fill the void and reach as far as the Ābhāsvara Heaven (*Ābhāsvara-deva*), raining down everywhere to wash the celestial palaces and cleanse the world below, from the Brahma... [text continues].
From the celestial palaces of the Kāyika devas down to the mountains of the eighty thousand worlds, including Sumeru, the king of mountains—all were washed and cleansed.
The foul, salty, and bitter impurities within them flowed downward into the ocean, merging into a single flavor.
Second: In the past, there was a great rishi who cast a spell upon the ocean water, making it perpetually salty and bitter so that humans could not drink it.
3. The Miscellaneous Abodes of Sentient Beings. Their bodies are large and tall, reaching from one hundred *yojanas* up to seven hundred *yojanas*.
Because of their inhalation and exhalation, as well as their discharge of urine and feces, the waters of the ocean are salty and bitter; here, "ocean" refers metaphorically to the ocean of karma.

Suffering has ten thousand aspects, yet through ritual practice and study, there is no difficulty in attaining liberation. To speak of "spontaneity" means that no forced effort is required. Having finished speaking:
It concludes thus: it is ultimately not in vain. Therefore, practitioners should be single-minded in their resolve. If one is single-minded, whatever is sought will surely be attained;

one shall emerge from suffering and realize bliss. This is the heart of the True Teacher’s entrustment in the celestial palace, as well as Kṣitigarbha’s intention to transform beings on the dark paths.
It is vital that you practice with exclusive dedication; cause and effect do not deviate by even a hair's breadth.
Thus, with these two phrases, the protection of the intention is concluded as in the text.
*The Commentary on the Sections of the Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s Fundamental Vow Sūtra*, Scroll Five;
*The Commentary on the Sections of the Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva’s Fundamental Vow Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Lingcheng of the Ancient Yan Kuang’an Qinglian Monastery, son of [Name]. Section Two:

Benefits Derived from Seeing and Hearing and the Circulation [of this Text]. It is said that there are none who do not obtain great benefit upon seeing the image of Kṣitigarbha or hearing the name of Kṣitigarbha;
this is analogous to the case of Avalokiteśvara, where those who hear his name, see his body, or contemplate him in their minds are all able [to attain liberation].
To see the cessation of suffering and pay homage to the body is the occasion for bodily action (*kāyakarman*); to hear the name is the occasion for verbal action (*vākkarman*);

and for body and speech to arise from the mind is the occasion for mental action (*manaskarman*). Once these occasions have been established, the responses—whether hidden or manifest—accord naturally, just as the grasses and trees upon the earth are all equally moistened by a single rain.
The benefit of its circulation is immeasurable. This concludes the title of the first chapter.
Chapter Twelve: Benefits of Seeing and Hearing.

△ The text of these two chapters is divided into two parts: first, Śākyamuni manifests signs and praises the virtues [of Avalokiteśvara]; second, Avalokiteśvara requests that [the teaching] be spoken for the sake of its circulation.
The first part is further divided into two: first, light is emitted from the crown of the head to certify the matter.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays from the great hair-tuft on the crown of his head.
From that moment until the address to the great assembly, all is the narrative text of the chronicler.

That the emission of light occurs precisely after the "Chapter on the Earth Deity Protecting the Dharma" is to serve as a proof for what follows, causing all sentient beings to perceive the signs and attain awakening.
The mind: each and every one knows for themselves that this is a single segment of the inconceivable, primordially existing, eternal radiance.

From the two lines beginning with "From the crown": this provides the general heading. Its Sanskrit name is *uṣṇīṣa*, which here is translated as "Buddha’s Crown. As for the term "gate" (*mon*), the *Zen Biyao Jing* (Sutra on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna) states:
"The human body has three divisions: the navel is the central plain; the head is the hall; and the crown is the celestial gate."
Therefore, it is called the "Crown Gate" (*uṣṇīṣa-mukha*). For the head is the sovereign of the entire body, and the crown is the most honored part of the head.

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* records that the seer Asita said: "Among the parts of the head, the mark of the crown (*uṣṇīṣa-lakṣaṇa*) has no one who can see its summit; whether among gods or humans, there is none superior to it.
It symbolizes the Wisdom of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), transcending causes and reaching the ultimate fruit. A gate is that which enables passage; it is the very essence [of the path].
There are two meanings. By means of this wondrous image and auspicious name of Kṣitigarbha, those who gaze upon, worship, and recite it can advance toward the ultimate fruit;
this is the power of its capacity to penetrate [reality]. This crown is inherently possessed by every person and requires no external borrowing.

Thus, the six realms and Kṣitigarbha are, in total, one and the same body; sentient beings and the Tathāgata have never been two distinct entities. It is right here and now—*dangxia*—that [this is realized].

This is so. Why borrow from entering through the gate? It is the meaning of realizing the essence itself. As for "the superior," light radiates from the crown of the head, signifying that from the ultimate body of wisdom (*jñāna*), this great function of radiant light arises.
Its essence is fundamentally one, for it is equally possessed by both sentient beings and Buddhas;

yet its functions are not one, as they are established according to the capacities of those to be guided. This is precisely the ultimate principle of the "three thousand worlds in a single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa-trisahasra*), which are mutually interpenetrating.
Because they possess mutual pervasiveness, there are hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions of rays of light from the great *ūrṇā* hair-tuft (*ūrnā-kośa*).

These represent the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*). "Great" refers to the *dharmakāya*, because it is all-pervasive. The hair-tuft represents *vimukti* (liberation), because it is solid on the outside and empty within.

The light represents *prajñā* (wisdom), because it illuminates and discerns the myriad dharmas. Since the body is great, the hair-light is also great; since the hair is empty, the great light is also [empty].
Emptiness. Because it illuminates, the Great White Hair also illuminates. The three and the one are not separate from one another; yet the one and the three are not to be confused.

They do not exist side by side, nor are they distinct in their vertical or horizontal arrangements. Both sentient beings and Buddhas equally possess this realization. Having provided this general indication, the following sections clarify it specifically.
These are known as: the light of the white ūrṇā-kośa mark, the light of the great white ūrṇā-kośa mark, the light of the auspicious ūrṇā-kośa mark,

the light of the great auspicious ūrṇā-kośa mark, the light of the jade ūrṇā-kośa mark, the light of the great jade ūrṇā-kośa mark, the light of the purple ūrṇā-kośa mark, the light of the great purple ūrṇā-kośa mark,

the light of the blue ūrṇā-kośa mark, the light of the great blue ūrṇā-kośa mark, the light of the emerald ūrṇā-kośa mark, the light of the great emerald ūrṇā-kośa mark, and the light of the red ūrṇā-kośa mark.
The light of the great red ūrṇā-kośa; the light of the green ūrṇā-kośa; the light of the great green ūrṇā-kośa; the light of the golden ūrṇā-kośa;
the light of the great golden ūrṇā-kośa; the light of the auspicious cloud ūrṇā-kośa; the light of the great auspicious cloud ūrṇā-kośa; the light of the thousand-spoked wheel ūrṇā-kośa;

the light of the great thousand-spoked wheel ūrṇā-kośa; the light of the jewel wheel ūrṇā-kośa; the light of the great jewel wheel ūrṇā-kośa; the light of the sun wheel ūrṇā-kośa; the light of the great sun wheel ūrṇā-kośa.

Light; the light from the hair-tuft of the lunar disc; the light from the hair-tuft of the great lunar disc; the light from the hair-tuft of the palace; the light from the hair-tuft of the great palace;
the light from the hair-tuft of the ocean-clouds; the light from the hair-tuft of the great ocean-clouds.
The mark of the white tuft (ūrṇā-kośa) is one; it is the substance (*tattva*) that gives rise to its function. Its radiance and colors differ, which are the functions of that very substance.

In the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra), the five colors are used as metaphors for the five destinies (*pañca-gati*): blue represents the causes and effects of hell; yellow represents hungry ghosts; red represents animals;

and white represents humans and devas (the asuras are subsumed within these four destinies, though black is omitted). Small-colored images represent the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*), while large-colored [images] represent...

The short physical form illustrates the Bodhisattva of Universal Enlightenment (Samantabhadra); the long physical form illustrates the Bodhisattva of Particular Enlightenment (Pratyekabuddha); and the long and short physical forms together illustrate the cause and fruit of the Buddha.
The opening and closing of these various passages may be adjusted according to one's inclination. In the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, the long and short forms are added;

this is because in the *Lotus Sūtra* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka), the nine realms all return [to the One Vehicle] and the three vehicles are fully integrated. Therefore, the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) cites this passage. Now, regarding Kṣitigarbha’s particular compassion: [End of excerpt]
Because there are the six realms and the three miserable paths, let us take the five realms as an illustration; matters are each specifically assigned.

The light of the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft between the eyebrows) is one of the thirty-two marks. In Sanskrit it is called *śvetavarṇa*; here it is translated as "white," which is the primary color of the West.
White is the fundamental essence and precedes all other colors. White can receive dye and gives rise to the colors of various lights; if one gathers [these],...

That which can be perceived is called "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*); that which blazes like a flame is called "light" (*prabhā*). The *Mahācakra* states: "The white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*) stands between the eyebrows;

its white light surpasses lapis lazuli. Because, while practicing the causal stage of giving, he was able to accord with the intentions of others, thereby giving rise to the causal conditions for sovereign karma (*vaśitā-karma*), and because he further praised and chanted the virtues of dwelling in seclusion, he thus possesses the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, externally complete."
The eight facets are hollow and spiral to the right. The merit of the thirty-two marks increases a thousandfold to form the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa) between the eyebrows.
The merit of this single tuft of hair increases a hundredfold to form the mark of the cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa).
For this reason, the Tathāgata is most supreme and honored. Now, from the very summit of his head, he emits light from the tuft of hair, fully manifesting [his glory].

This is an inconceivable matter. Regarding the term "great," it signifies being even more excellent and sublime than what preceded; hereafter, follow this pattern. ○ Regarding the "Auspicious Hair-Whorl Radiance" (*śrīvatsa-prabhā*):
jade is called "auspicious" (*shui*) because it serves as a token of trust; it is also a "favorable omen" (*xiangruì*). Heaven [bestows it] because the ruler possesses virtue.
I shall grant him many years; I shall grant him the five blessings. First, this is manifested as a token of faith; now it is displayed throughout the six realms.
By riding upon the power of Kṣitigarbha, those in the three miserable paths are purified and ascend, while humans and devas attain Buddhahood.

Therefore, these auspicious signs of the white tuft of light are revealed. ○ Regarding the light of the jade-hair mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*): jade is the refined essence of heaven and earth, possessing the virtue of warmth and moisture. (As the *Wénfù* says: "The mountain has...")

Like jade that becomes more lustrous through polishing, it can be fashioned into a vessel. This represents the five paths of existence: it leaves behind the parching heat of the burning house and increases the moisture of the mountain of its nature;
it emerges from the non-vessels of the three miserable realms and enters the *hu* and *lian* (precious ritual vessels) of the four noble ones.
○ Regarding the purple-hair-mark radiance (*śikhā-lakṣaṇa*), the Sanskrit name is *racā* or *lakṣa*, which translates here as "purple. It is a color between black and red.

This indicates that various classes of sentient beings obtain benefit. The *Zhiguan* states: "Sentient beings receive benefits differently; there are those who receive mixed benefits and those who receive unmixed benefits.
This is precisely what is meant. Regarding the light of the blue-hair mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*), its Sanskrit name is *nīla*, which in this [Chinese] context means "blue."
The East belongs to Wood; it arises from Water. It is dark yet light, and its color is radiant. This represents the black karma of the hells.
From this, vital energy (qi) becomes full and overflowing, causing the branches and twigs of the Bodhi tree to sprout.
○ Regarding the mark of the azure-white hair (ūrṇā-kośa), the *Shuowen* states that it refers to the beautiful blue of stone. The *Zengyun* says it is a deep blue color. This represents the earth.
Those with sharp faculties within the hells are like Devadatta in prison, who experienced joy as if in the third dhyāna;

or like King Ajātaśatru, who entered the *pāṅgu* (ball-beating) hell, entering only briefly before being released. ○ Regarding the light of the red-hair mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*), its Sanskrit name is *aruṇa*, which here means "red.
The south corresponds to fire; its energy is vigorous and bright, taking the great fire as its essence. One should simply observe this subtle red.

It is dark; therefore, it is specifically called "red. "Red" (hóng) consists of the radicals "silk thread" (mì) and "craft" (gōng). This represents the labor and skill of women in spinning, weaving, and sewing. This signifies the realm of animals.
By hearing its name or seeing its image, one immediately gives rise to the mind of awakening and applies oneself to practice; this is the primary cause for being deluded.
It is manifested through this, sharing the same efficacy as the vermilion letter. ○ The green light of the ūrṇā-kośa (hair-treasure): "Green" (lǜ) means clarity.

When looking down at spring water from above, it appears clearly green; it is a color between blue and yellow. It collectively symbolizes that the beings of the hells and the hungry ghosts likewise enter the stream of the Dharma.
○ The golden light of the ūrṇā-kośa: The Sanskrit name is *aineya*; here it is translated as "golden. Gold...
There are five colors; gold is the primary one. It does not change even after being buried for a long time, nor does it become light despite being fired a hundred times.

This symbolizes that although hungry ghosts have been buried in evil realms for a long duration, their Buddha-nature is not lost. When the treasury of the Middle Way is opened, they are suddenly liberated from their hollow emptiness.
**The Auspicious Cloud and the Light of the Ūrṇā:** The *Xijing zaji* states that auspicious clouds are called "auspicious clouds" (*qingyun*) or "splendid clouds" (*jingyun*).

When a cloud displays five colors, it is termed "auspicious" (*qing*) or sometimes "ministerial" (*qing*). This signifies the departure from the afflictions of the five abodes (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) and manifests as an omen of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*).
**The Thousand-spoked Wheel and the Light of the Ūrṇā:** The light of the wheel below this [the thousand-spoked wheel] is even more excellent than the scattered light.

This serves to indicate that it expounds the Perfect Dharma, is intended for those with perfect faculties, enters through the Perfect Gate, and attains the Perfect Benefit. Thus, the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* states:
"The 'wheel' (cakra) is like the light of the full moon; cool, unobstructed, and pervading all of space, it illuminates and touches everything within the realm of non-obstruction.
According to the *Yiyu*, the term "lun" (wheel/line) is explained as "encompassing and surrounding. The *Jingyun* states: "It is by means of this that a vehicle proceeds..."
As for its "revolving," it is because its form is circular; yet its wondrousness lies especially in the emptiness within.

To speak of "a thousand" refers to the hub with a thousand spokes, which manifests the six realms as a single thought-moment and the thousand suchnesses; here, these become manifest, revolving perfectly and without obstruction.
The jeweled wheel and its light rays are the same as above; here, the character "jewel" (pao) is emphasized, as a sutra says: "If a land..."
A member of the Kṣatriya caste, having succeeded to the position of consecrated sovereign, bathed and ascended the throne on the fifteenth day. Suddenly, a precious golden wheel appeared in the east;
its wheel had a thousand spokes, complete with hub and rim, radiating wondrous light as it came to attend upon the king. This certainly signifies a Golden Wheel-turning King.
This represents those who possess the five faculties and are endowed with the roots of goodness, who receive the Dharma from the Earth Store Bodhisattva.
The Water Consecration (abhiṣeka) signifies transcending toward the Perfectly Facing Golden Wheel, as one is about to succeed to the rank of Dharma King.

During this interval, there may be entry into the Iron Wheel, or even up to the Maṇi Wheel; these cannot be definitively fixed. The ray of light from the *ūrṇā* of the Sun Wheel manifests the palace of the Sun Deity (*Sūryadeva*).
"Sun" signifies reality (*satya*). Its radiant brilliance and fullness symbolize that the wisdom-light of the Bodhisattva is impartial.
It is illumination. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Just as the Sun Deity, out of compassion for sentient beings, travels around the four continents together with his palace of seven jewels;

from beginning to end, he never tires or rests. His sunlight shines universally, without hatred or favoritism, illuminating everything according to its height or depth, its profundity or shallowness. The Bodhisattva is also like this: from the first moment of generating the mind..."

He delivers sentient beings without weariness or rest. Having emerged from the world, he dwells in the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and abides in empty space, radiating the light of wisdom to extinguish false views and frivolous discourse (*prapañca*), just as morning dew vanishes upon seeing the sun; such is the case.
The crescent moon and its rays of light manifest the palace of the Moon Deity (*Candradevaputra*). The moon is that which wanes; when it is full, it wanes.

This signifies that the Great Being possesses the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*); thus, he is able to remove the feverish afflictions of the five realms of existence and bestow the coolness of liberation upon the fourfold assembly.

Furthermore, these two wheels specifically represent the Great Being’s two types of wisdom—expedient means (*upāya*) and reality (*bhūta-artha*)—which illuminate the principle and discern the capacities of beings.
Regarding the "palace" and "light from the hair-tip": the light manifests as the palace. The explanation of the "palace" follows the title. As for the "hall" (*diàn*), it refers to the main chamber.
As for its great height: it possesses the marvels of soaring loftiness and towering majesty, manifesting the beauty of brilliant and expansive splendor.

It symbolizes the transcendence of the three realms of suffering into the human and celestial worlds, and reveals that the five paths of existence ultimately converge in the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, it manifests this appearance of sublime height.

The Sea-Cloud Hair-Ray: with clouds of light pervasively covering all, like a sea without bound, this symbolizes that the Buddha and sentient beings are of one essence, the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual, defilement and purity share the same source, and suffering and joy are no different—just as the sea’s limits cannot be measured.

Just as clouds originally possess no discrimination, one thus realizes that it is consciousness that gives rise to discrimination; while phenomena appear distinct and separate, wisdom enters into the oneness of non-duality, such that all things are equal.
This is truly why [the sutra] concludes with "Ocean-like Clouds. △ Second, the Wheel of Speech issues forth sounds to praise the matter.
Having emitted such rays of light from the *ūrṇā-kośa* on the crown of his head, he uttered a subtle and wondrous sound,
addressing the great assembly of devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, humans, and non-humans: "Listen as I today, in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
proclaim and extol the deeds of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha— his benefits for humans and devas, his inconceivable deeds, and his transcendence of the causes of the sages."
Matters: the matter of realizing the ten stages; the matter of never regressing from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The first two phrases conclude what preceded. "Below 'emerging' (*chū-wēi*)," it is the formal address. "Thus" (*rú-shì*) is a term used to point to and praise [the Buddha].
Because the light from the *ūrṇā-kośa* on the Buddha’s crown is supreme and foremost, he points to it and praises it by asking, "Is there such a thing? However, "thus" (*rú*) is a name for...
They are not different; this is called "non-existence of non-being. Thus, both the sentient being and the Buddha equally proceed from the true aspect (dharmatā).
Both right and wrong accord with True Suchness (tathatā). This is the fundamental intent of our Buddha’s entrustment, and the original purpose of the Great Being’s reception of that mandate.
Purity and defilement both enter into a single light; the environment and its inhabitants together become one color. Therefore, the compilers of the sutra describe the inconceivable realm, and...
He sighed, saying, "It is thus. Therefore, we know that the initial emission of light symbolizes the three secrets of the Ultimate Sage;

since preaching the Dharma is the essential means, the light issues from the mouth. This symbolizes that the six realms of existence are destined to achieve the perfect cause and are about to proceed toward the ultimate fruit;

since realization and entry [into the truth] are the essential means, the light is emitted from the crown of the head. While the lights are similar in appearance, their respective significances each have their own specific destination.
The "great assembly" is the general term; "devas, nāgas, and so forth" are the specific ones. All are the recipients of this address.

As for those who listen to me, it is not only because the matter concerns profound depths and the transformation of beings from beginning to end, but furthermore, as I entrust this to humans and devas for the future, it is by no means an ordinary or minor affair.
You must listen with single-minded devotion to understand my immeasurable majestic power over humanity.
The "Chapter on the Conclusion of the Name" concerns matters such as the benefits [of reciting the name], for by chanting the name and reading the sutra, both humans and devas attain liberation.
The "Chapter on the Conclusion of the Substance" concerns inconceivable matters; however, while substance belongs to principle (*li*), why does it here point to phenomena?

One should know that what is relied upon from beginning to end possesses both delusion and awakening simultaneously; it is the phenomenon that is itself the principle. Therefore, it alone is appropriate [to be the subject].

The "Inconceivable Matters" section consists of two phrases that transcend the mundane. The "Establishing the Doctrine" chapter concludes with the phrase "the doctrine necessarily establishes both cause and effect," because the doctrine must necessarily bring about the simultaneous fulfillment of both.
The "Non-retrogression from Bodhi" section concludes the "Function" chapter; it is because Kṣitigarbha skillfully employs expedient means to cause beings to achieve bodhi.

If one follows the fourfold structure of the *Lotus Sūtra*: first, the initial phrase praises the teaching; second, the establishment of the teaching is intended for those of appropriate capacity, as humans and devas thereby obtain benefits. Next...

The first three phrases praise the unity of principle; it is because all things are replete with principle that they can subsequently function as phenomena. The third and fourth phrases praise the benefit of practice;
for practice must transcend causes in order to be able to realize the fruit. The fifth phrase praises the person:

having attained ultimate bodhi, one is the foremost person in both the mundane and supramundane realms. All these are called "phenomena" (or "matters") because they accord with the Tathāgata of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It is for the sake of the one great cause and condition that [the Buddha] appears in the world.

Indeed, whether mundane or supramundane, internal or external, good or evil, great or small, sage or ordinary person—there is not one who does not engage in their respective affairs; it is only that their modes of operation differ.

This is like the lute, the zither, and the harp: their tones and melodies are similar, yet the players and pluckers are different. Nevertheless, if we examine the meaning of the concluding eulogy, [it becomes clear].
It appears that all [the preceding sections] refer to what follows. Why is this? It is because the matters inquired about by Avalokiteśvara are entirely different from those before;

they specifically reveal the wondrousness of the four chapters, which permeates both the preceding and the following. By using what follows to illustrate what precedes, the profound intent is further clarified.

One must not judge the former as inferior and the latter as superior, thereby losing the essential point by following the literal text alone. △ Second: Avalokiteśvara requests the teaching for the sake of its circulation.

II. The Initial Request Made by the Appropriate Audience. This section has two parts: first, the naming and description of the ritual protocol by the sūtra’s narrator; second, the praise and permission granted by the Tathāgatas. Regarding the first part, it has two sub-sections:

first, the naming and description of the ritual protocol by the sūtra’s narrator. At the time this speech was being delivered, there was in the assembly a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva named Avalokiteśvara, who rose from his seat...
Rise. Kneel with your right knee on the ground and join your palms.
This is the wondrous resonance of the guest and host striking one another, the mutual response between teacher and disciple in their call-and-response.

It was for this reason that the World-Honored One, addressing the assembly, offered a concluding eulogy; his intention was to initiate the praise of the Avalokiteśvara Vehicle and to proceed with inquiry. Therefore, the Buddha spoke thus.

When these words were spoken, Avalokiteśvara immediately rose and addressed the Buddha: "This is what is meant by 'the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching. In the Western language [Sanskrit], his name is *Avalokiteśvara*;

here it is translated as "Observer of the Sounds of the World. "Observation" (*avalokita*) refers to the wisdom that observes, which illuminates the true nature through the three types of wisdom and examines both the fundamental and the derivative.
"Sounds of the World" (*īśvara*) refers to the objects of observation—the myriad phenomena that are distinct and manifold.

They are distinct. Though their sounds differ, the Bodhisattva’s vast compassion causes all to be liberated from suffering. Because the object and wisdom are unified in his manifestation, he is named Avalokiteśvara (The One Who Observes the Sounds of the World).

[In the country of Malakūṭa, on the southernmost coast of India, there is Mount Potalaka in the great ocean to the south. Therein lies a stone celestial palace, the permanent abode of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.]
△ Section Two: The Two Great Beings Expressing Praise and Requesting the Teaching. This has three parts. First, expressing praise for the merits previously described, which further has two parts.
First, describing the majestic spiritual power of Kṣitigarbha.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha is endowed with great compassion and takes pity upon those who have committed offenses.”
For the sake of suffering sentient beings, he manifests thousands of millions of billions of bodies throughout thousands of millions of billions of worlds;
such are his merits and his inconceivable power of majestic spiritual authority.
The World-Honored One wished to extol various matters. Avalokiteśvara opened his mouth and immediately asked about their origins;

thus one knows that both the questions and the answers do not go beyond these. Yet, it was necessary to rely upon Avalokiteśvara because they shared the same aspirations and both possessed great karmic affinities with Jambudvīpa.
This is just as when [the Buddha] praised Kṣitigarbha for possessing great compassion.
Even up to his inconceivable spiritual powers—these too are merely the actual manifestations of Avalokiteśvara.
According to the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he was formerly the eldest crown prince of King Araṇemin, named Akṣobhya.
Having been exhorted by the brahmin Ratnākara, he subsequently made a great vow; thus the Buddha Ratnagarbha said: "You behold the devas and humans, as well as those in the three evil realms..."

Seeing all sentient beings, you have given rise to great compassion, desiring to sever the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings, desiring to sever the various defilements of sentient beings, and desiring to cause sentient beings to abide in peace and happiness. Therefore, I shall now name you Avalokiteśvara.
When you were practicing the bodhisattva path, you already possessed hundreds of thousands of immeasurable billions of nayutas [of followers].
Sentient beings shall be freed from suffering and affliction. When you were a bodhisattva, you were already able to perform great Buddha-works (and so forth).

Because their virtuous deeds are equal [to his], they are then able to give rise [to the aspiration]; therefore, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) is invoked to respond to the occasion and submit the request.
△ Second, the description of the praise of the virtues by all Buddhas:
I have heard that the World-Honored One, together with immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, with one voice and in unison, praised the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, saying:
"Even if all Buddhas of the past, present, and future were to speak of his merits, they could not exhaust them."
The words of praise uttered by all Buddhas contain the meaning but not the explicit text. There are two aspects to this meaning.
The remote sense refers to the occasion when the Buddha was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the abode of the various Ṛṣis and Munis, where he extensively offered praise during a great assembly;

this is the first. The proximate sense refers to the occasion when the Buddha was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven palace, where the Buddhas of the ten directions gathered together and [divided the teaching].

The Earth Store Bodhisattva appeared together with Śākyamuni. Precisely at the time when Śākyamuni was extolling the various deeds of Earth Store, how could one know that the Buddhas of the ten directions were not likewise praising him?
This is second. For what reason do even the Buddhas of the three periods of time fail to exhaustively describe his merits?
It is because the mountain of Earth Store’s practice rises higher than Mount Sumeru, and the ocean of his vows is deeper than the vast abyss.
How much more so for wisdom and supernatural powers, all of which are inconceivable; how could they ever be measured? △ Second, the description of the benefit of what he now wishes to praise:
Previously, I was further graced by the World-Honored One’s universal proclamation to the great assembly, expressing his desire to extol the benefits and other matters concerning Kṣitigarbha.
The "former" fingers also have both distant and proximate meanings. The distant refers to the text at the beginning of the "Chapter on Praise" (Pūjā-parivarta);
the proximate refers to the events following the emission of light, when [the Buddha] addressed the assembly. △ Third, the formal request to extol his virtues for the sake of the multitude.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for the sake of all sentient beings of the present and future, extol the inconceivable deeds of Kṣitigarbha,
so that the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, may gaze upon him, pay homage, and obtain blessings.
This clarifies the intent behind extolling Kṣitigarbha: it is precisely for the sake of the eight classes of devas and nāgas, who obtain blessings through beholding and paying homage.
This is because all sentient beings are delusively attached to the notions of self and person; arrogance has become their nature, and they have been shrouded in ignorance for kalpas.

Failing to recognize the Triple Gem, they follow the current of folly and stupidity, rarely encountering the Ten Sages. How could they know that life is like a candle in the wind, difficult to preserve?
This sojourn is like a spark on a stone; how could it endure for long? Moreover, the five turbidities encroach from all sides, and the four snakes constantly press upon us.

Without paying homage to the Triple Gem, it is difficult to cross the four currents. Therefore, the practitioner must always maintain mindfulness and not allow themselves to fall into negligence, fearing that impermanence may arrive suddenly, leaving no way to pay homage.
It is like a mouse entering a horn; when the path is at an end, where can one go?

Therefore, a verse by the Buddha says: "Life is like a lamp in the wind; one knows not the moment of its extinction. From today until tomorrow, one fails to realize that the wheel of death has arrived.
Enveloped in darkness, one follows the conditions of karma, unaware of which realm one shall be reborn. How much more so when beholding and paying homage to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas:
at such times, one extinguishes the sins of immeasurable births and deaths and accumulates the merit of hundreds of thousands of virtuous conditions.
As stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*: "There are five merits in paying homage to the Buddha: first, physical beauty; second, obtaining a wondrous voice;
third, possessing abundant wealth; fourth, being born into a noble and high-ranking family; and fifth, being reborn in the heavens.

Therefore, when humans and devas gaze upon and pay homage to Kṣitigarbha, they naturally obtain blessings. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s praise and approval, in four parts: First, praising his virtues (in two parts). [End of section]
Praising the merit of those with whom he shares a karmic affinity in the Sahā world, the Buddha said to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "In the Sahā world, you possess great causal conditions.
Whether they be devas, nāgas, men, women, spirits, ghosts, or even sentient beings of the six realms suffering from the retribution of their sins—whosoever hears your name..."
Those who see your form, those who yearn for you, and those who praise you—all such sentient beings will certainly never regress from the unsurpassed path.
They shall constantly be born among humans and devas, fully experiencing sublime bliss. When cause and effect reach maturity, they will encounter a Buddha and receive a prophecy of enlightenment.

First is the general praise. If one were to praise it specifically, it would indicate that [the Buddha] has a karmic affinity with the Sahā world; thus, his spiritual resonance is particularly suited to this realm.

Nevertheless, in the transformative activities of a Great Being, there is no land where he does not appear. As for "great causes and conditions," this refers to the generation and supportive accomplishment [of enlightenment], which possesses inconceivable and supreme merit.
As the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* states: "A virtuous friend is a great cause and condition. Regarding this...

This means transforming and guiding sentient beings so that they may attain the vision of the Buddha. As stated in the *Akṣayamati-paripṛcchā-sūtra*: "By what causes and conditions is he named Avalokiteśvara?
The Buddha answered by explaining the matter through the seven calamities and two requests. The *Bie xing shu* (Separate Commentary) states:

"The causes and conditions are exceedingly numerous; here we speak briefly of object and wisdom. If we consider sentient beings, then the two types of stimuli—good and evil—serve as the cause. As for the Sage..."

With spiritual wisdom and compassion as the conditions (*pratyaya*): if one considers the perspective of the Sage, contemplative wisdom and compassion are the cause (*hetu*), while the karmic resonance of sentient beings is the condition.
This, in essence, does not transcend the four *siddhāntas* (the four levels of truth) [and so forth].
In the "Separate Praise," it is stated that through the three pairs and six types of karmic capacities, as well as the transgressions and blessings of the six realms...

This is to manifest the great causes and conditions. "Heavenly beings" and "dragon spirits" form one pair of the upper and lower realms; "men" and "women" form another pair of the internal and external;

"gods" and "ghosts" form yet another pair of the hidden and the manifest. The intermediate classes—the Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas, as well as the two assemblies of the ordained and the laity, along with the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas—are omitted;
hence the phrase "up to and including. Nevertheless, heaven and dragons are singled out for mention.

[The phrase] "and so forth" refers to the fact that all beings possess birth, old age, sickness, and death. "Hearing the name and so forth" refers to hearing the name and seeing the body as described in the Universal Gate Chapter (*Pumenpin*);

these can extinguish the sufferings of all realms of existence (*bhava*). As for those who feel longing and yearning, because the Great Being possesses majestic spiritual power (*vibhūti*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and bestows fearlessness (*abhaya*), he causes all living beings to feel affectionate attachment and deep yearning. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "They rejoice and desire to see [him]."
To remember [the Buddha] without forgetting and to give rise to a heart of longing and devotion—this is it. When such longing is unceasing, one then offers praise;
yet the power of his majestic spiritual authority is such that praise can never exhaust it. Examining the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Pumen pin*) below, the efficacy and verification are clarified:

having received these benefits, one will ultimately attain Buddhahood. Although he manifests bodies in response to sentient beings, appearing in the various distinctions of the forty-eight [forms], his teaching...
The Dharma adapts to the capacities of beings and is divided into nineteen distinct categories. However, the fundamental intention of the Mahāsattva lies in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By stating that he is constantly reborn among humans and devas and so forth, it clarifies that until he attains the Buddha-way, he will ultimately never fall into the evil realms.

Receiving joy among humans and devas, he cultivates and accumulates wholesome causes; when these causes are perfected and the fruit ripens, he encounters a Buddha who bestows upon him a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). All of these constitute the great causes.

This is because it concerns the causal conditions of phenomena. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to know the causes and conditions of all dharmas, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Consequently, although they universally deliver sentient beings and lead them into the realm of nirvāṇa, they are like a master illusionist delivering his illusory disciples;
both parties are free from attachment and have severed all views. △ Second, praising the audience for proclaiming the teachings of Kṣitigarbha.
Virtuous One,
you now possess great compassion and pity for sentient beings, as well as the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas.
Please listen as I proclaim the inconceivable benefits of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.

The first three phrases correctly point out the benefit of being able to hear and proclaim [the Dharma]. This should be cited in full from the *Bie xing shu* (Commentary on the Separate Practice), in the passage concerning "Universal Compassion":
"When the Great Being sees any sentient beings suffering, he gives rise to great compassion, causing the sprout of Bodhi to grow.
Therefore, it is said: through the invocation of the three karmas, one receives the sprout of liberation from suffering; the Four Great Vows serve as...
I vow that you shall be moistened by the supreme bliss; this is precisely the True Body (dharmakāya) extracting suffering and the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya) bestowing bliss.

Why then do you say, "Now possessed"? It is solely out of compassion for future sentient beings, so that they may specifically hear the proclamation of the benefits of Kṣitigarbha, that I have pointed to your words "now" and "you. △ Third, the admonition to listen.
"You should listen attentively; I shall now speak of it.
△ Third, the request to hear:
Avalokiteśvara said, "Indeed, World-Honored One, I wish most earnestly to hear it."
All is as stated in the text. △ Fourth, the formal address, which has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part [the prose] is further divided into three sections.

First, the specific demonstration of inconceivable matters, which consists of eight segments. From the first, the transformation of the signs of decline among devas and humans, up to the eighth, the settling of dangerous paths for those on land and water—each is termed "inconceivable" because these are the profound spheres of practice of the Great Being (Mahāsattva).
This flows forth from the nature. Now, for the first part, there are two sections; first, the manifestation of the five signs of decay.

The Buddha addressed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "In future and present worlds, there are devas and humans whose celestial merit is exhausted and who manifest the five signs of decay; some among them fall into the evil realms."
The various devas of the three realms each ride upon their past karma. Those whose past merit is profound and substantial advance toward the ranks of the noble ones;
those whose prior merit is meager and inferior are still dragged away by evil karma. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:

"Although there are no great sufferings or afflictions in the heavens, because their bodies are soft, supple, and delicate, when they behold the five signs of decay, they undergo extreme suffering equal to that of the hells."
The distinction is as follows: it is like honey mixed with poison, sweet at first but bitter in the end.

According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, when the lives of various devas come to an end, two kinds of fivefold signs of decay (*pañca-vyasanāni*) appear beforehand: the minor and the major. As for the five minor signs of decay:

first, an unpleasant sound issues from the body; second, the bodily radiance becomes faint and dim; third, bathing water adheres to the body; fourth, one cannot relinquish attachment to sensory objects; fifth, [the eyes blink].
The body becomes emaciated and the eyes blink frequently. As for the five great signs of decline: first, one's clothing becomes soiled; second, the radiance of the flower crown withers;
third, sweat flows from both armpits; fourth, a foul odor arises from the body; fifth, one finds no pleasure in one’s own seat.

When these minor signs appear, if one does not take refuge and seek protection, and the five great signs of decline manifest, one will certainly die and fall from the celestial realm. *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*.

It is said: "When karma is exhausted, one harbors sorrow and distress; one abandons all celestial maidens. At the time of falling away, there is great suffering and affliction that cannot be illustrated by any analogy.
Therefore, one must seek refuge. Or there are those who fall into the evil realms, descending into the five destinies according to the power of their karma.
As the *Sūtra on the Subjugation of Arhats* states: "Formerly, in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there was a deva whose lifespan was about to end."

There are seven kinds of omens that appear: the light fades, the flowers wither, the complexion changes, dust settles on the robes, sweat breaks out from the armpits, the body becomes emaciated, and one leaves one’s original seat.
Then, one reflects for oneself: "My life has ended and I shall be reborn below in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, as a pig within the womb of a mangy sow.
This is precisely such an example. △ Second, the transformation of what is seen and heard; first, showing the increase of the heavens.
Merit. Thus, when these gods and humans—whether male or female—behold such signs, they may see the image of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha or hear the name of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha;
by looking upon him even once or prostrating before him, the celestial merit of all these gods and humans shall further increase, and they shall receive [its fruits].
Great happiness! One shall never fall into the retribution of the three evil realms.

Initially, as a cause for cultivation, one displays signs of fear; when small or great signs of decline appear for men, women, devas, and others, if they see an image of Kṣitigarbha or hear the name of the Great Being, their body and mind will both be moved, and they will all arrive to gaze upon and pay homage to him, thereby attaining supreme merit.
Once cultivation has begun, the signs of decline are extinguished. This section clarifies the transformation of retribution and the increase of merit.
For example, when Śakra, Lord of the Devas, suddenly perceived signs of both minor and major decline, fear arose in his mind and he thought:
"Who can save me from such calamity? To whom shall I take refuge? He then realized that, apart from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, there was no one capable of providing protection. Immediately...
He went to the Buddha’s dwelling and, seeking compassion, entreated him for deliverance. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he immediately attained the vision of the Truths (satyadarśana).
His signs of decay vanished all at once, and filled with joy and exultation, he spoke these verses of affectionate words: "O Great Sage, you should know:
even upon this very seat, I have regained my celestial life-span. I pray only that the World-Honored One will remember me as I now gaze upon Kṣitigarbha."
"Rituals (li) cause decline to transform into the increase of merit; it is just like this. (According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, they cause those devas to increase five blessings:

first, the lifespan of devas; second, the beauty of devas; third, the fame of devas; fourth, the pleasure of devas; fifth, the majestic power of devas). As for 'never falling into the evil realms,' it is like the aforementioned deva who had been a pig.
Distressed and suffering, he did not know what to do. The other devas said to him: 'Only the Buddha can deliver you from your transgression. Thereupon, he went to the Buddha."
He prostrated and posed his question. The Buddha said, "If you wish to escape this pig's body, you must constantly recite the Three Refuges.
The deva immediately took refuge. Seven days later, he was reborn in Vaiśālī as the son of a householder. As soon as he was born and fell to the ground—
He also knelt and took the Three Refuges. When he was nearly seven years old, while playing by the side of the road, he encountered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.

The boy paid his respects to them and invited the Buddha to his home. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him; the boy, along with his parents and kinsmen, all attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression).
Viewed in this light, if one gazes upon and pays homage to Kṣitigarbha, how could it merely prevent one from falling into the evil realms? It is also [the cause for attaining non-retrogression].
One is able to enter the stages of the noble ones instantaneously; thus we know that the power of repentance can bring about the bliss of both body and mind.
△ Second, how much more so regarding the benefits of making offerings:
how much more so when one sees or hears of Bodhisattvas making offerings of various incenses, flowers, clothing, food and drink, precious gems, and necklaces?
The merit and benefits obtained from making offerings are immeasurable and boundless.
Merely by seeing the image or hearing the name, and by single-mindedly performing acts of veneration, one increases in merit, experiences happiness, and does not fall into the evil realms;
how much more so for those who see and hear [the teachings] and further extend their offerings? Therefore, the merit and blessings obtained are immeasurable and boundless. As it is said:
In the *Maitreyaparipṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra*, it is asked: "What is the fruit of giving? The answer is:

"There is one kind of fruit for giving, namely, the fruit of enjoyment (*paribhogaphala*). Furthermore, there are two kinds of fruits, namely, the fruit experienced in the present (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīyaphala*)."
Regarding the future reception of fruits, there are again three kinds of fruits; namely, these two kinds plus *prajñā*.
Having now obtained merit and virtue, which is precisely in accord with *prajñā*, it is therefore like empty space, being without limit or measure.
△ Second, the transformation of evil karma at the time of death, in two parts: first, hearing the name at the time of death and escaping suffering.
Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara, if in future or present worlds, sentient beings of the six realms, at the time of their death,

should hear the name of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha such that it passes through their faculty of hearing even once, these sentient beings shall never again experience the sufferings of the three evil paths.
△ Second, the transformation of the reward through clay statues of the retinue. Part one: The causes for creating the clay statues.
How much more so at the time of death! When parents and kinsmen take the house, wealth, treasures, and clothing of the dying person and fashion clay or painted images of Kṣitigarbha;
△ Second, the manifestation of the two [types of karma] before they have been repaid: First, regarding the patient’s knowledge of the cause.

Either the patient themselves, or someone acting on their behalf, while still alive and before the end of life, sees or hears with their eyes and ears that the relatives and associates are using the house, treasures, and other assets to fashion or paint an image of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva for the sake of the deceased.
All is as previously stated. △ Second, receiving the merit and transforming it: First, the immediate recovery from serious illness and the increase of lifespan.
If this person is one whose karmic retribution would otherwise entail suffering from a serious illness, by virtue of this merit, the illness is immediately cured and their lifespan is increased.
For what reason must one perform offerings and fashion images at the site of the Earth Store (Kṣitigarbha) for the sake of the sick? It is because this can cure illness and prolong life.
The *Zhiguan* states: "One fears the evil realms; human life is impermanent. With a single breath not followed, one departs forever for a thousand years.
The path to the underworld is vast and distant, and there are no provisions for the journey. The sea of suffering is deep and wide; where can a boat or raft be moored? [Year...]
As the matter gradually recedes, the "wind-sword" (the agony of death) will not spare you; how could you afford to remain complacent while awaiting such bitter suffering?
It is like a jackal that has lost its ears, tail, and teeth, feigning sleep in hopes of escaping [its fate] (and so forth). Therefore, one should cultivate merit to eliminate calamities immediately;
this will surely cure the illness and further extend one's longevity. It is comparable to taking the "five stones" elixir: not only does it stop the disease from worsening, but one also attains...
The body is filled [with merit]. △ Second, the exhaustion of life ends obstacles and leads to birth in the heavens.

If such a person’s karmic retribution has reached the end of their lifespan, and they should have all manner of transgressions and karmic obstructions that would otherwise cause them to fall into the evil realms, by virtue of this merit, after the end of their life, they will immediately be born among humans or devas, experiencing supreme and wondrous bliss. All transgressions...
All hindrances are completely extinguished.

As for those whose karmic retribution has exhausted their lifespan, it is because both their merit and their life-force have been exhausted. Nevertheless, although both merit and life-force are exhausted, the cultivation of meritorious deeds did not falter;
therefore, they must have incurred the karmic obstacles of the five heinous crimes and the karmic obstacles of the ten evil acts, and thus should fall [into the lower realms].
Those suffering in the evil realms, by virtue of the merit from inheriting and selling a house to have an image cast, will immediately be reborn among humans or devas to experience happiness;
furthermore, both their prior karmic offenses and the two hindrances will be entirely extinguished without remainder. As the Great Sūtra records, Jīvaka said to King Ajātaśatru:
"Cultivating a single virtuous thought can destroy a million kinds of evils, just as a small vajra can shatter Mount Sumeru."
Furthermore, it is like a small fire that can burn everything, or like a small amount of poison that can harm sentient beings;
so too is even a small good deed capable of destroying great evil. Although it is called "small good," its reality is actually great. For this reason, one must perform repentance.
If a person can do this, they will provide virtuous support for their posthumous blessings. △ Third, showing the rebirth of those who have passed away.
In the second section on realms, the matters of recollection are first described.
Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, if in a future age there are men or women who, at the time of nursing, [should hear this...]
Or those who, at three, five, or ten years of age or younger, have lost their parents,
or even lost their brothers and sisters— once these people have grown up, they long for their parents and kinsmen, not knowing in which realm they have fallen,
in which world they have been born, or in which heaven they dwell.
Regarding the period of nursing: this refers to an infant in its swaddling clothes. "Milk" (nu) refers to the fluid from the breast, which is a fleshy sac.

The fluid drunk by the child is transformed from the mother's blood. Before the child is born, it exists within the body as blood; once born, the blood rises upward and becomes milk. The *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Five Paths* states:
"By the time a child reaches three years of age, they have consumed a total of one hundred and eighty *hu* of milk."

(Three *sheng* of antiquity are equivalent to one *sheng* of the present). Excluding the portion of blood consumed while in the womb. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Pu" means to chew; it is composed of the radical 口 (mouth).

Just as the sound [of the child] is made, the mother chews food and gives it to him. As the *Yìlín* says: "The crow and the sparrow eat grain; opening their mouths, they receive nourishment. The *Yìyǎ* states:
"When a small child’s breath is labored, it is called *bù*. *Bù* means 'dew. When one is fed while chilled by dew, the milk-food is not digested, and this illness arises.
Nowadays, when adults eat too much and contract cold, a sour, rancid stench like that of *bù* arises in the chest.

It is so. From the time of nursing until the third year of life, although one loses one's parents and the circumstances before and after differ, there is no difference in the fact that one is ignorant of their size.
Once one has grown older and begins to reflect upon them, this is the innate goodness of a filial son, which cannot be suppressed.
The *Fan dong jing* (Brahmajāla-sūtra) says: "My body’s four great elements and six sense bases were born from my parents; [they provided] milk..."
They nourish and raise us, providing food and clothing until we grow up, caressing and protecting us throughout our lives.
Yet, there are those who never once contemplate from where their bodies have come, nor the arduous toil of those who nurtured them.

Should one not reflect upon the lamb that kneels to suckle its mother, the compassionate crow that regurgitates food for its parents, or the fledgling sparrow that steals grain and, when caught by a hawk, remembers its mother and endures hunger? How can a human being fail to surpass these creatures?
Are they birds or beasts? That which I now contemplate is that I do not know in which realm my kinsmen have fallen;

their ascent or descent is unfathomable. I do not know in which world they have been born; whether they are in the central or peripheral regions is difficult to determine. I do not know in which heaven they have been reborn;
whether they are in the state of form or formlessness is beyond my knowledge. Therefore, whether awake or asleep, I think of them, desiring only to know their destiny. II.2.

Demonstrating the Merit of Cultivating Reverence (Part Three): First, the liberation of those who have passed away; second, a full account of the realms of rebirth; third, the attainment of wondrous rewards in the present life.
Regarding the first, there are two further sections: first, cultivating superior causes.
If such a person can mold or paint an image of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, or even hear his name, and offer a single gaze or a single prostration—
From one day to seven days, do not retreat from your original resolve. Upon hearing the name or seeing the form, gaze upon it with reverence and offer worship;
do not retreat from your original resolve. A single awakening is the most essential admonition.

Among the people of this age, those who choose the good and hold fast to it—I long for them every morning, yet have not yet met them. As for those who cultivate merit, they may initially desire to do much, but in the end...
[The number] decreases. Those who study the Way advance with vigor at the beginning, but later become indolent and weary. As it is said:
"There are none who do not have a beginning, yet few are able to reach the end. Only the sages possess both the beginning and the conclusion. Therefore, a sutra says:
"The seeds of fish and the flowers of the mango—these three things are abundant during the causal stage, yet when the fruit ripens, they are few."

The admonition that their initial resolve must not regress is profoundly significant. △ Second, obtaining the retribution of happiness, in two parts: First, those who have fallen into evil realms are liberated.
These are the person’s kinsmen.
Because they rely on the causal conditions of karma, those who had fallen into evil realms—calculating by the number of kalpas—are now sustained by these sons and daughters.
Brothers and sisters, by molding or painting images of Kṣitigarbha and performing the merit of gazing upon and worshipping them, one shall immediately attain liberation.

Regarding the "three provisional designations" (tri-vidhā saṃvṛti)—provisional designation as cause-and-effect (*hetu-saṃvṛti*), provisional designation as continuity (*santati-saṃvṛti*), and provisional designation as mutual dependence (*apekṣā-saṃvṛti*)—they are called "provisional" because they are empty, false, and unreal.
As the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "Provisional designation as cause-and-effect refers to external objects and internal faculties; provisional designation as continuity refers only to..."

Regarding the internal faculties, they depend upon one another: vertically, they depend on the non-existence of cessation; horizontally, they depend on the non-existence of the three unconditioned states.
For all ordinary beings who have not yet ascended to the Noble Path, even the slightest arising of conceptual calculation is entirely a "view.

Because these views exist, the three provisional aggregates, suffering, and its origin follow along with afflictions; karmic bonds spread like weeds, and the cycle of birth and death becomes vast and boundless. Therefore, it is said:
