They fall into the evil destinies; "calculating the number of kalpas" refers to the fact that these kinsmen receive birth due to their karma.
"Relying on this [merit] below" means ascending by virtue of blessings. "Immediately attaining liberation" is because their faculties respond swiftly, and their benefit is swift.

For example, when parents cherish their children with deep affection, possessing abundant wisdom and wealth as well as great power, they are able to rescue them immediately from any peril into which their children have fallen.
Now, the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha possesses a profound heart of compassion, deep mastery of both provisional and ultimate wisdom, an abundance of the noble riches, and sovereign spiritual powers;
thus, whenever any of his kinsmen fall into the evil realms, he delivers them instantly.
They are liberated. △ Second, regarding those born among humans and devas as increasing the causes:

those who are born among humans and devas and experience supreme, wondrous bliss do so by virtue of this merit, which further increases their noble causes and leads them to receive immeasurable happiness.

An ancient worthy said: "Those who have already been born into the good realms should increase their meritorious achievements; those who have not yet escaped the wheel of suffering should be born early into the Pure Land.
This is the intended meaning of these two passages. By further increasing one's holy causes, one enters the stages of the Three Vehicles and receives supramundane bliss.
As stated in the *Ekottara Āgama*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Ordinary people do not perform meritorious deeds."
If one does not receive the four types of offerings and yet cannot avoid the suffering of the three evil realms, this is called "neither body nor mind being at ease.
An Arhat who cultivates merit receives the four types of offerings without any lack or deficiency, and furthermore avoids the suffering of the three evil realms;
this is called "both body and mind being at ease. Now that you have increased your noble causes, you shall experience both body and mind at ease.
△ Second, the complete account of the realm of birth, in two parts. First, the manifestation of the Bodhisattva’s body upon the initial thought.
This person can further, for a period of twenty-one days, single-mindedly gaze upon and pay homage to the image of Kṣitigarbha and recite his name.
Upon completing ten thousand recitations, one shall attain the Bodhisattva’s manifestation of boundless bodies. One should inform this person’s kinsmen and the realm of sentient beings;

beyond merely fashioning an image for veneration, one must exert oneself with utmost sincerity and single-mindedly invoke the name. Internally, one should be diligent in reverence, inclining the heart with utmost devotion.
Thus, the Bodhisattva will swiftly manifest before one. As it is said: "The Bodhisattva is like the cool moon, constantly traversing ultimate emptiness. For sentient beings..."
When the water of the mind is pure, the reflection of Bodhi appears within it; thus, there is no discrepancy between the response and the stimulus. Question:

There are those today who, despite many years of practice, have not attained even a fraction of efficacy. Why is this? Answer: One must understand that the single mind possesses both the phenomenal (shī) and the noumenal (lǐ).

If neither of these two paths is grasped, how can one move the sages? It is like facing a mirror while looking behind oneself, or shouting into a valley while swallowing one's voice; how could such actions produce a result?

As for the influence [of this practice], regarding the "Boundless Body" (Anantagātra): from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*), the boundless is itself the boundary; from the perspective of principle (*li*), the boundary is itself the boundless.
Now, by means of the single mind that unifies the acts of prostrating to the image and reciting the name, one enters into the single mind of the principle that is as boundless as empty space.
It is like an empty valley responding to an echo, or a clear mirror manifesting a form; thus, the Boundless One appears.
He personally informs them of the realm in which they have been born. △ Second, the deity leads them to see their kinsmen.
Or, within a dream, the Bodhisattva manifests great supernormal powers and personally leads this person to various worlds, where they behold their kinsmen.

The above illustrates the manifest capacity (*karana*) and the manifest response (*pratividhāna*); thus, at the moment of invocation and prostration, he manifests his body to inform [the practitioner] of his realm.
This belongs to the hidden capacity and the hidden response; therefore, he informs [the practitioner] within a dream.

This is identical to the case in the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, where a deva appears in a dream; it is indeed a true dream. However, one must understand that matters concerning good and evil, or ordinary beings and sages, are all nothing but dreams.
Initially, because those who encountered people in their dreams did not know the realms where their dream-families were born, they fashioned dream-images of Kṣitigarbha.

By gazing upon and paying homage to these images while dreaming and calling his name, he would manifest his form within the dream to inform them of their destinies. Therefore it is said: "Exert yourself as if in a dream;

when delusive names are severed, look back upon the world and see that all things are but events within a dream. Only the great awakening is luminous and clear—this is called 'awakening from the great dream.'"
△ Third, one obtains a wondrous reward in the present life.

Furthermore, if one can recite the Bodhisattva’s name a thousand times every day for a period of a thousand days, that person shall receive the protection of the spirits of the local land dispatched by the Bodhisattva for their entire life.
In this world, their food and clothing will be abundant and increased, and they will be free from all illnesses.

Suffering; even calamities shall not enter their door, let alone afflict their person. Such people will ultimately receive the Bodhisattva’s hand upon the head and the bestowal of a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Since the causes cultivated herein are superior, the fruits realized are likewise superior; this is vastly different from what preceded. [The spirits of the land...]
The deities are those who preside over soil and grain and protect the people; there are also those who protect dwellings and protect individuals.

Now, may they all provide eternal protection for one’s person, so that in the present one obtains three joys and in the future receives a sublime prediction. First, when food and clothing are abundant and beneficial, both the elderly and the young shall enjoy peace and security.
Second, being free from all illness and suffering, body and mind shall be harmonious and well-adjusted. Third, all untimely deaths are severed.
As for these matters, they will abide in tranquility. This is the retribution experienced by people in the present world; such matters are still minor.

When that person ultimately receives the Bodhisattva’s consolation through the touching of their crown and is personally granted a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), then the true cause will be realized and the wondrous fruit will be attained.
There will be nothing—whether mundane or supramundane—that is not accomplished. Their majestic power and benefits will be such as this.
This is it. △ Four: Accomplishing the Deliverance of Sentient Beings and Realizing the Fruit. Part One: Describing the Arising of the Mind to Deliver People.

Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, if in future ages there are good men or good women who wish to give rise to a vast mind of compassion to rescue and deliver all sentient beings; who wish to cultivate unsurpassed bodhi; who wish to emerge...
To be detached from the three realms is the mind of a great bodhisattva. Because they practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to give rise to the aspiration to deliver sentient beings.

Although compassion is inherently present, in the past they were attached to the notions of self and person, and thus distinguished between "self" and "other. Now, they know that all are of one essence.
Therefore, one arouses an impartial mind. Because of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one contemplates that sentient beings obtain happiness and also bestows upon them the causes of happiness.

Because of great compassion (*karuṇā*), one takes pity on sentient beings who undergo suffering and also delivers them from the realm of suffering. Hence, it is said that one "rescues and delivers all sentient beings."
To universally take the Dharma-realm as one's object is called "vast"; to universally deliver the deluded multitudes is called "great.

Those who wish to cultivate unsurpassed Bodhi—this clarifies seeking the Buddha-fruit for oneself—correctly employ śamatha and vipaśyanā to investigate the four noble truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Realizing that one’s own dharma-nature is non-dual and indistinguishable from all phenomena, they seek enlightenment above and transform beings below, thereby giving rise to the bodhicitta. [They] depart from the three...

Regarding the "realms" (*dhātu*): this refers to the first through seventh stages of faith in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), wherein the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) are first eliminated, and one departs forever from the wheel of suffering within the three realms.
△ Second, explaining the cultivation of causes to fulfill vows.
If these people see the image of Kṣitigarbha or hear his name, and take refuge in him with a sincere heart, or offer incense, flowers, clothing,
precious gems, food, and drink, and pay him homage, then the aspirations of these good men and women shall be swiftly fulfilled.
There shall be eternal freedom from obstacles.
The text is divided into three sections: first, seeing, hearing, and taking refuge; second, "or" and so forth, making offerings with utmost sincerity;
third, "this is virtuous" and so forth, the fulfillment of the aspiration. According to the preceding text, generating the bodhicitta is the matter of the superior *siddhi*.
It is as stated in the Susiddhikara Sūtra: "It can cause various siddhis to be accomplished and increase merit and virtue, even bringing to fulfillment the Dharma of the Dharma-Prince;
how much more so other worldly matters? Therefore, not only will one's aspirations be swiftly fulfilled."
And there shall forever be no obstructing conditions or hindrances. △ Five: Accomplishing Desires and Seeking Wishes. Part One: First, describing the wishes sought.
Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara, if in future ages there are good men or good women who desire to seek [attainments] in the present...

Regarding future aspirations numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions and so forth, as well as the activities numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions and so forth:

the aspiration and mindfulness reside within, while the objective phenomena rely upon the external. In terms of both the mundane and supramundane realms, there are thus hundreds of thousands of millions of billions.
Either they seek the fulfillment of fruits in the present life, or they aspire for them in future lives according to their wishes. As stated in the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*:

"O son of good family, wherever there may be sentient beings—whether for the sake of extensive learning, pure faith, pure ethical discipline, pure meditative concentration, supernormal powers, wisdom, liberation, or for exquisite forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures; or for gain, fame, or merit—"
Flowers, fruits, groves of trees, couches, mats, dwellings, and so forth—these are [the requisites]. △ Second, explaining the accomplishment through the cultivation of causes, in two parts:
first, the accomplishment of fulfilling vows.
One should simply take refuge in, gaze upon, pay homage to, make offerings to, and praise the image of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva; in this way, one's wishes will be fulfilled.
All that is sought shall be fully accomplished.
According to the various rituals of the Secret Section (*Guhyatantra*), the three and five grades of *siddhi* are clearly elucidated.

Now, according to the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, when seeking various kinds of mundane and supramundane benefits and happiness, one may encounter various anxieties and sufferings during the pursuit.

When those who are oppressed by such [suffering] are able to sincerely recite the name and invoke the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha with devotion and offerings, this son of good family—by virtue of his meritorious, wondrous samādhi, and majestic spiritual power—causes all of them to be freed from sorrow and suffering, and their wishes and desires to be fulfilled.
This is it. △ Second, the dream-vision of the touching of the crown.

Furthermore, I pray that Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, endowed with great compassion, will forever protect me. May this person, within their dreams, receive the Bodhisattva’s empowerment upon the crown of the head and his bestowal of a prophecy.
He returned to offer worship in accordance with the Dharma, entreating with all his heart. Consequently, he was moved by the Great Being’s bestowing of a prophecy within a dream;

this was precisely the bestowing of a prophecy coinciding with the initial arousal of the bodhicitta. By stroking his head, [the Bodhisattva] granted consolation regarding the ultimate fruit; by bestowing the prophecy, he enabled him to realize the perfect cause.
Were it not for the firmness of the power of faith, how could there be such auspicious signs? △ Sixth, the manifestation that gives rise to wisdom:
First, describing the previous obstacles and dull faculties.
Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, if in future ages there are good men or good women who, regarding the Mahāyāna...
These good sons cherish the sūtras deeply and give rise to an inconceivable resolve, desiring to read and recite them.

Even if they encounter an enlightened teacher who instructs and supervises them until they are proficient, they forget what they have just learned; though months and years may pass, they remain unable to read or recite them. These good sons...
Because there are karmic obstacles from past lives that have not yet been eliminated, one lacks the disposition for reading and reciting the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Regarding the capacity to receive the Dharma among both the male and female assemblies: the Mahāyāna sūtras are the teachings of the Vaipulya.

The way of the sovereign is recorded in registers and is called "canons" (diǎn); thus, the books of the Five Emperors are called the "Five Canons" (Wǔdiǎn), which constitute the constant norms of the state.
It is a *jing* (scripture). It is composed of the character 冊 (*ce*) placed above the character 六 (*jiǔ*, pronounced as *jǐ*). This conveys the sense of veneration;

by treating it with reverence as if it were natural, one can then open up one's own *tian* (heaven). Within our Buddha-dharma, it is likewise able to open up the *tian* of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Those who feel deep appreciation and esteem do so because the Buddha-dharma is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), capable of producing all manner of treasures; therefore, they treasure and revere it with love.
This is a matter of great importance. What is meant by "giving rise to the inconceivable mind"? The *Rāhula-kṣānti-sūtra* states: "The Buddha’s clear Dharma is contrary to worldly ways;
that which the world prizes is what the Great Way holds in contempt. Therefore, those who are attached to desire do not favor my practice of desirelessness.
(Text). Now, since you have already cherished this resolve and are reading and reciting it, then the mind and the Dharma are one.
As for their essence, who could fathom the depth or shallowness of their minds? This clarifies the excellence of their initial resolve (*cittotpāda*).

Next, it clarifies that their faculties are dull. Regarding the teacher: one who is fully proficient in both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), as well as the stages of practice (*pratipatti-bhūmi*) and cause and effect (*hetu-phala*), and who is worthy of being a model for humanity—such a person is extremely difficult to encounter throughout thousands of births and ten thousand kalpas. Now, having fortunately met such a one, he instructs them.

He examined the scriptures and ordered them to read and recite them until they were thoroughly mastered. However, because their faculties were dull and obtuse, as soon as they became proficient, they would immediately forget it again.
Year after year, month after month, they were unable to achieve reading from the text itself or recitation from memory.
This illustrates the meaning of dull faculties; because the obstacles of past karma have not yet been eliminated, they lack proficiency regarding the scriptures.
The nature of one's capacity for recitation is merely a matter of the ear-faculty. As before, there are many causes and conditions for dull faculties and the obstructions of past karma.
Generally speaking, the recitation of the sutras is the seed of the "revealing cause" (*vyañjana-hetu*). Because one did not recite or practice them in past lives, the revealing cause lacks its seed.
This is what Baizhang Huaihai meant when he said: "If this life passes in vain, the next life will be obstructed. Or, it may be that in the past one was unable to draw near to the Buddha-dharma.

They showed reverence to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, yet they obstructed others from preaching the Dharma, obstructed others from studying the scriptures, obstructed others from reciting them, and obstructed others from copying them.
Furthermore, they became addicted to fermented grains and malt, thereby losing the seed of wisdom.

Consequently, even if they encounter an enlightened teacher who instructs and trains them in this life, they are unable to recite [the teachings]. II. Showing the Cultivation of Causes to Generate Wisdom. A. First, the cultivation of causes.
Furthermore, regarding the first of two [cases], one presents their mind before the object:
such a person, upon hearing the name of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva or seeing an image of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, expresses their original intention in its entirety.
With reverence, I make this declaration:
"Hearing the name and beholding the image, I declare my original aspiration. For the name of Kṣitigarbha arises from wisdom, and the image of the Great Being is established through merit;
therefore, by invoking the name and making offerings to the image, one immediately awakens the nature of wisdom.
However, one must first cultivate reverence in order to be able to move [the Buddha's] heart. For sincerity can move things;

that which lacks sincerity has never been able to move anything, let alone a Great Being (Mahāsattva). △ Second, seeking the method for attaining wisdom. Part three: First, the method of practicing reverence.
Furthermore, one should offer incense, flowers, robes, food and drink, and all manner of playthings to the Bodhisattva.

Using material objects to convey one's intention, and relying on these activities to manifest the mind: through incense, one takes up purity and distant penetration; through flowers, one expresses perfection and joyful delight;

through robes, one reveals tranquil endurance and non-abandonment; through food and drink, one manifests that the life of wisdom constantly endures; and through playthings, one signifies the state of wandering [in liberation].
This is a playful manifestation of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). Therefore, I borrow this ritual form to express my sincerity and reverence. △ Second, the method for consuming water:
Take one cup of pure water and leave it before the Bodhisattva for one full day and night. Thereafter, join your palms and request to consume it.
Turning one’s head toward the south, as one approaches the entrance, one should with utmost sincerity and gravity use pure water.
This is to rely upon conditions to give rise to wisdom. For the wise delight in water;

water possesses the function of flowing through and cleansing impurities, and the merit of moistening things and fostering growth. Now, by means of this, one cleanses past obstructions, moistens the parched ignorance, and fosters [virtue].
Reading the *Xing* (Nature) is the gateway to penetrating wisdom. Thus, the *Shenshui jing* (Scripture on the Divine Water) says:
"Water in a river is river water; water in a well is well water; water that enters the Buddha’s bowl is Buddha-water; water that enters the belly is true water."
Using the clear to purify the turbid, and using the correct to rectify the deviant; when all deviance is severed, one knows that water is the truth, and thus it is now employed.

One cup represents the singular purity of the Way. One day and night represent the restraint of the mind upon a single point. The day represents the clarity of wisdom; the night represents the darkness of ignorance.
Placing it before the Bodhisattva, one seeks their empowerment for progress and attainment. With palms joined, one requests to partake of it.
The *biao* (tablet/standard) is worn facing forward, representing the mind. Turning the head toward the south represents having one’s back to *kan* (the north) and facing *li* (the south).

The *Yiyá* states: "Zheng" means a field plot (*tǐng*, with the initial tone as the third tone). Because the ground there is mostly level, it is "plot after plot" (*tǐngtǐngrán*). Thus, the *biao* signifies a profound resonance with equality;
it is the mark of one of great wisdom. △ Third, the Precepts for Caution and Reverence.
Once the practice of consuming water is completed, one must be careful regarding the five pungent vegetables, alcohol, meat, sexual misconduct, false speech,
and all forms of killing for either seven days or twenty-one days.
This demonstrates the assistance for opening the nature of wisdom; therefore, one must be careful regarding the five pungent roots and so forth. In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Mahāmati asks:
"For those bodhisattvas who are resolved to seek the Buddha-way, how should they regard wine, meat, and the various types of onions? The Buddha replies:
"All kinds of meat, onions, leeks, garlic, and the like, as well as various intoxicating liquors that lead to heedlessness—these are what the practitioner [must avoid]."

One should always remain far removed from the five pungent roots (*pañca-garjara*). As stated in the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*: "The large garlic (the *Guǎngyùn* glosses this as *húsuī*, coriander), and the *gécōng* (the upper character is pronounced *gé*; it is a mountain onion)."

*Cīcā* (the formal name for *cong*; scallion). *Lángcōng* (small garlic). *Xiàngqú* (*jíjí*; that is, asafoetida). Now, "fatty" (*hūn*) and "pungent" (*xīn*) have two distinct meanings: "fatty" refers to a foul odor.
Pungent but not aromatic: asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) is such. Aromatic but not pungent: mustard and ginger are such. Both aromatic and pungent: the five pungent plants (*pañca-kaṣāya*) are such.
In Sanskrit, these are called *madhu* or *surā*, both of which are translated as "alcohol. There are differences between grain-based liquors, fruit-based liquors, and medicinal liquors.
For the laity, alcohol is considered an essential substance; as the *Hanshu* (Book of Han) states regarding alcohol: [text continues].
This is the sublime provision of the heavens, by which all under heaven are nourished and sustained; it is used for offerings and prayers, to support the infirm and care for the sick.

Within the monastic community, it is considered an object that must be strictly cautioned against. As the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* states: "The Buddha taught that [the retribution for] body, speech, and mind..."
Among the evil deeds of the three karmas, alcohol alone is the root; it further leads one to fall into other misdeeds.
Regarding the prohibition of meat, as previously established, among all evil karmas, sexual misconduct is the most grave. Once a single perverse thought sprouts, perverse conditions converge upon it.

Various virtuous vows are extinguished by this; various evils and calamities arise from it. Therefore, upon the iron placards of the myriad realms, lust is invariably ranked as the foremost of all evils.
Yet one ultimately fails to reflect that the pleasures found beneath the moon and amidst the flowers are finite.

How could one know that there are iron beds and copper pillars, where suffering is endless? Yet commoners and worldly folk openly transgress the manifest path of conduct, showing no regard or restraint;
as for scholars and literary men who read books and discourse on the Way, they boastfully speak of the "seeds of passion"—how can their numbers be counted?
Their reckless acts of killing and harming are as described before. For seven days, or twenty-one days, one must clearly issue warnings and observe these strict time limits.
One must certainly seek to transform dullness into sharpness and eliminate folly to achieve wisdom.

If there is no response after one week, there has never been a case where it did not manifest by the third week—provided one excludes those who harbor doubts and lack faith, as well as those who fail to cultivate sincerity.
This is the intent of seeking a response within a fixed period. △ Second, the development of wisdom.
These sons and daughters of good family shall, within their dreams, behold the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha manifesting his boundless body.
He will bestow the water of consecration upon that person. Upon awakening from the dream, they will immediately attain clarity of mind;
having heard this sutra but once with their faculty of hearing, they shall remember it forever, never forgetting even a single word or a single verse.
The signs of generating wisdom do not arrive suddenly. If one does not move through the power of sincere devotion, how can there be a hidden response that accords with one's capacity?
Regarding sleep and dreams: there are those who sleep without dreaming, and those who sleep and dream.

According to the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra*, when one sleeps with an undefiled mind, this is called "sleeping while not associated with dreaming"; when one sleeps with a defiled mind, it is called "dreaming."

"Dream. This refers to that which is associated with sleep. Now, this is a dream occurring within a defiled mind, wherein one fully perceives [the Buddha's] body and so forth, manifesting a superior physical form with complete sense organs.
If one has not deeply accomplished the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), how could one be able to see the boundless body?

Therefore, the Great Master said: "Entering contemplation is like dreaming; emerging from contemplation is like waking. Zhiyi (Sì-míng) judged this as belonging to the stage of semblance (*sadr̥śa-bhūmi*), or perhaps it is the stage adjacent to it.

There are two kinds of resemblance: resemblance to that which is near to the Real (zhēn), and resemblance to that which is near to the Ultimate (jí). Now, perceiving the Boundless Body (wúbiānshēn) through contemplative practice (*guānxíng*) constitutes resemblance to that which is near to the Real;

it signifies the manifestation of the eight phases of attaining enlightenment (*bāxiàng chéngdào*) within the first stage (*chūzhù*), such as manifesting emanated bodies throughout the hundred realms and receiving the water of consecration.

This is resemblance to that which is near to the Ultimate: the conferral of the water of Dharma (*fǎshuǐ guǎndǐng*) and the succession to the rank of Dharma King (*fǎwáng wèi*). Although this is based on the mind, [it is nevertheless a manifestation of the ultimate].
Regarding the realization of the fruit: the beginning must necessarily lead to the end. Receiving a prophecy within a dream ensures that realization will be attained without difficulty;
it may even bear a resemblance to being near the ultimate state. The Sanskrit name is *abhiṣeka*, which here means "consecration.

By pouring the water of the five wisdom Tathāgatas upon the crown of the head, one is like a Kṣatriya prince who has received the ceremonial sprinkling and is destined to succeed to the position of great sovereignty. This clarifies...
The auspicious signs within the dream correctly clarify the manifestation of wisdom in that person—referring to the men and women of dull faculties who seek wisdom.
"Dreaming" refers to the phenomena of ignorance and perversion; "awakening" refers to the method of observing through enlightened wisdom to realize the principle.

Because one can resolve what was previously deluded, it is called "awakening from a dream. One must know that the name "Buddha" (Awakened) is like awakening from a great dream. Now, when observing practice, it is like a Buddha;
in this sense, it is called "dream-awakening. Whether one develops a semblance of understanding or enters the stage of partial truth, both possess the meaning of "dream-awakening.
As for "attaining clarity and intelligence," this is not like the worldly sense of having keen ears and bright eyes, such as the excessive claims of Wang Chong.

Shicheng Lan: Yang Xiong’s vision was immediately clear whenever his eyes met an object. He then said that once one has awakened from a dream, what one perceives is merely the flesh born of one's parents.

Yet, he could hear all manner of sounds throughout the three thousandfold world-system with the eyes of flesh born of his parents, and he could see all manner of forms throughout the three thousandfold world-system with those same eyes of flesh. This is the profound contemplation of deep faith.
Thus, he has generated supreme wisdom and is currently at the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"As the sūtras say, among all sentient beings, there is none who knows the Buddha-mind; yet if the Buddha were to cause them to know it through his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-bala*), even insects would be able to know it.
Now, the Great Being Kṣitigarbha causes that person to know it through his supernormal powers. Where could this go?"
Because he does not forget, all the scriptures pass through his faculty of hearing and are recorded forever; he never loses even a single phrase or a single verse.
This is the transformation of the karmic obstacle of "revolving and forgetting" (the tendency to forget what one has heard). Question: Regarding a sutra spoken by a single Buddha—
There are eighty-four thousand scrolls [of the Dharma] in circulation. How can one possibly remember them all without forgetting? Answer:

Because the Bodhisattva possesses the power of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining, he is able to receive [the teachings]; because he possesses the power of the *dhāraṇī* of firm mindfulness, he does not forget them.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The Buddha rains down the rain of the Dharma from his own mouth; except for those who practice the *prajñāpāramitā*..."
The Bodhisattva Madhu: there was no one else capable of receiving [the teaching]. That he is now able to receive it—is this not the power of the Great Being’s *prajñā*?
△ Seventh: The Transformation of Evil Characteristics and the Subsequent Seeking of the Two Truths. Part One: An Account of His Evil Deeds by Day and Night.

Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, if in future ages there are those who lack sufficient food and clothing, whose prayers for what they seek go unfulfilled, or who suffer from many illnesses, or much misfortune;
whose homes are not at peace, whose kinsmen are scattered, or who encounter many calamitous events that afflict their persons;
and who experience much terror even within their dreams—[they should call upon me].

Regarding such things as the insufficiency of food and clothing—the most grievous of human sufferings—there was, for example, the householder Dīpāṅgulika of Rājagṛha (so named because the light from his finger at birth was like a lamp;

he had obtained it by previously repairing a finger on a clay image in a stūpa with gold). His family was as immensely wealthy as Vaiśravaṇa, but later, due to a plundering by a band of thieves, his wealth was completely exhausted, his wife and children were abandoned, and his servants fled. Even those who had long been his close relatives...
Those who were once close now treat him as an enemy; when he forcibly begs for food, he is immediately met with contempt and disdain. Thereupon he sighed and said:
"For all those who are impoverished, every movement—whether walking, stopping, speaking, or bowing—is entirely a source of reproach. Such is the lot of the poor."
Like a *vetāla* (reanimated corpse), like encountering a terminal illness that is difficult to cure, poverty is likewise; it brings many hardships.
Furthermore, it can give rise to hunger and cold, resentment and hatred, restlessness, confinement, sorrow, bitter suffering, and the reproach of guilt and debt.
Such manifold sufferings arise from poverty. Alas! How strange! Poverty possesses great power. It can...
This causes those who are close to abandon me with extreme speed. Thus Lu Ji said: "Relatives fall away day by day;
friends fade out until they are sought in vain. Xu Wenchang said: "When one's occupation is neglected, family members abandon him; when the household is impoverished, guests are scarce.
Therefore, within the space between poverty and wealth, the true nature of friendship is revealed. This arises from [the conditions of] past lives.
It is due to stinginess and greed that one encounters the calamities of this present life. "Héng" (橫) means to encounter adversity; it signifies opposition and transgression.
This refers to the phrase from the *Lotus Sūtra*: "to suffer calamity through adversity. Regarding "sleeping dreams and terrors," these are like the "strange dreams" (*qǐ mèng*;

*qǐ* pronounced as *jī*) mentioned in the *Rites of Zhou*, or the "terrifying dreams" (*jù mèng*) described in the *Liezi*. The *Guanwu Liangshou Jing* (Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Buddha’s Crown) states: "Evil and heterodox demonic arts and sorcery..."
Strange omens follow in succession; one sees evil dreams while lying down and feels sorrowful during the day. The text states:
"Regarding 'evil dreams,' when the mind is hidden in its depths, karma manifests therein; thus one sees unpleasant things in a dream (text). Therefore, there is much alarm and fear.
△ Second, eliminating [suffering] through the cultivation of goodness and attaining peace and happiness.
If such persons as these hear the name of Kṣitigarbha, see the form of Kṣitigarbha, and with a sincere heart pay him respect and recite his name ten thousand times,
all these unfavorable matters will gradually vanish, and they shall immediately attain peace and happiness. Their food and clothing will become abundant, and even in their dreams,
they shall experience complete peace and happiness.

To be "sincerely respectful" means to penetrate to the very source and bottom. To hear the name without being deluded, and regarding the name and its appearances, not to cling to those appearances, but to enter into silent resonance with the foundation of ultimate reality—only then can it be called a sincere heart.

If one recites [the name] ten thousand times with such a mind, then the ten thousand delusions will be completely dispelled and the ten thousand virtues will be perfectly manifested. Therefore, whatever matters may be unfavorable, they will gradually...
Upon their total extinction, one immediately attains peace and happiness. What was formerly a lack of food and clothing now becomes abundant and overflowing;
even the terrors experienced in dreams are entirely transformed into physical and mental tranquility and joy.
This turning of misfortune into auspiciousness is as swift as the beating of a drum—truly an inconceivable matter. (8)
When traversing perilous waters and land routes, whether entering or departing, coming or going, one cannot avoid the hardships of wading and climbing;
on land, one mounts carriages or rides horses, and on water, one drives boats or rides rafts, never escaping the threats of fish, dragons, tigers, and leopards.

How can one avoid the anxieties of standing on the brink of a deep abyss or treading upon thin ice? If one can invoke the name of Kṣitigarbha, one may then escape such calamities as falling or drowning.
The difficulties [of this passage] are divided into two parts. First, an account of the experiences of evil events.

Furthermore: "O Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, if in future ages there are good men or good women who, whether for the sake of making a living, for public or private affairs, for the sake of life and death, or due to urgent matters, enter into mountain forests or cross over rivers..."
Rivers, seas, and even great waters; or traversing perilous paths.
First, the persons involved in the undertaking are identified; next, the places passed through are clarified. Regarding "governing life" (*zhisheng*):

Xunzi says, "To manage [it] from youth is called 'governing' (*zhi*). (This means that when one grasps the essentials and establishes order, it is termed "governing. The *Yijing* says, "The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called 'life' (*sheng*)."

This refers to managing the affairs of one's livelihood. Regarding "public" and "private": "public" may mean for the sake of the state or household; "private" arises from pursuing one's own interests.
However, to be devoted to such pursuits is for humans to behave like beasts, chasing after desires.

[The character for "private"] consists of "eight" (八) and "self" (厶, an ancient form of 私). One must distinguish and depart from this; only then will heaven, earth, and the myriad things be vast and open.
They are of the same substance. △ Self-cultivation: The ancients had profound insight into the subtleties of the mind’s workings and acted accordingly.
○ They did not manifest external forms to convey their intent to others. ○ This is the Way of Heaven; this is the Way of Earth.

Now, to act contrary to this is not the great and correct sentiment of Heaven and Earth. To initiate activity from within one's own physical shell is merely to cultivate for oneself. Depart from this!
When I depart, it is for the sake of benevolence (*ren*); does this depend on oneself or on others? It may be because of birth or death;
perhaps it is to repay the debt of giving birth or to face one's own demise, such that one cannot help but enter into these circumstances. "Urgent matters" refers to matters of dire distress.
Whether it be being seized by government officials, plundered by bandits, suddenly beset by fire or water,
or encountering an enemy; in all such matters of sudden urgency and calamity— this applies to them all— at such times,
one must enter high mountains or dense forests, and must cross deep rivers or the great ocean, or traverse vast waters.
Whether dispatched on official business or seeking private gain, one cannot avoid traversing perilous paths.
As for private enterprise, it involves engaging in commerce and trade, crossing the seas to seek rare treasures. As the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:
"Agriculture yields a hundredfold; commerce and trade yield a thousandfold; official service yields ten thousandfold; and returning safely from the sea is beyond measure."
One shall obtain immeasurable multiples [of merit]. Therefore, one enters the sea. △ Second, showing the benefits of reciting the name:
This person should first recite the name of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva ten thousand times. Wherever they travel, local spirits and deities will provide protection.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, they shall forever abide in peace and happiness; even when encountering tigers, wolves, lions, or any other poisonous harms, none shall be able to injure them.
This demonstrates the benefit of reciting the name. "These people" refers generally to those within the nine realms, for even a Bodhisattva of the first stage [does not yet...]

One is spared from the perils of tigers and wolves; how much more so from those below this level? That it must be done ten thousand times is to illustrate the ultimate number and manifest the utmost sincerity.
Therefore, wherever one passes through lands, one will naturally receive the protection and guardianship of immeasurable great spirits and benevolent deities.
Amidst the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—one shall forever abide in peace and happiness, free from [harm].
It was during the reign of Emperor Yu. When encountering tigers, wolves, and the like, the *Shilun* (Ten Wheels Sutra) states:

"If any sentient beings are bitten by venomous snakes or poisonous insects, or struck by various kinds of poisons, or confronted by tigers, wolves, and lions, should they be able to invoke this name with a sincere heart, all shall be freed from their fears and preserve their lives and spirits. This is due to Kṣitigarbha."

The Bodhisattva skillfully enters the power of the Samādhi of the Illumination of the Lamp-Torch of All Buddhas, causing all heterodox influences, malevolent poisons, and evil insects and beasts within those Buddha-lands to be completely extinguished; therefore, it is called an inconceivable matter.
△ Second, a general statement on the inexhaustible benefits.
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "This Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva has a great affinity with Jambudvīpa.
If one were to speak of the benefits for sentient beings who see or hear him, even in a hundred thousand kalpas, one could not finish describing them."

This is the intention behind the fact that Kṣitigarbha is specifically associated with Jambudvīpa. The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbhasūtra* states: "Those who take refuge in and pay homage to Kṣitigarbha shall have all their requests fulfilled.
He possesses the merit of perfect giving and has compassion for all sentient beings; even were one to spend a hundred kalpas [praising him]..."

Even if one were to praise and speak of its merits, they could not be fully exhausted; therefore, all should offer worship to it. This is exactly the same as the present text, so I have explained it briefly.
There are eight kinds of inconceivable matters in total. △ Third, the conclusion and exhortation for the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) to disseminate [this teaching].

Therefore, Avalokiteśvara, by means of your supernatural powers, propagate this sutra so that the sentient beings of the Sahā world may enjoy peace and happiness for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
These two Great Beings both possess a profound karmic affinity with Jambudvīpa; thus, by means of them, [this teaching] shall be propagated.

This may be called "like-sounds responding to one another" and "like-essences seeking one another. Then, for the sentient beings of the six realms within Jambudvīpa, what concern need they have that their karmic obstructions will not be purified, or that merit and blessings will not be gathered?
Naturally, throughout hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, they shall forever enjoy [the fruits of] human life.
It brings peace and happiness to the three vehicles of the heavens. A verse from the *Daśacakra Sūtra* says:
"The true Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha bestows happiness upon all sentient beings and delivers them from the suffering of the three realms of existence, raining down immeasurable kinds of rain.
Such a supreme and true scripture is truly the eyes for sentient beings, a bright lamp in a dark room, a treasure trove for the poor, and [a remedy] for those afflicted by disease.
How could a skilled physician not urgently circulate [this work]? The prose section concludes. II. Verse Summary. Why are there verses?
The *Vibhāṣā* of Nāgārjuna states: First, it follows the customs of the land;

in India, there are traditions of "scattered flowers" and "strung flowers," similar to the prefaces and postscripts here in this region. Second, it follows preferences; some prefer scattered flowers, while others prefer strung flowers.

It is said that there are three ways of attaining understanding: either through the joy of the verses and phrases, or by gaining understanding from the prose exposition, or by gaining understanding from the verses and phrases;
fourthly, according to the capacity of those who are sharp or dull—the sharp-witted realize it upon hearing it once, while the dull-witted realize it only after repeated explanation.

Because this accords with the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*, there are these reiterated verses. This section is divided into three parts: first, a general verse on the inexhaustibility of the supernatural power.

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse: "I observe the majestic spiritual power of Kṣitigarbha; Even in kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it would be difficult to exhaustively describe.
In a single moment of seeing, hearing, gazing upon, or paying homage, It brings immeasurable benefit to humans and devas."
The eye of the Tathāgata is like a thousand suns; it illuminates and examines past and present as clearly as one views fruit in the palm of one's hand.
Therefore, it is said, "I observe [all things] as equal. As the Buddha told Śakra Devendra:
"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha is adorned with immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable, supreme merits that encompass all worlds."

This great bodhisattva cannot be fathomed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), he rains down all manner of wealth and treasures, satisfying every aspiration as it arises (and so forth).
Therefore, even for those who merely see, hear, behold, or pay homage to him, giving rise to a single thought, there are immeasurable ways in which they benefit humans and devas;
thus, it would be difficult to describe these benefits even over kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This is the exhaustion of the power of his majestic spiritual authority. △ Second, the separate verses on the inconceivable matters consist of six chapters;
while the prose section has eight sections, the second and fifth are here omitted, thus leaving only six. Now, first, the verse on the manifestation of signs of decline:

Whether male or female, or even a nāga or spirit, when their retribution is exhausted, they shall fall into the evil realms; yet by taking refuge with a sincere heart in the body of the Great Being, their lifespan will increase and their karmic obstacles will be eliminated.

The *Śakradevendra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: Śakra-devendra and the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven dispatched the musician deity Pañcaśikha to inquire after the World-Honored One’s well-being. The Buddha replied:

"May you, Śakra-devendra, and the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven have long lives and enjoy happiness free from affliction. Why is this? Because [you are honored by] the devas, the people of the world, and the asuras."
All sentient beings alike crave long life, peace, and freedom from affliction;
therefore, it is now said that their lifespan increases and their karmic obstacles are eliminated. △ Second, the verse indicates the realm of birth.
For those who, at a young age, have lost the affectionate love of their parents and do not know where their spirits and souls now abide;

for brothers, sisters, and all kinsmen whom they have not recognized since birth— by fashioning or painting an image of the Great Being (Mahāsattva), gazing upon it with mournful longing and paying homage without ceasing for even a moment,
and reciting his name throughout the three weeks of twenty-one days, the Bodhisattva shall manifest his boundless form and reveal himself to their kin.

Regarding the realms where one is born: even if one falls into the evil destinies, one will swiftly emerge from them. If one can remain without regressing from this initial resolve, one shall immediately receive the empowerment of the crown of the head and the holy prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

This passage consists of three sections: the first two lines of verse concern the recollection of past events; the subsequent three lines of verse concern the proclamation to the realms of birth. All...
According to the text, the third verse of the first chapter records the prediction of receiving retribution in the present life. Based on the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, there are four kinds of predictions:

namely, for those who have not yet resolved their minds, those who have just resolved their minds, those who are present before one, and those regarding non-arising; all of these receive a prediction. The present case is a prediction for one who has resolved their mind.

This is explained according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). However, as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "One receives the prediction from the arising of Suchness; one receives the prediction from the cessation of Suchness.

Since Suchness is without arising or cessation, one knows there is no prediction. Furthermore, the *Cintāmaṇi-cakra-sūtra* says: "I vow not to hear the name of 'prediction'"; and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:

"Receiving a prediction is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). All of these are explained according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Yet, other sutras record that [the Buddha] did not predict [the enlightenment of] the virtuous ones.

He predicted their evil destinies; he predicted they would be male but did not predict they would be female. That now all are predicted is identical to the revelation and manifestation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
△ Third, the verse on the accomplishment of saving sentient beings:
"Those who wish to cultivate unsurpassed bodhi... until they emerge from the suffering of the triple world"—such people have already given rise to great compassion.

As for the mind: first, one should gaze upon and pay homage to the image of the Great Being (Mahāsattva). All vows will be swiftly fulfilled, and no karmic obstacles will ever be able to obstruct them.

As for the fulfillment of all vows as previously described and the absence of karmic obstacles to obstruct them, this refers specifically to the stage of emerging into the provisional [world] within the Separate and Perfect Teachings.
He transforms and teaches sentient beings, remaining unconfused by the sands of worldly dust. Uncontaminated karma does not obstruct his guidance and transformation.
△ Fourth, the verse on the manifestation of wisdom has two parts; first, the verse on past obstructions and dull faculties.
There are those who resolve their minds to contemplate the sūtras, desiring to deliver the deluded masses and transcend to the other shore.

Although they establish such inconceivable vows, as soon as they read, they forget, and much is lost and neglected. Because these people possess karmic obstructions and delusions, they are unable to retain the Mahāyāna sūtras in memory.

In Sanskrit it is *tāra*, which in the language of Qin means "shore. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one hears the syllable *ta*, one immediately knows that all dharmas are unattainable as either this shore or the other shore;
one has already reached the further shore (*pāramitā*) of perfection. Karmic obstructions and delusions constitute the three paths.
Now, since there are those of sharp and dull faculties, and since there are those who progress or are indolent in their practice, you have now resolved to awaken the mind and bring it to mind.
The Sūtras are intended to deliver the deluded masses and lead them all to the other shore; they are thus part of the stream of diligence and certainly not for those who are indolent.
However, although one’s aspiration may be sublime, it is of no avail if one’s innate capacity is truly dull; consequently, one forgets as soon as one learns and frequently suffers loss and neglect.
This arises from a lack of depth in the causes of practice, heavy karmic obstructions from past lives, and an absence of the merit gained through extensive hearing, recitation, and study.
Therefore, it is a nature characterized by little memory. △ Second, the verse on cultivating causes to give rise to wisdom (in four parts): First, the verse on cultivating causes:
"Offering to Kṣitigarbha with incense and flowers, clothing, food and drink, and various playthings."
△ Second, the verse on drinking water:
Place pure water before the Mahāsattva and seek to drink it for one day and one night;
everything is according to the text. △ Third, the verse on observing the precepts with care.

Arouse a heart of profound sincerity and be careful regarding the five pungent roots; abstain from alcohol, meat, sexual misconduct, and false speech. Within the twenty-one days, do not commit acts of killing or harm.
With a sincere mind, constantly recollect the name of the Great Being.

Question: Although the five pungent roots have a foul odor, they do not take the lives of sentient beings. For what reason does eating them obstruct the holy path and cause one to fall directly into the Avīci Hell?
Answer: Their nature is uniquely filthy and turbid, capable of giving rise to many faults. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Cooked [pungent roots] arouse lust."
Eating them raw increases one's anger; the celestial beings and immortals of the ten directions loathe their stench and stay far away. Hungry ghosts lick one’s lips;

one constantly dwells with ghosts, and one’s merit and virtue daily diminish, resulting in long-term lack of benefit. Thus, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: "Those who eat the five pungent roots defile the Triple Gem;
upon death, they fall into the Hell of Excrement and Filth. After emerging, they become jackals, pigs, or dogs. Even if they should obtain a human body..."
Its substance is foul-smelling. Thus, the Indian śramaṇa Juecheng said: "In my country, those who eat meat or the five pungent vegetables are driven out beyond the city walls.
The *Sengjing lu* states: "When Zhu Tanyou was prostrating at the Stone Beam of Tiantai, he encountered a holy monk who said to him:
'When your mother was pregnant with you, she passed through a garden of onions; the fetal energy was defiled by impurity, so you must not reside in this monastery.'"
The *Xianzhuan* (Biographies of the Immortals) states that when Le Zichang led his entire family to ascend to heaven after drinking the wine of the immortals, only his son fell to the ground.
A celestial deity declared, "This man consumed garlic; therefore, he may not go. For this reason, the *Daozang* (Canon of the Dao) says: "Recite the *Huangting jing* (Scripture of the Yellow Court)."

One must abstain from eating the five pungent plants. When a Daoist receives the Dharma, they must avoid the lingering impurities of the five pungent plants. Nowadays, many masters of our school neglect this matter;
therefore, I have recorded it here in detail. △ Fourth, a verse on the development of wisdom.
Within the dream, he beheld the Infinite One; upon waking, his faculty of hearing was immediately sharpened.

Surely the teachings of the sutras must have passed through his ears, so that throughout millions of lifetimes he never forgot them. By means of this inconceivable power of the Great Being, he has enabled this person to attain such wisdom.

The first part is the main verse; the latter is the concluding indication. This is because the Great Being’s dhāraṇī is profound and vast, capable of making the dull-witted sharp and the ignorant wise;

therefore, it is called an "inconceivable matter. (According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Tang*, there was an Ācārya Cen at Jingkong Temple in Xiangzhou during the Sui dynasty. His surname was Yang, and he was a native of Linyuan.)

To the west of the monastery, by the spring of Mount Sangai, he constructed a Hall for Reciting Sutras. Whenever he recited the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, he was moved by the appearance of the Four Heavenly Kings who came to listen. Later, when he read the Tripiṭaka, he never forgot anything. How could it be otherwise now?
△ Fifth, the verse on the transformation of evil signs, in two parts: first, the verse on evil events during day and night.
Poor sentient beings and those afflicted by disease; households facing misfortune and decline, separated from their kin; all find no peace within their dreams.
Those who seek have their efforts thwarted and find no fulfillment.
As stated in the text: △ Second, a verse on the peace and happiness resulting from cultivating the cause:
"If one gazes upon and pays homage to the image of Kṣitigarbha with a sincere heart, all evil matters will be extinguished; even in dreams, one shall attain complete peace.
Food and clothing will be abundant, and gods and spirits will provide protection."

Abundance in food and clothing is governed by spirits and deities. As stated in non-Buddhist texts, the Official of the Balance of Heaven presides over abundance, while the Assistant Judge of the Year-End presides over scarcity.
Now, since you have paid reverent homage to the sacred image of Kṣitigarbha with a sincere heart, your provisions of food and clothing will increase.
It causes the frugal to become abundant and fills what is deficient. △ Sixth, the verse on the security of both land and water. First, the verse on experiencing evil matters:
"Desiring to enter mountain forests or cross the sea, [one encounters] venomous and wicked birds and beasts, as well as wicked people, malevolent spirits, evil ghosts, and various evils."

Wind. Regarding all calamities and all sufferings and afflictions, the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra* explains that snake venom differs according to whether it has one fang, two fangs, three fangs, or four fangs. If one encounters the venom of one or two fangs, it can still be treated.
If it is from three fangs, death is more likely than survival. If it is from four fangs, death is certain and cannot be saved.
"Evil people" refers to those who啸聚 (assemble in bands) in the green forests and those who plunder on the roads.
"Evil deities" refers to all the various spirits of mountains, rivers, and forests who arrogantly exercise power and fortune. "Evil ghosts" refers to *rākṣasas*, the ghosts that devour humans.
Regarding "evil winds," the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* says: "Black winds and swirling waves. Furthermore, in the *Ratna-rājasamādhi Sūtra*, there are six [types of such winds].
The "Wind of Form" (rūpa-vāyu) refers to black, red, and blue—the earth, sky, and fire. The *Bie xing shu* (Commentary on the Separate Practice) states:
"Wind is black because its terror is extreme. The *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* says: "Swift winds, fierce waves, drowning, destruction, and being devoured by hungry ghosts—how extremely perilous it is!
The remainder is as in the text. △ Second, the verse on the benefits of reciting the name.
One should simply gaze upon, pay homage to, and make offerings to the image of the Great Being Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva;
thus, within these mountains, forests, and great oceans, all evils shall be extinguished.
The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states: "How does a bodhisattva roar like a lion?
For example, when a lion bellows, the wild beasts and jackals scatter in terror in every direction; no wild beast whatsoever can harm him.
The *Yingyan Zhuan* (Records of Miraculous Responses) relates that more than a hundred foreigners set sail from Siṃhala Island across the sea.

While heading toward Funan, they were suddenly struck by a violent wind and cast adrift into a realm of ghosts, who intended to devour the entire ship. The people were terrified and invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara.
Among them was a śramaṇa of the Hīnayāna school who refused to call upon the name. The ghosts then singled out this śramaṇa for their prey.
Even one who has fallen into distress and humbly adopts this title shall likewise escape calamity. Since the responsive manifestations of Guanyin are thus, so too are the benefits of Dizang.
Therefore, by invoking his name and paying him homage, all evils are extinguished. △ Third, the concluding verse universally announces its circulation, in three parts:
first, the exhortation to hear of Dizang’s spiritual power.
Avalokiteśvara, listen with a sincere heart to my words. The inexhaustible and inconceivable power of Kṣitigarbha could not be fully recounted even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas;
such is the great Bodhisattva’s power as it is widely proclaimed.
The sincerity of mind is as described before. The reason for exhorting one to listen with a sincere mind is that the matters involved are inexhaustible and inconceivable.

If one does not merge with the ultimate limit of the three truths (*triratna-satya*), how could one exhaust their boundaries and reach their very depths to fully realize the profound treasury of the Great Being?
Inexhaustibility is precisely the perfection of the three truths; as it is said: "Form itself is emptiness; it is not that form ceases for there to be emptiness. This...

The perfect emptiness (*pariniṣpanna-śūnyatā*) is inexhaustible. As it is said: "All dharmas, whether causes, conditions, fruits, or retributions, are inexhaustible," and so forth, up to "they are able to contain all Buddha-dharmas";
therefore, it is called inexhaustible. This is the inexhaustibility of the perfect provisional (*pariniṣpanna-prajñapti*).
As it is said: "Whether dharmas are exhausted or not exhausted, they are all inexhaustible. Appearance is itself emptiness; where there is emptiness, there is nothing that exists.
Because there is both exhaustion and non-exhaustion, one knows that it is neither exhausted nor inexhaustible; this is the true meaning of inexhaustibility.
This is the inexhaustibility within the Perfect [Teaching]. How could such inexhaustibility be conceivable?

Thus, even if one were to speak for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas—speaking in every atom and in every land, speaking with fervent intensity—one could not fully exhaust its matters. Therefore, I now, before the devas, nāgas, and great...
Within the assembly, he extensively proclaimed the such majestic spiritual power of Kṣitigarbha. The two characters "such as this" (rúshì) also refer to the Three Truths.
Otherwise, how could he manifest the various causes and conditions of Kṣitigarbha, none of which fail to be identical with emptiness, the provisional, and the middle?
Therefore, his power is called "inconceivable. △ Second, a general verse on hearing and beholding.
Benefit and happiness.
If anyone hears the name of Kṣitigarbha, or even sees his image and pays homage, offering incense, flowers, clothing, and food, they shall receive a hundred thousandfold sublime joys.
If one can dedicate this merit to the Dharma-realm, one will ultimately attain Buddhahood and transcend [samsara].
Regarding "birth and death":
the first four phrases conclude the preceding discussion on hearing the name, beholding the image, and so forth, asserting that one will certainly receive the sublime joys of humans and devas.

The final two phrases conclude the preceding dedication to the Dharma-realm, asserting that one will certainly transcend birth and death to attain Buddhahood. This is because it possesses the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*.
It is for the sake of benefit. The reason it is so is that by using the name of Kṣitigarbha and so forth to provide a world-classified exposition, one can cause people to obtain the benefit of joy;
if one explains the individual characteristics of names and forms to each person, one can cause them to obtain the benefit of generating wholesome roots;
and even when the five signs of decay appear among devas and humans, or when they are traversing perilous paths.
By invoking the name and prostrating before the image, calamity is transformed into auspiciousness, enabling people to attain the multitude of qualities that destroy evil.
If these aforementioned practices are dedicated toward the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they can enable people to gain the benefit of entering into the principle.

Furthermore, the reason each of these is dedicated to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is that Kṣitigarbha exists only as a name; the nature of a name is emptiness, abiding neither within, nor without, nor in between.
[The text] merely manifests images; yet the nature of these images is also detached [from inherent existence], equal to the empty flowers reflected in a mirror.

Offerings such as incense and flowers are, in essence, products of causes and conditions, yet they do not depart from the Middle Way of Buddha-nature. Those who experience sublime bliss for hundreds of thousands of kalpas do so within the voidness of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), ultimately finding no one who experiences it;
this is entirely due to the power of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, in the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation):

It is said: If one investigates a single dharma, one immediately penetrates the Dharma-realm, reaching its limits and its depths, exhausting both the horizontal and vertical dimensions, and being fully endowed with both phenomena and principle.
With the aspiration to seek enlightenment above and transform beings below, all is complete therein; only then can it be called the arousal of the bodhicitta. "Bodhi" means the Way (*mārga*);
because the Way can lead one across to the other shore—both horizontally and vertically—it is called the *cittotpāda-pāramitā*. Thus, one attains the ultimate.

One becomes a Buddha of the Dharmakāya through the perfected, perfect teaching; eternally transcending both *paricchinna* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) birth-and-death, one must therefore direct oneself toward the Dharma-realm in every respect.
△ Third, the conclusion, exhortation, and proclamation.
"Therefore, Avalokiteśvara, you should know; proclaim this throughout all lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
As for the word "therefore," it refers back to the eight matters mentioned above.

That is to say, regarding such inexhaustible and inconceivable matters, none other than you, Avalokiteśvara, is able to know them or to proclaim them; therefore, he exhorts you to know and to proclaim them universally.
It is an announcement; to say "announced everywhere" implies it should encompass all nine realms. To say "all lands" (zhū guó), how could it be restricted to the realm of shared residence?

Therefore, we know that the Dharma-gate of Kṣitigarbha encompasses the entire Dharma-realm without exception, reaching its ultimate limit across both the horizontal and vertical dimensions, toward which all beings return.

△ Third, regarding the entrustment and circulation: as for the distinction of names, this name is specific to this sutra; as for the commonality of names, it refers to the entrustment found in every sutra.
Although it belongs to this present sutra, despite being general, it remains specific. This concludes the title of the first chapter.

Chapter Thirteen: Entrusting to Humans and Devas △ Section Two: The Text of this Chapter is Divided into Two Parts. First, the Transformation Master grieves for humans and devas and entrusts [the teaching]; second, Ākāśagarbha asks about the blessings and benefits of paying homage.
The first part is further divided into two: first, the World-Honored One strokes their heads and entrusts [the teaching]; second, Kṣitigarbha kneels crosswise and receives it.

The first part of the main section also has two sub-sections. First, the invocation of the name and the great praise of his merit. Second, the preliminary description of raising the arm and touching the crown of the head.
At that time, the World-Honored One raised his golden arm and again touched the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.

The "Erl" (爾) is explained as "ji" (即), meaning "immediately. This refers to the point when the benefits of seeing and hearing [the Buddha] for Avalokiteśvara have been fully expounded, and he further entrusts the world of humans and devas to Kṣitigarbha.

Furthermore, since the great assembly has already heard the two successive cycles of propagation by the Earth Deity and Avalokiteśvara and their joy is complete, it is appropriate to hear the entrustment concerning the generation of goodness in humans and devas. Moreover, it is heard that...
The aforementioned inconceivable matters of benefit have already destroyed the conditions for falling into suffering through various evil dharmas.
Now, the assembly further desires to hear the entrustment concerning Kṣitigarbha’s salvation, which serves as a perpetual remedy against all evils.
Furthermore, having heard the two preceding inconceivable events, those who have attained the Way are now complete; they further hear this great assembly of the entrustment.

Among this multitude, there was no one who did not awaken to the principle (the First Noble Truth). Because there are the causes and conditions of the four *siddhāntas*, he again extended his entrustment;
thus it is said, "At that time. As for "raising the golden arm": gold is originally yellow, symbolizing the Middle Way.

The arm possesses the power of lifting and pulling up, precisely manifesting the act of supporting and guiding those in the six realms of existence so that they all return to the single nature of the Middle Way. Therefore, [he] again...

He raises [his hand] and first strokes their heads to comfort them for the hardships of delivering sentient beings. Now he strokes their heads to entrust them with the toil of rescuing and uprooting them.
Previously, one hand stroked the heads of immeasurable beings, signifying mastery over the one and the many.
Now, one arm strokes each individual head to signify that they are fundamentally of one path; this reveals that within the six realms and nine worlds, there is no other path. △
Second, praising his inconceivable multitude of virtues, he spoke these words: "Kṣitigarbha! Kṣitigarbha! Your spiritual power is inconceivable; your compassion..."

Inconceivable is your wisdom; inconceivable is your eloquence. Even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions were to praise and proclaim these inconceivable matters of yours, they could not exhaust them within a thousand million kalpas.

That the World-Honored One specifically called upon the name of Kṣitigarbha amidst this great assembly of devas and humans was truly because his love for him was profound and the trust he placed in him was weighty.
It is like a great king on the verge of death whose heir is still an infant and of a stubborn and wayward nature;

wishing to entrust the orphaned state to a great minister for assistance, he would surely take the man by the hand and call out repeatedly, "My beloved minister," for while the son is young, the kingdom is vast, and the days [of the king] are few.
Yet their hearts were long; within them there was a sense so full that it could not be fully expressed in words.

Therefore, our Buddha raised his arm and touched their heads, calling out their names one by one. Following the display of your spiritual power, the Buddha himself praised your virtues, like a king entrusting a matter to his subjects.
He also first praised the virtues of his aged ministers. Now, the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa are of unsettled disposition;

were it not for extraordinary implements that transcend the common, how could one possibly rescue the sands of the world from the realms of darkness and light? Therefore, the various virtues to be praised below [are set forth].

This does not transcend the three wheels of transformation. The first phrase praises the wheel of body (*kāya-cakra*) manifesting supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). That which the various sages cannot fathom is called "divine" (*śen*);
the eight forms of self-mastery are called "powers" (*bala*). Regarding the term "inconceivable" (*acintya*), according to the *Mahā-śāstra*, there are five things that are inconceivable:
namely, the number of sentient beings, the retribution of karmic results, the power of those who practice dhyāna, the power of the nāgas, and [the power of] the Buddhas.

The powers of all Buddhas. The power of a Buddha is most inconceivable. When a Bodhisattva enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they give rise to inconceivable supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)—namely, the supernormal power of swift ubiquity according to wish. Thus, within a single thought-moment, they reach the worlds of all Buddhas in the ten directions and manifest infinite bodies.
These are such that no holy ones or sages can practice them or reach them; therefore, they are inconceivable.
Consideration: However, the manifestation of supernatural powers by the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*) must arise from the discernment of capacities by the mind-wheel (*manas-cakra*).

The mind-wheel is precisely compassion that bestows and removes [suffering]. If one wishes to bestow and remove, one must necessarily manifest supernatural powers; therefore, it is said that the body-wheel arises from the mind.
This is the great kindness and great compassion of Kṣitigarbha, which is truly able to universally bestow and remove [suffering] all at once; thus, it is inconceivable.

Nevertheless, although one may possess internal insight and external manifestation, if one lacks wisdom and eloquence, how could one possibly respond to the capacities of sentient beings to preach the Dharma?
Thus, we know that wisdom and eloquence rightly praise the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*). For the supernatural powers of the body do not function without wisdom;
as the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna said: "By the power of wisdom, one is able to turn all dharmas. This refers to the small [capacity].
He can become large; being large, he can become small. He can take countless billions of *kalpas* and make them a single day, and he can likewise take a single day and make it a billion *kalpas*.
This Bodhisattva is the sovereign of the world; his desires are self-sovereign—what wish could remain unfulfilled?
For these reasons, the Bodhisattva, by means of the power of supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*), is able to swiftly transcend ten [thousand worlds].
Throughout the worlds, is it not the case that wisdom is the very foundation of spiritual powers (*abhijñā*)? The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* states:
"Wisdom is profound and vast, like the great ocean; eloquence is unimpeded, like water driving a wheel; therefore, it is inconceivable.
This is because the Great Being is perfectly endowed with the three secret wheels, and thus is able to manifest forms throughout the realms of sand. My Buddha praised this virtue.
How could it be said that this is in vain? "Even if" (zhèngshǐ) below refers to being the same as all Buddhas. "Even if" (*zhèng*) is used in contrast to a provisional expression;
if one says "if" (*jiǎ*), the meaning becomes superficial and vague, whereas saying "even if" (*zhèngshǐ*) makes the word manifest its true reality.

Yet, how can the Great Being Kṣitigarbha cause the Buddhas of the ten directions to offer praise? As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If there is a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with the ten..."

The immeasurable, pure Buddha-dharmas, such as the stages, the six pāramitās, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities—[the Bodhisattva] dwells for a long time in saṃsāra for the sake of sentient beings, yet does not grasp at unexcelled bodhi, but extensively delivers sentient beings.
Such a Bodhisattva is praised by all Buddhas; this is precisely what [the Buddhas] are doing now.
This is the meaning of the Buddha’s simultaneous praise with a single voice. Yet for what reason does he praise and describe these matters as being inexhaustible even in ten million kalpas?

It is also as the treatise says: "The Bodhisattva emerges from the triple world and manifests countless transformation bodies to enter the cycle of birth and death and teach sentient beings. Such rare and wondrous deeds all arise from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."

"If [the Perfections] arise"—this is precisely the meaning of the inexhaustible intent behind the current praise. △ Second, calling out their names and entrusting them to humans and devas, divided into two parts:
first, the prose; second, the verse. The prose section is further divided into two: first, do not let sentient beings in the burning house fall into suffering;

second, do not let sentient beings with slight roots of goodness regress or lose [their gains]. The first part is further divided into two: first, the actual [instruction]; *Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence. The translation reflects the structure and content as presented.*
The devas and humans of the three realms entrust [this matter] to Kṣitigarbha.

Kṣitigarbha, Kṣitigarbha, take note of this today: within this great assembly of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, [I] record it.
All sentient beings, including humans and devas, who have not yet emerged from the triple world and remain within this burning house, are entrusted to you.
Do not allow these beings to fall into the evil destinies, let alone to descend into the five realms of uninterrupted suffering or the Avīci hell,
where they would pass through thousands of millions of billions of kalpas without any prospect of escape.
Calling out names previously was with words of affection and joyful tones; calling out names now is with words of suffering and mournful tones. Previously, it was to praise their virtues;

now, it is because of the entrustment of this matter. "Bear us in mind" means to entrust us so that we shall not forget these final words—just as a filial son engraves his father’s testament upon his bones and never forgets it.
The phrase "the great assembly and others" is used to rely upon the testimony of the multitude to manifest [this truth].
This is a momentous matter; it is not a trivial one. How does this differ from the "entrustment of the business" by the elder in the *Lotus Sūtra*, where he gathers his kinsmen?
Why is that? In that teaching, the disciples who had been transformed for a long time reached the point where the great task was successfully accomplished.

Having gathered the assembly to entrust the business, it was as simple as pushing open a door or dropping a pestle into its mortar—what difficulty could there be further? This present entrustment, however, concerns an assembly that is not yet fully disciplined, intended to ensure the continuity of the Buddha-seed.
It is uninterrupted, like rescuing one's children from water or fire; yet, in the end, one does not know how the matter will conclude. Therefore, it is not the same.
As for the phrase "to entrust with," "with" (以) means "to take" (將). Previously, human and celestial beings were already entrusted; now, this assembly is once again committed to you.
Regarding the phrase "not yet emerged," it refers to the period from after my parinirvāṇa until Maitreya attains the Way.
Previously, all those who were within this burning house of the five desires of the triple world have now been entrusted to you.
