You must ensure that these beings do not fall into the three evil realms, even for as short a time as a single day or night;
how much more so must you provide urgent rescue, lest they further fall into the Avīci Hell of Uninterrupted Suffering.
Within the prison, one undergoes extreme suffering and pain for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas; it is difficult to expect the time of release from this prison.
I entrust these words to all worthy ones: do not辜负 (betray) the Buddha’s grace. Seek early to emerge from suffering and hasten to cross over to the ford of birth. Exert yourselves! Exert yourselves!
△ Second, it further clarifies that the nature of beings has no fixed form or shape.
Kṣitigarbha, the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa are of unfixed disposition; they mostly habituate themselves to evil.

Even if they give rise to a wholesome mind, it recedes in an instant. If they encounter adverse conditions, [their evil] increases with every thought-moment. For this reason, I have assigned this [task].
He manifests hundreds of thousands of billions of transformations to deliver beings, liberating them according to their individual capacities and natures.
This passage merely reiterates what was previously stated to clarify the intent behind my entrustment.

It refers to all sentient beings who have not yet attained liberation—those such as those in the Southern Jambudvīpa—as mentioned in the "Chapter on the Response to Karma," whose fundamental consciousnesses and natures are not fixed.
The passage beginning with "I observe these sentient beings of Jambudvīpa," etc., is from the chapter on "Benefits for the Living and the Deceased" where Kṣitigarbha makes his report.
From "By this" onwards, it reveals two sections of text: first, the Buddha’s own emanations manifesting; second, Kṣitigarbha’s transformation bodies appearing in secret.
This is precisely as stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-saṃgraha* (Fu fǎzàng jīng): "The dispositions of all sentient beings are not fixed; they follow..."
Regarding what is cultivated through habitual conditioning: if one associates with evil friends, one will create evil karma and transmigrate through birth and death without end.

If one associates with virtuous friends and listens to the Dharma with a respectful mind, one will certainly leave the three miserable realms and receive the most supreme bliss (like the white elephant of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra).

Hearing the Dharma gives rise to compassion; seeing slaughter increases malice. How much more so for human beings—how could one not be affected by such habits? Yet, when those of good character ascend the mountain, it is logically difficult to climb; whereas evil is like a collapsing precipice, truly easy to follow.
For this reason, the celestial palaces are vast and spacious, yet those who come there are few;

the hells are like caged enclosures, yet those who go there crowd together. Thus, I manifest various forms to transform and deliver them; this is the reason for my weaving [of these teachings]. II. A Brief Account.
"O virtuous beings, do not allow them to fall back or lose what they have attained. First, protect those who have planted even a small amount of merit so that they do not regress.
Kṣitigarbha, I now earnestly entrust you with the multitudes of devas and humans.
In future ages, if there are devas, humans, or good sons and good daughters who plant even a small root of goodness within the Buddha-dharma—be it a single hair or—"
"Like motes of dust, grains of sand, and drops of water—by your power of the Way, protect these people so that they may gradually cultivate the Unsurpassed and never fall back or lose their way.
The first two lines reiterate the previous matter; yet, upon seeing the two characters 'earnest' (yinqin), I could not help but shed several rows of tears."
Now, "yin" (殷) means flourishing; "qin" (勤) means toil. It is the winding complexity of the mind. This refers to the mind with which one serves those above:

the body is vigorously toiling while the mind is full of such complexity, striving diligently to attend to one's duties with circumspection, not daring to have even the slightest laxity or negligence (*tuo-chi*).

(*Tuo* [音託] means to fall away from restraint; *chi* [音始] means to abandon and neglect the observance of ritual standards. In the "Annals of Emperor Wu of the Han," it refers to "men of *tuo-chi* conduct. Now, as for me...
For the sake of future sentient beings, the Buddha condescended from his exalted status to the lowly and humbled himself by descending from above to below.
Unaware that his words had reached this point, he now reveals the intent of his entrustment to those below, declaring that all sentient beings equally possess the Buddha-nature.

Although the icchantikas are evil, their inherent goodness remains intact. Should there be gods, humans, or virtuous sons and daughters in future ages who do not lose sight of their original aspiration,
and who are able to plant even a small seed within the unsurpassed field of merit of the Buddha-dharma—
be it as slight as a hair, a speck of dust, a grain of sand, or a drop of water— you should, by means of the power of your expedient wisdom, protect them.
He protects such people of minor merit, gradually causing them to practice for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. As the *Bodhisattva-pūrva-caryā-sūtra* states:

"If there is a person who can perform even a slight, minute good deed within the Buddha-dharma, as small as a hair or a pore, the retribution they receive in their place of birth will be vast and great, without end.
(Text). Therefore, one knows that the merit of giving arises from the mind; how could it be otherwise?
Because the objects of giving range from the vast to the minute, I entrust you with their protection; do not allow them to be lost or diminished along the way.
As the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra* says: "A blind turtle might, at some time, happen upon the hole of a floating log; yet once a person loses the root of their life-force," [it can never be recovered].
Even over a hundred million kalpas, this would be difficult to surpass. The waters of the ocean are deep and vast—three hundred and thirty-six [yojanas].
If a single needle were cast into the sea, it might still be found by searching for it; yet once the human body and life are lost, it is even more difficult to regain than that.

Thus we know that a single retrogression results in a loss no small matter. Now I pray, O Kṣitigarbha, that you will nurture me like a compassionate mother raising an infant, and certainly cause me to...

This is established. Do not be even slightly negligent, lest you meet an untimely death. This is my earnest exhortation to you today, amidst this great assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, before the multitudes of devas and humans;
it is the sincere effort of my heart. II. Reciting the Buddha’s Name to Shatter Hell and Be Born in Heaven.
1. First, falling into the evil realms according to one's karma.
Furthermore, Kṣitigarbha, in future ages, whether gods or humans, according to the retribution of their karma, shall fall into the evil realms.
As the sutra says: "Even if it be hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the karma one has created does not perish; when the causes and conditions meet, one must receive the fruit and retribution oneself.
Thus we know that shadow and form follow one another—who can escape them? Formerly, there was a person who died and arrived at Yama’s...
When his crimes were investigated at the king’s court, he was destined to fall into the Iron City (Ayas-tāla).

Yet, because the man’s sister’s son was the king’s chief consort, she urged the king to consider her own brother and not punish him for his offenses. The king commanded that he remain within his palace and not go outside.
However, seized by the prison officials, the man unknowingly entered the Iron City himself; even the king could not save him, as he followed [his karmic retribution].
The retribution for karma cannot be altered by even a hair’s breadth of forced effort.

According to the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*, there are ten types of karma each that lead to falling into the four evil destinies (and so forth). △ Second, salvation through the skillful means of supernatural power.
When these sentient beings are on the verge of falling into the miserable realms, or have already reached the gates thereof, if they are able to recollect the name of even one Buddha,
the name of one Bodhisattva, or a single phrase or verse from a Mahāyāna sūtra— then, by your supernatural power and skillful means,
you should rescue these sentient beings. Manifesting an infinite body before such persons, you shall shatter the hells and dispatch them to be born in the heavens to receive [their rewards].
Supreme and wondrous bliss.
As for those on the verge of falling [into hell] who reach the gateway: once they have entered the prison, it is difficult to escape quickly.
Therefore, at the moment of entering, one is made to recite the Buddha’s name to avoid suffering. As the *Dṛṣṭānta-sūtra* says: "In the past, there was a king who murdered his father and..."

He stood there. There was an Arhat who knew that the king’s remaining life would not exceed seven days, and that upon the end of his life, he would surely fall into Avīci Hell to suffer for one kalpa.
He immediately went to convert him, instructing him to recite "Namo Buddha" with a sincere heart, without ceasing for seven days.

As he was about to depart, [the Buddha] addressed him once more: "Be careful not to forget this. The king then pressed his palms together and recited [the name of the Buddha] with single-minded devotion, never ceasing day or night.

When his life ended after seven days, his soul reached Avīci Hell. Recalling his previous mindfulness of the Buddha, he recognized it as hell and immediately cried out in a loud voice, "Namo Buddhāya!
When the sinners in the hell heard the sound of the Buddha's name being invoked, they all at once—
As soon as they uttered these words together, the fierce fire was immediately extinguished and all attained liberation.
They were reborn among human beings, and later, when an Arhat preached the Dharma for them again, they attained the stage of Srotāpanna. Furthermore, the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states:
